SERMONS I SERMONS ON OLD TESTAMENT SCRIPTURE
“My joy is full and true when I listen, not when I preach” (Serm. 179,2: PL 38,967). "Since the external preacher of the Word of God is vain if he is not an internal hearer" (Serm. 179,1: PL 38,966).

Approaching the rhetorical work of Saint Augustine involves capturing in a global synthesis the human, scientific, cultural and religious personality of the rhetor of Tagaste. The multiplicity of facets that can be found in this section of the saint's writings has been carefully studied by several authors, who have tried to bequeath us the image of the preacher along with his doctrinal baggage and the idiosyncrasy of a people who lived pending the word of this man of the Church.' His perennial concern was none other than to lend his personal wealth to put it at the continuous service of the Word, living daily listening to it in order to be able to translate it into the language of the people who hear him, always remaining faithful to it 2. We, men of the 20th century, will not be able to approach the reading of his rhetorical work if it is not starting from these assumptions, extracted from a knowledge that is the fruit of a continued dialogue with the saint, which makes us present this preacher of the 4th century. Through his literary work we find the imperative need that he shows to live flooded by the Spirit, after thorough preparation on Scripture and the faith of the Church. However, it is not the work of research that is at the forefront of the exposition of the Augustinian sermon. It is a victim of the inspiration of the moment, enhanced by the daily experience of the message. All authors have spoken of this character of spontaneity and sincerity of the exposition of their homilies as a key criterion for putting into action the meaning of speaking the Word of God in human language 3. Hence the reader should not be surprised that, when speaking of this facet of spontaneity and sincerity in the composition of sermons, it is precisely in this part of Augustine's work where we can find his richest and most authentic personality. The overly prepared and non-spontaneous speech bears the traces of a certain concealment of the personality, while the word that comes from an experience manifests the being of the speaker with the clairvoyance of the man who seeks to approach man and engage in the dialogue of love and testimony. It is not at all strange that we can also find ourselves in the Augustinian exposition, following the indicated line, with pastoral and catechetical concern, placing clarity and effectiveness as its basis. As we will have occasion to verify, the public to which Agustín addresses his speech is a most heterogeneous public. Patricians and slaves, poor and rich, men of the people with their rudimentary culture, heretics and indifferent men come together when listening to the Christian speaker 4. Hence, his concern to approach everyone and his continuous effort to present the Word clearly and, at the same time, with simplicity, was the first intention of his dialogue with the people in the Church. He listens to the Word in order to be able to announce it5, but he is aware of human mediations with their burden of limitation and weakness 6. Likewise, given this multifaceted figure of the saint in the exposition of the Word, scholars have stopped at the analysis of the Augustinian projection. Pontet insists on the most human Augustine, where the burden of his personality is reflected in a positive way 7; Mersch will find Augustine "less pessimistic" 8 within the very disparate context of the presentation of his work in different environments and situations; while Van der Meer finds Augustine in his plenitude 9. Our attempt in this introduction is simply to limit ourselves to presenting the context in which Augustine's preaching takes place, in order to capture the environment more closely in order to understand the meaning of his work. In this way the reader will be able to approach his reading away from presuppositions, perhaps foreign to the saint, and will be able to read it in its most genuine context. We also try to provide the possibility of consulting works dedicated specifically to the study of the various themes in Augustinian oratory. It is not, therefore, our intention to make an exhaustive study of the oratorical personality of Tagaste's rhetor or of the study of the doctrines that here or there he analyzes and expounds. Without a doubt, nothing is better when approaching the reading of the Augustinian sermon than the reading itself. The conclusions that can be drawn will be conditioned by the factors that should always be kept in mind in this work of hermeneutics. 1.
THE RHETORICAL WORK OF AUGUSTINE

The work, so called rhetoric, of Augustine comprises three series of sermons: a) The Sermons proper; b) the Tractaius or comments on the fourth gospel and the first letter of Saint John; c) the Ennarrations to the Psalms.

The translation we present is limited only to the properly called Sermons ad populum. All authors who have dedicated themselves to the study of Augustinian sermons agree on dividing the compilation of Augustinian rhetorical work into three stages. The first would be limited to what Verbraken properly calls the compilation stage16; a second, where all the so-called Sermons post Maurinos reperti, published by Dom Morin 17, are introduced; and the third, which would include the latest findings regarding these sermons of Augustine that Verbraken has chosen to classify as Sermones post Morinum reperti1S. The Benedictine edition printed in Paris in 1683 always remains as the base edition. The Maurines assign 394 sermons, and among them, 363 would be authentic, and 364 to 394 would be rather doubtful. They add another 27 fragments and in the appendix they also place 317 apocrypha 19. Migne reproduces this edition20. Under a number of 396 it includes all the sermons, some authentic and others doubtful. They add two more to the Maurines, since they were found by the Benedictines when the work was in the process of publication. In this way, the Maurinos have 365 as definitively authentic. However, critics still remove four of them. 40, which is part of 339, and three others that belong to Cesáreo de Arles. Both ancient editors and current critics fully agree on this. CRITERIA OF AUTHENTICITY IN THE RHETORICAL WORK OF AUGUSTINE

Both Pontet and Lambot, subsequently, have taken care to present the criteria through which it is possible for us to discern the authenticity of Augustine's sermons. We are going to stop in our study on the contributions presented by Lambot, as a wise researcher and concerned throughout his life to detect the saint's sermonary through archives and study centers around the world. His starting point has been to focus on a synthetic study of the internal critical work of sermons, presenting concrete examples of it and subsequently moving on to the study of what he describes as rules of authenticity, general rules on a methodical plan. GENERAL CONTEXT IN WHICH AUGUSTINE PREACHED

Regarding the place where the preaching takes place, we could place all his sermons in a certain local context, given the importance that finding Augustine preaching in Hippo, in Carthage or in his hometown may have for many today. Possidius clearly shows us what Augustine's attitude was in this regard: "His disposition was such that wherever the bishop was called to go to preach, he was always prepared to give an account of the faith and hope that had God as its basis" 34. In fact, we know from other sources that Augustine traveled quite a bit 35, with Hippo being the central place of his preaching, ' like his episcopal city, with Carthage following in the number of sermons preached there. Pontet specifically presents the other places of preaching. It says verbatim: «He preached in Bulla Regia (Denis, 17); at Chemton, near Hippo (10th century); in Bizerte, at the dedication of the Florence basilica (c.359; c.396); in Constantine, in Utica, in the Basilica of the White Mass {In Ps. 144); in Tagaste (In Ps. 34; s.l and 2); in Argentario (s.286); in Vallis, in the Basilica of Saint Vincent (277th century); in Boseth and in Ai Tunga (Indic. c.8)36. Carthage can be placed as the city-center of Augustinian eloquence of a rather scientific type, given the context of this cosmopolitan city and with international accents of all kinds. In Carthage, a multitude of disparate ideas and, from the Christian point of view, heterodox orientations of thought also converged. It was here that Augustine had to present the full force of his eloquence in contrast to other ideologies. He himself feels impressed by Carthage and continually evokes it 37. A leisurely reading of this work by Augustine could lead us to a detailed study of the doctrinal content. We have already indicated how, among the authors who have approached this work of Augustine, each one has chosen a theme and has developed it carefully, something that goes beyond the work of an introduction like this one. Augustine feels compelled to announce the Christian message, and for this he resorts to all possible means to make it present in the community. AT THE SERVICE OF THE WORD

When we open Augustine's work, we see his deep sense of the mystery of preaching, placing himself in an attitude of listening to that mystery, manifested to men in Christ Jesus: "These are things," Augustine will say on one occasion, "more worthy of being admired than of being said." 73. He cannot remain in indifference and passivity when he is aware of being a mediator of the revealed Word and feels, on the other hand, his limitation and inability, since he observes his weakness and sinfulness in accordance with the people to whom this Word will be addressed 74. The awareness of human limitation when it comes to translating this Word of God into the word of man makes him become more and more convinced of the need to continue hearing it continuously, to listen to the inner Master who presents it to him in a graduated manner and prepares his person with that inner illumination, preparing his spirit to speak75. It is the voice of the Master, which, with a silent timbre, invites you to make room inside to continue listening to him. The weakness of the man who has the audacity to pronounce that Word, as the mediator that he is, is continually reinforced by the love that the Spirit instills in the heart of the preacher and guides him towards a deeper understanding of the mystery that he is preparing to participate with the people. In his preaching and in the experience of it, Augustine once again questions us believers in our technological and sophisticated century at the same time, making us flee from illusory formulas and abstruse theories around preaching, introducing us more seriously to the need to polish our language of faith and making us look for its significance for this man who seeks liberation through it. Through reading his sermons we find an environment where he actually knows how to unite the simplicity of preaching with the depth of the mystery that is preached. Concerned as he is to bring the Word closer to man, to make that dead word speak in writing, knowing clearly and in a real way the elementary techniques of a hermeneutics faithful to the text and faithful, in turn, to the man with whom it dialogues and to whom it is addressed. Hence it does not surprise us that, along with these thoughts, of a theology that we can call preaching, we also find the hermeneutic of the Word as its condition. He challenges the people, examines their reactions, takes events from daily life and, through them, tries to make that Word meaningful. We frequently encounter such plastic expressions in the mouth of Augustine that they themselves make us enter into the dialogue that is established between the pastor Augustine and the people of North Africa in their diverse historical and cultural contexts83. The principle of his preaching is basically biblical. Part always of his own conviction that he cannot be a good preacher of the Word who does not know how to continue listening to it within himself and in the Scripture86. The limited condition of human existence prevents us from grasping the deep meaning of the biblical text, since we were all born sinners in Adam 87. This condition needs to be overcome through methods capable of infusing light into the heart of man, and it will be through Scripture that man will be able to progressively introduce himself into the revealed mystery88. However, the Scripture bears the letter, which further obscures its intelligence; lyrics that, on the other hand, show the traces of this man, but to which God has adapted over time. This purification that man needs will come from personal effort and a positive response to the questions that this same text proposes to existence. It will, therefore, be a medicinal text, preparing the person for the presence and intelligent awareness of mystery 89. No one will dare approach the revealed mystery without first making room in their existence through a profound attitude of faith. It is the process insistently proclaimed by Augustine: Believe in order to understand. After a multitude of difficulties that his strongly rationalist spirit goes through, he cannot help but proclaim that principle, describing his process like this: «You said you understood in order to believe; I said, so that you can understand, believe. The dispute is known, let's go to the judge. The prophet answers: Unless you believe, you cannot understand" (Is 7:9) w. This attitude of faith, a condition without which man will not be able to begin his reflection on the action of God in the history of man, also entails uniting the experience consistent with that attitude 91. But the reader of the Bible also demands and is asked for a reasonable reading of it, in order to be able to give an account of the faith that he manifests in his life. This rationality must follow the line of the incarnation. For Augustine it is clear that every intelligence of faith corresponds to the personal conviction of its reasonableness and, therefore, there must be the possibility of its foundation. Scripture is strewn with light and dark elements that appear on one side and the other of it, and thus the reader will encounter issues that, at first glance, appear clear, and, once he pays attention to them, they become more confusing; and initially confusing issues, with the passage of time, become clear to him. It is the mystery, which approaches or recedes to the extent that man commits his being to this approach. Augustine will say in this regard that we must be convinced that only the man who places his spirit in an attitude of openness and simplicity will be able to approach the mystery, since the very richness of the mystery gives rise to thought and suggests much more than what appears at first sight: "Perfect eternity remains close to him and in himself, which cannot be understood by human understanding nor can it be said by any human language." 93. TESTIMONY OF THE CHURCH THAT PRAYES IN TIME

In this general overview of the themes that Augustine presents to us through his homiletical ideology, we cannot overlook the insistence on one of the key facets of his preaching: focusing on the Church, which prays in diverse circumstances. It shows us the bishop following the liturgy of the time, insisting on the key aspects of that time in the experience of the mystery, and he goes through the entire liturgical cycle, leaving his life and thoughts incarnated in that same liturgy. "The Augustinian reflection regarding the liturgy could be summarized in two fundamental aspects: Firstly, the analysis carried out by the preacher in the various liturgical times occupies a front-line position, examining the work of Christ extended through various stages and lived in the Christian community during the liturgical cycle. Secondly, the analysis carried out in the presentation of the meaning of the saints in the divinizing work of their community and that of all times. His ideas are left to us captured in fragments of a speaker who responds to the demands of the public or a pastor concerned for the good of his people, but always taking as a central point the mystery of Christ lived through the itinerant time of the Church. We will leave aside insisting on the most predominant aspects in the consideration of people who have lived through the time of the pilgrim Church and who are considered saints. In this Augustine makes clear his general thought, reflected in other works, and we will dwell on the meaning of the. lived liturgy, where he leaves his thoughts expressed and can guide us on how the Church of the 4th century lived and expressed its faith through the liturgy 9?.

There is a catechesis, as recorded in Augustine, to reach this new life, where there is a graduation from the catechumens, passing through the competent, and reaching infants. The preaching of the first times of Lent is directed above all to the competent and the faithful in general; it is preparation for baptism; while the preaching of the Easter octave is rather directed to those who have finished being baptized m. In the initiation rites we find several moments: It begins with the registration for baptism, following the scrutiny with the delivery of the symbol, or what has been commonly called the Tradiíio Symboli, about fifteen days before Easter 107. A week before the celebration of Easter the first ritual ceremony took place: the solemn exorcism 1C8 and the reading of the symbol m. All this constituted the counting ceremony. A second phase was the reception of baptism on the Easter eve, after reciting the symbol: "Retain, therefore, these prayers that you must recite by heart within eight days. Any of you who did not recite the symbol perfectly by heart still has time to learn it; learn it, because on Saturday you will have to give it by heart before being baptized; It is the last business day to give it from memory» m. The rite of baptism, with all that it entails of preparation for it and its meaning, is followed by the rite of laying on of hands, with the deep sense of the Spirit as a sanctifying force in the life of the believer: «What does fire mean, that is, this anointing of oil? Fire is a sacrament of the strength of the Holy Spirit... The Holy Spirit approaches after the fire of water» m. The rite and preparation of the anointing of the Saint is followed by the rite of the imposition of the white vestment, which had to be worn throughout the following week: "Their heads must be veiled, since it is a sign of freedom" 113. Moses says, they affirm, that in the beginning God made heaven and earth; but he does not name the Son, through whom God made all things, while John says: The beginning was the Word, and the Word was in God, and God was the Word. This was in the beginning in God. Everything was done through him, and without him nothing was done. Is there a contradiction here, or are those who, in their ignorance, prefer to learn what they do not understand rather than investigate with piety, contradict themselves? What will they say when I reply that this "beginning" is the Son of God, in whom God made heaven and earth, according to Genesis? Or will I not be able to prove it, knowing that I have witnesses of the New Testament on my behalf, to whom, whether they want to or not, they submit, having broken the neck of their pride? Thus said the Lord to the unbelieving Jews: If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me. How can I not understand that the Lord himself is the principle in which God the Father made heaven and earth? Indeed, it was Moses who wrote: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the voice of Christ himself confirms that Moses wrote about Christ. Or is he not already a beginning? Nor does this admit of doubt, since, according to the Gospel, when the Jews asked the Lord who he was, he answered: The beginning, well, I am speaking to you. This is the principle in which God

He made heaven and earth. So God made heaven and earth in the Son, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. Therefore, agreeing the Gospel with Genesis, let us retain the inheritance, according to the consensus of both Testaments, and let us leave those litigious slanders to the disinherited heretics. 3. It should not impress your prudence that John did not say: "All things were made in him," but all things were made by him. This does not force us to read: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," but in the beginning God made heaven and earth. Because the Apostle says: He will now show us the mystery of his will according to his good will, which he purposed beforehand, to bring it about in the fullness of time: to establish in Christ all things, those that are in heaven and those that are on earth. Thus, when you hear here that it says in him, you must understand "by him"; for in the same way, when John says everything through him, you are forced to understand "in him." Likewise here subsists the sense according to which I understand that all things were made in him when I read by him; Likewise, in Genesis, when I read that heaven and earth were made "in him," no one forbids me to understand "by him." Unless the Manichaeans transfer the dispute to the two Testaments, raising it between both most blessed witnesses of the New Testament, Paul and John, since one says in him and the other through him. There are many other texts that we could cite according to these rules of speaking about the divine scriptures 5. 1. The renowned piety of our father Abraham returns to our memory thanks to the recent reading. It is already wonderful that there is no heart so forgetful that this could fall from memory. However, I don't know how, every time it is read it seems to impress the listener's spirit as if it were happening at that moment. Great was the faith, great was the piety not only towards God, but also towards the only son; The father believed that nothing bad could be for the son whatever the one who created him commanded about him. Because Abraham could be the father of his son according to the activity of the flesh, but not his creator and maker according to the work of majesty. In fact, as the Apostle says, Isaac was not born of Abraham according to the flesh, but by promise. It was not that the flesh had not intervened, but that he had received it when he was totally desperate. Without the intervention of the promise of God, no posterity dared to wait for the old man from the womb of his wife, also old. And since he believed that he was going to be born, he did not cry for him as if he were going to die. His right hand was chosen for sacrifice, in death;

Sermon IV Esau and Jacob

It will be greater, since the greater precedes in time; the minor, in power. When Jacob cooked the lentils, Esau wanted to receive them before reaching this blessing. And Jacob said to Esau: Give me your birthright and I will give you the lentils that I cooked. He sold his birthright to the youngest. The one took the temporary pleasure; the other, eternal dignity. That is why those in the Church who seek temporal pleasure eat lentils. Jacob cooked them, but did not eat them. Especially in Egypt, idols enjoyed the greatest favor. Lentils are food from Egypt. All the errors of the Gentiles are symbolized by lentils. And since the Church, more eminent and manifest in the younger son, would come from the Gentiles, it is symbolically said that Jacob cooked the lentils and Esau ate them. While the Gentiles abandoned the idols they worshiped, the Jews served idols. Converted in heart towards Egypt, they were led through the desert. When their adversaries had died in the sea and their enemies were buried in the waves, they coveted to make an idol, because they did not see Moses. They did not see God present among them, but, placing their hope in the presence of man, not seeing man with their eyes, they began to think that God was not there, when it was he alone who did so many things through Moses. They sought man with eyes of flesh, because in their hearts they did not have eyes to see God in Moses. They lost their primacy, because turning their hearts toward Egypt, they ate the lentils. Understand it. It is the Christian people. But in that same sed ipse minor etit maior: ille enim tempote praecedit, iste virtute. Namque cum coxissetentem Iacob, desideravit Esau accipere, antequam vinoet ad istam benedictionem: et ille ait illi, Da mihi primogenita tua, et dabo tibi lentem quam coxi (Gen 25,31). Vendidit primogénita sua minori: abstulit ille voluptatem temporalem, abstulit ille dignitatem sempiternam. Ergo qui temporalibus voluptatibus serviunt in Ecclesia, lense manducant. Quam quidem coxit Iacob, sed non manducavit Iacob: idola enim magis in Aegypto viguerant. Lens cibus est Aegypti. Per lentem omnes errors Gentium signifitur. Quia ergo Ecclesia eminentior et manifestior in filio minore of Gentibus ventura significatur, lense coxisse dicitur Iacob, et manducasse Esau.

They committed frauds, they continue their frauds; If they swore lying, they continue perjuring; If they maliciously harassed the innocent, they continue to harass him; If they processed the homicide, they continue to process it; If they fornicate, if they get drunk, they continue doing the same thing as before. Because there are subjects in the Church who fear to mix with sinners, lest by the consortium of sin they become defiled in their unity and perish through heresy and schism. 15. And what is said to the hirsute Esau, who did not behave well at home? Well, that is also said about such: He was a wild hunter, while Jacob behaved without fraud at home. That's why his mother loved him, because she noticed his gentle behavior. This is Jacob, who was afterwards called Israel, when he wrestled with the angel; This also has great mystery. If, then, this man was an Israelite because there was no idol in him, there would be no idol in Israel itself. Well, why is it said: Your brother came with deceit and took away your blessing? quae antea faciebant. Si ergo ideo iste Israelite, quia non est in BO dolus; in ipso Israel utique non erat dolus. Quid sibi ergo vult, quod dicitur, Venit frater tuus cum dolo, et abstulit benedictionem (Gen 27:35)? Sine dolo eum commendat Scriptura conversantem in domo: Dominus etiam perhibet testimonium, quia sine dolo erat, cum dicit de Nathanaele, C A„ 7

truly an Israelite in whom there is no fraud. For what does it mean when it is said: He approached with deceit and snatched away the blessing? 16. Let us listen and see in the meantime what fraud means and what Jacob should do. He bears the sins of others, and bears them with tolerance, even though they are foreign. This is having the skin of a goat, that is, patiently putting up with what is other people's things, not getting attached to what is one's own. Therefore, all those who tolerate the sins of others for the unity of the Church imitate Jacob. Because Jacob himself is in Christ, since Christ is in Abraham's seed. Thus it was said: In your seed all people will be blessed. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who committed no sin, bore the sins of others. And is he ashamed of bearing other people's sins who were forgiven of his own? If, then, Jacob passes over to Christ, he carries other people's sins, that is, goatskins. And what is fraud? 17. Esau arrived late, presented what the father had ordered, found that his brother had been blessed in his place and that he gave him no other blessing. Those two men were two peoples, and a blessing means the unity of the Church. The two peoples identify themselves with Jacob. But the two towns that belong to Jacob are figured in different ways. mind the promises of the Lord; They did not desire to receive the land they desired carnally, but they spiritually desired that city in which no one is born carnally, because in it no one dies either carnally or spiritually. 18. CAPUT XVII.—18. Duo haedi, duo populi.—Hanc ergo cum coepissent desiderare, coeperunt pertinere ad Iacob, qui crediderunt in Christo, et factus est grex Domini in ipsa Iudaea. Sed quid dicit Dominus de ipso grege? Habeo alias oves, quae non sunt de hoc ovili; ford, adducam eas, et erit unus grex et unus shepherd (lo 10,16). cornerstone, for the psalm says: the stone that the masons rejected was turned into the head of the corner. And the Apostle says: the supreme cornerstone being Christ Jesus himself. sions. Why is it called lion? For the strength. Why stone? For the firmness. Why lamb? For innocence. Why calf? For being a victim. Why mount? Because of the magnitude. Why manna? For the sweetness. Why fraud? Let's see what fraud is, and we will find out why it is called fraud. We know what a stone is; But a man who is absurd and hard is called a stone, and also a man who is robust and firm. To praise you focus on firmness, and to blame, on hardness. We know the firmness of the stone and we say to Christ a stone: And Christ was the stone. In the lion we recognize strength, and yet the devil is also called a lion. Well, what do we recognize in the idol to take the idol as a figure, as we take the stone and the rest? 23. What, then, is fraud? There is fraud when one thing is done and another is simulated. This is how we speak of fraud when there is one thing in the intention and another in the facts. According to its property, fraud is reprehensible, as is a stone according to its property. Whoever says that Christ was properly a stone is blaspheming, just as anyone who says that Christ was properly a calf is blasphemous. The calf on his property is a beast; in the figure, a victim. In its property, the stone is hardened earth; in the figure it is firmness. Fraud, strictly speaking, is fraud; in the figure it is the same figure. Every figurative and allegorical lesson or locution seems to say one thing carnally, and imply another spiritually. He therefore gave this figure the name of fraud. quaeramus. Quare dictus est leo? Propter fortitudinem. Quare dictus est petra? Propter firmitatem. Quare dictus est agnus? Propter innocentiam. Quare dictus est vitulus? Propter victimam. Quare dictus est mons? Propter magnitudeinem. Quare manna? Propter dulcedinem. Quare ergo dolus? Iam quid sit dolus videamus, et inveniamus quare dictus sit dolus. Novimus enim quid sit petra: et tamen dicitur de homine absurd et duro petra, et de homine robusto et immobili dicitur petra; et ad laudem inde duxisti firmitatem, et ad vituperationem duritiam. Novimus in petra firmitatem, et accepimus Christum petram: Tetra autem erat Christus (1 Cor 10:4). In leone fortitudinem novimus: et tamen leo etiam diabolus nominatus est. In dolo quid novimus, ut accipiamus in figura dolum, quemadmodum accipitur et mons, quemadmodum accipitur leo, quemadmodum accipitur agnus, quemadmodum accipitur petra, et cetera? CAPUT XXII.—23. Dolus in Jacob quid. lacob a mendacio defenditur.—Dolus ergo quid est?

Dolus est quando aliud agitur, et aliud simulatur. Quando itaque aliud est in intentione, aliud in factis, dolus dicitur. Dolus ergo in proprietate reprehensibilis, quomodo petra in proprietate. Qui dixerit petram in proprietate Christum, blasphemat: quomodo vitulum qui dixerit in proprietate Christum, blasphemat. Vitulus in proprietate pecus est; in figura, victim: in proprietate lapis terra obdurata est; in figura, firmitas. Dolus in proprietate fraus; in figura, ipsa figura. What does it mean then: He came with deceit and took away your blessing? Since what was being done was figurative, it was said: He came with deceit, because the father would not have confirmed the blessing to a deceitful man to whom a just curse was due. Therefore it was not a true idol, especially because he did not lie when he said I am your eldest son Esau: he already had a pact with his brother, and he had sold him his birthright. So he told his father that he had what he had bought. What Esau had lost had passed to Jacob. The honor of the firstborn was not taken away from Isaac's house. That honor was preserved in her. But it was no longer in the one who had sold it. Where was he then, if not in the minor? Knowing this in mystery, Isaac confirmed the blessing and said to his son: What shall I do? And he answered: Bless me also, father; Well, you don't have a single blessing. But Isaac knew she was unique. 24. Why unique? Help me the Spirit to explain myself and understand me. We see those blessings, the one that Jacob received and the one that Esau received. Isaac himself said to Jacob: Are you my son Esau? He answered: yes. So he said: Bring me and I will eat your game, son, and my soul will bless you before I die; but give me a kiss. He hadn't kissed the other one. The blessing of this one began for peace. confirmaet, cui debenbatur iusta maledictio. Non ergo erat verus ille dolus: máxime quia non est mentitus dicendo, Ego sum jilius tuus maior Esau: iam enim pactus erat ille cum fratre suo, et vendiderat primogénita sua. istum transierat. Non enim primogeniti honor exclusus erat de domo Isaac: primogeniti honor ibi erat; in illo non erat, qui eum vendiderat: si non in minore erat? benedictio (Gen 27,37.38). Isaac autem sciebat unam. CAPUT XXIII.—Quare unam? Aderit Spiritus sanctus, et intellegatis.

Ipse Isaac ad lacob: Tu es filius meus Esau? Reply lacob: Ego. And say: Appone mihi, et manducaba de venatione tua, fili, et benedicat te ani[46]ma mea, antequam moriar; sed admove mihi osculum. Illum non Paz is equivalent, without further ado, to our “giving each other peace” of the liturgy. Then it was carried out through the kiss, which is discussed below. See C. MOHRMANN, La struc ture du latín paléochrétien, in Eludes sur le latín des ch-étiens IV (Rome 1977) p.15.

kiss? Because precisely for peace Jacob bore the sins of others, and he approached and kissed him. And he breathed in the fragrance of her dress. The thing is that he had his brother's stole, that is, he had the dignity of birthright that the other badly lost. She breathed in the fragrance of his dress, blessed him and exclaimed: Hey, the fragrance of my son is like that of a rich field that the Lord blessed! He perceived the fragrance of the dress and announced the fragrance of the field. Within the interior mystery he understands Christ and understands the Church as clothed with Christ n. 25. Understand your holiness. In many ways it can be meant as a reality. For example, before the two goats meant the Church, now that dress means it: the same reality is meant in many ways, since nothing is said by evidence, but everything is said in figure. The lamb cannot be a lion, and the lion cannot be a lamb. But our Lord Jesus Christ could be a lion and a lamb. He was neither a lion nor a lamb in evidence, but rather in figure. In the same way, the two kids cannot be one dress, and the dress cannot be a kid. On the other hand, the Church, which is neither kids nor clothes in evidence, is kids and clothes in figure. That can apply to everything. 26. He sniffed his clothes and said: Hey, the smell of my son is like the smell of a rich field that the Lord blessed! est osculatus: a pace coepit huius bencdictio. Quare osculo confirmavit pacem? Quia et ille propter pacem portabat aliena peccata. Et accessit, et osculatus est eum: et odoratus est odorem vestís eius. Stolam enim habebat fratris sui: id est, dignitatem primogenitorum, quam ille perdiderat, iste habebat. In isto iam bene olebat, quod ille male perdiderat. Odoratus est odorem vestís eius, et benedixit eum, et dixit: Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, quem benedixit Dominus. Odorem vestimenti accepit, et dixit odorem agri. Intellege Christum in mysterio interiori, et intellege vestem Christi Ecclesiam. CAPUT XXIV.—25. Una res multis modis significata.—Intellegat Sanctitas vestra. Multis enim modis significatur una res: id est, Ecclesiam, quam signifier illi duo haedi, ipsam significat vestís ista. Quia una res multis modis significatur, quae níhil horum est per essentiam, omnia per figuram. Agnus non potest esse leo; leo non potest esse agnus: Dominus autem noster Iesus Christus et leo potuit esse, et agnus: sed quia nec leo nec agnus per essentiam, et leo et agnus per figuram.

Sic haedi non possunt esse vestís, et vestís non potest esse haedi: Ecclesia vero, quia nec haedi nec vestís per essentiam, et haedi et vestís est per figuram; et quidquid aliud dici potest. CAPUT XXV.—26. Ecclesia ager. Odoratus est ropa eius, et u It is the concrete application of the principle formulated in sermon 46,33: "Almost all the pages (of Scripture) speak of nothing other than Christ and the Church." The systematic application of this principle can be seen above all in the Enarrations to the Psalms. See supplementary note 6: The spiritual meaning of the OT, p.745.

This field is the Church. We will demonstrate that this field is the Church. Listen to the Apostle who says to the faithful: You are God's agriculture, you are God's factory. Not only is the Church a field, but God is a farmer. Hear from the Lord himself: I am the vine, you are the branches, and my father is the farmer. That is why the Apostle, who worked in this field as a worker and expected eternal wages, assumes nothing but what corresponds to the worker, and says: I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore, neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God, who gives the increase. How well he kept his humility, to belong to Jacob and to the field itself, that is, to the Church, so as not to lose the stole whose fragrance was like that of a fertile field, so as not to pass into the arrogance of Esau, understanding carnally, filling himself with pride! He smells the field because of his son's dress. But that field is nothing by itself, and that is why he adds: the one the Lord blessed. The Lord will give you the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, and abundance of wheat and wine. And the nations will serve you, and you will be lord of your brother, and your father's sons will worship you. Whoever curses you is cursed; and whoever blesses you, blessed will he be. This is Jacob's blessing. If Esau had not also been blessed, there would be no problem. This one is also blessed, but not with the same blessing, although not completely different either. 27. Let us hear how Esau is blessed and see the difference between the carnal and spiritual children of the Church, dixit: Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni quem benedixit Dominus.— Ager iste, Ecclesia est. Probemus quia ager est Ecclesia. Audi Apostolum dicentem fidelíbus: Dei agriculture estis, Dei aedificatio estis (1 Cor 3,9). Non solum ager est Ecclesia, sed et agricultural Deus. Audi ipsum Dominum: Ego sum vitis, vos sarmenta, et Pater meus agricultural est (lo 15,1 et 5). In hoc ergo agro laborans operanius, et sperans mercedem sempiternam, ipse Apostolus nihil sibi arrogat, nisi quantum decet operarium. Ego, inquit, plantavi, Apollo rigavit; sed Deus incrementum dedit. Itaque ñeque qui plantat est aliquid, ñeque qui rigat; sed qui incrementum dat Deus (1 Cor 3,6 et 7). Quomodo servavit humilitatem, ut ad Iacob pertineret, ut ad ipsum agrum, id est, Ecclesiam, ne amitteret stolam, cuius odor erat sicut odor agri pleni, et transiret ad superbiam Esau, carnaliter intellegens et typho plenus?

Olet ergo ager de veste filii: sed non ager ille ex se aliquid est, ideo adiecit, quem benedixit Dominus. Et dabit tibi Dominus de rore caeli desursum, et ab ubertate terrae, et multitudinem frumenti et vini: et servient tibi gentes, et eris dominus fratris tui, et adorabunt te filii patris tui. Qui maledixerit te, maledictus erit; et qui benedixerit te, benedictus erit (Gen 27,19-29). Haec benedictio Iacob: T47] si non benediceretur et Esau, nulla esset quaestio: benedicitur et ipse. sed non ipsa benedictione; nec tamen ab hac penitus aliena. CAPUT XXVI.—27. Benedictio Esau.—Audiamus ergo quomodo benedicitur Esau; et videamus quid intersit Inter spirituales Ecclesiae filios,

between those who tolerate the sins of others and those who bear their own, between those who always live spiritually and those who always delight in carnal pleasures. Isaac answered and said to Esau: Who then hunted the game for me and served it to me? blessed be. And it came to pass, when Esau heard the words of Isaac his father, that he cried out with a loud voice, and said, Bless me, father, me also. And he said to him: Your brother came with fraud and received your blessing. 28. And Esau said: Well they called his name Jacob. Because Jacob means impersonation. But let us not believe that the impersonation was in vain, because it is taken in figure, as fraud. There was not yet enough malice in the brother for him to try to supplant his brother. He was called a supplanter when he held the foot of his brother who was being born with his hand; then he was called an impersonator. The supplantation of carnal things is the life of spiritual things. Therefore, when the carnal in the Church envy the spiritual, they are supplanted and become worse. Listen to the Apostle who says the same thing, even mentioning the smell, which Isaac expressed here when he said: Hey, the smell of my son is like that of a rich field that the Lord blessed! Thus says the Apostle: We are a good smell of Christ in every place, and he adds: for some, a smell of life to live; and for others, a smell of death to die. And who will be suitable for this, that is, to understand how we are a smell of death to the death of men through no fault of our own? The spiritual ones follow their paths and only know how to live well. And those who envy the carnal; inter eos qui spiritualiter vivunt, et eos qui semper carnalibus gaudiis delectantur. Respondens autem Isaac, say to Esau: Quis ergo venatus est mihi venationem, et intulit mihi? benedictas sit. Factum est autem ut audivit Esau verba Isaac patris sui, exclamavit voce magna, et dixit: Benedic et me pater. Et dixít illi: Venit frater tuus cum dolo, et accepit benedictionem tuam. 28. lacob supplantatio.—Et dixit Esau: Iuste vocatum est nomen eius lacob. Supplantatio enim vocatur lacob. Et nec ipsa supplantatio inanis est: quia in figura accipitur, quomodo dolus. Non enim iam erat tanta malitia in fratre, ut veUet supplantare fratrem suum. Tune enim dictus est supplantator, quando manu fratris sui nascentis pedem tenuit: tune supplantator est dictus (Gen 25,25). Supplantatio autem carnalium, vita spiritualium est. CAPOT XXVII.—Omnes enim carnales, cum in Ecclesia invident spiritualibus, supplantantur, et fiunt peiores.

Audi Apostolum hoc ipsum dicentem, máxime quia ibi commemoravit odorem, quem hic expressit Isaac, dicens, Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, quem benedixit Dominas. Ait ergo Apostolus, Christi bonus odor sumus in omni loco: et adiecit, Alus quidem odor vitae, in vitam; alus odor monis, in mortem: et ad haec quis idoneus (2 Cor 2,15.16)? id est, ut intellegat quomodo odor mortis sumus in mortem hominum, nulla nostra culpa. Those who live in innocence commit serious sins, for which God condemns them. Thus that smell is death for them, although for others it is the smell of life. The Lord himself first became a good odor of life for believers and a bad odor of death for persecutors. Since many believed, the envy of the Jews arose, and they committed their great crime by killing the innocent, holy of holies. If they did not, the good smell of Christ would not have been deadly to them. Thus Esau was supplanted in the father's blessing. 29. Isaac answered and said to him: I have made him your lord. Esau could not understand otherwise what was said: and all his brothers will serve him. And what will I do to you, son? And Esau said to his father: Nevertheless, bless me also. And as if Isaac saw himself squeezed, that is, as if he saw himself coerced. Great thing, great sacrament, I hope we understand it! He blessed him under duress. See what this means. Let's look at blessing and understand what coerced blessing is. 30. Isaac answered (the father did not kiss Esau) and said to him: Come, your habitation will be of fertility of the earth and of dew from heaven above! He had also said to the other: of the fertility of the earth and the dew of heaven. That is, then, common to Esau and Jacob. What is characteristic of Jacob? All your brothers will serve you; whoever blesses you will be blessed; and whoever curses you, etenim vias suas spirituales, nihil aliud norunt quam bene vivere: et qui innocenter vivostibus invident, faciunt peccata gravia, unde iUos puniat Deus; et fit eis ille odor in mortem, qui est alus odor ad vitam. Nam ipse Dominus prius factus est odor bonus ad vitam credentibus, et odor malus ad mortem persequentibus. Quia enim multi illi crediderant, inviderunt Iudaei, et fecerunt tantum scelus occidendo innocentem, Sanctum sanctorum: quod si non facerent, ad mortem eis non valeret bonus odor Christi. Ergo supplantatus est Esau in benedictione patris. 29. Iterum de benedictione Esau.—Respondit autem Isaac, et dixit ad illum, Dominum illum tuum feci: non enim aliud potuit accipere Esau quod dictum est, Et omnes fratres eius servient illi: tibi autem quid faciam, fili? Et dixit Esau ad patrem suum: Benedic tamen et me. Cum strangulatus esset Isaac: id est, cum coactus esset. Magna res, magnum sacramentum, utinam capiamus: coactus benedicit, et tamen benedicit; et quod benedicit, verum est, sed tamen coactus benedicit. Quid sit hoc, attendite.

Videamus ipsam benedictionem, et intellegamus quid sit coactum benedicere. CAPUT XXVIII.—30. In benedictione quid pro[48]prium, quid comtnune lacob et Esau.—Respondit autem Isaac (pater sane Esau non est osculatus), et ait illi, Ecce a fertilitate terrae erit habitatio tua, et a rore caeli desuper. Dixit hoc et illi, ab ubertate terrae, et a rore caeli: hoc ergo commune est lacob et Esau. What is proprium lacob? Servient tibi gentes. What is proprium lacob? Omnes fratres tui tibi servient: et qui te benedixerit, benedictus erit; et qui, te maledixerit, maledictus erit.

will be cursed. There was still a certain property for Esau that was not mentioned to Jacob: you will live by your sword and serve your brother. But in order not to suppress free will 13, we already talked about this yesterday M, added: it will happen when you break and shake off the yoke from your neck. What does it mean when you break and shake off the yoke from your neck? You have freedom, if you want, to convert; and you will no longer be two, but one Jacob. For all who convert from Esau belong to Jacob. Similarity does one thing, and dissimilarity creates diversity. What does it mean then: of the dew of the sky and the fertility of the earth? That's common. The people and your brothers and your father's sons will serve you; That's just Jacob. You will live by your sword: it is Esau's alone. Something affects both of them and something affects each one. 31. There are evil people in the Church who belong to Esau, since they are children of Rebekah, children of the mother Church, born from her womb, hirsute, persevering in their carnal sins, but born from her womb. They participate, therefore, in the dew of heaven and the fertility of the earth; From the dew of heaven come all the Scriptures, all the divine word; and from the fertility of the earth come all the visible sacraments; because a visible sacrament belongs to the earth. The good and the bad have both things in common in the Church. Indeed, they have and participate in the sacraments, even (what the faithful know) in wheat and wine. And they have the dew of heaven, because the word of God descends on everyone from heaven. The word Habet comes et íste nescio quid proprium, quod non dictum est Iacob: Et in gladio Vives, et fratri tuo servies. Sed ne tolleret liberum arbitrium (iam hinc et hesterno diximus), adiecit, Erit autem, cum deposueris et solveris iugum de eolio tuo. Quid est, Erit autem, cum deposueris et solveris iugum de eolio tuo (Gen 27,39.40)? Liberum tibi est, si volueris, convertí: non quasi duo eritis, sed unus Iacob. Omnes enim qui convertuntur ab Esau, ad Iacob pertínent. Similitudo unum facít, dissimilitudo facit diversitatem. Quid ergo? A rore caeli, et a fertilitate terrae, both habent. Servient tibi gentes et fratres tui et filii patris tui, solus Iacob habet. In gladio autem tuo Vives, solus Esau. Quiddam commune habent, quaedam singuli. 31.

Scripturae et Sacramenta bonis et malis communia.—Sunt mali in Ecclesia pertinent ad Esau: quia et ipsi filii Rebeccae, filii matris Ecclesíae, de uterus ipsius nati, et pilosi in peccatis carnalibus perseverantes, de iílius tamen uterus nati. Habent ergo a rore caeli, et a fertilitate terrae: a rore caeli omnes Scripturas, omnem sermonem divinum: a fertilitate vero terrae, omnia visibilia Sacramenta; visibile enim Sacramentum ad terram pertinet. Haec omnia communia habent in Ecclesia et boni et mali. Nam et ipsi habent et participant Sacramentis: et quod norunt fideles, a tritico et vino. Et habent de rore caeli: quia super omnes
Typical theme of the Pelagian controversy. See sermon 5,4.

of God and water. But look who waters and what they water. It waters some and others, namely, the good and the bad. But the wicked turn good rain into the root of brambles, while the good turn rain into good fruit. At the same time the Lord rains on the harvest and on the bush; but it rains in the harvest for the barn, and it rains in the bush for the fire. However, rain is unique. Thus, the word of God rains on everyone. Let each one see what root he has and what he uses the good rain for. If it is used to raise brambles, should we blame God's rain? Before reaching the root, that rain is sweet. Sweet is the word of God before it reaches the evil heart; but this turns the rain of God into fraud, turns it into hypocrisy, takes it to the roots of evil lusts, to their perversities and depravities. Brambles begin to sprout, but with a good rain, since it comes from the dew of heaven. And since not all evil people are excluded from the sacraments of God, what all those who already wanted to participate in the mysteries of the faithful know also comes from the fertility of the earth. 32. Although these things belong to both, all people belong to the spiritual ones, since these belong to the Church, which filled the entire globe of the earth. Pay attention, brothers, and discern as much as you can or as much as the Lord allows you. Every spiritual person sees that the Church, spread throughout the world, is one, true, Catholic. Nothing arrogates and tolerates sins

descendit sermo Dei de cáelo. Venit sermo Dei, et irrigat: sed qui irriget, et quid irriget, attend. Nam et illos irrigat et illos, bonds et malo: sed illi bonam pluviam in radicem spinarum convertunt; illi autem ad fructum bonum pluviam trahunt. Nam simul pluit Dominus super segetem et super spinas; sed segeti pluit ad horreum, spinis ad ignem: et tamen una est pluvia. Sic Verbum Dei omnes compluit. Videat quisque qualem radicem habeat; videat quisque quo trahat pluviam bonam: si eam trahit, ut generet spinas, numquid ideo pluvia Dei aecusanda est? Antequam veniat ad radicem, dulcís est pluvia illa; dulce est verbum Dei, doñee veniat ad cor malum, et convertat ad fraudm suam pluviam Dei, convertat ad hypocrisim, convertat ad radices malarum concupiscentiarum, ad perversitates et depravationes suas. Incipit quidem generate spinas, thirst for good rain: habet enim a rore caeli. Et quoniam non excluduntur omnes mali a Sacramentis Dei, habet et [49] ab ubertate terrae, quod norunt illi, qui iam voluerunt esse participas mysteriorum fidelium. CAPUT XXIX.—32. Omnes gentes spiritualibus subiectae.—Cum ad both pertineant ista, non tamen pertinent omnes gentes nisi ad spirituales, quia ipsi pertinent ad Ecclesiam, quae implevit totum orbem terrarum. Attendite, fratres, and discern quantum potestis, vel quantum vobis Dominus dat. Otnnis spiritualis videt quia Ecclesia per totum

of men, whom he cannot eliminate from the Sunday threshing floor before that last beler arrives who cannot deceive himself and cleanses his threshing floor, putting the wheat in the granary and delivering the straw for the bonfire. Because it is up to him to exclude the chaff, and separate it from the wheat, and prepare the granary for the wheat and the fire for the chaff. And because he knows it, he tolerates sinners to finally separate them. In all nations, the sinful and carnal are mixed with the spiritual and at their service. On the other hand, spiritual people do not serve the bad, since they take advantage of the bad when they decline. Listen, my brothers! I will say it, if I can, without fear. I will not remain silent, because I feel the urgency to say it. And if by chance some get irritated, forgive me. Indeed, I feel fear: may they forgive me for my fear. Christ feared no one. And we, out of fear of Christ, speak, lest, because we do not grieve some, he will not forgive us. Deign to listen and pay careful attention to what I want to say. Both Esau and Jacob received the dew of heaven and the fertility of the earth. Both possess what we said, that we know and that you know. But only Jacob received the service of the people, because in the Church, throughout the entire world, the carnal do not serve but the spiritual. Because? Because thanks to them the spiritual progress. And that is why carnal men are called servants. If they do what they do not want, the bad behavior of the carnal benefits the spiritual, since they progress by the same treatment and are crowned by their tolerance. otbem terrarum est una, vera, catholica, et nihil sibi arrogat, et tolerat peccata hominum, quos non potest purgare de zona dominica, antequam venial ílle ultimus ventilator, qui falli non potest, ut purget aream suam, et frumentum mittat in horreum, paleas autem det ad comburendum (Mt 3,13): quia ipse habet excludere paleam, et segregare a frumento, et praeparare horreum tritico, paleis ignem. Itaque quia novit, tolerat peccatores in fine separandos. Per omnes gentes peccatores et omnes carnales mixti sunt spiritualibus, et serviunt eis: spirituales autem non serviunt; quia de illis proficiunt, cum ipsi deficiunt. Attendite, fratres mei; dicam, si possum, et non timeam, non tacebo: urgeor enim ut dicam: etsi mihi forte aliqui succensuerint; sed dent veniam, timeo enim, ut dixi; rudder dent veniam.

Christus neminem timuit: nos autem Christum timendo non parcimus, ne nobis, dum tales nolumus contristare, ílle non parcat. Quid velim dicere dignifiedmini audire, et attemptissime advertere. Acceperunt ambo a rote caeli et ab ubertate terrae, Iacob et Esau; both illud habent quod iam diximus, quod novimus, quod nostis: sed ut serviant ei gentes, non accepit nisi Iacob; quia carnales in Ecclesia per totum orbem terrarum non serviunt nisi spiritualibus. Quare? Quia de illis proficiunt spirituales. Nam ideo carnales nomines servi dicuntur: et si quod nolunt faciunt, prodest tamen spiritualibus mala conversado carnalium; quia et ex eadem conversatione proficiunt, et per tolerantíam coronantur.

33. Let your holiness pay attention to what we say. Esau was not given the nations, because all the carnal ones in the Church are either divided or easy to divide. There you have the party of Donato 15, who came from there, one of those carnals who feel carnally. They were carnal, but, as they sought their own honor, they lost patience, found opportunity and divided. They loved their honor, they gave it too much importance, they became inflated with the arrogance of pride, they had no tolerance, that is, they had no charity. Because it is written: charity tolerates everything, endures everything. He does not envy, he does not puff up, he does not act with malice. For this reason, even though they had other things, since they did not have what makes the most of what they have, they were divided 17. All the heresies, separations and schisms that have been consummated were done by these carnals. Sometimes they felt carnally and created images of their fantasies and fell into error, and the Catholic faith rebuked them, and when they were argued, they were excluded by their own weight. Other times, creating disputes and competitions between men, they divided. Who were divided, but those to whom belongs the sword of which it was said: Thou shalt live by thy sword? It is not that the sword lacks good sense. In the same way as CAPUT XXX.—33. Camalibus cur non subiectae gentes.—Intendat Sanctitas vestra quod dicimus. lili autem Esau non sunt datae gentes: quia omnes carnales, qui sunt in Ecclesia, aut divisi sunt, aut Fácil sunt ad divisionem. Ecce pars Donati inde facta est, inde est, de ipsis camalibus carnaliter sentientibus. Carnal weret: sed quia quaesierunt honorem suum, vel patientiam perdiderunt, invenerunt aditum, et divisi sunt: ​​amaverunt honorem suum, multum ei tribuerunt, typho superbiae tumuerunt, non habuerunt tolerantiam, id est, non habuerunt caritatem. Scriptum est enim: Caritas omnia tolerat, omnia sustinet; non aemulatur, non inflatur, non agit perperam (1 Cor 13,7.4). Itaque quidquid aliud haberent, quia illud non habebant per quod prodest quidquid habetur, diviserunt se. Et quotquot haereses vel praecisiones et schismata facta sunt, per hos carnales facta sunt. Aut enim carnaliter senserunt, et fece[50]runt sibi imagines phantasmatum suorum, et erraverunt, et reprehendit eos fides catholica; et cum arguerentur, exclusi sunt foras pondere suo: aut invenientes sibi lites et simultates cum hominibus, diviserunt se.

Qui se ergo diviserunt, nisi ad quos pertinet gladius ille, de quo dictum est, In gladio tuo vives? Non quia gladius non accipitur in bono: nam quemadmodum dicta sunt illa superiora, id est quomodo Donatus of Casa Negra, or Donatus the Great, was not the initiator, but he was the chief and main organizer of the African schism that is named after him. It is known that he wrote at least one letter (which Saint Augustine refuted in a work entitled Against the Letter of the Heretic Donatus, which has not been preserved to us) and another work On the Holy Spirit, in which, according to Saint Augustine (The Correction of the Donatists 1,1), he defended doctrines very close to the amanas. See note 6 to sermon 10, p.186. "See complementary note 11: The Donatist schisms, p.746.

Above we said, that is, how the stone means firmness in attention to Christ and rebuke in attention to the fool; As Christ was called a lion for one reason, and also the devil for another, so the sword is sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one. But for some reason the sword was not given to Jacob, but to Esau, because part of the mystery has a bad meaning. Thus, servitude is not excluded from the mystery either; namely, when it was said: You will serve your brother, since this was said with a profoundly mysterious meaning. 34. Therefore, brothers, those who divide are those who have the sword, those who die in it and live in it. But what the Lord said is true: He who strikes with iron dies with iron. See, then, my brothers, how those who separated themselves from unity then divided themselves in vain. You know how many parties Donato's party created, and I think it is not hidden from your holiness that he who strikes iron with iron dies. It was said: by your sword you will live. So are those who did not separate from the Church, but live as if they were outside it. For those who in the Church love their honors, such are they absolutely; Those in the Church who love their secular comforts are also chaff. Since the wind does not blow, they do not fly out of the threshing floor. I say briefly that the temptation is missing, because they would fly out of the threshing floor. When the Church takes some measure against them, how easily they separate! How easily they gather abroad and refuse to leave their principalities! How they are prepared to die for their principality! How accipitur lapis Ule, et ad firmitatem propter Christum, et ad reprehensionem propter stultum; quomodo leo dictus est Christus propter aliud, et leo dictus est diabolus propter aliud: sic accipitur gladius aliquando in bono, aliquando in malo. Sed hic non sine causa non datus est Iacob, sed datus est Esau: nisi quia aliquid mysterii significatur in gladio. Quomodo et ipsa servitus non est aliena a mysterio; id est, quod dictum est, Servies fratri tuo: nam et hoc in magno mysterio dictum est. CAPUT XXXI.—34. Contra schismaticos.—Ergo, fratres, qui se dividunt, ipsi habent gladium divisionis, et in gladio suo moriuntur, et in gladio suo vivunt. Sed quia verum dixerat Dominus, Qui gladio percutit, gladio morietur (Mt 26,52); Videte illos, fratres mei, qui se ab unitate praeciderunt, in quot frusta praecisi sunt.

Nostis quot parties fecit pars Donati, nec arbitror latere Sanctitatem vestram, quia qui gladio percutit, gladio peribit. Dictum est illi, In gladio tuo Vives. Sic et illi qui non recesserunt ab Ecclesia, et such sunt, quales si foris essent. Who enim loved his honors in Ecclesia, omnino such sunt; who loved in Ecclesia commoda sua saecularia, et ipsi palea sunt; sed ventus deest, ideo non volant de area: hoc est quod dico breviter, tentatio deest, nam volant de area. Denique when contra illos aliquid egerit Ecclesia, quemodo facile_ se praecidunt? quomodo facile extra colligunt, et nolunt dimitiere principatum suum? quomodo pro ipso principatu mori volunt? quomodo

They want to retain the people in their obedience, and do not let them go to the unity of Christ! How they intend to become their sheep, those they did not redeem with their blood and those they despise because they did not buy them! What need is there to discuss that further? Observe them throughout the Church, look at them, now at those who are within, now at those who, when the opportunity offered, flew from the threshing floor and want to take the grains with them. But the true and full grains tolerate the chaff and remain on the threshing floor until the end, until the last welder arrives; Like Jacob with the goat skins, he tolerated the sins of others and deserved to receive his father's blessing. 35. Why did Isaac bless coerced? Either out of necessity, or out of coercion, the father said to his son: Hey, in the fertility of the earth your habitation will be and in the dew of heaven! And lest you think you are good, you will live by your sword and serve your brother. But so that you do not despair, since you can correct yourself, that will happen when you shake and break the yoke from your neck. He will receive, therefore, from the fertility of the earth and from the dew of heaven. Isaac, coerced, threw the blessing at him, he did not give it to him. Doesn't that happen now in the Church with the evil ones, who want to disturb the Church? They are tolerated by the need for the same peace; They are admitted and enjoy the common sacraments. Sometimes they are known to be bad, but they cannot be discovered. It cannot be demonstrated to them, to make them amend, to be degraded, excluded or excommunicated. If someone tries to do so, sometimes it leads to the destruction of the Church. The ruler tenere volunt sub se plebes, et non dimíttere plebes unitati Christi? Quomodo volunt faceré oves suas, quas suo sanguine non emerunt, et ideo viles habent, quia non emerunt? What opus est hinc diutius disputare? Attendite illos per universam Ecclesiam, videte tales, et eos qui intus sunt, et eos qui inventa occasione de area volaverunt, et volunt secum trahere grana; sed grana vera et plena tolerant paleam, et manent in zona usque in finem, quousque veniat ultimus ventilator: sicut ille cum pellibus haedinis toleravit aliena peccata, et meruit accipere benedictionem paternam. CAPUT XXXII.—35. Extorta benedictio.—Quare autem sugillatus Isaac benedixit? Iam enim necessitate, iam coactus pater eius dixit illi, Ecce ab [51] ubertate terrae erit tibi habitatio et a rore caeli. Et ne ideo te putes bonum, In gladio tuo vivirs, et fratri tuo servies.

Sed ne de te desperes, quia potes te corregere, Erit autem, cum deposueris et solveris iugum de eolio tuo. Ecce ab ubertate terrae et a rore caeli accipiet; sed Isaac sugillatus proicit illi benedictionem, non dat. Nonne fit moda in Ecclesia malis hominibus, qui volunt perturbare Ecclesiam, ut toleratentur ad necessitatem ipsius pacis, ut admittantur, ut habeant Sacramenta communia? Et aliquando scitur quia mali sunt, et convinci forte non possunt ut emendentur et degradentur; ut excludantur, ut excommunicantur, non possunt convinci. Si institerit aliquis, aliquando itur in disruptiones Eccle-

of the Church is forced to say: Hey, you will have the fertility of the earth and the dew of heaven! Use of the sacraments; Eat your own damnation and drink your own damnation. For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks his condemnation. You know well that you are admitted by the need for the peace of the Church and in your heart you only have disturbances and divisions. Therefore, you live by your sword. You do not live, then, from what you receive, from the dew of heaven and the fertility of the earth. This does not delight you nor is the Lord gentle on you. For if this delighted you and the Lord were gentle to you, you would imitate the humility of the Lord and not the pride of the devil. Therefore, although from the dew of heaven and the fertility of the earth you receive the mystery of humility from the Lord, you do not abandon the pride of the devil, who always enjoys seductions and dissensions. Although that communion comes to you from the dew of heaven and the fertility of the earth, you live by your sword, you enjoy and suffer in seduction and dissension. 36. All this that I have said, brothers, perhaps is little according to the greatness of the mysteries, but it is a lot for the space we have and for our and your strength. If the problem has not been discussed more clearly, it is partly due to the greatness of the mystery, and we can clarify it if we explain it. Be patient because of the pressure of time, because of our strength and because of your capacity. If you want to understand better, grow; If you want to grow, live well. Because whoever doesn't want to live well, doesn't want to grow. This banquet has been given to us. Cogitur gubernator Ecclesiae tanquam dicere, Ecce ab ubertate terrae erit tibi, et a rore caeli: utere Sacramentis, tibí manducas iudicium, tibi bibis iudicium: Qui enim manducat et bibit indigne, iudicium sibi maniucat et bibit (1 Cor 11:29). Nosti quia admitteris ex necessitate pacis Ecclesiae, non habes in corde nisi perturbationes et divisions. Ideo in gladio tuo Vives: nam in eo quod accipis a rore caeli, et ab ubertate terrae, non ibi Vives; non enim hoc te delectat, aut suavis est tibi Dominus. Si enim hoc te delectaret, et suavis tibi esset Dominus, imitareris humilitatem Domini, non superbiam diaboli. [Quamvis ergo accipiat mysterium humilitatis Domini a rore caeli et ab ubertate terrae, non tamen deponit superbiam diaboli; cui nihil faciam, qui semper dissensionibus et seditionibus gaudet].

Quamvis sit tibi is communio a rore caeli et ab ubertate terrae; tamen in gladio tuo vivis, seditionibus et dissensionibus aut gaudes aut terreris. Muta ergo te, et tolle iugum a eolio tuo. offered our holy God and Lord on the birth of his martyr Vincent. It is the name of victory 18. Love, then, to win. Because there is no shortage of persecution. The devil is the persecutor and the opportunity to deserve a crown is never lacking. It is enough for the soldier of Christ to understand the battle and know who he defeats. Is it because you are not harassed by a manifest and bodily enemy that you are not harassed by a hidden persecutor with the attractions of the flesh? How many evils it suggests to you, now through lust, now through fear! With what charms he persuades you to consult spell-casters and mathematicians 19 when your head hurts! Those who leave God and seek diabolical bonds are defeated by the devil. On the contrary, suppose that someone is suggested to accept the devil's remedies according to his body, because it is said that another was cured by them; Upon receiving his sacrifice, the devil stopped pursuing his body, having captured his heart; Suppose those detestable remedies are suggested to him and he replies: 'I will die before using such remedies; If God wants, he will flagellate me and save me; If he knows it is necessary, he frees me; and if he knows that I must leave this life, whether I am sad or happy, I will follow the will of the Lord: with what face will I have to present myself to the Lord in a short period of time, since the devil's remedies do not provide me with what the Lord gives me, eternal life, and that is why I condemn my soul by buying bene vivite. Who enim non vult bene vivere, non vult crescere. You have vobis epulas exhibituerit Dominus Deus noster per natalitia martyris sui Vincentii. Vincentius nomen victoriae est. Amate autem, ut vincatis: non enim deest persecutio; diabolus persecutor est, nunquam desit occasio coronae: tantum miles Christi intellegat pugnam, et sciat quem vincat. Numquid quia non te urget hostis manifestus corporis, non te urget persecutor oceultus illecebris carnis? How much bad suggestion? quanta per cupiditatem, quanta per timorem? Quibus illecebris persuadet ut eas ad sortílegos, ad mathematicos, quando [52] dolet caput? Qui dimittunt Deum, et eunt ad ligamenta diabolica, victi sunt a diabolo.

Contra si cui suggestum fuerit, secundum corpus fortasse efficere remedia diaboli, unde alius sanatus esse dicitur, quia accepto ab illo sacrifice suo, deserit persequi corpus, quia cor obtinuit: ergo cuicumque suggesta fuerint ista remedia scelerata, et dixerit, Moriar potius, quam talibus remediis utar; if vult Deus, flagellat et liberat me; si novit quia necessarium est, liberate me; si autem scit quia debeno exire de hac vita, sive contrister, sive laeter, sequar voluntatem Domini. a few days for my body? He who says this and does not go, and does not incline his heart to apply bad remedies, undoubtedly wins. I have cited a case by way of example. You surely see how many things the devil suggests. But where is it? You see that the sick man languishes, you see him lurking in the bed, you see that he can barely move his limbs, that he barely moves his tongue: he is dying, he conquers the devil. Many were crowned in the amphitheater for their fight with wild beasts. Many are crowned in their beds for their struggle with the devil. Here it seems that they cannot move, and inside their hearts they have so much vigor and fight such a fierce battle. Where the hidden battle is, there is the hidden victory. 37. Why do we say all this, brothers? So that, when you celebrate the birth of the martyrs, you imitate the martyrs; Do not think that we may lack opportunities to be crowned because such persecutions are now lacking. Even now and every day there is no shortage of persecutions from the devil, either by suggestion or by some bodily discomfort. It is enough for you to know that you have an Emperor who has already preceded you going to heaven. He opened the way for you to follow him; pay attention to him. And when you conquer, do not boast proudly, as if you had fought with your strength; rather he boasts of the one who gave the strength to conquer because he himself conquered the world. And you will always be crowned and you will leave here a martyr if you overcome all the temptations of the devil. quod praestat Deus, vitam aeternam. Quare ergo damno animae meae emo paucos dies corpori meo? Qui haec dicit, et non it, nec applicat cor suum ut faciat mala remedia, utique vincit. Unam rem dixi exemplí gratia; videtis certe iam quanta diabolus suggerit. Vides illum certe languere, vides anxiousantem in lecto, vides vix moventem membra, vix moventem linguam, lassus iste diabolum vincit. Multi coronati sunt in amphitheater pugnantes ad bestias: multi in lecto vincentes diabolum coronantur: videntur non se moveré posse, et intus in corde tanta vires habent, tantam pugnam exercent. Sed ubi es hidden struggle, ibi hidden victory. CAPUT XXXIV.—37. Martyres imitandi.—Quare ista diximus, fratres? Ut quando celebratis natalitia martyrum, imitemini martyres; nec putetis ideo vobis deesse posse occasions coronae, quia moda desunt such persecutions. Nec moda enim desunt quotidie persecuciones a diabalo, sive per suggestionem, sive per moles aliquas corporis.

Tu tantum scito te habere Imperatorem, qui iam praecessit in caelum: dedit tibí viam qua sequaris, teñe te ad illum. Noli cum viceris, per superbiam tibí tribuere, quasi de viribus tuis luctatus fueris: sed praesume de eo qui dedit vires, ut vinceres, quia ipse vicít saeculum (lo 16,33): et semper coronarís, et martyr hinc exies, si omnes temptationes diaboli superaveris.

Why did the Lord at first choose a few who were neither noble, nor wise, nor elegant, having before his eyes such a crowd (which in comparison to those few was scarce, but full of its kind of rich, noble, learned, wise) whom he later attracted? The Apostle exposes that mystery: God chose the weak in the world to confuse the strong; God chose the foolish things of this world to confuse the wise; God chose the ignoble part of this world to render useless the things that are not, that is, that are not esteemed, as those that are. Because he had come to teach humility and combat pride. God had come humbly: there was no way he was going to seek the high ones first, having come so humble. First, because he chose to be born to that woman who was married to a worker. He did not choose a dominant lineage so that the nobility would not become proud on earth. He did not even choose to be born in a powerful city, but was born in Bethlehem of Judea, which was not even

Theme: Jacob's combat with the angel (Gen 32, 22-32). Date: Different opinions. Location: Unknown.

1. The Christian man has the greatest need for this rule of discipline: that he hear the word of God while he lives in this century, waiting for him who first came to the century to save him with mercy and then by discernment in judgment. That is why our Lord Jesus Christ was proposed to us as a model of imitation, so that, since we are Christians, we may imitate him or those who have imitated him. There are some who call themselves Christians and are not; The Church distinguished some as dung, for example, to heresies and schisms, which are at the same time compared to the sterile branches, pruned from the vine, or to the straw that the wind snatches from the threshing floor before the fork. But there are others who, even though they are evil, are retained in the Catholic communion, whom the good Christian is forced to tolerate until the end, since the fork of this harvest and this era is nothing but the day of judgment. We have always told you this, and we hope in the name of Christ that it has been appreciated.

2. Many are coming, and now is the time for them in the name of the Lord to hasten to receive the grace of baptism, believing that they are forgiven all the sins they previously committed, all of them at all; They believe that they come out of the water without owing anything to the Lord; like that servant who, upon rendering an account to his master, found that he owed him ten thousand talents, and retired without owing anything; and not because the debt did not exist, but because the master was merciful, canceled the debt and absolved the debtor. Yet, brothers, how much fear does that same servant instill in us! Because he did not want to forgive his companion or defer the payment of one hundred denarii, and then his master demanded the ten thousand talents that he had previously forgiven him. Therefore, those who will emerge from baptism owing nothing, absolved of all their sins, fear; lest, if someone has offended them and they refuse to forgive, not only will they not be forgiven, but everything that was lost to them will also be claimed.

Therefore, that Jacob who has just been mentioned in the reading means the Christian people. He is the youngest son, since the Jewish people are Esau. Without a doubt, the Jewish race was born from Jacob, but in figure the Jews like Esau are better understood, since the older people were reproved and the lesser people took over the principality. When they were fighting in the mother's womb, and she became impatient because they shook her insides, she said: What's wrong with me? Sterility was better for me than suffering this. The Lord told her that two peoples and two races were fighting in her womb, and that the older would serve the younger. And what was said when they were in the womb was repeated in the blessing of Isaac, when he blessed the younger thinking that he was blessing the older. Isaac represented the law. It seems that the law was given to the Jews, but the kingdom was given to the Christians. Consider that the law seems to promise the kingdom. It is said to the Jews: for this reason they will take the kingdom from you and give it to people who do justice. Esau will be taken away and given to Jacob. Esau had been born hirsute and hairy, that is, full of sin; sins adhered to him. On the other hand, Jacob, to receive the birthright, placed goat skins on his arms, and thus his father blessed him by feeling his arms and finding him hirsute. But Jacob endured the hairs and sins that were attached to him. In the same way, the Church of God bears the sins of others, not its own, tolerating them until
