Let us remember the episode of the Gospel. The Pharisees, wanting to tempt the Lord, presented him with a woman caught in adultery. Against this sin there was a specific penalty in the law, in that law given by the servant of God Moses. The Pharisees approached the Lord with a malicious and fraudulent intention, so that, if he ordered that defamed woman to be stoned, they could accuse him of lacking meekness. If, on the contrary, he prohibited compliance with the law, he could be considered a violator of the law. But those who asked him about the legality of paying the tribute when Caesar defeated them through his own mouth, questioning them in turn whose coin they showed him was and what image and inscription it had; The same people who had asked him answered that the image of Caesar is on the coin, and he answered them according to his own words: Give to Caesar the things of Caesar and to God the things of God, in order to warn them that the image of God in man had to be given to God just as the image engraved on the coin had to be given to Caesar. Unfortunate is he who does not care about discipline. We could well add to this sentence: just as he who disregards discipline is unfortunate, he who rejects it is cruel. I have dared to tell you something that, due to the difficulty of the subject, I am forced to explain more clearly. I repeat what I said: he who despises or does not care about discipline is an unfortunate person. This is evident. He who rejects it is cruel. I maintain and defend that a man can be pious by punishing and can be cruel by forgiving. I present you an example. Where do I find a man who is pious in punishing? I will not go to strangers, I will go directly to the father and son. The father loves even when he punishes. And the son does not want to be punished. The father despises the son's will, but pays attention to usefulness. Because? Because he is a father, because he prepares the inheritance, because he nourishes the successor. In this case, the father, punishing, is pious; hurting, is merciful. Present me a man who is cruel when forgiving. I don't distance myself from the same people, I continue with them before my eyes. CAPUT I.—1. Pauper verus quinam sit.—Cantavimus Domino, et diximus, Tibi derelictus est pauper, pupillo tu eris adiutor. Quaeramus pauperem, quaeramus pupillum. Nec mirum sit quod admoneo [112] ut quaeramus, quos sic abundare cernimus et sentimus. Nonne pauperibus plena omnia? nonne pupillis plena sunt omnia? Tamen inter omnia quaero pauperem, quaero pupillum. Ac prius ostendendum est Caritati vestrae, id quod putamus, non hoc esse quod quaerimus. Qui enim dicuntur pauperes et sunt, in quos a Deo mandatae elemosynae fiunt, de quibus fatemur scriptum, Include elemosynain in corde pauperis, et ipsa exorabit pro te Dominum (Eccli 29,15): abundat quidem hoc genus hominum; sed altius intellegendus est iste pauper. From illo genere est iste pauper, from quo dictum est, Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum (Mt 5:3). Sunt pauperes non habentes pecuniam, victum quotidianum vix invenientes, alienis opibus, misericordia sic indigentes, ut

goods and mercy from their neighbor, who are not ashamed to beg. If it has been written about these poor people: The poor are in your charge, what will we do if we belong to this type of poor? Therefore, we, who are Christians, are not protected by God? And what other hope is there for us if we are not protected by the one who does not abandon us? 2. Learn, therefore, to be poor and to put yourselves in the hands of the Lord, my brothers! One is rich, one is superb. In these riches, which the common people call so, to which what is generally understood by poverty is opposed; In these riches, I say, nothing is to be avoided with more interest than the disease of pride.' He who does not have money, lacks great powers, has nothing to be proud of. He who has nothing to be conceited about is not praised for not being conceited; On the other hand, he who has is praised if he does not become conceited. Why do I praise the humble poor who has nothing to be proud of? Who tolerates a poor arrogant person? Praise the humble rich, praise the poor rich. The Apostle wants these, who, writing to Timothy, says: Command the rich of this world not to be conceited. I know what I'm saying: send them this. They have riches, certainly; but those riches internally invite them to arrogance; They have wealth, so it is difficult for them to be humble. Give me a Zacchaeus, possessor of great riches, chief of tax collectors, confessor of sins, small in stature and smaller in spirit, who climbs a tree to see the one passing by who had de etiam mendicare non erubescant: si de his dictum est, Tibi derelictus est pauper; nos quid facimus, qui hoc non sumus? Ergo nos qui christiani sumus, non sumus Deo derelicti? Et quae allia nobis spes est, si non sumus illi derelicti, qui nos non derelinquit? 2. Divitibus cavenda superbia.—Discite ergo esse pauperes et Deo relinqui, o compauperes mei. Dives est, superbus est. Nam et in divitiis, istis, quae vulgo appellantur divitiae, quibus est contra vulgaris ista paupettas; in divitiis ergo istis nihil est sic cavendum, quam superbiae: morbus. Qui enim non habet pecuniam, non habet amplissimas facultates; do not habet unde se extollat. Si ergo qui non habet unde se extollat, non laudatur pro eo quod non se extollit: qui habet, laudetur, si se non extollit. Quid ergo laudo humilem pauperem, qui unde superbiat, non habet? Quis autem ferat et inopem et superbum? CAPUT II.—Lauda divitem humilem, lauda divitem pauperem.

4. Let us distinguish, then, who are the poor and who are the rich. Why do you provoke me to understand other things? The poor are visible and the rich are visible. Listen to me, oh poor thing!, about what you have proposed to me. When you say that you are that ulcerous saint, I am very afraid that, out of pride, you are not really what you say. Do not despise the merciful rich, the humble rich; and to say in a word what I announced before: do not despise the rich poor. Oh poor man, be poor too; poor, that is, humble! If a rich man has become humble, how much more must the poor become humble? The poor man has nothing to be proud of; The rich man has something to deal with. Listen to me: be truly poor, be pious, be humble. If you glory in your ragged and ulcerating poverty, because such was the poor man who lay before the rich man's house, you only pay attention to the fact that he was poor and do not pay attention to anything else. "What should I attend to?" you say. Read the Scriptures and you will find what I say. Lazarus was poor, but the one to whose bosom he was carried was rich. The Scripture says: It came to pass that the poor man died and was carried away by the angels. Where to? To Abraham's bosom, that is, to the mysterious place where Abraham rested. Do not understand this in a carnal way, as if the poor man had been taken to the lap of Abraham's robe. It was called "bosom" because it was a secret place, just as it is said in the psalm: Return our neighbors to their bosom. What does it mean to your breast? To his secret. What does it mean: return them to their bosom? Turn them to

his conscience. Lee; If you cannot read, listen to what is read, and you will realize that Abraham was very rich in land, gold, silver, family, animals and possessions. However, this rich man was poor, because he was humble. He was certainly humble: Abraham believed God and justice was imputed to him. He was justified by the grace of God, not by his own presumption. He was a believer and acted righteously. He was ordered to sacrifice his own son, and he did not defer offering what he had received to the one from whom he had received it. He was tested by God and set as an example of faith. God already knew him, but he had to manifest himself to us. He did not take pride in good works as if they were his own, because this rich man was poor. And so that you may realize that he did not boast of good works as if they were his own—he truly knew that what he had was due to God, and he gloried not in himself, but in the Lord—listen to the apostle Paul: If Abraham was justified by works, he can boast, but not before God.

CAPUT III.—4. Pauper et dives in eadem sorte jelicitatis, si uterque humilis. Sinus Abrahae. Discernamus ergo, inquit mihi, pauperes et dívites: quid me ad alia intellegenda exhortaris? Aperti sunt pauperes, aperti sunt divites. Audi ergo me de hoc quod proposuisti, domne pauper. Cum enim illum sanctum ulcerosum te esse dicis, timeo ne superiendo non sis quod dicis. Noli contemnere divites misericordes, divites humiles; et ut citius dicam, quod paulo ante dixi, divites pauperes noli contemnere. O pauper, this is your pauper; pauper, id est, humilis. Si enim dives factus est humilis, quanto magis pauper esse debent humilis? Pauper non habet unde infletur, dives habet cum quo luctetur. Audi ergo me. This verus pauper, this pius, this humilis. Nam si de ista pannosa et ulcerosa paupertate gloriaris, quia talis Fuit ille qui ante domum divitis inops iacebat; attendis quia pauper Fuit, et aliud non attendis. Quid, inquis, am I attending? Lege Scripturas, et invenies quod dico. Lazarus pauper Fuit: in cuius sinum levatus est, dives Fuit. Contigit, inquit, mori inopem illum, et auíerri ah angelis. What? In sinum Abrahae, id est, in secretum, ubi erat Abraham. Nolíte enim carnaliter intellegere, quod velut in sinum tunicae Abrahae levatus sit pauper. Sinus erat, quia secretum erat. Unde dicitur, Redde vicinis nostris in sinum^ eorum (Ps 78,12). Quid est, in sinum eorum? Insecretaeorum. Quid est, Redde in sinum eorum?

5. You are now understanding that, although the poor abound, we look for the poor; We search for him among a great crowd, and we barely find him. A poor person appears before me, and I look for the poor person. In the meantime, extend your hand to the poor person you have found. Whoever you seek, you seek with your heart. You say: "I am poor like Lazarus." However, this humble rich man does not say: "I am rich like Abraham." Therefore you exalt yourself and he humbles himself. Why are you conceited and not le Torque conscientiam eorum. Lege, aut si legere non potes, audi cum legitur, et vide Abraham opulentissimum Fuisse in terra, auro, argento, familia, pecore, possessione (Gen 13): et tamen dives iste pauper Fuit, quia humilis Fuit; Credidit enim Abraham Deo, et deputatum est illi ad iustitiam (ib., 15,6). Iustificatus est gratia Dei, non propria praesumptione. Fidelis erat, bene operabatur. Filium iussus est immolare; ñeque cunctatus est ei offerre quod acceperat, a quo acceperat (ib., 22). Probatus est Deo, constitutus est exemplum fidei. Iam Deo notus erat: sed nobis monstrandus erat. Non est inflatus quasi in bonis operibus suis; quia pauper erat dives iste. Et ut scias quia non est inflatus tanquam in bonis operibus suis (sciebatenim quia quidquid habebat, aDeohabebat; et non in se ipso, sed in Domino gloriabatur), audi [114] Paulum apostolum: Si enim Abraham ex operibus iustificatus est, habet gloriam, sed non ad Deum (Rom 4.2). CAPUT IV.—5. Verus pauper in pauperum peat vix invenitur. Videtis, quia cum abundent pauperes recte quaerimus pauperem: in peat quaerimus, et vix invenimus. Occurrit mihi pauper, et quaero pauperem. Interim tu manum porrige pauperi quem invenís. Corde quaeris, quem quaeris. You say, Pauper sum sicut Lazarus: dives iste meus humilis non dicit, Dives sum sicut Abraham. Ergo you extollis, ille se humiliat. Quid inflaris, et non imitaris. Ego, inquit, pauper levor in

do you imitate? "I, he says, as a poor man, am taken to Abraham's bosom." Don't you realize that the rich received the poor? Don't you realize that the rich are the ones who welcome the poor? If you become arrogant against those who have money and deny them belonging to the kingdom of heaven, when possibly there is a humility in them that does not exist in you, are you not afraid that after death Abraham will say to you: "Depart from me because you reviled me"? 6. Let us, therefore, advise our rich people the same thing that the Apostle advised: Do not be arrogant or trust in the uncertainty of riches. We are already warned. Those riches that you consider full of pleasures are also full of dangers. He was poor and slept safer; sleep came more easily to the hard earth than to the silver bed. Be attentive to the worries of the rich and compare them with the tranquility of the poor. But the rich man must learn not to exalt himself and not to trust in the uncertainty of riches. Use the world like someone who doesn't use it. Think that you are on your way and that you have entered the world of riches as in an inn. Repair your strength, you are a pedestrian; recover and continue traveling; Do not take with you what you found at the inn. Another traveler will come and find the same thing; He will use it, but he will not take it. Everyone must leave in the world what they acquired in the world. Job already says: Naked I came out of my mother's womb and naked I must return to the earth. The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it from me; but he did not remove himself, since in your charge sinum Abrahae. Non vides quia paupetem dives except? Non vides quia dives susceptor est pauperis? Si enim superbis contra eos qui habent pecuniam, et negas eos ad regnum caelorum pettinere; cum in eis fortasse inveniatur humilitas, quae in te non invenitur: non times ne tibi, cum mortuus fuerís, dicat Ábraham, Recede a me, quia blasphemasti me? 6. Divitiae plenae periculorum et periturae. Admoneamus ergo divites nostros, quod Apostolus admonuit. Non superbe apere, ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum (1 Tim 6:17), admoniti sumus. Divitiae illae, quas putatis plenas esse deliciarum, pleniores sunt periculorum. Pauper erat, et secutior dormiebat: somnus facilius accesobat ad duram terram, quam ad lectum inargentatum. Attendite curas divitum, et compárate securitati pauperum. Sed audit dives iste, ut non superbe sapiat, ñeque speret ín incerto divitiarum. Utatur mundo, tanquam non utens.

Sciat se viam ambulare, and in has divitias tanquam in stabulum intrasse. Reficiat, viator est: reficiat se, et transeat; non secum tollit quod in stabulo invenit. Alius viator erit, et ipse habebit, sed non auferet. CAPUT V.—Omnes hic relicturi sunt quod hic acquisierunt. Nudus, inquit, exii de uterus matrh meae, nudus revertar in terram, Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit (Job 4:21). Non abstulit, quia tibi derelictus est pauper. Nudus exii of uterus matris meae; nudus revert in terram.
Commentary on Psalm 9:14

there is the poor Naked I came out of my mother's womb, naked I must return to the earth. 7. Listen to another poor person: We have brought nothing into this world and we will take nothing from it. Having clothing and food. That's enough for us. Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and pernicious and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and perdition. Greed is the root of all evil; Those who wanted it gave up their faith and became entangled in many pains. Who are these who turned away from the faith and became entangled in many sorrows? Those who want to get rich. Let the poor ragged man answer me now. Let's see if he doesn't want to get rich. Answer and don't lie. I hear the murmur of his tongue, but I ask his conscience. Tell the truth if you don't want to get rich. If you want to get rich, you have already fallen into temptation, into vain and pernicious desires. I'm not talking about riches, but about desires. Because? Because he wants to get rich. And from this, what is derived? Many vain and harmful desires that plunge men into perdition. Do you notice what situation you are in? Why do you appear before me empty of goods when I present you with a multitude of desires? Compare these two men. One is rich, the other is poor... The rich man is already rich and does not want more: he is rich, either because of his parents, or because of his inheritance. Let us suppose and assume that he is rich because of his iniquities; but he no longer wants to accumulate more wealth, he put a stop to and set limits on greed; Now he fights wholeheartedly in the field of piety. 7. Pauper cupiditatibus divite peior. Audi aüum pauperem. Nihil intulimus in hunc mundum; sed nec auferre aliquid possumus: victum' et tegumentum habentes, bis contenti simus. Nam qui volunt divites fieri, incident in temptationem et desideria fines, stulta et noxia, quaemergunt homines in interitum et perditionem. Radix est enim omnium malorum avaritia: quam quidam appetentes, a fide pererraverunt, et inseruerunt se doloribus multis (1 Tim 6,7-10). Qui sunt isti qui a fide' pererraverunt, et inseruerunt se doloribus multis? Qui volunt divites fieri. Mode mihi respondat Ule pannosus. Videamus, si non vult dives: fieri; videamus, interrogemus eum, si non vult dives fieri: responderat,, non mentiatur. Audio linguam, sed interrogo conscientiam. Dicat si non vult dives fieri. If autem vult; iam incident in temptationem et dell5\ sideria fines, stulta et noxia. Non enim opes dico, sed desideria. Where? Qui vult dives fieri. Quid inde?

Desideria fines et stulta et noxia, quae mergunt homines in interitum et perditionem. Vines ubi sis? Quid mihi you boast nullas facultates, cum ego convincam so many cupiditates? Ecce iam compare duos. Iste dives est, ille pauper est: sed iste dives, iam est, non vult fieri. This dives est, aut de parentibus, aut de donis et hereditatibus. Ponamus, faciamus: dives est etiam de iniquitatibus. Iam non vult addere, imposuit modum, fixit limitem cupiditati, iam corde militar pietati,
Commentary on Psalm 9:14

8. He is rich, you say. I answer you: he is rich. Again you, accuser, respond and say: "He is rich through iniquity." So what if he makes friends with the riches of iniquity? The Lord knew what he was saying and he was not wrong when he said: Make friends for yourselves with the wealth of iniquity, so that they may receive you into eternal mansions. What happens because the rich man does this? He has put an end to his greed and now exercises piety. You have nothing, and you want to be rich. That's why you fall into temptation. Perhaps you became poor and needy because, having some paternal assets with which you supported yourself, they were taken from you due to the slander of some rival. I hear you moan and lament your fate; but, if it were in your hands, you would do the same thing you cry. Don't we see it every day? Don't these cases happen daily? Yesterday he who lost his property groaned; Today, having risen, he steals what belongs to others. 9. We find the truly poor, the truly humble pious who does not trust in himself; to the truly poor, to the member of the poor who, being rich, became poor for us. Consider our rich man who became poor for us, being rich; Behold this rich man: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. It is more worthy to create gold than to possess it. Perhaps you are rich in gold, silver, livestock, servants, farms and fruits; but you have not been able to create all those things. Behold that rich man: All things were made through him. Behold that poor man: The Word became flesh and dwelt

between us. Who will think worthily of his riches? How does he who is not made do things, how does he who is not created create; And how does he form the unformed and make the immutable things changeable, and the eternal things temporary? Who will think worthily of his riches? Let us think about their poverty, lest perhaps, being poor, we do not understand it. He was conceived in the virginal womb of a woman, enclosed in the maternal womb. Oh poverty! He is born in a small shelter, he is wrapped in poor swaddling clothes. Next, the Lord of heaven and earth, the creator of angels, the maker of visible things, sucks, cries, feeds, grows, endures age and hides majesty. And finally he is captured, despised, whipped, spat on, slapped, crowned with thorns, hung on a tree and pierced by a spear. Oh poverty! Here is the head of the poor that I seek, of which the true poor is a member.

CAPUT VI.—8. Rursum pauper cum divite comparatur.—Dives est, inquis. I answer, Dives est. Iterum tu accusator responders et dicis, De iniquitate dives est. Quid, if facit amicos de mammona iniquitatis? Dominus noverat quod dicebat: utique non errabat, quando praecipiebat, Vacite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut et ipsi recipiant vos in tabernacula aeterna (Luke 16,9). Quid si hoc facit iste dives? Iam finit cupiditatem, exercet pietatem. Tu nihil habes, sed dives vis fieri; incidents in temptationem. Sed forte inde factus es paupertimus et egentissimus, quia nescio quid habebas paternum, quod te sustainret, et calumnia aliqua competitoris abstulit. Gemis, audio, tempora aecusas: quod gemís, si posses, faceres. Annon videmus? annon quotidianis exemplis plena sunt omnia? Heri gemebat, quia perdebat sua; hodie pertinens ad maiorem, rapit aliena. 9. Verus pauper. Christus pauper et dives.—Invenimus verum pauperem, invenimus pium humilem, non de se fidentem, pauperem verum, membrum pauperis qui propter nos pauper factus est, cum dives esset (2 Cor 8:9). Vide divitem nostrum, qui propter nos pauper factus est, cum dives esset; vide illum divitem: Ómnia per ipsum jacta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Plus est aurum faceré, quam habere. Dives is auro, argento, pecore, familia, fundís, fructíbus; tibi ist creare non potuisti. Vide illum divitem: Omnia per ipsum jacta sunt. Vide illum pauperem: Verbum caro jactum est, et habitavit in nobis (lo 1,3-14). Quis worthy

10. Let us quickly search for the orphan, since we have tired ourselves in the search for the poor. Oh Lord Jesus! I look for the orphan, and I look for him tired. Answer me soon so I can find it. We are told: Call no one Father on earth. He who is an orphan on earth finds his immortal Father in heaven. Do not call anyone Father on earth. We have found the orphan. Let this orphan pray! Let us listen to him and imitate him. What is your prayer like?: My father and mother abandoned me. My father, he says, and my mother abancogitet divitias eius? Quomodo faciat qui non fit, quomodo creet non creatus, formet non formatus, mutabilia manens, temporalia sempiternus? Quis digne cogitet divitias eius? CAPUT VIL—Paupertas Christi.—Paupertatem cogitemus, ne forte pauperes vel ipsam capiamus. Concipitur uterus feminae virginali, including visceribus matris. Or paupers! In angustodiversotio nascitur, involutus infantilibus tegumentis in praesepio ponítur, fit cibaria iumentis pauperibus; deinde caeli et terrae Dominus creator Angelorum, omnium visibilium et invisibilium effector et conditor sugit, vagit, nutritur, crescit, tolerat aetatem, oceultat maiestatem: postea tenetur, contemnitur, flagellatur, illuditur, conspuitur, colaphizatur, spinis coronatur, ligno suspenditur, lan[116]cea perforatur. Or paupers! Ecce caput pauperum quos requiro, cuius pauperis membrum invenimus verum pauperem. 10. Pupillus quis.—Breviter quaeramus pupillum: quia in paupere requiring fatigueti sumus. Domine Iesu, pupillum quaero; fatiguetus quaero: I quote answer, ut inveniam. Ne vobis, inquit, dicatis patrem in terra (Mt 23:9). Pupillus in terra, immortalem patrem invenit in cáelo, Ne vobis, inquit, dicatis patrem in terra. Inventus est pupillus iste. Oret pupillus iste: audiamus eum, et imitemur eum. Quae est eius oratio? Quoniam pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me. Pater, inquit, meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me: Dominus autem assumpsit me (Ps 26,10). Si ergo S. Ag. 7
Commentary on Psalm 25:8

they donated; but the Lord took me into his charge. Therefore, if the poor are blessed in spirit because theirs is the kingdom of heaven; The poor man is in your charge. If my father and mother abandoned me, the Lord took me back; you are the orphan's help.
Topic: Commentary on Psalm 25,8. Date: Around the year 418. Place: Carthage, in the Petri basilica.

1. We love the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place of the tabernacle of his glory, if we are the house and tabernacle of the Lord. What is the beauty of the house of the Lord and the tabernacle of his glory, but his own temple, of which the Apostle says: The temple of God is holy, which are you? Just as your bodily vision is recreated in the buildings built by man, when they are elegant and sumptuous, in the same way, when the hearts of the faithful - living stones - are intertwined by the bond of charity, they constitute the beauty of the house of God and the place of the tabernacle of his glory. Learn, therefore, what you must love so that you can love it i. For he who loves the beauty of the house of God does not beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum (Mt 5:3); Tibí derelictus est pauper. Si pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me, Dominus autem assumpsit me; Pupil, you are adiutor.
VERSU 8 PSALMI 25: «DOMINE, DILEXI DECOREM DOMUS TUAE, ET LOCUM TABERNACULI CLARITATIS TUAE»

CAPUT I. — 1, Decor domus Dei. Ecclesia viva.—Decorem domus Dei, et locum tabernaculi claritatis eius diligimus, si et nos ípsi sumus._ Quis est ergo decor domus Dei, et locus tabernaculi claritatis eius; nisi templum eius de quo Apostolus dicit, Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos (1 Cor 3:17)? Sicut ergo in fabricis manufactis, cum elegantr et magnifice construuntur, corporalis noster mulcetur aspectus; ita cum lapides viví, corda fidelium caritatis vinculo continentur, decor est domus Precondition of love for anything is the knowledge of it, See the application that makes this principle in Confessions X 20,29

There is no doubt that he loves the Church, not because of the sumptuousness of the walls and vaults, nor because of the splendor of the marbles and the golden coffered ceilings, but because of the believing and holy men who love God with all their heart, with all their soul and with all their mind; and their neighbors as themselves. 2. But in the Church, in that which refers to the participation and communication of the sacraments, they have multiplied above all numbers. One thing is the number and another thing is the over-number. The number of believers is that of which the Apostle says: The Lord knows his own. The overnumber is that of which it is said: In the great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some for honor, others for contumelia. The number is the vessels of honor; the over-number are the vessels of ignominy. Since these two kinds of vessels exist, do we doubt where the beauty of the house of the Lord is found? If, then, you are determined to love the beauty of the house of the Lord, doing with righteousness what you have sung, seek the vessels of honor. And I don't want you to say: "I looked for them and couldn't find them." Maybe you looked for them and didn't find them because you weren't what you were looking for. Like adheres to like; and the dissimilar turns away from the dissimilar. If you are a vessel of ignominy, you will undoubtedly find it difficult to see the vessel of honor. Don't you hear what some say about another: nos es penoso Dei, et locus tabernaculi claritatis eius. Discite ergo quod amare debentis, ut amare possitis. Qui enim diligit decorem domus Dei, non est dubium quia Ecclesiam diligit: non in fabre factis parietibus et tectis, non in nitore marmorum et laquearibus aureis; sed in hominibus fidelibus, sanctis, Deum diligentibus ex toto corde suo, et ex tota anima sua, et ex tota mente sua, et proximum suum tanquam seipsum. CAPUT II.—2. Numerus et super numerum. Vasa in honorem, vasa in contumeliam.—Sed in congregatione christiana, quantum pertinet ad participationem et communionem Sacramentorum, multiplicati sunt super numerum (Ps 39:6). Alius est ergo numerus: alii super numerum. Numerus est, de quibus dicit Apostolus, Novit Dominus qui sunt eius. Super numerum autem: Quoniam in magna domo non solum vasa sunt áurea et argentea, sed et lignea et fictilia; alia quidem in honorem, alia in contumeliam (2 Tim 2,19,20). Numerus ergo, vasa [117] in honorem: super numerum, vasa in contumeliam.

Cum ergo sint ista duo genera vasorum, numquid dubitamus ubi sit decor domus Dei? Si ergo vis diligere, agens quod cantasti, decorem domus Dei, et locum tabernaculi claritatis eius; quaere vasa in honorem. Et nolo dicas, Quaesivi, et non inveni. Ideo enim quaesisti, et non invenisti, quia quod quaesisti tu non Fuisti. Similis simili cohaeret, dissimilis dissimilem refugit. Si fueris vas in contumeliam, procul dubio vas in honorem grave tibi erit et ad videndum. Non audis quomodo quidam de quodam dicant, Gravis nobis est etiam ad videndum

contemplate him? That which is annoying for you to contemplate, when will it be clear for you to find? These vessels are the interior of man. The righteous man is not known merely by his outward appearance. Both the just and the unjust have the same external appearance. They are both men, but, although they both call themselves Christians, they are not both the house of God. They are both vessels, but they are not both vessels of honor: one is a vessel of honor, and the other is a vessel of ignominy. 3. Should we leave the big house because of the bad vessels? God, the Lord of the great house, knows how to use the vessels of honor and the vessels of ignominy. Just as it is characteristic of the evil ones to use goods badly, it is characteristic, on the contrary, of God to use evils well. How many good things do bad people use! Every creature of God is good. Why do bad people use it badly? The Scripture severely rebukes them with these words: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrong; to spend it on your lusts. What name have those received who misuse God's goods? The same Apostle says: Adulterers. Why adulterers? Do you not know that the friend of this world is the enemy of God? He calls them adulterers. There are adulterous men, fornicating men: let's talk about them. Fornicating souls are those who clumsily give themselves over to countless false gods. Adulterous souls are those who, being united in legitimate marriage with God, do not maintain the chastity of the sacred bond. I will speak more precisely: the soul of the pagan is fornicatory; the soul (Wis 2:15)? Quod tibi grave est ad videndum, quando erit apertum ad inveniendum? Vasa enim ista, interiorum hominum sunt. Non utique cum visus fuerit iustus, iam agnoscitur iustus. Eumdem aspectum habet et iustus et iniustus: uterque homo, sed non uterque domus Dei. Et si ambo christiani appellanfur, utrumque vas, sed non utrumque in honorem; be aliud in honorem, aliud in contumeliam. CAPUT III.-—3. Malorum est male uti bonis; Dei contra, bene uti malis. Animae adulterae et fornicariae.—Numquid propter mala vasa deserenda est domus magna? Novit Deus uti, id est Dominus magnae domus, et vasis in honorem, et vasis in contumeliam. Sicuti est malorum male uti etiam bonis; sic e contra Dei bene uti etiam malis. Quantis bonis utuntur mali? Omnis enim creature Dei bona est (1 Tim 4,4). How do you male utuntur mali? Quomodo eos increpat Scriptura, dices, Petitis, et non accipitis, eo quod male petatis, ut in concupiscentiis vestris insumatis.

Quod nomen acceperunt isti male utentes bonis Dei? Sequitur, et dicit, Adulteri. Unde adulteri? Nescitis quia amicus huius mundi, inimicus Deo constituitur (Iac 4,3.4)? Adulteri, inquit. Sunt animae adulterae, sunt fornicariae: discutiamus eas. Fornicariae animae sunt, multis diis falsis quodam moda prostitutee: adulterae autem, tanquam legitimo iam coniugio copulatae, et ipsi legitimo coniugio non servantes animae castitatem. Ut autem hoc dicam expressius, pagani anima fornicaria est,
Commentary on Psalm 25:8

of the bad Christian is an adulteress. The fornicating soul of the pagan does not have a legitimate man and is corrupted as soon as it gives itself over to various demons. Why is the soul of the bad Christian adulterous? Because she neither loves purity nor abandons her husband. And you do not ask me: "Why do such souls dwell in the house of God?" I would answer you: they are vessels of ignominy. God knows how to use them. He who created them knew them; because if he could create them, he also knew how to organize them, so that each one had its own place in his great house. But if you ask me: "How does God use them well?" I will sincerely confess that, as a man, I cannot explain the mystery of God. I am filled with wonder, just like the apostle Paul when he thought about this counsel of God; stunned, he exclaimed: Oh depth of the riches of the science and wisdom of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and how impenetrable are his ways! Who knew the mind of the Lord or who was his counselor? Or who gave it to him first, so that he might repay him later? For all things are made of him, through him, and in him, to him be glory forever and ever. We only have consideration, admiration, trembling, and exclamation before these unfathomable mysteries of God, since we cannot understand them. Now God, what is owed to Him? Glory forever and ever. Whether through the vessels of honor, or through the vessels of ignominy: to him be glory forever and ever. He crowns some, condemns others, but he is never wrong. Test some, test through others, but order all. christiani mali adulteres. Pagani anima fornicaria, legitimum virum non habet, per diverse daemonia prostitute corrumpitur: christiani autem mali quare adultera est? Quia nec castitatem diligit, nec virum deserit. Non ergo dicas, Quare sunt isti in domo Dei? Respondetur tibi, Vasa sunt in contumeliam. Novit eis uti Deus: non errat qui creavit; quoniam qui potuit creare, novit ordinare: habent in domo magna locum suum. Si autem quaeras a me, quomodo eis bene utatur Deus: fateor, Dei consilium, sicut homo, explicare non possum. Novi enim cum Paulo apostólo expavescere, quod etiam ille cumconsideret, expavit, et expavescens exclamavit: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiae et scientiae Dei! quam inscrutabilia sunt indicia eius, et investigabiles viae eius!

Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis consiliarius eius Fuit? aut quis prior [118] dedit Mi, et retribuetur ei? Quoniam ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omitted: ipsi gloria in saecula saeculorum (Rom 11:33-36). Nobís considered, admired, tremor, exclaimed: quia mile penetrated. Ipsi autem quid? Glory in saecula saeculorum. Sive de vasis in honorem, sive de vasis in contumeliam, ipsi gloria in saecula saeculorum. Alios coronat, alios damnat, nusquam errat: alios probat, de alus probat, omnes ordinat.
Commentary on Psalm 25:8

4. What do bad men do in this world? he asks. Answer me: What does straw do in the silversmith's oven? I believe that chaff is not meaningless where gold is purified. Let us consider all the things that are there: there is an oven, there is straw, there is a fire and there is a silversmith. The first three: gold, straw and fire, are in the oven; but the silversmith is attentive to the oven. Now consider this world: the world is the furnace, the chaff is bad men, the gold is good men, the fire is tribulation, the silversmith is God. Stay attentive and realize: the gold is not purified if the straw does not burn. Consider also in this psalm, where we love the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place of the tabernacle of his glory, the voice of gold. He desires to purify himself: Test me, O Lord, and tempt me; burn my kidneys. Try me and tempt me. He who should fear temptation asks for it. Test me, he says, O Lord, and tempt me. Look what the fire also asks for: Try me and tempt me; It burns my kidneys and my heart. Are you not afraid of fainting in the fire? No, he says. Because? For your mercy is before my eyes. Here, he says, is why I feel secure and say: Try me, O Lord, and tempt me; Burn my kidneys and my heart, not because I am able to withstand the fire of temptation with my own strength, but because your mercy is before my eyes. He says: You, who granted me to be tested like gold, will you allow me to perish in the furnace? On the contrary, you throw me into the oven to purify me and you take me out already purified. The Lord keep your entrance

da and your exit. Contemplate the exit and contemplate the entry into the oven. Consider it as a reward when you find yourself in various trials. You already heard the entrance: now look for the exit. Entering is easy, leaving appears difficult. But do not fear: God is faithful—no doubt because you had entered you were already thinking about the exit. God is faithful to such a point that he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but will offer you the same way out along with temptation. What does exit mean? May you endure temptation. You entered, you were tempted, you endured the temptation and you came out safely. 5. The abundance of the bad is a great means for the purification of the good. Although the good are mixed among the multitude of the bad, the Lord knows his own. Under the skill of such a great craftsman, not even a speck of gold can perish among so much chaff. How abundant is the straw and how scarce is the gold! But do not be afraid: the craftsman is so great that he can purify and not lose the gold. Contemplate the Apostle, who is gold, in what way he is tested in the furnace of this world, and thus you will realize how the Lord knows how to use well the vessels of ignominy that are in the great house. What did the Apostle say when he felt tested in difficulties? Dangers at sea, dangers in the wilderness, dangers from my lineage, dangers from the Gentiles. All these dangers were external. But now attend to the inmates: dangers from the false brothers. I talk about the gold of God, I talk about the vessels of honor, I talk about the

CAPUT IV.—4. Ad quid malí in mundo.—Quid faciunt, inquit, in hoc mundo homines mali? Reply mihi, in fornace aurificis palea quid facit? Puto non ibi esse sine causa paleam, ubi aurum purgatur. Videamus quae ibi sint omnia: fornax est, palea est, aurum est, ignis est, artifex est: sed illa tria, aurum, palea, ignis, in fornace; artifex, ad fornacem. Attend etiam istum mundum: mundus fornax est; palea, homines mali; aurum, homines boni; ignis, tribulatio; artifex, Deus. Attende et vide: aurum non purgatur, si palea non uratur. Vide aurum in hoc ipso psalmo, ubi diligimus decorem domus Dei; et locum tabernaculi claritatis eius. Vide ibi aurum, vide vocem auri; purgan cupit: Proba me, Domine, et tempta me; ure renes meos et cor meum. Proba me, inquit, Domine, et tempta me. Qui timere debuit temptationem, petit temptationem. 1. What we have just sung: Rejoice, righteous, in the Lord, it is fitting to praise the upright, it invites us to rejoice in the praise of God and to live with dignity praising God. If it suits the upright, it does not suit the wicked. The righteous are those same righteous people who are said to rejoice in the Lord; Therefore, praise is fitting for them. Who are the wicked, but the sinners and the wicked, who cannot rejoice in the Lord, since praise is not convenient for them? With good reason it is said in another psalm: God says to the sinner: why do you announce my righteousness and put my law in your mouth? Since it is decorous to praise the upright, and since justice and the law of the Lord are found where praise is given nita cogitans; spem saeculi irridens, spem caelestem exspectans, mutans amores et mores: oleum sanctitatis est in torculari, vas in honorem est in domo magna, aurum est in fornace, granum est in hórreo. to the Lord, it is rightly said elsewhere: praise is not beautiful in the mouth of the sinner. Where it is not suitable, it is not beautiful; and where it is beautiful, there it is suitable. 2. Examining the Scripture we find who are the righteous men; and thus each one will know if the praise of God is beautiful in his mouth. A psalm says: How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart! And he adds: My feet have almost staggered, since I was envious of sinners when I contemplated their peace. Here the danger is confessed, not the aversion and the fall. It does not say that he fell, but rather that his feet staggered and he almost fell. It goes like this: How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart! My feet almost staggered. The author of this psalm seems to confess that he was once not upright in heart and that because of this his feet almost staggered. It says that the God of Israel is good to the upright in heart. But to me, however, it once did not seem good, because I was not upright in heart. He did not dare to say, "God did not seem good to me," but he said it. By saying: The God of Israel is good to the upright in heart, but my feet almost trembled, he shows that it did not seem good to him, since his feet staggered. Why didn't God seem good to you? My feet almost slipped. What does this almost mean? Because I was envious of sinners when I contemplated their peace. He says: «I saw sinners who do not praise God, who blaspheme him and irritate him. And I also saw that they abound in peace and happiness. and it seemed to me

that God does not judge rightly in granting happiness to those who blaspheme. When he contemplated this, when he contemplated the happiness of the wicked, he says that his feet staggered, since God did not seem good to him. Later he came to know, as it says in the same psalm: I tried to know; and he adds: this is painful for me, he says, until I enter the sanctuary of God and know its end; that is, until I learned that to the wicked, to whom happiness is now temporarily given, eternal punishment is reserved for the last day. Once he knew this, he became upright in heart, began to praise God in all things, both in the works of the good and in the joys of the evil, thinking that God will be a just judge on the last day. He understood why he now grants temporary happiness to some, reserving eternal misfortune for them; He also understood why He exercises many pious men in tribulation and reserves eternal happiness for them. And he understood that it is appropriate that fortunes be changed, just as the fate of the rich man who ate sumptuously every day was changed and that of the poor ulcer patient who lay stretched out at the rich man's door and wanted to satisfy his hunger with the crumbs that fell from the potentate's table. Once they were both dead, one went to the pains of hell, and the other went to rest in the bosom of Abraham. And as the rich man seemed unworthy and longed for a drop of water from the little finger of Lazarus, longing for a drop of water from the finger of him who desired the crumbs from his table,

He heard from Abraham the sentence of the just God: Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus, on the contrary, bad things; but now Lazarus rests and you are tormented. And he who was envious when contemplating the peace of sinners and doubted that God was good, now entering the sanctuary of God, directs his gaze towards these last moments. And knowing that the judgment of God is true and right, although now it is carried out in darkness and later in the sight of all, having converted his heart from his own perversity and having applied to himself the rule of God's justice, by which the straying heart is straightened, he breaks out in this exclamation and says: How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart! Now I understand the good, because I have been made upright in heart. Previously it did not seem to me that God was good, because my feet wavered: I was envious of the sinners contemplating their peace. 3. If God already seems good to you, even when he gives happiness to the wicked, which is why you used to murmur against God, it is a sign that your heart is right and praise is decent to you: praise is convenient for the upright. If you are perverse, praise is not decent to you. Because? Because the praise with which you exalt God will not persevere, since you praise him when things go well with you and you insult him when things go badly with you; You like it when it offers you happiness and you dislike it when it punishes you. In this case you are not upright at heart nor can you sing that of

psalm: I will bless the Lord at all times; His praise is always in my mouth: How will he always be if you praise him only when things are going well for you and not when things are going badly for you? What seems like an evil to you is a good if you come to understand that it is a father who punishes. The foolish child often loves the soft teacher and hates the punisher. However, the intelligent child considers both the one who flatters and the one who punishes to be a good teacher. Praise so that the child is encouraged and punish so that he does not fail. So, when you have a heart that does not feel upset when something unpleasant happens to you, you praise God safely and sing faithfully to God: I will bless the Lord at all times; His praise is always in my mouth. However, he scourges everyone he receives as a son. What do you choose? To be punished and received, or not to be punished and not received? Consider what kind of son you are. If you desire paternal inheritance, do not refuse punishment. If you reject the punishment, renounce the inheritance. Why does he correct you, if not to give you the inheritance? To be your father's heir, did he not rebuke you, rebuke you, punish you, and whip you? And why did he do this? So that you would inherit a house that will fall over time, so that you would inherit a field that will be temporary or so that you would inherit the gold that will not remain in this world longer than yourself. Certainly, either in life you have to lose what you have, or you have to abandon it in death. For this temporal inheritance you endured the father's punishments, and did you murmur?

bant de mensa divitis saturari concupiscentis. Cum autem mortui essent ambo, Ule in poena in inferno esse coepit, ille in sinu Abrahae requievit; et cum indignum videretur diviti, et vellet sibi de modico digit Lazari stillari guttam aquae, vicissim de digito ipsius desiderans guttam, de cuius mensa ille desideravit micam, audivit ab Abraham sententiam recti Dei: Fili, inquit, memento, quia percepisti bona in vita tua, Lazarus autem mala; I never saw any requiescit, tu autem torquerh (ib., 25). Inhaec new intendit aspectum intrans in sanctuatium Dei ille, cui non videbatur bonus Deus, quia zelavit in peccatoribus pacem peccatorum intuens; et agnoscens iudicium Dei verum et iustum, quod quidem moda agitur, sed occulte, futurum in fine in manifestatione, et tanquam correct corde ex pravitate propria, admota velut regula iustitiae Dei, qua cor tortum corrigeretur, erupit in hanc vocem et ait: Quam bonus Deus Israel rectis corde! Modo intellego bonum, quia factus sum rectus corde; antea vero non mihi videbatur bonus, quia nutabant pedes mei: zelavi enim in peccatoribus, pacem peccatorum intuens. 3. Si ergo iam tibi videtur bonus Deus, et quando malis dat felicitatem, unde solebas murmurare adversus Deum, factus es rectus corde, decet te laudatio: rectos enim decet laudatio; si autem sis pravus, non te decet laudatio. Quare non te decet? Non erit perseverans laus, qua laudas Deum: laudas enim Deum, quanto tibi bene est: blasphemas Deum, quando tibi male est. Etenim tune tibi placet, quando dat felici-

tatem; displicet autem, quando punishat: non es rectus corde, non poteris dicere canticum illud aíterius psalmi: Benedicam Dominum in [127] omni tempore, semper laus eius in ore meo (Ps 33,2). Quomodo enim semper, si tune quando tibi bene est laudas, non et quando tibi male est? Quia et ipsum quod dicitur male tibi esse, bene est, si punishatorem patrem esse intellegas. Puer insensatus amat plerumque magistrum blandientem, odit caedentem; puer vero intellegens intellegit magistrum bonum, et blandientem, et caedentem; blanditur enim ne puer deficiat, caedit ne pereat. Tale itaque cor cum quisque habuerit, id est rectum, ut non ei displiceat Deus, et quando facit quod forte illi ad tempus adversari videatur, securus laudet Deum; quia semper laudabit, et veré illum decet laudatio, et veré fideliter cantat: Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus eius in ore meo. Flagellat autem omnem filium quem recipil (Heb 12:6). Quid ergo you choose: flagellari, et recipi, an non tangi, et non recipi? Vide qualis sis filius: si hereditatem paternam appetis, flagellum ne recuses; si flagellum respuis, nega hereditatem. Quo enim te erudit, nisi ut det hereditatem? Heres patris tui ut esses, non te increpavit, non obiurgavit, non punishavit, non verberavit? Ut quid hoc? Ut ei succederes in domum quandoque ruituram, et fundum quandoque transiturum, et aurum non diutius in hoc saeculo mansurum quam tu ipse, qui aurum possides: etenim aut vivirs amissurus es quod habes, aut moriens relicturus. Propter istam tamen temporalem hereditatem pertulisti flagella
Commentary on Psalm 32:1

Are you now of God who corrects you to give you the kingdom of heaven? 4. When you are such that it pleases you that God punishes you - since there is something in you that must be corrected by punishments or your very righteousness must be tested - when you are like that, I repeat: praise. You praise safely. Because? Because you praise decently, because you praise constantly. I no longer fear that you will praise now, and blaspheme a little later. I no longer fear that you praise when you are healthy, and curse when you are sick. I no longer fear that praise comes from the mouth of the healthy, and that from the mouth of the sick one looks for the astrologer or the spell-reader 2, one looks for the sorcerer or the one who offers healing with sacrilegious bandages. I am not afraid of any of that, because you already understood that God is good even when he punishes, and you know well that he who punishes his son also knows how to forgive him. It will be decent for you to praise, because you will always and constantly praise and at all times the praise of God will be in your mouth. You already welcome the father who flatters and also the father who punishes; You don't run to him when he caresses and you run away from him when he punishes. If you did this you would be like the child who, fleeing from the father who punishes, throws himself into the hands of the seducer who caresses 3 and, judging him good, prefers the deceptions of flattery to the truth of punishments. And by doing so he prefers to lose his inheritance and fall into slavery. Change your counsel and make your heart straight.

God does not change because he punishes you, but it is you who changes. He acts in such a way that you, changing for the better, receive the inheritance. Because, if he doesn't care about you and abandons you, even if it seems good to you, his anger flares up. Let your charity pay attention to what God's Scripture says in another psalm: The sinner provoked the Lord. Why did it irritate you? Consider where God's irritation comes from. Truly, the sinner irritated the Lord greatly: The Lord did not seek him, due to his great indignation. 5. On the contrary, holy Job, blessing the Lord at all times, always having the praise of the Lord in his mouth, being rich, blessed the Lord in his riches, doing with them all those good works that are described in his book: he gave bread to the hungry, he clothed the naked, he welcomed the pilgrim, he carried out all those things in which the rich use their wealth. Such rich people do not enrich themselves or boast of the earnings they leave to their children, since they do not know who will enjoy, after their death, the efforts of their work. About this vanity the Scripture says: Truly every living man is vanity who hoards things and does not know for whom he accumulates goods. All the profit that can be obtained from riches is the kingdom of heaven. That is why the Lord advised that you move your gold so as not to lose it. The Lord does not say to you: “You lose it if you give it,” but rather: “You have it in a bad place on earth; I will keep it for you in heaven. Why are you afraid to lose?

patris tui; et murmuras ad Deum erudientem, ut det tibi regnum caelorum? 4. Cum ergo talis es, ut placeat tibi Deus, et punishns placeat tibi—aut enim est in te aliquid quod flagello corrigatur, aut ipsa rectitudo tua in flagello probatur—cum ergo talis es, lauda; securus enim laudas. Quate securus laudas? quia decenter laudas, quia perseveranter laudas. Non enim timeo, ne moda laudes, post paululum blasphemes: non timeo, ne sanus laudes, et aegrotus blasphemes: non timeo, ne de sani ore proceedat laus Dei, de aegroti lingua quaeratur mathematicus aut sortilogus, quaeratur praecantator et remedyrum diabolicorum alligator; non timeo, quia iam intellexisti bonum Deum esse et cum punishat; et seis, quia ille qui peteutit filium, novit et quando parcat. Decebit et laudare, quia semper perseveranter laudabis, et erit semper laus Dei in ore tuo. Accipis libenter blandientem patrem, accipis [128] libenter et flagellantem patrem: non ad illum curris cum blandí tur, et fugis ab eo cum flagellat. Si enim hoc feceris, eris tanquam puer, qui, cum fugeret a flagellante patre, incurrit in blandientem mangonem, et putavit eum bonum, patrem vero suum malum, et praetulit dolos blandimentorum veritati flagellorum; The same in sermon 63 A 3 (= Mai 25) and 4,36. See note 19 to the latter. This comparison frequently appears in Augustinian preaching: Ennarration to Psalm 127:11; Treatises on the first letter of Saint John 3,9 and 7,6.

praeferendo autem amisit hereditatem, incurrit in condicionem. Muta tu consilium, et fac cor tuum rectum: non enim mutatus est Deus, quia flagellat te, sed tu mutabilis es; agit ille aliquid per commutationem, ut tu in melius commutatus percipias hereditatem. Nam si relinquat te, et neglegat te, quando tibi videtur bonus, tune multum irascitur. Intendat caritas vestra, quid dicat in alio psalmo scriptura Dei; irritavit TSominum peccator, ait. Quare irritavit? Videte ubi exclamaverit de irritato Deo. Utique ad iracundiam maiorem irritavit Dominum peccator: Prae magnitudeine, inquit, irae suae non exquiret (Ps 10 sec. Hebr., 14). 5. Contra Iob sanctus, benedicens Dominum in omni tempore, in cuius ore semper erat laus eius, cum esset dives, benedixit Dominum in divitiis suis, faciens de lilis omnia opera bona quae in libro eius enumerantur: frangens panem esurienti, vestiens nudum, suscipiens peregrinum, et cetera, quae sola divites de divitiis suis percipiunt, quae divites sola lucrantur. Ñeque enim lucrantur, aut praesumunt de lucris, quae filiis suis relinquunt: nesciunt enim, quis post eorum mortem tú possessurus labores ipsorum. Et hanc vanitatem scriptura dixít: Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivos; thesaurizat, et nescit cui congreget ea (Ps 38,6.7). Ergo lucrum totum, quod fit de divitiis, thesaurus est regni caelorum; unde Dominus dedit consilium, non ut perdas, sed ut mutes locum auro tuo. Non enim ait tibi, Cum dederis, perdes; sed, Male habes in terra, in cáelo ego tibi servabo. What times do you lose? in cáelo

it? You put your riches in heaven, having Christ as your guardian. If you are looking for a place, let it be heaven; If you are looking for a guardian, let it be Christ. Why are you afraid of losing him? When Job acted like this, with his own works he praised God and blessed the Lord with those goods received from his hands. Riches should not be censured in themselves. When you see bad rich people, do you think that riches are bad? Riches in themselves are not bad; They are bad. Riches are gifts from God. Give them to the righteous and see how he does good things with them. Is wine bad because someone gets drunk? Give it to the sober person, who uses it well, and you will understand it as a gift from God. Give gold to the greedy man and you will observe that, to become richer than he is, he tries to perpetrate all kinds of crimes. Offer gold to the just man and you will see how he distributes it, how he helps the needs of men as much as he can. Therefore the evil is not the wealth itself, but the misuse of it. Job used them well, as did Abraham. Brothers! That poor ulcer patient who lay before the rich man's door was so needy that the dogs licked his sores. This is how we read it, since it is written. And where was he taken? To the bosom of Abraham. Review the Scriptures. Consider if Abraham was poor. You will realize that he had a lot of gold, silver, abundant flocks, a lot of servants and considerable property. But the poor man was taken to the bosom of the rich man. If poverty obtained him this reward, Abraham would not have preceded him in this rest nor would he have received him. ponies, guard Christo. Si locus te sollicitat, caelum erit; yes custos, Christus erit. What times do you lose? Ergo cum haec de taíibus faceret Iob, utique operabatur, et in ipsis operibus eius Deus laudabatur, et benedicebat Dominum in his quae acceperat. Non enim veré, fratres, divitiae accusantur. Putatis, quando videtis divites malas, divítias esse malas? Divitiae non sunt malae, sed illí; divitiae autem dona Dei sunt. Da illas iusto, et vide quae bona inde faciat. Numquid ideo [129] malum vinum, quia nescio quis se inebriat? Da sobrio bene utenti, et vide munus Dei. Sic da aurum homini avaro: ut amplius faciat hoc quod habet, quaerit committere omnia facinora. Da aurum homini iusto, et vide, quemadmodum distribuat, quemadmodum inpertiat, quemadmodum quibus potuerit necessitatibus hominum subveniat. Non ergo divitiae, sed utens male divitiis ipse est malus.

Cum ergo bene uteretur Iob, sicut bene usus est Abraham... Certe enim, fratres, ille mendicus ulcerosus iacens ante ianuam divitis ita egens erat, ut canes lingerent ulcera eius; sic certe legimus, sic scriptum est; et tamen quo ablatus est? In sinum Abrahae (cf. Luke 16, 22). Pray scriptures, vide si pauper hic Fuit Abraham: invenies illum habuisse hic multum auri, multum argenti, multum pecorum, multum mancipiorum et praediorum. Ergo pauper levatur in sinum divitis. Si meritum illi paupertas faceret, non eum ad requiem Abraham ipse praecederet, et eum succedentem susciperet; sed quia hoc in paupere Lázaro
Commentary on Psalm 32:1

But since poor Lazarus had the same as rich Abraham, that is, humility, piety, observance of divine commands, neither was one harmed by wealth nor the other by poverty, but their true merit was piety. That is why in the rich, who changed destiny badly, it is not his wealth that is reproved, but his spirit. He dressed in linen and purple and feasted lavishly every day, and at the same time he tolerated the ulcerous beggar lying before his door and, proudly despising him, he did not satisfy his poverty. What do you think the rich man said to the annoying beggar? "Why does this one lie here?" No wonder that same tongue, which despised the beggar, then begged for a drop of water from the poor man's hand. 6. Even though holy Job had much wealth, he praised God, was tempted and was tested; and it was tested for our teaching. This teaching is hidden not only from men, but from the devil himself, who is much sharper than men 4. What Job truly was was hidden, although the Lord knew him. The tester allowed the tempter; but not for himself, but for us, to show us what we should imitate. Nor did he want to reveal himself to the devil, but to us through the devil, so that we would have a model to imitate once the devil was defeated. And Job, having lost all his possessions suddenly, and not little by little, says: The Lord gave them to me and the Lord took them away from me. As it pleased the erat, quod erat in divite Abraham, id est humilitas, pietas, Dei cultus, Dei observantia, nec illi obfuerunt divitiae, nec huic paupertas, sed illius meritum pietas Fuit. Inde in illo divite, qui male mutavit vices, non reprehenduntur divitiae ipsius, sed animus ipsius: Induebatur enim purpura et bysso, et epulabatur cotidie splendide, et patiebatur ulcerosum mendicum iacere ante ianuam suam, et eum superbe contemnens non satiabat eius inopiam. Quid putatis dixisse divitem fastidientem mendicum? Quid hic icet iste? Sed merit illa lingua, quae contempsit pauperem, guttam de digit eius desiderabat. 6. Cum ergo Iob sanctus, ut dixi, haberet fines divitias, laudavit Deum, temptatus ut proveretur, probatus ut ostenderetur: latebat enim non solum homines, sed et ipsum diabolum latebat, qui diligentius inspicit quam quisquam hominum. Latebat ergo eum quis esset Iob, sed Dominum non latebat. Permisit temptatorem probator; probator autem non sibi, sed nobis, ut nobis manifestet quid imitari debenamus.

Non enim ipsi diabolo voluit ostendere Iob, sed per diabolum nobis, ut diabolo victo nos haberemus quod imitaremur. Ergo amissis omnibus, non paulatim, sed suddenly, ait: Dominus dedit, et Dominus abstulit: sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est: sit nomen Domini bene\\l>ü\dictum (Iob 1,21). See the city of God (IX 21): "He made himself known to the demons... by certain temporary effects of his power and signs of his most hidden presence, which could be visible to the angelic spirits, even the evil ones, more than to human weakness."
Commentary on Psalm 32:1

Lord, this is how it was done. Blessed be the name of the Lord. As it pleased the Lord, so it was done. That which pleased the Saint cannot be perverse. What pleased the Good cannot be evil. The God of Israel is good to the upright in heart. Job was a man with a right heart, and that is why it was fitting for him to praise. The Lord gave it; the Lord took it away. As it pleased the Lord, so it was done. Praising God he made this confession, as he says: Blessed be the name of the Lord. The Lord gave it and the Lord took it away. Before he was rich; now, poor thing. Things have changed for me, but he remains unchanged. Sometimes rich, sometimes poor; but he remains always rich, always upright, always a father. Blessed be the name of the Lord. The name of the Lord could not be blessed in wealth and cursed in misery. Far be it from me this way of thinking. Job said all this, full of interior riches. He had lost his entire house, but his heart was full. He had lost the house, the gold, but his heart was full. God was present in him in place of all those goods that had been granted to him before. The Lord gave it, the Lord took it away. Learn to understand the supreme power. So all power is in God; so that you do not pretend to praise God because of the kingdom of heaven and do not pretend to fear the devil because of the goods of the earth. The devil intended to do harm, but, if he had not been given permission, he would not have been able to. The power is in God. Because, if the devil were allowed everything he craves, how many Christians would be left? What worshiper of God would be left on earth? Don't you see

their temples reduced to rubble, their false images broken and their priests converted? Don't you think that the devil is tormented and hurts because of this? If the devil had power, what Church would be left on earth? Although the holy Job lost all his possessions through the schemes of the devil, the devil was not granted any power. When Job praises God he does not say, "The Lord gave it to me and the devil took it from me," but he says, "The Lord gave it, the Lord took it away." The devil has nothing to brag about. When I was rich, I was rich because of God; and when I am poor, I am poor because of God. And even if he were allowed to tempt, he has not been allowed to drown. He would have drowned not by twisting and breaking the neck, but by chaining the spirit. If Job, in enduring the anguish of tribulation, had uttered a blasphemous word, he would have spoken in an extremely choked manner, removing from him the true spirit of life. And he did not do it either in that sudden poverty or in that last calamity. 7. What's more, since the devil did not think it was enough to have taken away everything he owned, he even took away the children he had, leaving him only his wife. And the woman left him knowing what she was doing. He knew that Adam had fallen for Eve; She rather reserved a cooperator for herself than a consoler for her husband. 5 Having taken away all his things and leaving him only one to tempt him again, it still seemed little to him. He also asked to strip him of his bodily health. And it was granted to him, so that, even in that situation of misery, the righteous Job continued to praise God, not changing his attitude in any way.

Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est; non potest pravum esse, quod recto placuit; non potest malum esse, quod bonus placuit: bonus enim Deus Israel rectis corde. Rectus corde erat Iob, ideo decebat eum laudatio. Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit; sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est. Confessus est laudans: sit nomen Domini benedictum. Dominus dedit, et Dominus abstulit. Erat copy, nunc est inopia: apud me res nunc mutatae sunt, ille non est mutatus: ego aliquando dives, aliquando pauper; ille semper dives, semper rectus, semper pater, sit nomen Domini benedictum; non enim benedictum erat nomen Domini incopia mea, et maledictum erit in inopia mea: absit hoc a me. Hoc dicebat Iob divitiis interioribus ditatus. Totam domum amiserat, sed pectus plenum erat; amiserat domum, aurum, impleverat pectus: Deus, pro his omnibus quae dederat, ipse aderat. Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit. Videte quemadmodum intellegat supereminentissimam potestatem. Ne forte Deum velis colere, o christiane, propter regnum caelorum, et diabolum timeas propter bona terrena: omnino penises illum est tota potestas et summa. Diabolus nocere tantum voluit; nisi permissus non potuit. Apud illum ergo potestas est. Ceterum, si tantum liceret diabolo quantum vult, quis christianorum remaneret? Quis Dei culturar in terra relinqueretur? Non yidetis templa eius cadere, simulacra confrmgi, priests eius ad Deum

did I convert? Non putatis bine doleré et torqueri diabolum? Si ergo pro dolore suo et potestas ei esset, quae ecclesia in terra remanet? Proinde cum Iob sanctus per diaboli insidias omnia perdidisset, non dat ei aliquam potestatem. Cum laudat Deum, non ait, Dominus dedit, diabolus abstulit; sed ait, Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit. Nihil sibi arroget diabolus: et quod dives eram, Dei erat, et quod pauper sum, Dei est. Et si permissus est ut temptaret, non est permissus ut suffocaret: suffocaret autem, non gulam tenens et confringens, sed spiritum intercludens. Si forte ille tribulationis passus anguishes unum verbum blasphemum ex ore emitteret, tune exhalaret extremum suffocatus, excluso a se spiritu vitae. Hoc nec in illa sudden paupertate fecit, nec in illo ultimo vulnere. 7. Nam, cum parum Fuisset diabolo abstulísse omnia quaecumque ille possidebat, abstulit et filios, quibus ille possidebat, sola relicta [131] uxore; solam enim illam non abstulit, et hoc utique sciens quid faceret. Noverat Adam per Evam deceptum: servabat ergo suam potius adiutricem, quam mariti consolatricem. Cum ergo abstulisset illa omnia, et reliquisset unam per quam rursus temptaret, parum ei Fuit: petit etiam auferre sanitatem corporis. Et ipsam permissus est auferre, ut et in illo
See the same in seimon 22 A 3 (= Mai 15).

position. Now his wife approaches him, inviting him to blasphemy, and says: "How many evils we suffer! Curse God and die. At first, Eve, invited by the devil to life, was seduced and met death. The devil says: You will not die the death. And thinking that he would have life, he found death, since he acted against the commandment of the Lord and persuaded the man against the commandment of God. Now, on the contrary, he says: Curse God and die. Enough with that Eve who persuaded to act against the divine precept. She was still Eve, but he was no longer Adam. She was still full of the devil, but Job was corrected by example. Job in the dunghill was better than Adam in paradise. So that you understand what a right heart is worth, how did Job overthrow the devil, in the midst of his poverty and his wounds? Answering the woman and saying: You have spoken like a foolish woman. If we have received good things from the hand of God, why should we not receive evil things? He blessed the Lord at all times, always keeping praise in his mouth. He was a man with a right heart, so it was good for him to praise God. If you want praise to be worthy on your lips, you also be men of upright heart. And if you want to be upright in heart, let God displease you in nothing. Because, one of two: either you understand the reason why God acts this way, and seeing the reason, you do not censure him; or, if you do not understand the reason for God's actions, know that he acts in such a way that no one can be displeased.

vulnere positus Iob laudaret Deum rectus corde, in nullo varians, quem decebat laudatio. Accessit ad eum illa ad hoc relicta, et persuasit, immo suasit blasphemiam. Ait enim: Quanta mala patimur! Dic diquii in Deum, et morere (Iob 2,9). Primo Eva a diabolo quasi ad vitam tumbata seducta est, et invenit mortem; etenim diabolus ait: Non mor te morieris (Gen 3,4). Et putans se habituram vitam, mortem invenit, quia contra praeceptum Dei fecit, et contra praeceptum Dei viro persuasit. Mode contra: Dic aliquid in Deum, et morere. Sufficiat Eva quia persuasit faceré contra praeceptum Dei. Illa adhuc Eva, ille iam non Adam; illa a diabolo impleta, ille exemplo correctus. Melior Iob in stercore, quam Adam in paradiso. Ut noveritis quantum sit rectum cor habere, Iob quomodo prostravit diabolum in illa inopia, in illo vulnere? Respondit enim muliere, et ait: Tanquam una ex insipientibus mulieribus locuta es. Si bona percepimus de manu Domini, mala non sustinebimus? (Iob 2,10). Benedixit Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus eius in ore illius; rectus enim erat corde, propterea illum decebat laudatio. Si ergo vultis ut et vos deceat laudatio, estote recti corde; si vultis autem esse recti corde, non vobis displiceat in aliquo Deus. Aut enim vides causam, quare faciat quod facit, et causam intuens non reprehendis; aut, si causa te latet, scito quia ille facit, qui in nullo poterit displicere.
Commentary on Psalm 32:1

8. Someone demolishes his own house and is rebuked. But if you know the cause, perhaps you will not rebuke the one who does it. Now we find ourselves in this basilica, it seems narrow and small to us; But it pleased the Lord that we built another one, and this one must be destroyed 6. Anyone who sees the demolishers, when it begins to be demolished, will say, “Wasn't there prayer here? Has not the name of the Lord been invoked here? What harm does it do to be destroyed? This action is distasteful because the reason is unknown. This is how God also acts. Why does he act like this? If you are upright in heart: either you know it and praise it or you ignore it and believe it. He is of upright heart who praises God in things known and does not treat God as a fool in things he does not know. Without any reason and foolishly, he who ignores your reasons and your plans censures you. And you, do you dare to censure the ruler of the entire world, the creator of heaven and earth, because he made the wind blow and the vineyards withered or because he formed the clouds and hail fell? Don't murmur! He knows how to govern and evaluate all his works. You could not create heaven and earth, and yet, if you were allowed, you would say to God: "If I ruled, I would not do what you do." When you dislike something done by God, don't you try to be a governor yourself? Be ashamed. Who do you want to put yourself before: the one who is to die over the immortal, man over God? It is better to submit to God than to try to take precedence 8. Deicit nescio quis domum suam, reprehenditur; si causam noveris, fors non reprehendis hominem facientem. Utique in hac moda basilica sumus, et angusta est, et habet aliquid parvum, et placuit Domino alteram fieri, et destruenda erit haec. Quicumque forte viderit deicientes, cum coeperit deici, dicit: Hic non oratum est? Hic nomen Dei non evocatum est? Quid patiuntur isti ut deiciant? Displicet opus, quia latet consilium. Sic ergo et Deus aliquid facit: quare faciat, aut [132] six, et laudas; aut nescis et credis, if rectus is corde. Ipse est enim rectus corde, qui et in ipsis causis quas novit laudat Deum, et in his quas nescit non dat insipientiam Deo. Iniuste et stulte reprehenderis, homo gubernator domus tuae, ab ignaro causarum et ignaro consiliorum tuorum; et tu audes gubernatorem totius mundi, et creatorem caeli et terrae reprehenderé, quia flavit ventus, et aruerunt vites, aut surrexit clouds, et fudit grandinem? Tu certe non potuisti fabricare caelum et terram; et tamen, si tibi liceret, díceres Deo: O si ego gubernarem, non facerem quod facis. him. Submit to God, since He is God; and if by chance he acted against your will, he did not act against your benefit. How many things doctors do against the will of the patient and yet they do not act against health! And the doctor makes mistakes from time to time, but God never makes mistakes. If, then, you surrender to the doctor who errs from time to time, you surrender to human advice. And you do it not so that I use a synapism, which is a mild thing, or a painless plaster; but many times you put yourself in their hands so that they burn, cut, amputate a member of your own body. And you don't say: Maybe he's wrong and I'm left without a finger. You allow him to cut off your finger to try to save your entire body. And shouldn't you allow God to amputate, to take away some of your assets, when possibly with that decrease in assets you find true correction? 9. Brothers! Be upright, therefore, of heart. May God displease you in nothing. I'm not saying don't pray. Pray as much as you can in affliction. It's not raining: ask for it. If it rains, praise God; If it doesn't rain 7, praise him too. The humble soul heads towards the greatness of God, if God helps it in its need, to thus manifest its consolation to the Deo; melius est te illi cedere, quam quaerere succedere. Cede Deo, quia Deus est; etsi forte contra voluntatem tuam fecit, non est forte contra utilitatem tuam. Quanta faciunt medici contra aegrotorum voluntatem, et tamen non faciunt contra sanitatem. Si ergo committis te medico aliquando erranti, committis te humano consilío, non ut adhibeat poultice, quod leve est, aut emplastrum, unde tibi dolorem non faciat, sed plerumque ut urat, ut secet, ut auferat membrum tibi et tecum natum; committis te illi, non dicís, Hic forte errat, et ego minum habebo unum digitum; permittis ut tollat ​​unum digitum, ne forte inde totum corpus putrescat; et non permittis Deum secare, ut tollat ​​aliquid de fructibus tuis, si forte in ipsa moderatione habeas dísciplinam? 9.
