DE EO QUOD SCRIPTUM EST IN PSALMO 33,13: «Quis EST HOMO QUI VULT VITAM, ET DILIGIT VIDERE DIES BONOS?»
CAPUT I.—1. Vita praesens nec vita est.—Vocans humanum genus Spiritus Dei, iubendo quid faceré, et promittendo quid sperare debenamus,

wait. The same spirit inflames our minds with the desire for the reward, so that we are more willing to execute what is commanded out of love than to execute what bothers us out of fear. Who is the man who loves life and wishes to see happy days? He wonders about this man as if there were anyone who does not have such desires. Who will there be who doesn't want to live? And where will we find the one who does not want to see happy days? Listen, O mortal!, to what follows; Listen, you who love and long for this: Turn your tongue away from evil and let your lips utter no lie. Turn away from evil and do good; Seek peace and pursue it. Of all these things, the first demands are a precept, while the last words contain a reward. We are commanded to turn our tongue away from evil so that our lips do not utter lies; We are commanded to turn away from evil and do good so that we may seek and achieve peace. What kind of peace is this, if not that which the world lacks? What kind of peace is this, except that which is not found in this life, which, in comparison with true life, is not life at all? Certainly, it could not be said of the present life: Who is the man who loves life?; nor would we be exhorted by previous mandates to retain it and extend it as if no one wanted it. We desire this long, although not eternal, human life; and through it reach eternal life. However long the present life may be, is it not in itself a finite thing? What seemed long will be nothing; because when it existed it could not last forever, when prius mentem nostram inflammat ad praemium; ut quod praecipitur magís bonum amando, quam malum timendo faciamus. Quis est homo, inquit, qui vult vitam, et diligit videre dies bonds? Sic intertogatur quis iste sit, quasi possit invenid qui non sit. Quis enim non vult vitam? Who can't read these bonds? Audi ergo quod sequitur, quicumque hoc vis et diligis, homo; audi quod sequitur, omnis homo: Cohibe, inquit, Un guam tuam a malo, et labia tua non loquantur dolum. Declines to bad, et fac bonum; quaere pacem, et sequere eam (Ps 33,13-15). Horum omnium cetera superiora sunt in praecepto, ultimum in praemio. Nam ut cohibeamus linguam nostram a malo, et labia nostra non loquantur dolum, declinemus a malo, et faciamus bonum, ut quaeramus pacem [122] praecipitur nobis: ut autem sequamur eam, promittitur nobis. Quae ista pax est, nisi quam non habet mundus?

Quae ista pax est, nisi quam non habet ista vita, quae in huius vitae comparisone nec vita est? Ñeque enim de hac vita saysret, Quis est homo, qui vult vitam? et ad istam vel retinendam velproductodam praeceptis consequentíbus hortaretur, tanquam et istam quis non vellet. Nam et haec optatur saltera prolixa, quia non potest esse sempiterna: et per hanc potest homo pervenire ad illam, si quemadmodum vult eam longam, sic velit et bonam. Quantum est autem in hac vita, longum, quod erit aliquando finitum? Et quod erat
Commentary on Psalm 33:13

was produced did not increase, nor did it grow by adding time to time, since, as it approached, it disappeared. 2. Anyone who is a lover of a long life, rather be a lover of a good life. Since, if you want to live badly, living long will not be truly good, but rather a prolonged evil. Look how foolish and perverse you are when you clearly confess that you love life more than a town; and, on the other hand, you prefer a good town to a good life; since to satisfy your lust you get a good villa leading a life of fraud. However, if you were asked whether you would rather not have the good life by losing it or lose the bad life by dying, you would respond, if you cannot retain both, that you are prepared to lose the life. Why don't you love the good life so much that you come to prefer it to all good things and even to the bad life? You truly wish for a long life, even if it is bad. Well then: make that life good and do not fear that it will be short. If I invite you to do good, I also assure you that it will be brief; and then eternal life will come, blessed forever and without any fear. About that life the question is asked who says: Who is the man who loves life and wants to have good days? The Apostle, who commands that in this life we ​​take advantage of the time, since the days are bad. And what does it mean to take advantage of or rescue time, if not to seek and acquire, even to the detriment of temporal goods, true eternal goods? Therefore the Lord also says: If anyone wants longum, erit nullum: quia et quando erat, non stabat; when producebatur, non augebatur; nec addendo crescebat, quia coming recedebat. CAPUT II.—2. Vita bona hic sectanda. Redimere tempus quid.—Quisquis igitur is amator longae vitae, this potius bonae vitae. Nam si male vivere volueris, longa vita non erit verum bonum, sed erit longum malum. Vide autem quam sis absurdus atque perversus: cum te vitam fatearis plus amare, quam villam, villam vis potius bonam habere, quam vitam. Nam ut inhiando et male concupiscendo adipiscaris villam bonam, fraudando efficit vitam malam. Tamen si tibi diceretur, si a te quaereretur, utrum malíes villa bona carere perdendo, an vita mala dying; You will respond, te, si utrumque retiñere non posses, patatiorem esse ut villa tibi auferretur. Cur igitur non sic amatur vita, ut sit etiam bona, quae abs te omnibus tuis bonis praefertur etiam mala?

Cupis certe ut longa sit, licet mala sit: immo fac ut bona sit, et noli timere ne brevis sit. Nam if I solicit you bene agitur, I will surely quote you finietur. Succedet ei namque vita aeterna, sine metu beata, sine fine longa. De illa quippe interrogat, qui dicit, Quis est homo qui vult vitam, et diligit videre dies bonds? In hac autem vita iubet nos Apostolus redimere tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt (Eph 5,16). Et quid est redimere tempus, nisi, cum opus est, etiam detrimento temporalium commodorum ad aeterna quaerenda et capessenda spatia temporis comparae? Unde et Dominus praecipit, they say, Si quis voluerit tecum indication contendere, et tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte illi et
Commentary on Psalm 33:13

fight with you and take your tunic, also give him the mantle, so that, once you have abandoned the temporal good, you can invest in peace the time that you had to spend in the lawsuit. 3. The following words of the psalm show us that the Spirit of God does not speak of the days of this life when he says: Who is the man who longs for life and desires to have good days? He then added some precepts through which we could have a good life and days, so that this life that passes and these days that we have should be lost in compliance with those precepts. Therefore, if we understood about this present life what is written: Who is the man who longs for life and wishes for good days?, and to obtain this life we ​​fulfilled the indicated precepts, what would we do if a powerful man threatened us with death if we did not bear false testimony? If we fulfill what is ordered here: Turn your tongue away from evil, and because of the precept we reject a fallacious testimony, we would be disappointed, since we have set out to fulfill the precept in order to retain life, and it turns out that we lose it by fulfilling it. Suppose we understand the eternally blessed life, which God will give us if we obey Him, and of which the Lord said to someone: If you want to attain life, keep the commandments; To the one who asks us: Who is the man who longs for life? We will answer that we long for life and we will confess the truth, even if we have to take the blow.

of the pursuer's sword. By despising death in the world, we will achieve life in heaven. 4. Understand everything said in reference to good days. Because if, because of the days of this century, which seem good and are not, you dedicated yourself to burying your heart with banquets, with bacchanals of lust and wine, with clumsy pleasures of gluttony; If because of these days, I repeat, you had received the precept that our lips do not speak lies, often these days would force their lovers to speak lies. Furthermore, such days would be denied to those who do not tell lies. What else is a lie but pronouncing one thing with the lips while hiding another in the heart? ' This is what the occupation of flatterers is directed towards, since they do not stop lying so as not to be excluded from good invitations and sumptuous banquets; and they would be excluded from all this if they always told the truth while loving God. Because of these days that they judge to be good, flatterers continue to speak lies, since, if they do not tell lies, they are excluded from such days. Therefore, we must conclude that there are other good days; and we are advised that, if we want to see them, we must turn our tongue from evil by not telling lies. Such good days are not of this world; They are not the possession of the heaven that passes away, but of the heaven that remains; The land of those who will die does not know them, but the land of those who will live. Everyone who has understood and loved these days

pallium (Mt 5:40): ut scilket amissa re aliqua temporali, impendas ad quietem, quod eras impensurus ad litem. CAPUT III.—3. Vita in Psalmo quaenam proponitur.—Quod itaque non de vita et diebus huius temporis loquatur Spiritus Dei, they say, Quis est homo qui vult vitam, et cupit videre dies bonds? teaching sequence Talia enim praecepta subiungit, quibus obaudiendo vitam et dies bonds habere possimus, ut haec vita quam nunc agimus, et hi dies pro eisdem praeceptis implendis plerumque amittendi sint. Proinde [123] si hanc vitam, in qua nunc sumus, intellexerimus in eo quod dictum est, Quis est homo qui vult vitam? et propter hanc habendam quae conectuntur praecepta facíamus; quid acturi sumus, cum aliquis in malitia potens mortem nobis fuerit comminatus, nisi falsum testimonium dixerimus? Profecto enim si fecetimus quod hic iubetur, Cohibe linguam tuam a malo, ut propter hoc praeceptum testimonii fallaciam recusemus, quasi decepti videbimur: quia propter habendae vitae cupiditatem praeceptum servare suscepimus, et eam magis praeceptum servando perdidimus. Porro si vitam intellexerimus in aeternum beatam, quam post istam Deus dabit oboedientibus sibi; de qua Dominus dixit ad quemdam, Si vis vinore ad vitam, serva mandam, (Mt 19:17): tune vero interrogati, Quis est homo qui vult vitam; responderus nos velle vitam, et si etiam sub ipso percussoris ictu veritatem servabimus in testimony, mortem contemnimus in mundo, vitam consequimur in cáelo.

4. Dies boni in psalmo, non huius saeculi, sed aeterni promittuntur. Loqui dolum.—Hoc de diebus bonis intellegamus. Nam si propter dies praesentis saeculi, qui boni dicuntur, et non sunt, in sepultura cordis per epularum ageres, in luxuriae ac vinolentiae gurgitibus, in turpissimis ingluvium voluptatibus: si ergo propter istos dies, quasi propter dies bonds, susceperimus praeceptum, ut labia nostra non loquantur dolum; plerumque such dies cogunt amatores suos loqui dolum, et such dies negantur eis qui non loquuntur dolum. Quid enim aliud est, loqui dolum, nisi aliud labiis promere, cum aliud claudatur in pectore? Ad hoc maxime adulatorum exarsit negotium; quia penis semper, ne prohibeantur ab opimis mensis apparatisque conviviis, brandishing non tacent falsum; et ab his prohibition, si loving Deum díxerint verum. Ergo propter istos dies, quos putant bonds, ut eis exhibitantur, loquuntur dolum; et eis negantur, si non loquuntur dolum. CAPUT IV.—Alii sunt igitur dies boni, de quibus admonemur, ut si eos videre diligimus, cohibeamus a malo linguam, nec dolum loquamur. Non sunt de isto saeculo dies illi: non eos habet caelum quod transiet, sed quod permanebit; non eos novit terra morientium, sed terra vivostium. Hos quisquís intellexerit et dilexerit, linguam cohibet a malo: et

good: turn your tongue away from lies; and even if the terror of death incites him to do evil, let his lips not utter fallacies. And if you are deceived to obtain the good days of the world: turn away from evil even in the midst of the same good things and practice good even in the midst of the same bad things. Seek that peace that does not exist on earth and find it in him who made heaven and earth. 5. For the same reason, brothers, desire true life and love to see good days where there will never be night. Love that life in which there is no fear of a bad day; Love those good days where life has no end. But, if you love that inheritance, try not to flee from the work for which it is the reward. Keep looking for that true peace. Work with your hands before God during the night and you will not be disappointed. What does it mean to work with your hands? With your good works. What does overnight mean? In the tribulation. What does it mean before God? The purity of conscience. Living like this and loving all this you will possess God, and in him you will possess life without end, you will have good days without shadow, you will have peace without discussion. si eum terror mortis cogat ad malum, labia eius non loquuntur dolurn: et si diebus fallaciter bonis invitationtur ad dolum, declinat a malo etiam inter bona, facit bonum etiam Inter mala; quaerit pacem, quae non est [124] super terram, et sequitur eam in illo qui fecit caelum et terram. 5. Quanto ardore quaerenda pax et vita aeterna.—Proinde, fratres, concupiscite vitam, et diligite videre dies bonds ubi nulla nox erit: vitam in qua dies malus non timeatur; dies bonds, in quibus nunquam vita finiatur. Sed si hanc mercedem diligitis, cávete ne opus, cuius ea merces est, recusetis. Mam enim pacem quaerendo sequimini: quaerite autem manibus vestris nocte coram Deo, et non decipiemini (Ps 76,3). Quid est enim manibus vestris, nisi operibus vestris? Quid est nocte, nisi in tribulatione? Quid est coram Deo, nisi conscientiae puritate? Sic vivirdo et hoc loving, habebitis Deum in contemplatione, et in illo vitam sine defectione; dies bonds sine contenebratione, pacem sine dissensione.
Topic: Commentary on Psalm 38:13. Date: The year 411. Place: The Basilica Maiorum, Carthage.

1. It is a Christian requirement to progress every day in the knowledge of God and to rejoice in his gifts. The time of our trip around the world is short, but our homeland lacks time. Between time and eternity there is a great difference. Here you conquer piety, there you rest. As good businessmen, we should know what we earn every day, since we must not only be careful in listening, but also diligent in doing good. This school, in which only God is the teacher, seeks good, assiduous and dedicated students. The Apostle says it: Do not be negligent in your dedication, have a fervent spirit, be joyful in hope. In this school we learn every day: one thing in the precepts, another in example and another in the sacraments.' All this is the medication for our wounds and the stimulation of our zeal. We just said: Lord! Hear my prayer and my prayer;
FROM RESPONSORY PSALMI TRICESIMI OCTAVI: «EXAUDÍ ORATIONEM MEAM ET PRECEM MEAM, DOMINE». ET DE MULIERE IN ADULTERIO DEPREHENSA

1. Christianorum est, cotidie in Deum proficere, et de Deo vel de donis eius semper gaudere. Peregrinationis enim nostrae tempus brevissi[112]mum est, et patria nostra sine tempore est. inter aeternitatem enim et tempus multum distat: hic conquiritur pietas, illic requiescitur. Inde cotidianis diebus quasi boni negotiatores noverimus quid profecerimus; non tantum enim studiosi esse debenmus in listening, be vigilant in operating. Haec schola, in qua Deus solus magister est, bonds quaerit disciples, non fugitives, be studious. Apostolus dicit: Studio non pigri, spiritu ferventes, spe gaudentes (Rom 12,11.12). In hac ergo schola, fratres, cotidie discimus: aliud discimus in praeceptis, aliud in exemplis, aliud in sacramentis. Sunt is medicamenta vulnerum nostrorum, et foment studiorum nostrorum. Respondimus mode: Exaudí orationem meam The precepts are the decalogue and other commandments; The examples are the good actions of the patriarchs and other characters in the Old Testament; sacraments sister the rites and the set of liturgical ceremonies that are a sign of future realities. In this sense, that is, as soon as they hide and imply something, they receive that name.

turn your ear, that is, perceive my tears in your ears. What do you think he should ask for who, above all, longs for God to be favorable to him? What should you ask for with your greatest desire? Let's see and learn. Perhaps riches, perhaps happiness in this life? Tell us what to order. He realized what he couldn't get on his own and he could get it from God. I had heard that expression: ask and you will receive. I already knew what he who prayed to the Lord above all had to ask: listen to my prayer. And as if he had been asked: "What do you want, why are you calling, what do you demand?" I will listen to what you want. «What do I want? May you listen to my will and perfect my work. This is my will: I will keep my ways so as not to sin with my tongue. He proposes a difficult thing, but he does not hesitate, since he has previously prayed to the Lord. He knew in fact Paul's sentence: Not I, but the grace of God with me. 2. I said, therefore, I will keep my ways. What kind of roads? Perhaps the paths of the earth? Do we, by chance, walk the earth with our tongues? On earth we walk with our own feet, or with the feet of others; We are either carried by animals or we walk with our feet. What is it about? What kind of path do you seek so as not to sin with your tongue? This is a great teaching! Listen, brothers! Can we speak and be silent in the same moment, just as we can in an instant eat food and walk away satisfied? Just as we have eyes to see, ears to hear and

other senses to perceive their own objects, we also have language to speak. We have a great need for language: either to respond to what we hear or to say what we have to teach. Do you perhaps intend to speak with your eye and not with your tongue? If you listen with your ear, it is with your tongue that you have to respond. What do we do with that useful member? With our tongue we pray to God, we satisfy Him, we praise Him, we sing to Him in chorus, we do daily works of mercy: speaking to others or giving them advice. What do we do now? Our own language is presenting the mystery to you. What must we do to not sin with it? We must pay special attention to what we were told: Death and life are in the power of the tongue. And on another occasion: I saw many succumb to the blow of the sword, but not as many as succumbed to the tongue. And also: The tongue, which is between the members of the body, defiles our entire body. And finally: They taught their tongue to tell lies. They taught! Telling lies is already a habit; and even if you don't want to, the same language speaks fallaciously. Just as when you turn a wheel it spins by itself by virtue of its round shape, so we do not need to teach our language to speak fallaciously. Once released, it spontaneously goes towards what is easiest for it. You have one thing in your heart, but something else slips on your tongue by virtue of habit. What is to be done? You see, brothers, the balance

et precem meam, Domine; inaurire, hoc est, auribus percipe lacrimas meas (Ps 38,13). Quid whores iste petiturus est, qui primo sibimet Deum cupit propitium esse? What ab illo expetiturus is? Videoamus, discamus. Forte divitias petiturus? Forte in hac vita aliquam congratulate? Dicat ergo nobis quid petiturus est, qui primo Deum deprecatur. Vidit enim quod ex se habere non potuit, sed a Deo habere potuit; audierat enim, petite, et accipietis (Mt 7,7). Noverat ergo quid esset petiturus, qui primo Deum rogavit. Ergo exaudií Deus orationem meam. Et quasi interrogatus. What do you see, what do you press, what do you cry, what do you question? Audiam quid vis. What flew? Audi voluntatem meam, et perfice operam tuam. Quae est voluntas mea? Dixi custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea (Ps 38,2). Arduam rem iste available; sed non dubitat, quoniam primo Dominum deprecatus est; noverat enim magisterium Pauli: Non ego, sed gratia Dei mecum (1 Cor 15:10). 2. Dixi ergo, custodiam vias meas. What routes? Earthly? Numquid per linguam ambulamus in terra? Aut pedibus nostris in terra ambulamus, aut pedibus alienis; aut animalibus vehimur, aut pedibus nostris imus. What is ergo? Quam iste viam quaerit, ne delinquat in lingua sua? Great doctrine. Videte, fratres, numquid enim, quemadmodum una hora possumus cibum accipere, et refecti recedere, sic possumus momento uno loqui etiam et silere? Quemadmodum enim habemus oculos ad videndum,

aures ad audiendum, ceterosque sensus [113] ad percipiendum, sic iterum linguam ad loquedum. Est nobis magna necessitas linguae. Aut aliquid auditurus es, ut responderas; aut aliquid dicturus es, ut twelves. Numquid oculo dicturus, et non lingua? Et si aure auditurus es, lingua responsurus es. Quid facimus de tam utili membro? Inde Deum rogamus, inde satisfiimus, inde laudes dicimus, inde una voce concinentes Deo cantamus, inde cotidianis diebus aut misericordes efficimur, cum alus loquimur, aut consilia damus. Quid facimus nunc? Ipsa lingua nostra vobis ministerium exhibitat. Quid facimus, ut non delinquamus in lingua? Maxime cum dictum sit, mors et vita in manibus linguae (Prov 18,21), et iterum dictum sit, multos vidi cadentes per casum gladii, sed non sic quomodo qui ceciderunt per linguam (Eccli 28,22). Iterum dictum est: Et lingua in membris nostris constituitur, quae maculat totum corpus nostrum (Iac 3,6). Inde iterum idem Dominus: Docuerunt linguam suam loqui mendacium (Ier 9,5). Or docuerunt! Facit enim consuetudinem loqui mendacium: etiam si non vis, illa loquitur mendacium. Quemadmodum enim, si rotam volvas semel, iam, ut manu impuleris, illa ipsa figura et rotunditate, vel ipso instabili et quasi naturali cursu currit, sic et lingua nostra opus non est utdoceatur loqui mendacium; iam enim inita sponte currit ad id, ad quod facilius potest moveri. Aliud habes in corde; aliud illa aliquando volvit ex more. Quid facturus is it? Quae, videtis, fratres, quae statera

verve that must exist in the heart for the language to speak! The tongue does not move spontaneously; Inside is the one who moves it. 3. There is a certain faculty that moves itself and the organs subject to it. It is absolutely necessary that he who governs be good so that, helped by grace, he can overcome any evil inclination. The soldier has weapons in his hands, but if he does not use them, the weapons are useless. So also the tongue is among our members the weapon of our soul. It has been said about her: a restless evil, O restless one! Who made her evil but restlessness? Do not be restless and this evil will not occur in you; do not exalt yourself and he will not be exalted. It is not a spirit to move. It is a body that lies at rest. Don't move it and it won't move. Pay attention to how you move it. The tongue is a member that is given free rein to those eager for fraud and those who are greedy for wealth; and this tongue, which was made for the praise of God, they now use to blaspheme against God, saying: “By Christ! I bought for so much and I sell for so much. Because? I asked you. Swear to me: how much do you sell it for? I asked you: how much do you sell it for? «I sell it for ten joles, for twenty joles» 2. You swear by Christ. Swear rather by your eyes and by your children, and you will see that at that very moment your conscience will tremble. Oh impious tongue! You despised the Creator and kept the creature. Oh restless evil, full of deadly poison! cordis facienda est, ut lingua aliquid ptoferat! Ñeque enim sponte movetur, intus est qui movet. 3. Est enim quaedam vis, quae et cetera ministry sua movet. Opus est ut bonus sit ille qui regit, et quamlibet malam consuetudinem adiutus per gratiam vincit; bonus sit minister, et quiescit ministerium. Miles habet arma, sed, si non fecerit, níhil faciunt arma: sic et lingua in membris nostris arma animae nostrae sunt. From ipsa dictum est: Inquietum malum (Iac 3,8). O inquietuml Quis fecit istud malum, nisi inquietus? Tu noli esse inquietus, et non est hoc malum; tu noli agitare, et non est quae se agitate. Ñeque enim animus est, ut moveatur: corpus est enim, iacet: noli moveré, et non movetur. Vide autem quomodo [114] moves. Ipsa est illa, de qua multi fraudibus studentes, et avaritiae servientes, cum coeperint de negotiis aliquid agere, eiciunt membrum factum ad laudem Dei, et ibi blasphemant Deum, et dicunt: Per Christum! Tantum emi, tantum vendo. Quare? I asked you, Iura mihi, how much are you selling?

That's what I asked you, Oantum vendis? Decem folübus vendo, viginti follibus. Per Christum iu-as. Per oculos tuos iura, per fílios tuos iura, et ipsa hora contremescit conscientia. O itrreietas linguae! Creatorem contemnsisti. crea ture m custodisti. O inauietum malum, plena veneni mortiferüln ipsa benedicimus Deum et Patrem: sed Deum et Follis was a bronze coin of little value (two denarii).
Commentary on Psalm 38:13

With it we bless God and the Father; God by nature, Father by grace. And with it we curse man, who was made in the image of God. Realize, brothers, what you carry with you! And I am also a man with you. But let's continue. 4. Lord, hear my prayer! The Jews we read about in the Gospel were of that type. Their own language led them to death. We have just heard it in the Gospel. We are told that the Jews presented Jesus to a prostitute to tempt him, saying: Master, this woman was caught a moment ago in adultery. According to the law of Moses, any woman caught in adultery must be stoned to death. You, what do you say? The tongue spoke like this, but it did not know its Creator. Those Jews did not want to pray and say: free my soul from the lying tongue. They had approached Jesus in a malicious way, trying to carry out their purpose. The Lord had not come to repeal the law, but to fulfill it and forgive sins. The Jews said to each other: "If he says that she must be stoned, we will tell him: where is the one who forgives sins?" Are you not the one who says: Your sins are forgiven? And if he says: Let him be free, we will say: How is it that you came to fulfill the law and not to destroy it? Behold a lying tongue before God. Jesus, who had come as a redeemer, not as a condemner—he had come to redeem what had perished—turned away from them as if he did not want to see them. This distancing from them is not meaningless; something special is Patrem, Deum propter naturam, Patrem propter gratiam; et in ipsa maledicimus bominem, qui factus est ad imaginem Dei (Iac 3,8.9). Attendite, fratres, quid portetis: ecce dico, quid portemus; et ego enim vobiscum homo sum. Be recurramus. 4. Exaudi Deus orationem meam. Inde sunt illi Iudaei quos moda in gospel legimus: utique lingua illos perduxit ad mortem. Enim mode in gospel audimus. Adduxerunt, inquit, Iudaei quamdam mulierem, licet meretricem, ad Dominum, temptantes illum, et dicentes: Magister, haec mulier moda comprehensa est in adultery. In lege Moysi scriptum est, ut quaecumque fuerit in adultery comprehensa lapidetur: Tu quid dicis? (lo 8,3-5). Hoc lingua dicebat, sed creatorem non agnoscebat. Nolebant isti orare, utdicerent: Eripe animam meam a lingua dolosa (Ps 119,2). Dolóse enim accesserant: hoc enim volebant agere. Venerat enim Dominus, non legem solvere, sed implere (cf. Mt 5:17), et peccata dimitiere.

Dixerunt ergo apud se Iudaei: Si dixerit, Lapidetur, dicemus ei, Ubi est, quod peccata dimittis? Non tu es, qui say: Donata sunt tibi peccata tua? (cf. ibid., 9,2 etc.). Si dixerit, Dimittatur, dicemus, Ubi est, quod legem venisti adimplere, non solvere? Videte linguam dolosam ad Deum. lile, qui venerat Redemptor, non damnator—venerat enim redeemere, quod perierat—aversus est ala ipsis, quasi conspicere eos nolens. Non vacat aversio ista ab ipsis: intellegitur aliquid in hac aversione. Quasi says:

transparent in this action. As if to say: "You sinners brought me a sinner!" If you think that I must condemn sins, I will begin with yourselves. And he who came to forgive sins says: He who among you believes he is without sin, let him cast the first stone against her. Oh answer! If they had tried to throw the stone at the sinner, at that very moment they would have been told: With the judgment that you have judged you will also be judged. You condemn, then you will be condemned. The Jews, however, although they did not know the Creator, they knew their own conscience. Therefore, turning their backs on each other, since they were ashamed and did not even want to see themselves, they all left, starting with the oldest to the youngest, as we are told in the Gospel. The Holy Spirit had said: All have gone astray; There is no longer anyone who does good, there is not even one left. 5. They all left. Jesus and the sinner were left alone. The Creator remained with the creature; misery remained with mercy; remained the one who recognized his sin with the one who forgave it. This means writing on the earth. When man was created, he was told: You are earth. When Jesus offered forgiveness to the sinner, he wrote on the earth. He offered forgiveness; But when he offered it to her, he raised his face towards her and said: Did no one stone you? At this, she did not say: Why? What did I do, Lord? Am I a prisoner? The sinner did not speak in that way, but said: No one, Lord. It was accused, Peccatricem mihi adducitis, peccatores; si putatis quia damnare [115] debeno peccata, a vobis incipio. Et ipse, qui venerat donare peccata, ait: Qui se scit vestrum sine peccato esse, prior in illam lapidem mittot (lo 8,7). O responsio, vel propositio! Si mittere voluissent lapidem in peccatricem, ipsa hora iterum recitaretur: In quo indication iudicaveritis, iudicabitur de vobis (Mt 7,2). Damnastis, damnabimini. lili tamen, etsi creatorem non agnoscebant, conscientiam suam sciebant: exponents invicem faciem post faciem, ut nec ipsi se propter confusionem videre vellent, a senioribus—hoc dixit evangelista—usque ad minores (lo 8.9 sec. gr.) omnes egressi sunt. Dixerat cním Spiritus sanctus: Omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt; non est qui facial bonum, non est usque ad unum (Ps 13:3). 5. Et exiemnt omnes.

Remansit solus et sola: remansit Creator et creatura: remansit miseria, et mercy: remansit quae suum reatum agnoscebat, et qui peccatum dimittebat. Nam ipsum est, quod conversus scribit in terra. Scripsit enim in terra. Quando enim peccavit homo, dictum est ei, terra es (Gen 3:19). Peccatrici ergo cum daret indulgentiam, dans scribebat in terra. Indulgentiam ibat: sed, cum daret indulgentiam, erigens faciem suam ad illam, nemo, ait, te lapidavit? Et illa non dixit: Quare? Quid fecí, Domine? Numquid enim rea sum? Non hoc dixit, sed ait: Nemo, Domine (lo 8,10.11). Semetipsam accusavit. I will try illi non
Commentary on Psalm 38:13

Well, to herself. The Jews could not prove the crime; and they left. She confessed the sin that the Lord was not ignorant of; but the Lord, at the same time, sought faith and confession. Did no one stone you? —No one, Lord, she responded. He said no one because of the confession of sins; and he said Lord because of forgiveness. Nobody, sir. I know both: who you are and who I am. Before you I confess, since I heard: Confess the Lord because he is good. I recognized my guilt and I recognized your mercy. And he said: I will keep my ways so that my tongue will not be deceitful. The Jews sinned by acting with deceit, but the sinner freed herself by confessing. Did no one condemn you? —No one, and keep quiet. Jesus writes again. He wrote twice, as we are told: Once, when granting forgiveness; another, by renewing the precepts. Both things are done when we receive forgiveness. The emperor signed; and when this formality is renewed, other precepts are given again 3. These precepts are those that we have heard in the Apostle 4 commanding the observance of charity. We have heard that reading before. And the Lord himself says it: You will love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength; and you will love your neighbor as yourself. The entire law and the prophets are contained in these two precepts. 6. So that we would not have difficulty in understanding, only two things were proclaimed: God and our neighbor; he who potuerunt, subduxerunt se: sed illa confessa est, cuius Dominus non reatum nesciebat, sed eius fidem atque confessionem quaerebat. Nemo stoned you? At illa: Nemo, Domine. Et nemo propter confessionem peccatorum, et Domine propter indulgentiam meritorum. Nemo, Domine. Utrumque agnosco: qui sis novi, quae sim novi. Tibi enim confiteor: audi enim, confitemini Domino, quoniam bonus est (Ps 117,1). Novi confessionem meam, novi misericordiam tuam. Ista said: Custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea (Ps 38,2). lili deliquerunt dolóse agendo; ista magis se absolvit confitendo. Nemo stoned you? Et illa, nemo, et tacet. lile iterum scribit. Bis scripsit, [116] hoc audivimus, bis scripsit: semel indulgentiam daring, iterum praecepta renewing. Utrumque enim fit, cum indulgentiam accipimus. Subscripsit imperator: cum iterum forma procedit, quasi iterum alia praecepta dantur. Ipsa sunt, per quae primo in apostólo audivimus caritatem illam inperatam (cf. Iac 2).

Primo enim ipsam lectionem audimus; inde hoc ipse Dominus dixit: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum de toto corde tuo, et de tota anima tua, et de tota virtute tua; et diliges proximum tibi tanquam te ipsum. In his duobus praeceptis tota Lex pendet, et Prophetae (Mt 22,37.39.40). 6. Ne aliquis nostrum laboraret, duo quaedam sunt dicta: Deus et It refers to the fact that the emperor signed the laws. In this way, normally, the fact that one began to write meant the birth of a new law. It refers to the apostle James, from whose letter the second chapter had been read. See number 11 of this same sermon.

He made you and with whom he made you. No one has told you: "Love the sun, love the moon, love the earth and everything that has been made." In all these things God is to be praised, the Creator is to be blessed. How great are your works; You did all things wisely! They are yours; you have done them. Thanks be given to you! But above all things you made us. Thanks too! We are your image and your likeness. Thank you! We have sinned and were sought by you. Thank you! We have abandoned you, but you did not abandon us. So that we would not forget your divinity and lose you, you took our humanity. Thanks be given to you! When should we not thank you? Therefore I said: I will guard my ways so that I do not fall with my tongue. That woman, presented to Jesus as an adulteress, accepted forgiveness and was absolved. Will it be difficult for us to receive forgiveness of all our sins through baptism, through confession and through grace? But let no one say now: «That woman received forgiveness. I am still a catechumen. I will commit adulteries 5, since I will also receive forgiveness. Imagine that I am like that woman. She acknowledged her sin and was absolved. Our God is good. If I sin, I will confess it to him and he will forgive me. You are very attentive to his goodness, but you must always keep in mind his justice; since, just as he is good at forgiving,

proximus; qui te fecit, et cum quo te fecit. Nemo tibi dixit: Dilige solem, dilige lunam, dilige terram, et quaecumque facta sunt. In his laudandus est Deus, benedicendus est factor. Quam magnificata sunt opera tua! Dicimus, omnia in sapientia fecisti (Ps 103,24). Tua sunt, tu fecisti omnia: gratias tibi. Sed us fecisti super omnia: gratias tibi. Sumus enim image and similarity of yours: gratias tibi. Peccavimus, quaesiti sumus: gratias tibi. Negleximus, non sumus neglecti: gratias tibi. Cum nos te contemneremus, non sumus contempti; ne divinitatem tuam obliti Fuissemus, et te amitteremus, tu etiam nostram humanitatem suscepisti: gratias tibi. Ubi non gratias? Dixi ergo, custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Illa enim mulier, cum offerretur causa adulterii, accepit indulgentiam, liberata est: onerosum nobis est, quoniam per baptismum, per confessionem, per gratiam accipiunt omnes omnium peccatorum suorum indulgentiam? Sed nemo nunc dicat: Illa accepit indulgentiam; ego adhuc catechumenus sum: faciam adultery, quoniam accepturus sum indulgentiam. Pone et me unum esse, quemadmodum illa mulier: confessa est, et liberata est. Deus noster bonus est: et si peccavero, confiteor illi, et dimittet mihi. Bonitatem ipsius attendis, sed iustitiam eius considera: quomodo This way of reasoning must have been quite common. It is enough to remember the text of the Confessions (I 11,18): «Where does it come from now that from one and another reaches our ears from all sides: 'Let him; let it work; who is not yet baptized'; However, let's not say about the health of the body; 'Let him receive even more wounds, since he is not yet healthy?'
Commentary on Psalm 38:13

He is also just in condemning. Therefore I said: I will guard my ways so that I do not fall with my tongue. I would like to know if now, while I am preaching, no one has sinned with his tongue. Possibly, in the time we have been here, none of you has spoken evil; but perhaps someone has thought wrong. Stay tuned! I will guard my ways so that I do not fall with my tongue. Say truly: I put a lock on my mouth when the sinner came against me. 7. Pay attention! I put a lock on my mouth when the sinner came against me. An evil man comes to you, insults you, and says against you what you have not done. You put a lock in your mouth. I said, I will keep my ways so that my tongue will not be deceitful. Let him speak; you listen and be silent. Two things can happen: he tells the truth or he tells a lie. If it says true, you did what it says; and perhaps it is even an act of mercy. In the event that you do not want to hear what you did, God, who cares for you, tells you through another what you did, so that you resort to medicine6, confused by modesty. Do not return evil for evil; You don't know who it is that speaks to you through him. But if he tells you something you did, recognize that you have obtained God's mercy; You must think that it was told to you, either because you forgot, or for your confession. If you didn't: your conscience is free. Why are you disturbed? Why are you angry about what you haven't done? What happens if he says to you: "Thief, drunk"? Enter immediately into the secret bonitotem ad indulgentiam, sic iustitiam ad poenam. Dixi ergo: Custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Vellem scire, si in hoc tempore, quo sermonem vestrae caritati ministramus, nemo delinquat in lingua sua. In hoc tempore, quo hic sumus, forte nemo nostrum aliquid locutus est mali, sed forte cogitavit aliquid mali. Attendite. Dixi, [117] custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Dec I will see: Posui orí meo custodiam, dum consistit peccator adversus me (Ps 38,2). 7. Pay attention. Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consistit peccator adversus me. Stat adversus te aliquis inprobus, conviciatur tibi, dicit quae nescis; you put ori tuo custodiam. Dixi, custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Dicat ille: tu audi, et tace. Duae enim res sunt: ​​aut verum dicit, aut falsum.

Si verum dicit, tu fecisti ut diceret, et forte hoc misericordia est: cum enim tu non vis audire quod fecisti, Deus, qui curam tui gerit, per aliquem tibi dicit quod fecisti, ut vel ipso gordo confusus aliquando ad medicinalm recurras. Noli ergo rependere malum pro malo; nescis enim qui tibi per ipsum loquatur. Ergo, si aliquid dicit quod fecisti, agnosce te misericordiam consecutum, ut aut oblitum te putes, aut ad confusionem tuam hoc dictum esse iudices; If you do not fecisti, release this consciousness. Quid quaeris? quid irasceris de eo quod non fecisti? In sermon 20:2 he will specify more, speaking of the medicine confessionis, that is, recognizing oneself as sinners.
Commentary on Psalm 38:13

of your conscience, contemplate yourself, be your own judge, be your own examiner 7. Search there. “Where do you think I have put the sins I did?” If they are not there, answer: "I did not commit them." If your conscience tells you that you did not commit them, then say: Our glory lies in the testimony of our conscience. Did your conscience tell you this? Be silent and pity the one who spoke; and then say to God: "Father, forgive him because he does not know what he says." Pray to God for him. I said, I will keep my ways so that I do not sin with my tongue. You put a lock on my mouth when the sinner came against me. Do not judge yourself as holy because no one tempts you. You will be when you are not disturbed by an injury, when you feel compassion for the one who insults you, when you do not worry about what you suffer, but instead take pity on the one for whom you suffer. There is full mercy. You feel sorry for him because he is your brother, because he is also your member. He is angry at you, he is sick, he is frenetic. Take pity on him, do not rejoice; Rejoice only in the peace of your conscience. He is only a man; and be careful not to see yourself equally tempted. It has been said: Bear each other's burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ. When he speaks now, you remain silent. Then, when he has calmed down8, say to him: «Brother! For your sake, why did you blame me for what I did not do? You sinned against me, but I pray to God for you. I offer you forgiveness and I pray for you to God, whom you insulted when Quid enim aít tibi: Fur? Did he get drunk? I quote you recurre intus ad secreta conscientiae: vide te intus: iudex this, discussor tui this. Quaere ibi: Ubi putas posui peccata mea, quae feci? Aut, si non sunt, dic: Non feci. Yes, Non feci, dicit tibi conscientia tua, dic, gloria nostra haec est, testimonium conscientiae nostrae (2 Cor 1:12). Dixit tibi haec conscientia tua; tace, dolé illum dicentem tibi. Dic etiam tu Deo: Pater, ignosce illi, quia nescit quid dicat. Roga pro illo Deum. Dixi, guard» vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consistit peccator adversus me. Noli enim putare, quia tune videris sanctus, si nemo te temptet: tune es sanctus, quando aliquo convicio non moveis, quando doles dicentem, quando non curas quod pateris, sed tamen doles eum, a quo pateris. Ibi est omnis mercy: doles, quoniam et ille frater tuus est, membrum tuum est.

Insanit adversum te, phreneticus est, aegrotat: dolé illum, noli gaudere; tantummodo de conscientiae tuae securitate gaude: inde dolé. Homo is enim: vide ne et tu tempteris (cf. Gal 6,1). Dictum est enim: Onera vestra pórtate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi (ib., 2). Mode, cum dicit, tace; post quam quieverit, dic ei: Frater, per salutem tuam, quare mihi dixisti quod non feci? Peccastiin me, I pray Deum pro te. Ego tibi quidem veniam do, et rogo pro te Deum See note
complementary 38: Augustinian interiority, p.757. Indicates what is the most opportune time to make fraternal correction. See complementary note 13: Fraternal correction, p.747.

you sinned against me. Don't do it again. "Do not be arrogant." I don't mean: may God punish him for what he said against me and that I didn't do. I refuse to say it, since I put a lock on my mouth when the sinner came against me. 8. I was deafened and humiliated - the psalm continues - and I kept silent about good things. I became deaf, I didn't hear him speak. How much progress has this Christian who, internally rejoicing in his brother's error and in the tranquility of his own conscience, seems to ignore what is murmured outside! What a good Christian he is, how secure he is, how happy he is! This is the Christian soul that says to God: I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the middle of your house. The destroyers were knocking at the door, but the house is safe. I was deafened and humiliated, I did not rise proud against him. And, humiliated, I kept quiet about good things, since it was not time to make them public. Now is the time to be silent; When he has become aware of himself, talk to him and he will understand you. Sick children frequently hit their parents; and parents, because of their children's illness, lament and cry. What affection men show to their children in the hope that they do not die and are cured! But you say: "He is not my son." It is the work of God, image of God, son of God. If you despise him because he is not your son, you do not despise him because he is a son of God, your brother. «Then I remained silent and was humiliated. I did not become arrogant, but I kept silent about good things and my pain was renewed, not for me, but for him, because I did not do what he said. I felt pain because he spoke this way. I had pain, since, meum, cui fecisti iniuriam, cum in me peccasti. Noli ulterius faceré, noli superbire. Non dico: [118] Redde illi, Deus, qui dixit mihi quod non feci; nolo hoc will say. Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consistit peccator adversus me. 8. Obsurdui, et humiliatus sum—hoc sequitur—et tacui a bonis (Ps 38,3). Obsurdui: non illum audivi dicentem. Iste animus quantum profecit, qui etiam intus in fratris errore et conscientiae suae securitate gaudens, quod foris latretur nescit! Qualis ista anima est, quam secura, quam gaudens! Ista est, quae dicit Deo: Ambulabam in innocentia coráis meí, in medio domus tuae (Ps 100,2). Fores effractors pulsabant, sed ideal erat domus. Obsurdui et humiliatus sum; non adversus illum superbus extisi. Et humiliatus silui a bonis; nec enim temporis erat, ut aliquid boní dixissem. Tempus est enim ut taceas moda: posteaquam ille sinceraverit, loquere, tune intelleget.

Plerumque filii aegrotantes paires suos caeciderunt; tamen illi propter infirmitatem filiorum et vapulabant, et plorabant. Quem affectum adhibent filiis nomines, ne moriantur, expectantes salutem filiorum! Sed non est filius meus, ais. Sed est opus Dei, filius Dei; si contemnis, quia non est filius tuus, noli contemnere, quia filius Dei est, frater tuus est. Ergo obsurdui, et humiliatus sum. Non superbivi, sed silui a bonis, et dolor meus renovatus est, non de me, sed de ipso, quia non feci quod dixit. Habui dolorem, sed quia ita dixit;
Commentary on Psalm 38:13

worrying about my brother, the pain was renewed in me. This is the way. This is what the Lord our Father did, who was also called husband. The husband's children shall not fast while the husband is with them. He was scourged by unscrupulous sons; unscrupulous sons killed him. And he prayed for them. I was humiliated, and in reflection the fire was kindled; and suddenly, without knowing why, something striking appears here, since after so many battles and so much work he says: I spoke with my tongue. The language of the soul is the movement of its own will. Just as speech is a movement of the body, will is a movement of the soul. There is the first word; From there we speak to God. The body language exercises its function externally with men; The other language, which is in the movement of the will, exercises its function internally, remaining in its sanctuary. This is the true language. Therefore the Lord said: Those who worship Him must worship in spirit and in truth. This is the true language. I said with my tongue: Make me, Lord, know my end and what is the number of my days, to know what remains to me. If your holiness has been attentive, first of all you will understand the sentence, and in this way it will be granted to us by the Lord, whose mercy never fails, to examine it and decide.

that works for love. Make me, Lord, know my end and dual is the number of my days. The number of our days is never stated, since, if each of us knew when we were going to die, we might decide to live a good life. Hence the Master himself, wanting to make us solicitous, once he was asked about the day and the hour, answered: No one knows the day or the hour. I didn't want them to know. That is why he said: • Not even the Son himself, that is to say: it is not convenient for you to know 10, since you would be negligent and lazy. The better you will live the more caring you are! It is not that I do not know the day, since all the things that the Father has are mine. Make me, Lord, know my end and what is the number of my days. Make this known to me so that I may always be solicitous, since I do not know when the thief will come, and so that I may always be aware of what I lack. 12. Brothers, let us be cautious to know what we lack. The temptation of Christians is their test, since he who is tempted realizes what he lacks. Two things are present: what he has and what he lacks.

He did not hesitate for a moment. He believed, he accepted; He deserved it and received it. The child was born, was raised, fed, grew. The Christian people who say in the plural: Our Father, are the same people who say: I said, Lord, have mercy on me, for I have sinned against you. Many would like to sin without attributing their own sins. See, your holiness, how proud men refuse to praise God. They do not want to take credit for the bad things they do and apologize saying that it was due to the influence of luck or fate. Some say, "The devil did it," instead of saying, "I did it." Therefore, let him who tries to apologize in this way remove all this from his world, since luck is a human chimera and fate is a hollow entity. 1. We have just sung: God will come manifestly, our God, and will not be silent. The Holy Scripture prophesied that Christ God will come to judge the living and the dead. When he came the first time to be judged, he appeared secretly; When he comes to judge, he will appear manifestly. That the first time he appeared hidden is deduced from what the Apostle says: If they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. When asked, he remained silent. And in this way the Gospel is expressed so that Isaiah's prophecy would be fulfilled: He was led to immolation like a sheep; and like a lamb before the shearer, without bleating; and he did not open his mouth. But it will come in a manifest way and will not be silent. He did not speak, because, upon being condemned, he remained silent. But when it comes to speaking to us when necessary, when did he remain silent? He was not silent through the patriarchs, he was not silent through the prophets, he was not silent through his carnal mouth. And if he were silent now, would he not speak through Scripture? The reader goes up to the platform, but Christ does not remain silent. The speaker expounds and, if he expounds well, he is Christ

Glass, although fragile, lasts a long time if treated with care; and in this way you find glasses of grandparents and great-grandparents from which the grandchildren and great-grandchildren still drink. So much cared for fragility has become old. We, on the other hand, are men and are exposed to innumerable daily dangers. And even if sudden death does not come to us, the truth is that we cannot live for a long time. All human life is short. It is short from childhood to old age. Even if Adam were still alive and had to die today, what would he have gained by having lived so long? To all this you must add that the present day itself, although bustling by nature, is uncertain due to a kind of radical illness. Men die every day. The living take them to bury them, celebrate their funerals and promise themselves a long life. No one says: "I will correct myself, lest tomorrow I be like this one whom I accompanied to the cemetery." You like words, but I look for facts. Do not sadden me with your perverse customs, since my delight in the present life is none other than your worthy life.

1. Welcome with pleasure the few words that, to move the minds of your charity, the Lord wants to suggest to me about this psalm. In this psalm, in which we have sung: God, our God, will come manifestly and will not keep silent, is prophesied about our Lord Jesus Christ. Our Lord Jesus Christ, our God, Son of God, came in a hidden way at his first coming, but he will come manifestly at his second coming. When he came in secret, he only made himself known to his servants; but when it comes in a manifest way it will appear before the good and the bad. When he came secretly, he came to be judged; when he comes manifestly, he will come to judge. When he was judged, he remained silent; and about this silence the prophet prophesied: He was led like a sheep to sacrifice; and like a lamb before the shearer he did not open his mouth. But God, our God, will come manifestly and will not be silent. When he comes to judge he will not be silent, just as he was silent when he came to be judged. In reality he is not silent now either, if there is someone who wants to listen; but it was said: then

ees will not be silent, since her voice will be recognized even by those who now despise her. At the present time, when the commandments of God are proclaimed, some laugh at it. Since God's promises are not now made manifest nor his threats are yet palpable, his commands are taken as a mockery. At the present moment, even bad men themselves enjoy the happiness of the world; while the good patiently endure the misfortunes of the world. Those men who believe only in present things and not in future things must be attentive, since the good and evil of the present century are shared by the good and the bad alike. If you desire wealth, you will see that both good and wicked men have it. If you are horrified by poverty, you should know that such misery is suffered not only by the good, but also by the bad. And they come to say within themselves that God does not care about human things nor govern them'; but, on the contrary, he simply let us move according to the whims of this deep corner of the world, without making his providence present to us. And this is the reason why contempt for what is commanded originates in them, since they do not see any sign of judgment. 2. Despite everything, man must now keep in mind that God sees and judges when he wants; and that he does not leave it for later, although, when he wants, he defers it. And why this? audit: sed dictum est: Tune non silebit, quando vocem eius agnoscent et qui moda contemnunt. Commentary on Psalm 49:3

Because if you never judge today, you would come to think that God does not exist; and if he judged everything now, he would reserve nothing for the day of judgment. Many things are reserved for the final judgment and some are judged in the present time, so that those for whom the judgment is deferred may fear and be converted. God's will is not to condemn, but to save, and that is why he is patient with the bad, to make them good. The Apostle says: The wrath of God will be revealed against all ungodliness, and God will give to each one according to his works. Admonish and correct the disdainful man saying: Do you perhaps despise the riches of God's goodness and generosity? Because he is good to you, because he is generous and patient, because he puts up with you and doesn't get you out of the way, you despise him and think that there will be no judgment from God at all. You ignore that God's patience provokes you to penitence. Because of the hardness of your heart you accumulate wrath for the day of wrath and the manifestation of the righteous judgment of God, which he will give to each one according to his works. 3. Everything that man now does he locks up in a treasure, but he does not know what he accumulates. This man acts like the rich who accumulate treasures on earth: they know well what they accumulate, but they do not know for whom they accumulate it. They are completely unaware of who will possess these riches after their death; and sometimes, those same riches end up in the hands of their enemies. Therefore, he who does not want to eat to get rich deceives himself, and another will enjoy his sweat in a lustful and disorderly manner. But just as some ammon-

They accumulate wealth knowing what they accumulate and not knowing for whom they accumulate it, on the contrary, the good know well what and for whom they accumulate in the heavenly treasure. The wicked do not know for whom they hoard. But the good man places in the heavenly treasure all those works of mercy that he did for the benefit of men; and he also knows that the guardian who guards what he deposited there is faithful. And although he does not see it, he is sure of his treasure, because the thief cannot steal there, nor does any stranger penetrate, nor will it be taken by a powerful and heartless enemy; It will remain there forever, because the omnipotent Lord guards it. If men place their goods in the hands of a faithful steward and feel secure, should they be restless when they place their good works in the hands of the almighty Lord? Good men knew perfectly well that whatever they deposited there was safe. Those who are faithful always trust in the power of their Lord. They trust him because he preserves the treasure and they find what he preserves. Are men who hoard money continually seeing the ark or the money in the ark? They pile it up and keep it, or bury it and hide it. Therefore, they do not see it, but they are very sure that it is where they placed it; although possibly the thief has already stolen it and those who hid it rejoice in vain. But, if we place our riches in the heavenly treasury, we are well assured of the custody of our Lord and we do not suffer from any thief nor do we fear any harm. Bad men also put all their bad works in the treasury, and God keeps them for them.

Hoc? Quia si numquam in praesenti iudicaret, non esse Deus crederetur: si omnia praesenti iudicaret, nihil iudicio reservaet. Ad hoc enim fines servantur iudicio, et quaedam in praesentia iudicantur, ut illi qui differuntur, timeant et convertantur. Non enim amat Deus damnare, sed salvare: et ideo patiens est in malas, ut de malis faciat bonds. Sed dicit Apostolus, quia revelabitur ira Dei super omnem impietatem (Rom 1:18), et reddet Deus unicuique secundum opera sua. Admonet autem et corripit hominem contemnentem; et dicit: An divitias bonitotis et longanimitatis eius contemnis? Quia bonus est in te, quia longanimis est in te, quia patiens est in te, quia differt te et non aufert te, contemnis, et omnino nullum iudicium Dei putas: Ignorans quia patientia Dei ad paenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem secundum duritiam cordis tui thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis iusti iudicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua (Rom 2:4-6). 3. Thesaurus operum, seu bonorum, seu malorum.—Quidquid ergo homo facit moda, in thesaurum mittit, sed nescit quid colligat: quomodo divites, qui in thesaurum terrae mittunt, quasi sciunt quid colligunt, sed nesciunt cui colligunt. Quis enim possideat divitias eorum post mortem ipsorum, prorsus ignorant: et aliquando divitiae eorum ad inimicos eorum perveniunt. Et ideo se quisque fraudat nolens man[130]ducare, ut ditescat, ut alius de laboribus eius fluat et luxurietur et dissolvatur.

CAPOT III.—3. Quomodo ergo colligunt quidem scientes, sed cui colligant, nesciunt: sic contra in thesaurum caelestem boni quid colligant sciunt, mali quid colligant, nesciunt. Bonus enim ponit in thesauro caelesti omnia opera misericordiae, quae fecit circa nomines quibus subvenit; et scit quoniam fidelis est custos, qui illi servat omnia quae reponit. Et non ea videt, sed de thesauro suo certus est, quia ñeque aliquid a fure subripitur, ñeque ab hoste invaditur, ñeque ab inimico et improbo et potent quasi e victo tollitur; sed semper manebit, quia a Domino potentissimo custoditur. Si enim pecunias homines fideli servo commendant, et securi sunt; Misericordias suas commendant potenti Domino, et solliciti sunt? Noverunt ergo quia quidquid reponunt, totum ibi salvum est: qui fideles sunt, potentiae Domini sui fidem iungunt. Credunt enim quia servat, et inveniunt quod servat. Nam et homines qui pecuniam colligunt, numquid vident arcam ipsam, aut in arcam pecuniam semper colligunt et mittunt, aut infodiunt et servant? He will also show them his own treasures there: I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was naked and you clothed me, I was a pilgrim and you welcomed me, I was imprisoned and you came to me, I was sick and you visited me. And they will answer him: Lord, when did we see you in such needs and help you? And he will say: When you did it to my little brothers, you did it to me. And since you did so: receive what you treasured, possess what you bought. You trusted me as a faithful custodian. He will then turn to those on the left and show them his tanks empty of any work mittunt in thesaurum omnia mala opera sua, et servat illis Deus. Hoc est quod Apostolus said: Thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae iusti iudicii Dei. CAPUT IV.—4. Suus quemque manet thesaurus pauperes divitibus laturarii.—Sed quoniam servatur quidquid mali fachant, et nesciunt: ubi venerit Deus noster manifestus, et non silebit, summona ad se omnes gentes, sicut dicit in Gospel, et separabit, quosdam pones ad dexteram, quosdam ad sinistram: et incipiet iam tractare thesauros utrorumque, quid quisque posit ut inveniat. Come, inquit, benedicti Patris mei, ad eos qui sunt ad dexteram, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab initio mundi. Regnum caelorum, regnum sempiternum, societatem cum Angelis, aeternam vitam, ubi nullus oritur, ñeque moritur, hoc percipite. Quando enim opera vestra in thesaurum mittebatis, regnum caelorum emebatis. Percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab initio mundi.

Etiam otendit illis thesauros suos: Esurivi, et dedistis mihi manducare; sitivi, et potastis me; nudus fue, et vestistis me; hospes fue, et adduxistis me; I went in prison, et venistis ad me; aeger I went, et visitatis me. Et respondert illi: Domine, quando te vidimus in bis necessitatibus constitutum, et ministravimus tibi? Et ille: Quando uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Quia ergo quando uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis, percipite quod misistis, possidete quod emistis. Mihi enim Servatori ideo credidistis. Deinde convertet se ad illos qui sunt a sinistris, et ostendet illis

good; and he will say to them: Go into the eternal fire that is prepared for the devil and his angels. I was hungry and you didn't give me food. If you put or locked something in the warehouse, think a little and it will be returned to you. They will tell him: we never saw you hungry. And he will answer: When you did not do it to my little brothers, you did not do it to me either. Maybe you didn't do that with me because you didn't see me walking on the earth. You are so evil that, if you had seen me, you would have crucified me like the Jews. Even today, those evil men who try - as much as they can - to destroy the divine precepts, those who try - as much as they can - to make the churches where such precepts are preached disappear, would they not kill Christ himself if they found him living on this earth? And they will still dare to say, as if the Lord were ignorant of man's thoughts: Lord, when did we see you hungry? It will be answered: If you did not do it to my little brothers, you did not do it to me either. I had put my needy little ones on earth. He will say: “I, as the Head, was seated in heaven at the right hand of the Father, but my members suffered on earth, my members had needs on earth. What you would have given to my members would have reached the Head. And you would have realized that, when I placed my needy little ones on earth, I made them bearers for you to carry your good works to my treasure. And you put nothing in his hands, and that is why you found nothing in me.

CAPUT V.—5. Paenitentia infructuosa.—Tune ergo non silebit, sed apparebit: ideo dictum est: Non silebit. Mode autem dicit illud Codex reader, et contemnitur: dicit illud de ore suo tractator aut disputator episcopus, et irridetur. Numquid sic itrideri habet, quando ab ipso iudke potentissimo dicetur? [132] DE EO QUOD SCRIPTUM EST IN PSALMO 50,5: «QUONIAM INIQUITATEM MEAM EGO AGNOSCO»: ET IN PSALMO 72, 1: «QUAM BONUS DEUS ISRAEL RECTIS CORDE!»

1. Rogandus Deus, ut faciem non a nobis avertat, sed a peccatis nostris.—Singers Dominum rogavimus, ut avertat faciem suam a peccatis nostris, et omnia facinora nostra deleat. Sed animadvertere potestis, fratres, quod in eodem psalmo audierimus, Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego Day of the amphitheater games. See supplementary note 25: Public shows, p.753. The Restituía or Perpetua Restituía basilica was the largest in Carthage, in which the remains of Saints Perpetua and Felicidad were buried. This is probably where the second name by which she is known comes from. The name Restituta, on the other hand, refers to the restitution to the Catholic Church, after having been the patrimony of the Donatist Church. See the ad boc note of ML 38,132. Facinus, iniquity, has a precise meaning in Augustine. In this regard, it is worth transcribing a text from The Christian Doctrine: «The act, committed by an indomitable greed (cupiditate), to corrupt the soul and its body, is called flagitium, clumsiness, and the act committed to harm one's neighbor is called facinus, iniquity. These are the two generative causes of all evils: but the clumsiness comes before. Indeed, when they have exhausted the soul and have reduced it to a certain degree of indigence, it launches itself into iniquities to remove the obstacles that oppose clumsiness, or seeks
auxiliaries to these" (III 10,16),

from me, to the same God to whom shortly before we said: Turn your face from my sins. The man and the sinner being one person, the man says: Do not turn your face away from me; The sinner says: Turn your face from my sins. What is said is this: do not turn your face away from him whom you created, and turn your face away from that which I made. Let your eye distinguish both things so that nature does not perish because of vice. You did something, and I did something too. What you made is called nature; What I did is called vice. Let the vice be corrected so that nature is saved 4. 2. I recognize my crime. If I recognize it, you forgive it. Let us live with dignity, but even if we live with dignity, let us not presume to be sinless. Let us praise in life and at the same time ask for forgiveness. Men without hope, the less they make an effort to recognize their sins, the more curious they are about the sins of others. Look not so much for a way to correct but for a way to criticize others; and as they cannot excuse themselves, they are always ready to accuse others. This was not the example of the psalmist: For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. The psalmist was not very attentive to the sins of others. He concentrated on himself; He was not conceited, but penetrated deep inside him and reached the depths of his heart. He did not forgive himself, and therefore he could be forgiven with all humility. Brothers, sin cannot go unpunished,

since, if it remained unpunished, it would be a clear injustice. Then without a doubt he must be punished. This is what your God tells you: "Sin must be punished either by you or by me." Sin is punished, either by the penitent man or by God the judge; either for you without you, or for God with you. What, then, is penitence, but indignation against oneself? He who repents becomes angry with himself. Where do chest-beating come from when it is not done falsely? Why hurt yourself if you don't repent? When you beat your chest, you repent in your heart to satisfy your Lord. In this way we can understand what is written: Be angry and do not sin. Be angry because you sinned, and by punishing yourself, sin no more. Awaken your heart with penitence, and this will be a sacrifice before God. 3. Do you want to appease God? Know what you have to do with yourself so that God pleases you. Look at the psalm; there it reads: Because if you had wanted a sacrifice, I would have given it to you; but you shall not delight in burnt offerings. Must you be without some sacrifice? Should you not offer anything to God, should you not appease him? What did you say? If you had wanted a sacrifice, I would have given it to you; but you shall not delight in burnt offerings. Continue reading, listen and say: Sacrifice for God is a contrite spirit. God does not despise a contrite and humiliated heart. Having discarded the things you offered, you have found what you must offer. You offered, in the style of the patriarchs, victims of animals.

agnosco, et peccatum meum ante me est semper. Dicitur autem Deo alibi, Ne avertas faciem tuam a me (Ps 26,9): cui diximus, Averte faciem tuam a peccatis meis. Cum sit ergo persona una homo et peccator, homo dicit, Ne avertas faciem tuam a me: peccator dicit, Averte faciem tuam a pecca tis meis. Hoc ergo dicitur: Ne avertas faciem tuam ab eo quem fecisti; averte faciem tuam ab eo quod feci. Oculus tuus, inquit, utrumque distinguat, ne propter vitium natura dispereat. Fecisti tu aliquid, feci et ego aliquid: quod tu fecisti, natura dicitur; quod ego feci, vitium vocatur: vitium sanetur, ut natura servetur. 2. Paenitentis est peccata propria et agnoscere et puniré.—Facinus, inquit, meum ego agnosco. Si ego agnosco, ergo tu ignosce. Bene vivamus, et bene viventes sine peccato nos esse minime praesumamus: sic vita laudetur, ut venia postuletur. Desperati autem homines, quanto minus intenti sunt in peccata sua, mucho curiosiores sunt in aliena. Quaerunt enim non quid corrigant, sed quid mordeant: et cum se non possint excusare, parati sunt alios accusare. Non sic iste nobis orandi et satis Deo faciendi demonstravit exemplum, they say: Quoniam facinus meum ego agnosco, et peccatum meum ante me est semper. Non [133] erat iste intentus in aliena peccata: advocabat se ad se; nec se palpabat, sed penetrabat, et in se ipsum altius descendebat. Sibi non parcebat: et ideo

ut sibi parceretur non impudenter rogabat. Peccatum enim, fratres, impunitum esse non potest: si peccatum impunitum remaneat, iniustum est: ergo sine dubitatione puniendum. Hoc tibi dicit Deus tuus: Puniendum est peccatum aut a te, aut a me. Punitur ergo peccatum, aut ab nomine paenitente, aut a Deo iudicante. Punitur ergo aut a te sine te, aut a Deo tecum. Quid est enim paenitentia, nisi sua in se ipsum iracundia? Qui paenitet, irascitur sibi. Nam si non ficte fiat, unde est et pectoris tunsio? Quid feris, si non irasceris? Quando ergo tundis pectus, irasceris cordi tuo, ut satisfy Domino tuo. Potest enim etiam sic intellegi quod scriptum est, Irascimini, et nolite peccare (Ps 4,5). Irascere quia peccasti, et puniens te ipsum noli peccare. Exsuscita cor paenitendo, et hoc erit sacrificium Deo. 3. Sacrifice contriti coráis placandus Deus. Vides antiquorum in Christum.—Placari Deo vis? Nosce quid agas tecum, ut Deus placetur tibi. In eodem psalmo warns: ibi enim legitur, Quoniam si voluisses sacrificium, dedisssem utique; holocaustis non delectaberis. Ergo sine sacrifice eris? nihil oblaturus, from nulla oblatione Deum plaqueturus? What did you say? Si voluisses sacrificium, dedissem utique; holocaustis non delectaberis. Sequere, et audi, et dic, Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus; cor contritutn et humiliatum Deus non spernit (Ps 50,5.11.18.19). Abiectis quae offerebas, invenisti quod offeras. Offerebas enim apud Patres victimas pecomm, et sacrificia vocabantur. Si voluisses sacrificium, dedissem utique.

them, which were called sacrifices. If you had wanted a sacrifice, I would certainly have given it to you. Therefore you do not seek those sacrifices and yet you seek a sacrifice. Your people say to you: what shall I offer? Why shouldn't I offer what I offered? This town is the same town, some are born and others die. The signs have changed, but not the faith 5. The signs with which something special was symbolized have changed, but what was meant has not changed. The ram, the calf, the goat, all of these meant Christ. The ram because it leads the flock: it was found among the brambles when the patriarch Abraham received the order to forgive his son; However, Abraham did not depart from there without having offered a sacrifice. Isaac also symbolized Christ, like the ram. Isaac carried the wood for the sacrifice: Christ carried his own cross. The ram was sacrificed in Isaac's place, but Christ was not replaced by another Christ. But Christ was symbolized in both Isaac and the ram. The ram was fastened by its horns to the bush; Ask the Jews what they crowned the Lord with. Christ is also a lamb, since it was said: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. There is also symbolism with the calf because of the sticks of the cross. And he is also a goat, by virtue of his resemblance to sinful flesh. All these things were veiled until the day dawned and the shadows disappeared. The ancient patriarchs believed in that Christ the Lord not only as the Word, but also as the mediator of

God and of men, the man Christ-Jesus; and they transmitted that same faith to us by preaching and prophesying. That is why the Apostle says: Having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: I believed and therefore I spoke. That same spirit that those who wrote had: I believed, therefore I spoke. We, having that same spirit of the ancients, also say: And we believe, and that is why we speak. When holy David said: If you had wanted a sacrifice, I would have given it to you; but you will not delight in burnt offerings, sacrifices were offered to God that are not offered to him now. Hence when he sang this psalm he prophesied, rejected those sacrifices and preannounced the gifts. Thou shalt not delight in holocausts, he said. If you will not delight in burnt offerings, will you remain without sacrifices? By no means. Sacrifice for God is a contrite spirit. God does not despise a contrite and humiliated heart. You already have something to offer. Do not look out for your flocks or prepare ships to go to distant nations in search of aromas. Search within your heart for that which is pleasing to God 6. Make yourself a contrite heart. Do you fear that a contrite heart will perish? The psalm says: O God, create in me a pure heart. In order for God to create a pure heart, the impure heart must be destroyed. 4. Let us be dissatisfied with ourselves when we sin, since God does not like sins. But since we cannot be without sin, let us at least be like God by feeling displeasure for that which displeases Him. Of

You somehow adhere to the will of God if you dislike what the one who created you hates. God is your maker; Look at yourself and destroy in yourself what did not come out of his hands. God created the upright man, as it is written. How good is the God of Israel to those who have a pure heart! If, then, you are upright in heart, God will not displease you, since He will always be good to you and you will praise Him. You must praise him in everything: when he gives you gifts and when he punishes you. He who said: How good is the God of Israel to those who have a pure heart!, had examined himself, coming to the conclusion that at some time he was not of a pure heart and that God displeased him. Some time later he realized that God was not wicked and he understood that he was the wicked one. Remembering the past times of his wickedness, and being conscious of his present correction, he says: How good is the God of Israel! But for whom? For those who have a pure heart. And you, what do you say? My feet almost staggered, but my steps did not slip, that is, I almost fell. And why? Because I was envious of sinners when I contemplated their peace. This is why his feet staggered and his steps slipped. He waited from God, ignoring that the promises of the Old Testament were signs for the future; I hoped, I say, for the happiness of this life; and he sought in this life what God keeps for his people in heaven. I hoped to be happy here, when happiness is not found here. Happiness is certainly a great thing, but it has its own region. region of happiness came Christ; but not even he himself found happiness here. Christ was mocked, despised, imprisoned, whipped, bound, slapped, spit upon, crowned with thorns, nailed to the cross; and finally found the way out of death. It is written in the psalm—here those who knew Psalm 7 applauded—and of the Lord the coming out of death. What happiness do you seek there where the Lord himself found death? That man of whom I spoke shortly before sought happiness not in his own region, and, to achieve that happiness in this life, he adhered to God and tried to fulfill his precepts as much as he could; He realized that what he sought in God was possessed by those who did not serve God, but worshiped demons and blasphemed the true God. Realizing this, he began to tremble as if he had lost the fruit of his labor. This is what sinners envied as they beheld his peace. Finally it was said to you: Behold, sinners obtained abundant riches in the world. Did I purify my heart in vain or did I wash my hands among the innocent and be scourged all day? I worship God, they blaspheme him. For them it is happiness; For me, calamity. Where is the equity? 8 That is the reason for regione felicitatis Christus venit, et hic eam nec ipse invenit. Irrisus est, exprobratus est, apprehensus est, flagella[135]tus est, vinctus est, palmis caesus est, affectus contumelia sputorum, spinis coronatus est, ligno suspensus: ad extremum, Domini exitus mortis. In Psalmo scriptum est (hi acclamaverunt qui cognoverunt), Et Domini exitus mortis (Ps 67,21). Quid hic ergo, serve, felicitatem requiris, ubi et Domini exitus mortis? Cum ergo in regione non sua felicitatem requireret ille, de quo loqui coeperam, et propter illam in hac vita adipiscendam cohiberet Deo, eique serveret, et eius praecepta, ut poterat, faceret; vidit noc magnum, vel pro magno, quod quaerebat a Deo, et propter quod Deo serviebat, esse apud eos qui Deo non serviebant, sed daemonia colebant, et verum Deum blasphemabant. Vidit, et commotus est, quasi perdidisset fructum laboris sui. Hoc est quod zelavit in peccatoribus, pacem peccatorum intuens. Denique habes ibi, Ecce ipsi peccatores et abundants in saeculo obtinuerunt divitias. Numquid sine causa iustificavi cor meum, aut lavi inter innocentes manus meas, et fue flagellatus tota die?
