Observe what danger he came to, demanding earthly happiness from God as the greatest reward. Learn, dear brothers, to despise this type of happiness if you have it and not to say in your hearts: "I am doing well in this life because I adore God." You will observe that, if things are going well for you, and those who do not worship God are also doing well, your steps are necessarily not firm. If you have that happiness for worshiping God, and those who do not worship Him also have it, you will think that you worship God in vain, since those who do not worship Him have the same happiness. And if you do not have it, you will murmur against God, who grants happiness to blasphemers and denies it to those who worship him. Learn, therefore, to despise the things of earth 9 if you want to serve God with a worthy heart. Do you possess that happiness? Do not think that for this you are good, but that you must become good for it. Don't you have it? Do not think that this is why you are bad, but that you should avoid the evil that the good does not incur. 5. This man coming to himself and rebuking himself because he had begun to think evil of God, longing to be a sinner and desiring the peace of sinners, rebuking himself he says: What is there for me in heaven and what did I want from you on earth? Reflecting, and with a right heart, he knew the value of the service of God, to which he had previously assigned

mind a low price when he asked God for happiness on this earth. He knew again what is due to the servants of God, where we should have the heart and where in fact we have it 10. And heaven grant that we do not lie, at least in this hour, in this instant of time in which we proclaim this. Looking at himself and correcting his heart, he surprised himself for having ever sought earthly happiness in the world as a reward for divine service. But rebuking himself he said: What is there for me in heaven? What's there for me there? Eternal life, incorruptibility, the kingdom with Christ, the company of angels; There I will be free of all annoyance, all ignorance, all danger, all temptation; there I will have true, certain and permanent security. Here is what will be for me in heaven. And from you, what did I want on earth? What did I want? Deplorable, expired and vain riches. What did I want? Gold, earthly shine; silver, lividity of the earth; honor, temporary smoke. Here is what I wanted from you on earth. But because I saw this in sinners, my feet staggered and my steps trembled. How good is the Lord to the upright in heart! What are you seeking, oh faithful prophet? Gold, silver, earthly riches? So, is the fidelity of a faithful wife worth as much as the behavior of a prostitute? Is the fidelity of the upright husband worth as much as the behavior of the comedian, the charioteer, the theatrical hunter or the thief? Not at all, my brothers; our faith is not worth that. Topic: Commentary on Psalm 50:12. Date: It is not clear whether it belongs to the era of the presbytery or the episcopacy. Location: Unknown.

1. With a voice of harmony and a heart of one accord we have prayed to the Lord on our behalf, saying: O God, create in me a pure heart and renew within me a steadfast spirit. I will show you, with the help of the Lord, the things that he deigns to inspire me with. This psalm is about a penitent eager to recover lost hope, who lies prostrate in his sin and who longs to rise with the help of the Lord, just as he was capable of hurting himself and feels powerless to recover his health on his own. Just as we can hurt and mistreat our own body at will and to heal it we have to turn to the doctor, since it is not in our power to heal us, in the same way the soul is self-sufficient to commit sin, but to heal the wound caused it implores the healing hand of the Lord. Hence it is said: I said, Lord, have mercy on me; Heal my soul because I sinned against you. It is said: I said, Lord, to make it clear that the will and decision to sin was born from his soul and that he is very capable of losing himself, but

Attendance at Augustine's sermons was not uniform. While on the great festivals, the church was completely filled, on other occasions, such as this sermon, the number was small. This happened especially when there were public shows at the same time. In such circumstances the majority had no qualms about choosing the amphitheater or the circus in preference to the church. Augustine consoled himself with the certainty that, at least those who remained faithful to him, really wanted to listen to him and were not waiting for him to finish as soon as possible.^ It is for these minorities that he has preached some of his longest sermons, such as sermon 51. See the introduction to it and F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.86.

1. Peccator non potest resurgere per se a peccato absque gratia.— Voce consona, corde concordi, pro ipso corde nostro Dominum deprecantes diximus: Cor mundum crea in me, Deus, et spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis. Hinc pauca quae Dominus dederit, in eius gratiam manifestabimus vobis. Psalmus [138] est paenitentis, amissam spem recuperare cupientis, lapsu suo iacentis, et Deum magnis deprecationibus urgentis, tanquam qui fuerit idoneus ad se vulnerandum, et non sit ad sanandum. Sicut enim ipsam carnem nostram percutere et vulnerare cum volumus, possumus; ut autem sanetur, medicum quaerimus; nec ita nostra potestate salvamur, ut nostra potestate sauciamur: ita ad peccandum quod peccatum laeserit, Dei medicinalem dexteram implorat. Unde dicit in alio psalmo: Ego dixi, Domine, miserere mei; sana animam meam, quia peccavi tibi. Ad hoc ait, Ego dixi, ut constitueret ante oculos voluntatem arbitriumque peccandi ex anima oriri, sibique sufficere ut perdat
Commentary on Psalm 50:12

that it should be God who searched for what had perished and who healed the wound. The son of man came to seek and save what he had lost. Let us all say together: Create in me, Lord, a pure heart and renew within me a firm heart. Let the soul that sinned proclaim this, lest it lose more by despairing than it lost by sinning. 2. First of all we must make a serious effort not to sin, not to create a familiarity and friendship with sin as we did with the serpent of paradise. Through its poisonous bite it killed the one who sinned; hence it is not necessary to establish a friendship and a relationship with her. If by chance the serpent has oppressed the weak, or has surprised the unwary, or has captured the traveler or deceived the stranger, let the soul not be ashamed to confess it or try to find excuses, but rather accept its own guilt. That is why it was said in a certain psalm: O Lord, set a guard over my mouth and surround my lips with a door of restraint, and do not incline my heart toward evil words to seek excuses for my sins. Does someone incite you to sin? The first thing to do is reject it. But did it convince you? Don't try to excuse yourself, but rather accuse yourself. The same one who said: Create, Lord, a firm spirit within me, had begun by saying: Lord, have mercy on me according to your great goodness. The great sinner implores great mercy. A big wound needs a big medicine. Right there it says: Take your eyes off

my sins and blot out all my iniquities. Create, Lord, within me a firm heart. God turns his face away from the sins of the penitent and the self-accusing, the one who implores God's help and mercy. He turns his face away from sins without turning his face away from the sinner. To the same one who is asked: Turn your face from my sins, to the same one is asked: Do not turn your face from me. He turns his face away because he does not punish, and if he punishes, he moves the man. It is said that judges argue before passing sentence on convicted prisoners. So that God does not behave like this we say: Turn your face from my sins. In order not to know them, he forgives them. As we call the noble noble and we do not call the ignoble noble, so we also call the one who knows the knower and the one who does not know the unknown. If you want to be forgiven, recognize yourself. Sin cannot go unpunished; It is not appropriate for it to go unpunished, it is neither fair nor appropriate. And since sin cannot go unpunished, let it be punished by you so that you may not be punished for it. May your sin have you as its judge, not its protector. Get on the tribunal of your mind against yourself and be guilty of yourself. Do not try to flee from yourself, lest God place you before you. Hence the psalm, to easily ask for forgiveness, says: For I recognize my iniquity and my sin is always before me. As if to say: since it is before me, let it not be before you; and since I recognize it, forgive him. Every sin receives its corresponding punishment: either by you or by God; or for you without you or for God with you. Be the punisher

se; Dei autem esse quaerere, et salvum facete quod se vulneraverat. Venit enim Filius hominis quaerere, et salvum facete quod peretat (Luke 19:10). Hinc ptecem fluxentes dicimus: Cor mundum crea in me, Deus, et spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis. Dicat anima quae peccavit, ne plus peteat desperando, quam se petdidit delinquendo. 2. Confessio peccati necessaria, ut venia impetretur. Puniendum peccatum, aut ab ipso peccatore, aut a Deo. Excusado peccati iniqua est et a diabolo suggeritur.—Ante omnia quippe danda est opera, ne peccemus, ne quamdam familiaritatem et amicitiam cum peccato, tanquam cum serpente faciamus. Morsu quippe venenato perimit peccantem, nec tale aliquid est, cum quo facienda sit amicitia: sed si forte aut infirmum oppresserit, aut cautiono surrepserit, aut errantem cepetit, aut in errors eundo deceperit, non pigeat animam confiteri, nec quaerat excusationem, sed sui aecusationem. Nam et inde oravit quodam in psalmo, et ait: Pone, Domine, custodiam orí meo, et ostium continentiae circum labia mea: et nons cor meum in verba maligna, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis (Ps 140,3 et 4). Peccatum quisque suadet tibi? ante omnia recusetur. Sed persuasum est? non excusetur, sed potius aecusetur. Nam et iste qui dicebat, Cor mundum crea in me, Deus, sic incoepit, Miserere mei, Deus, secundum magnam misericordiam tuam. Magnam Misericordiam Magnus Peccator implorat: Magnam Medicinam Magnum Vulnus Desiderat. Ibi dicitur, Averie faciem tuam a peccatis meis, et

omnes iniquitates meas dele. Cor mundum crea in me, Deus (Ps 50, 3.11.12). Avertit ergo Deus faciem suam a peccatis confitentis, et se ipsum aecusantis, Deique auxilium et misericordiam deprecarnos. Avertit enim faciem suam a peccatis eius, non avertendo ab ipso. Cui enim dicitur, Averie faciem tuam a peccatis meis, et omnes iniquitates meas dele; eidem alibi dicitur, Ne averías faciem tuam a me (Ps 26,9). Avertit, quando non advertit: nam si advertit, evertit. Ideo et iudices in convicts reos sententiam preferentes animadvertere dicuntur. Hoc ne faciat Deus, id est, ne animadvertat, dicimus, Averte faciem tuam a peccatis meis. Ne agnoscat, ignoscat: Quomodo autem nobilem dicimus nobilem, non autem nobilem [139] dicimus ignobilem: sic noscentem noscentem, non autem noscentem ignoscentem. Tamen si vis ut ille ignoscat, tu agnosce. Impunitum non potest esse peccatum: impunitum esse non decet, non oportet, non est iustum. Ergo quia impunitum non debent esse peccatum, puniatur a te, ne puniaris pro illo. Peccatum tuum iudicem te habeat, non patronum. In tribunal mentís tuae ascend contra te, et reum constitue te ante te. Noli ponat te post te, ne Deus ponat te ante se. Ideo dicit in eodem psalmo, unde facillimam impetret veniam: Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego agnosco, et peccatum meum ante me est semper (Ps 50,5). Tanquam you say, Quoniam ante me est, ne sit ante te; et quia ego agnosco, tu ignosce. Ergo peccatum aut a te punitur, aut a Deo: sed a te

from sin and thus you will find a defender in God. Say: "I did it." I said: Lord, have mercy on me. Save my soul, for I have sinned against you. I, he claims, said. I do not try to make excuses for my sin by asking who sinned in me or who caused me to sin. I don't say "luck did it", "fate did it". Nor do I say: "the devil did it." The devil has the power to persuade and frighten, and also to cause serious discomfort when he is allowed to. But we must ask God for the necessary strength not to fall under the seduction of flattery and not to feel destroyed by setbacks. May God grant us two virtues against the flattery and threats of the enemy: continence and fortitude'; contain our desires so that we are not seduced by the prosperity of the world and be strong in threats so that we are not defeated by adverse things. It is written: Knowing that no one can be continent except by the grace of God, I cried out: Create, Lord, within me a firm heart; and also: Woe to those who lost their strength.' Do not try to accuse anyone, lest you find yourself with an accuser against whom it will be impossible for you to defend yourself. Our enemy, the devil, feels happy when he is accused; He longs for you to blame him, he wants you to present him as a criminal, as long as you do not recognize your sin. Against this diabolical cunning the psalmist exclaims: I said, Lord. sine te, a Deo tecum. Te ergo habeat punitorem, ut tu Deum habeas defenderem. Dec: Ego feci. Ego dixi, Domine, miserere mei; sana animam meam, quoniam peccavi tibi. Ego, inquit, dixi. Ego non quaero ad excusationem peccati, quis de me peccavetit, aut quis me peccare compulerit. Non dico, Fortuna fecited. Non dico, Fatum hoc voluit. Postremo nondico, Diabolus fecit. On whatever day the wicked converts and does penance, I will forget all his iniquities. The soul is revived if it comes to believe these words about the evil of despair. But it can find a new grave, and that soul that could not perish in despair, now perishes in hope. Who is this that perishes in hope? He perishes in his hope who dares to say: "God has already promised forgiveness to all those who turn away from their sins, God will forget all their iniquities whenever they convert." God forgives all past sins. If we deny this we go against divine forgiveness, we oppose the words of the prophet, we reject the divine word. This is not typical of the faithful dispenser.

In you, says the servant to the Lord, the creature to the Creator, the workmanship to the Maker, the captive to the Redeemer, the defeated to the Liberator and, to put it in a word, man to God. Two things are proposed here to man: that he know God and himself; God to trust and himself to trust. Those men who think highly of themselves and despise others say in vain: “I do not trust man; Far be it from me to trust in man. Such expressions are sometimes born from humility, sometimes from pride. It is good not to trust man as long as you do not trust yourself. He who trusts in himself either trusts in man or he does not consider himself a man. Only one sincere word remains: Have mercy on me. What personal merits can I list so that you may have mercy on me? Neither my justice, nor my riches, nor my strength. Therefore I do not ask this because of my merits, but because my soul has trusted in you. My soul asked for the prize because it offered a sacrifice. What did he offer? He did not offer a bull, nor a ram, nor a goat, nor Arabian incense, nor gold ornaments, nor anything bought at a very high price, but that which is worth more than all: he offered himself. There is nothing of more value to God than his own image. 3.

Love humble things above all. Starting from the humble you reach the sublime. No one builds a tall building if he has not laid the foundation well.' My brothers! Consider these things calmly; Instruct yourselves and strengthen yourselves in faith so that you can see the path you must follow until you achieve what you desire. I know and know very well that none of you rejects immortality, eternal sublimity, as well as achieving the company of God. We all wish it. Let's see, then, where we have to get to them, since we love the place to which we are heading. I said, then: he who has to build a temporary house of hay does not worry about digging a firm foundation. If, on the other hand, you wish to build a large building, of great consistency and long duration, first of all you direct your gaze and your attention to the foundation that must be laid and not at the height that it must reach; and the higher the top of the building must be, the deeper the foundation trenches must be. Who doesn't want to see their harvests high? But before getting those high harvests he must stir the earth deeply to sow the seed. He who plows plows the depths of the earth. He who plows deepens the furrow so that the harvest may grow. The taller and more slender the trees are, the deeper their roots are, because all height comes from the bottom.

rejoicing You will ask where such joy comes from. Here you hear: The righteous will rejoice in the Lord, and elsewhere: Delight yourself in the Lord and he will give you the desires of your heart. What is announced to us, what is granted to us, what is given to us, what is commanded to us? May we rejoice in the Lord. Who will rejoice in what he does not see? Or do we see the Lord? It's something we have promised. In the present, however, we walk in faith; While we are in the body, we are pilgrims far from the Lord. We walk in faith without yet possessing reality. Until when will it be like this? Until what John himself says is fulfilled: Dearly beloved, we are children of God and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is. Then the great and perfect rejoicing will take place; then the joy will be full, when it is no longer hope that breastfeeds us, but reality itself that nourishes us. However, even now, before reality itself reaches us, before we approach it, let us rejoice in the Lord, for the joy produced by the hope of what will later become reality is not small. It also happens in temporal affairs, in the joy we have, not in the Lord, but in the world: many love some things without having yet achieved what they love. Even though they do not yet possess it, the ardor is fueled by the mere hope. For example: you love money; but you would not love it if you had no hope of possessing it. You love as a wife a woman whom you have not yet married, but whom you hope to do so; perhaps, before taking her as a wife, you love her, and once taken, you hate her. In that way? because

God is no body. God is spirit. That is why it was said: Those who worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth. Not in any corporal place, because it is not a body; not, for example, on a high mountain, so that you think of approaching God using the height of the mountain. Certainly the Lord is exalted, but he directs his gaze to humble things; He knows elevated things from afar, but not the humble ones. Without a doubt da amatur, ducta odio habebitur. Quare hoc? Plus ergo amabimus cum viderimus, si potuerimus amare et antequam videremus. Ergo mode in spe amamus. Ideo iucundabitur, inquit, tustús in Domino. estate. May he delight you from whom you receive anything that causes you satisfaction. I'm not talking about sin, because that's the only thing you don't receive from it. Except sin, whatever else you have of it you receive. 3. What I said: "Let him delight you from whom you receive whatever gives you satisfaction," do not understand it about sin or say: "Behold, sin gives me satisfaction, do I receive it from God?" Reflect a little first, in case it is not the sin that delights you, but something else present where you commit the sin. When you love a creature in a disorderly way, against honest and lawful use, that is, when you love a creature against the law and the will of the Creator himself, you are sinning.' Certainly you do not love sin in itself, but by loving badly what you love you remain trapped in the bonds of sin. You crave the bait placed in the net, and without realizing it you feed on sin. Then you defend yourself this way: "If drinking too much is a sin, why did God create wine?" If loving gold is a sin—I am nothing more than a lover of gold, not its creator—; the maker of gold is God—why did he create what constitutes an evil to love? You can ask yourself the same thing about the other things that you love badly, among which is all kinds of lust, an area in which all kinds of foolishness are committed 2. Pay attention, look, reflect and see that every creature of God is good and in it there is no sin except because you use it badly. Therefore listen, O man! You say: "Why did God create what

What prohibits me from loving? That he had not created and would not exist for me to love. That I had not created the creature that orders me not to love and what I could love would not exist and by loving it I could be condemned. If this creature that you love badly because you don't even love yourself could speak, it would answer you: "I wish God had not created me so that what you feel love for would not exist. What if I had not created you so that you who feel love would not exist? Consider now how stupid you are, and your very words reveal that you are extremely stupid. You would want God, who is superior to you, to create you and you would not want him to do any good thing inferior to you. Everything God made is good. Some goods are big, some are small, but all are goods. Some are from heaven, others from earth; some are spiritual, others corporal; some eternal, others temporary, but all are goods, because he who is good did good things. For this reason, in a certain place in the Scriptures it is said: Command love towards me. God made you as an inferior good to himself; He did something also inferior to you. You are inferior to certain things and superior to others. Do not incline to the lower good after abandoning the higher. Stay upright so that you may be praised, for all those who are upright in heart will be praised. Where does it come from that you sin, if not because you treat the things you received for your use in a disorderly manner? Use inferior things well and you will properly enjoy the superior good.

Manumission was called the legal act through which the master gave freedom to his slave. Emperor Constantine authorized in the year 321 that it could take place inside the church in the presence of the bishop. See Theodosian Code IV 7. It was one of many measures by which said emperor equated bishops with civil officials. The libellus mentioned is the formula by which the master publicly declared his intention to free the slave, and asked the bishop to ratify such decision. At the same time, the tables on which the slave purchase contract was written were broken; Therefore, they were the document of its status as such. Augustine will talk about this a little later.

A wonderful, simple, perfect and immutable joy remained in his heart. What he had, he possessed, was not possessed; However, he was possessed by the Lord. I trampled on those things and was attentive to him. Leaving aside those things that he trampled, he adhered to the one he was dependent on. This is what it means to rejoice in the Lord. The Lord gave it—look at the rejoicing—the Lord took it away. Did he turn away? What he gave, he took away; he who gave offered himself. He rejoices, therefore, in the Lord. The Lord gave it, the Lord took it away; As the Lord pleased, so it was done; Blessed be the name of the Lord. Why should what pleases the Lord displease the servant? «I lost the gold, he said, I lost the family, the livestock; I lost everything I had. But the one from whom I have it, I did not lose. I lost what was with me, I did not lose the one whose I am. My delight is him; my riches are also him. But why? Because he did not follow a crooked path, he did not reverse the order of things, he did not recklessly forget those who are above him and he loved things that are inferior to him. That is the perversity of misusing creatures. 10. Why do you accuse the one who gave the gold, you who are rightly accused of loving gold badly? Delectatio piorum in Deo amissis terrenh rebus.—Ideo delectare in Domino, iucundare in Domino, non in saeculo. In Domino enim iucundabatur ille, qui cum perdidisset totam iucunditatem saeculi, remansit ei Dominus, in quo iucundaretur: remansit ei in ira simplex, perfection et immutabilis iucunditas cordis eius. Quae habebat possidebat, non possidebatur; a Domino autem possidebatur: illa calcabat, ex illo pendebat: ille illis subtractis quae calcabat, haesit [148] in illo in quo pendebat. Ecce enim quid sit in Domino iucundari. Dominus dedit, Dominus, vide iucunditatem, Dominus abstulit: numquid se abstulit? Quod dedit abstulit; qui dedit, se obtulit; iucundatur in Domino. Ergo, Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit; sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est: sit nomen Domini benedictum (lob 1,21). Quare displiceat servo id quod placuit Domino? Aurum, inquit, perdidi, familiam perdidi, pécora perdidi, quidquid habui perdidi: a quo habeo, non perdidi.

You would also delight in the Lord; as righteous you will rejoice in it. Accusation against the Creator will have no place in you, but thanksgiving to the Redeemer. Amen. dedi tibi, bene utere. Ornari vis auto; orna potius aurum: honorem vis, decus vis ab auro; decus praesta auro, ne sis dedecus auti. Aurum habet scortator, fornicator, luxuriator: edit pompatic ludos, insane doll donat histrionibus; esurientibus pauperibus non donat: non est decus auri. Nonne qui recte attendit hoc, dicit, Doleo aurum quod in illum incurrit; or if ego illud haberem! Et tu aurum si haberes: moda enim dicis: Doleo aurum quod in istum incurrit; or if ego illud haberem! what are you doing? Pilgrims susciperem, inopes pascerem, knots will dress, captives redeem. Bona loqueris antequam habeas: vide loquaris quando habueris. Si sis talis, erit aurum in tuo ornatu. Si vero sic uteris auro, quia plus diligis eum qui creavit aurum, eris rectus, superiora plus diligens, inferioribus recte utens; et delectaberis in Domino, iustus in Domino iucundaberis. Non erit in te accusatio Creatoris, sed erit gratiarum actio Redemptoris. 'Agustín condemns the custom of the muñera, based above all on the immense amount of money that it entailed, so that sometimes the promoter was completely ruined. The holy preacher would have liked such sums to have been distributed to the poor, instead of being wasted on wild beast hunting and subsequent spectacles. He beautifully expresses the same thought in sermon 32:20.
Commentary on Psalm 67,3.
Date: Between the year 400 and 405. Place: Carthage?

1. We have heard with trembling what was prophesied in the words of the psalm. It goes like this: As the smoke vanishes, let them vanish; As wax melts in the presence of gambling, so may sinners perish in the presence of God. I do not doubt, dearly beloved brothers, that all our hearts have been shaken and that no conscience remained without experiencing fear under the weight of such words. Who will boast of having a chaste heart? Or who will boast that he is cleansed from sins? Therefore, when the Scripture says: As wax melts in the presence of fire, so sinners perish in the presence of God, who will not tremble, who will not be startled in fear? What to do then? What hope do we have, since these words are not sung in vain? Or perhaps, when the prophet says such things, he expresses a desire and does not rather predict what is to come? In the words the form of the one who desires certainly appears, but the prescience of the one who announces something is understood. Just as in the Scripture of the prophets certain things are

"SICUT DEFICIT FUMUS, DEFICIANT", ETC.

CAPUT I. — 1. Propheta utens optantis figura, visionis suae certitudinem significat.—Audivimus, et contremuimus, quod in voce Psalmi est prophetatum. Ait enim: Sicut deficit fumus, deficit; sicut fluit cera a facie ignis, sic pereant peccatores a facie Dei. Non dubito, fratres mei, quod omnium vestrum corda concussa sint, nec cuiusquam conscientia sub his verbis intrépida steterit. Quis enim gloriabitur castum se habere cor? aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a sin? Ac per hoc cum Scriptura dicit, Sicut fluit cera a facie ignis, sic pereant peccatores a facie Dei (Prov 20:9), quis non contremiscat, quis non pavibundus exsiliat? Quid ergo faciemus, aut quae spes nobis est? Ñeque enim frustra haec cantantur; aut vero cum haec dicit Propheta, optat ea hominibus, ac non potius ventura praevidet. [149] In verbis quidem figura optantis apparet, sed intellegitur praescientia nuntiantis. Sicut enim quaedam in Scriptura Prophetarum tanquam in praeteritum facta narrantur, cumfutura praedican-

They seem to have happened in the past; at the moment of being predicted, as future; In the same way, to say some things, they do it as if expressing a wish. Those who correctly understand what they hear recognize that whoever foreshadows it is already seeing it as having happened. These psalms were sung and written down long before the birth of the Lord. Not before Christ God, but before Christ born of the Virgin Mary. Indeed, the patriarch Abraham lived long before King David, in whose time these psalms were sung. The Lord said: I have existed before Abraham. He is the Word of God, by whom all things were made. He himself also, inspiring the prophets, predicted that he would come in the flesh. His passion, therefore, is a consequence of his incarnation, since he could not suffer what is written in the gospels, but in the mortal and passive flesh that he carried. There we also read that those who crucified him, once the Lord had been nailed to the cross, divided his clothes among themselves and, having found a tunic woven in one piece, they did not want to tear it, but rather divided it by lot so that the person whose turn it belonged to would wear it in its entirety, because it signified love, which cannot be divided. These things that, already accomplished, are narrated in the gospels, were written as having already happened and happened many years before in the psalm when they were foreshadowed as future. They drilled into my hands and my feet, they counted all my bones. They

tur: ita quaedam tanquam vow dicuntur optantis; sed qui recte intellegunt quod audiunt, visionem praenuntiantis agnoscunt. Longe autem ante nativetatem Dominicae incarnationis, isti Psalmi dicti atque conscripti sunt, Non ante Deum Christum, sed ante natum ex virgine María Christum. Nam profecto pater Abraham longe ante David regem, cuius tempore hi Psalmi cantati sunt, Fuit. Dominus autem dixit, Ante Abraham ego sum (lo 8,58). Ipse enim est Verbum Dei, per quod facta sunt omnia: sed ipse ímplens Prophetas, in carne se esse venturum per eos praedixit. Ad eius autem incarnationem pertinet passio. Ñeque enim potuit pati illa quae in Gospel scripta sunt, nisi in carne mortali et passibili, quam gerebat. Et ibi utique legitur, quemadmodum Domino crucifixo hi qui crucifixerunt eum, ropa eius diviserunt sibi, et cum invenissent in eú tunicam desuper textam, noluerunt eam conscindere, sed sortem super eam miserunt; ut ad quem perveniret, integra perveniret (ib., 19,23.24): qua significatur caritas, quae dividí non potest. Haec ergo cum in Gospel iam facta narrentur, longe ante multos annos in Psalmo cum future praenuntiarentur, tanquam gesta et transacta cantata sunt. Foderunt, inquit, manus meas et pedes meos, et dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea. Ipsi veroconsiderverunt et inspexerunt me: diviserunt sibi ropa mea, et super vestem meam miserunt sortem (Ps 21,17-19). Omnia tanquam praeterita dicuntur, et future praedicuntur. Sicut ergo in verbis
Commentary on Psalm 67:3

They looked at me and contemplated me: They divided, he said, my clothes and for my dress they cast lots. Everything is narrated as past, and in reality it is preached as future. Thus, just as future events are implied through words that indicate past time, in the same way the mind of the one who announces must be perceived in the figure of the one who desires. The same thing happens with regard to Judas the traitor; The prophet predicts what would happen by expressing a wish. Likewise with reference to the Jews: Let their table, he said, be a snare, a hunt, and a scandal. That this was predicted referring to them, the Apostle clearly states, just as the apostle Peter remembers that the things pre-announced under the same figure referred to Judas. 2. It is not without reason that things that are still future are narrated as having already happened 1. For God they are so certain that they are already taken for granted. The prophet seems to say, as an expression of a vow, what he foresees will certainly take place, as if to show, as it seems to me, that we should not be displeased with the sentence of God once known, a sentence which he has made fixed and immovable. For this reason, when in the Acts of the Apostles a certain prophet named Agabus announced that the apostle Paul was going to suffer greatly in Jerusalem at the hands of the Jews and that he was even going to be imprisoned, upon hearing this the praeteriti temporis future facta signifitur; sic in figura optantis praenuntiantis mens intellegenda est. Sic et de luda Domini traditore, tanquam optat ei propheta, quod venturum esse praedicit. Et de ipsis Iudaeis, Fiat, inquit, mensa eorum in laqueum, et in venationem, et in scandalum (Ps 68,23). Quod de his praedictum esse sine dubitatione exponit: sicut de luda quae sub eadem figura praenuntiata sunt, apostolus Petrus commemorat (Act 1,20). CAPUT II.—2. In figura Prophetae optantis, intellegenda divini decreti approbatio.—Nec sine causa ea quaefutura sunt, tanquam transacta dicuntur. Deo enim sic certa sunt, ut iam pro factis habeantur; et tanquam optans videtur dicere Propheta, quod certum praevidet esse venturum: nihil aliud, quantum mihi videtur, ostendens, nisi nobis non debenré displicere cognitam sententiam Dei, quam fixam immobilemque constituit.

Et ideo in Actibus Apostolorum, cum quídam propheta, nomine Agabus, praediceret apostolum Paulum in Ierusalem a Iudaeis tumba esse passu1 In the previous number he affirms the fact, incontestable for him, that in the Bible, especially in the Old Testament, many future things are narrated as already past. He gives two examples: the passion of the Lord in Psalm 21 and the desertion of Judas in 68:23. In the present text he gives the reason for this procedure of the sacred writer. It is not sine causa that the future is narrated as having already happened. This cause is God's foresight. He sees everything so true that it can be taken for granted. This certainty is communicated to the sacred author. The example he gives below is interesting and explains the saint's thoughts well,
Commentary on Psalm 67:3

brothers wanted to change his mind and keep him from going there; But he said, What are you doing troubling my heart? I am willing not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. When the brothers saw the immovable strength of that man to endure everything, they said: God's will be done. Did they perhaps, because they said, May the will of God be done, desire that the Apostle suffer all those things? Was it not that they rather submitted their minds to God's sublime plan? In the same way, when he says: As wax melts in the presence of gambling, so sinners perish in the presence of God, the prophet is seeing that this will surely happen to sinners: he is pleased with what God has established, so as not to displease God himself. 3. What are we to do, brothers? Change our lives while there is still time, correct our actions if they need to be corrected; Thus, what will undoubtedly happen to sinners, will not affect us, on whom it will come; It will not reach us, not because we no longer exist, but because it will not find us such as those to whom it is predicted to happen. For this reason, the judge threatens that he will come: so as not to find someone to punish when he arrives. So that we correct ourselves, the prophets announce it out loud. If he wanted to condemn, he would remain silent. No one who intends to hurt says: "Pay attention." Brothers, what we have just heard through

of the Scriptures is the voice that warns: "Pay attention." Everything we suffer, the tribulations of this life, are a scourge from God who wants to correct now so as not to have to punish in the end. What each one suffers in this life is something that seems like cruelty; They are annoying things, they cause horror when told, extremely heavy things; But compared to the eternal fire, saying that they are small is an understatement, because in reality they do not exist. Both when we are punished and when others are punished, we are given a warning. All these things, brothers, in which we are wounded by the Lord, are warnings and stimuli for our correction. The eternal fire will come; referring to him, it will be said to those who will be placed on the left: Go into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. Then they will certainly repent, for it is written in a certain book called Wisdom: They will say among themselves, repenting and groaning for the anguish of spirit: Of what use has pride been to us, and what benefit has it brought us the boasting of riches? All that passed like a shadow. There they will move to penance, but it will be fruitless. The penance there will be painful, not medicinal. Now penance is fruitful, when it is free to correct oneself or not. Repent before the voice of Scripture, because before the voice of the judge who is judging your repentance will already be in vain. Then he will proclaim the sentence. When he is ready to dictate it, there will be no reason for you to reproach yourself. He was not silent before it. He did not defer it to you so that you could correct yourself, because he allowed the thief who was hanging

rum, et usque ad liga perventurum, cum hoc audito fratres revocare et retiñere vellent, ne illuc pergeret: Quid facitis, inquit, conturbantes cor meum? Ego enim non solum alligari, sed etiam mori [150] paratus sum pro nomine Domini nostri lesu Christi (Act 21,13.14). Atque ita cum viderent fratres immobilem viri ad omnia perferenda constantíam, dixerunt, fiat Domini voluntas. Numquid ergo quia dixerunt, Fiat voluntas Dei, optaverunt Apostólo, ut talia pateretur, ac non potius mentem suam sublimi et divino statuto devotissime subdiderunt? Sic et Propheta cum dicit, Sicut fluit cera a jacte ignis, sic pereant peccatores a facie Dei, videt hoc certissime peccatoribus imminere, et placet ei quod Deus statuit, ne Deo ipse displiceat. CAPUT I I I. — 3. Quibus modis Deus ad paenitentiam sollicitat. Flagellum Dei, admonitio nostra est. Paenitentia infructuosa, et fructuosa.— Quid ergo faciemus, fratres, nisi, ut, dum tempus est, vitam mutemus, et facta nostra, si qua mala sunt, corrigamus? Ut quod sine ulla dubitatione venturum est pecatoribus, nos non inveniat super quos veniat: non quia non erimus, sed ut non such inveniat, qualibus venturum esse praedictum est. Propterea se iudex venturum minatur, ut non inveniat quos puniat, cum venerit. Propterea illud cantant Prophetae, ut corrigamur. Si damnare vellet, taceret. Nemo volens ferire dicit, Observe. Totum, fratres, quod audiyimus per Scripturas, vox est Dei dicetis, Observa. Et totum

quod patimur, tribulationes in hac vita, flagellum Dei est corrigere volentis, ne damnet in fine. Quasi dura sunt, annoying sunt, horrent quando narrantur, quae quisque gravia valde patitur in hac vita: in comparatione autem aeterni ignis non parva, sed nulla sunt. Sive ergo nos flagellemur, sive cum alii flagellantur admonemur a Domino. Omnia ista, fratres, quae in hac vita inflictuntur a Domino, admonitiones sunt et stimuli correctionis nostrae. Veniet autem ignis aeternus, de quo dicetur illis qui ad sinistram constituendi sunt, Ite in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo et angelis eius (Mt 25,41). Tune acturi sunt quidam paenitentiam. Nam scriptum est in libro quodam Sapientiae: Dicent intra se, paenitentiam agents, et prae anguish spiritus gementes, Quid nobis profuit superbia? et quid divitiarum iactantia contulit nobis? Transierunt omnia illa, tanquam umbra (Sap 5,3.8.9). Erit enim ibi paenitentia, fruitless thirst: erit ibi paenitentia, sed dolorem habens, medicam non habens. Paenitentia is never fruitful, when correctio liberates. Paeniteat te ad vocem Scripturae. Nam ad vocem praesentis iudicis, sine causa paenitebit te. Tune iam ille sententiam dicturus est: et non erit quod reprehendas, quando sententiam dicturus est. Non enim tacuit ante sententiam. Non enim te distulit, nisi ut corrigeres te: quandoquidem latroni in cruz pendenti se mutare permisit. Tune enim latro pendens cum Domino,
Commentary on Psalm 67:3

with him on the cross. When the disciples doubted him, then the thief who hung on the cross next to the Lord believed in Christ. The Jews despised him who raised the dead, and the thief did not despise him who hung at his side of the cross. There is no reason to say at the end to the Lord: "You did not allow me to live well" or "You did not give me an extension to correct myself" or "You did not show me what I should desire and what to avoid." Know that he is not silent, know that he is in no hurry, know that he caresses, exhorts, threatens. All over the world it is read aloud to the entire human race. There is no longer anyone who can say: "I didn't know, I didn't hear anything." What is said in the psalm is being fulfilled: There is no one who hides from its heat. In the present his warmth is in his word. Turn away now from its heat and you will not melt like wax before the fire. 4. Sometime there will come, my brothers, what is now mocked by the wicked, what is now despised by those who laugh at it, what is now considered false when it is sung. It has to come sometime. If so many other things that were predicted did not come, let us not lose hope that this too will come sometime. If, on the contrary, we already see before our eyes and even hurt the eyes of the blind how many things were announced in advance about the future Church, why do we doubt that those too will come? When it was announced that the Church of Christ would spread throughout the entire world, few announced it and many laughed. Now what credidit in Christum (Lk 23:40-43) has been fulfilled, when the disciple titubaverunt. Contempserunt Iudaei mortuos suscitantem, non contempsit latro secum in cruz pendentem. Non est ergo quod in fine dicatur Domino, Non me permisisti betie vivere; aüt, dilationem correctionis non mihi dedisti; aut, non ostendisti quid appeterem, quid vitarem. [151] CAPUT IV.—Videte quia non tacet, videte quia differt, videte quia blanditur, hortatur, minatur. Constituit verbum suum in sublimitate; per totum mundum recitatur human universe generi. Non est qui iam dicat, Nescivi, non audiví- Impletur quod dictum est in Psalmo, Nec est qui se abscondat a calore eius (Ps 18,7). Modo ergo calore eius in verb eius est: mutare moda a calore eius, et non deflues sicut cera ab igne eius. 4. Iudicii futuri fides tot alus praedictionibus impletis firmatur.

Martyrum sanguis, semen.—Nam illud, fratres mei, venturum est aliquando, quod moda rident impü, quod moda contemnunt derisores, quod putant false cantori; aliquando venturum est. Si non venerunt tanta, quanta praedicta sunt; desperemus et illud aliquando venturum: si autem omnia quae de Ecclesiafutura praenuntiata sunt, iam videmus exhibita, et caecorum etiam oculos feriunt; quid dubitamus etiam illa ventura? When dicebatur Ecclesia Christifutura per totum orbem terrarum, dicebatur a paucis, et ridebatur a multis. Mode iam impletum est, quod both

It was predicted so far in advance: the Church is spread throughout the entire globe of the earth. A thousand years ago it was promised to Abraham: In your seed all people will be blessed. Christ arrived, born from the lineage of Abraham, and all peoples have already been blessed in Christ. Future schisms and heresies were predicted. We are seeing them. The persecutions were predicted. They were promoted by idol worshiping kings. The earth was filled with martyrs because of those who favored those idols against the name of Cyistus. The seed of blood was scattered, the harvest of the Church emerged2. Not in vain did the Church pray for her enemies: even those who persecuted her believed. It was prophesied that idols would also be cast to the ground through the name of Christ, as we also find this in the Scriptures. Not many years ago, Christians read that without seeing it yet; They expected it for the future, and with that hope they left this world. They did not witness them; However, they marched towards the Lord with the certainty that they were going to happen. Today these things are also realized. 3. What was predicted about the Church, we see realized. Is judgment day going to be the only thing that doesn't come? Is he the only one, of all that was prophesied, not going to arrive? Are we so hard and heart-of-stone that we read the Scriptures, see that absolutely everything that was written was fulfilled to the letter, and lose hope regarding what still remains? How much praedictum is: diffusa est Ecclesia per totum orbem terrarum. Ante millia annorum promissum is Abrahae, ln semine tuo benedicentur omneS gentes (Gen 22,18). Venit Christus ex semine Abrahae, benedictae sunt in Christo iam omnes gentes. Praedicta sunt schismata, et haereses futuree: videmus illa. Praedictae sunt persecuciones: factae sunt a regibus colentibus idola. Pro ipsis idolis adversus nomen Christi replete est terra martyribus. Sparsum est semen sanguinis, surrexit seges Ecclesiae. Nec frustra oravit Ecclesia pro inimicis suis: crediderunt et qui persequebantur. Praedictum est etiam quia ipsa idola evertenda essent per nomen Christi: nam et hoc invenimus in Scripturis. Ante paucos annos Christiani illa legebant, et non videbant; adhuc Futura illa exspectabant, et sic abierunt: non illa viderunt, sed tamen credentes quod Future Essent, cum fide abierunt ad Dominum: nostris temporibus etiam ipsa cernuntur.

Omnia quae ante praedicta sunt de Ecclesia, videmus impleta: solus dies iudicii non est venturus? Ipse solus praenuntiatur, et non veniet? Usque adeo sumus duri et lapidei cordis, ut legamus Scripturas, et videamus omnia prorsus ad litteram evenisse quae scripta sunt, et de his quae

Commentary on Psalm 67:3

What is left, compared to the things that have been shown to us? If God has shown us so many things, is He going to disappoint us in what remains? The judgment will come that will reward according to merit, good to the good and evil to the bad. Let's be good and wait calmly for the judge. 5. My brothers, pay attention above all to what I am going to say now. I don't want to tell you about what happened. Change your life starting today; May tomorrow find you converted into another. We in our perversity desire that God be merciful in such a way that He is not just. Others, on the contrary, being very confident in their own justice, want him to be just in such a way that they wish he were not: to be merciful. God manifests one thing and another, mercy and justice; In both things he remains firm. Neither does his mercy annul justice, nor does justice banish mercy. He is merciful and just. How do we prove that he is merciful? Forgive sinners now, grant forgiveness to those who confess themselves as such. How do we prove it is fair? Because the day of judgment must come, which momentarily defers, it does not abolish. When he arrives, he must give to each one according to his merits. Or do you want him to give to those who turned away from him what he will give to those who returned to him? Brothers, does it seem fair to us that Judas be placed in the same place as Peter? He would also be there if he had corrected himself; But desperate to achieve forgiveness, he preferred to tie the rope around his neck rather than ask the king for mercy.

6. Therefore, brothers, as I had begun to say, there is no reason to reproach God. When he comes to judge, there will be nothing we can allege against him. Let each one think of his sins, and correct them now, while he has time. May pain be fruitful, so that repentance is not sterile. God says something like this: “Behold, I have hinted at the sentence, but I have not yet proclaimed it. "I predicted it, I didn't set it." What are you afraid of, because I said: "If you change, it changes"? It is written that God repents. Does he do it in the same way as man? In fact, it was said: If you repent of your sins, I will also repent of all the evils that I was going to impose on you. Does God repent, as if he had made a mistake? In God the change of sentence is called penance. This is not wicked, but just. Why fair? The prisoner changed, the judge changed the sentence. Don't be terrified. The sentence changed, not the justice. Justice remains intact, because whoever is just must forgive those who have changed. As he does not forgive the obstinate, so he forgives those who have converted. He who is the giver of the law, the same is the king of mercy. He sent the law before; with it he brought forgiveness. The law had made you guilty; He who promulgated the law absolved you. Better, he didn't absolve you, because to acquit is to declare innocent. Rather, the converted forgives sins. Those who are involved in their sins are guilty. Nobody pretends to be absolved. Let's all apologize. But forgiveness is granted to those who have changed. Then we will be safe when

remnant despair? Quantum est enim quod remanet, ad ea quae iam nobis exhibita videmus? Tam plura Deus otendit, et de residuo nos fraudaturus est? CAPUT V.—Veniet iudicium redditutum pro meritis, bonis bona, malis mala. Boni simus, et securi iudicem exspectemus. 5. Deus et iustus et misericors.—Fratres mei, máxime nunc dicentem me audite. Nolo tecum computare praeterita: ab today die te muta, eras te alterum inveniat. Nos autem perversitate nostra sic volumus Deum misericordem, ut non sit iustus. Alii tursus quasi praefidentes de iustitia sua, sic volunt [152] iustum, ut nolint misericordem. Utrumque is exhibitedt Deus, utrumque praestat; nec mercy eius praescribit iustitiae, nec iustitia eius aufert misericordit. Misericors et iustus est. Unde misericordem probamus? Parcit moda peccatoribus, dat veniam confitentibus. Unde probamus quod iustus est? Quia venturus est dies iudicii, quem moda differt, non aufert; et cum venerit, redditurus est pro meritis. An: hoc vultis ut reddatur aversis, quod reddetur conversis? Fratres, iustum •videtur vobis, ut ibi ponatur ludas, ubi positus est Petrus? Et ipse ibi donderetur, si se correxisset. Thirst for venia desperans, potius sibi collum ligavit, quam Regis clementiam supplicavit.

CAPUT VI.—6. Mutato reo iudex mutatur.—Itaque, fratres, sicut dicere coeperam, non est unde reprehendamus Deum. Quid contra illum dicamus, non erit, cum venerit iudicare. Cogitet unusquisque peccata sua,, et moda illa emendet, cum tempus est. Sit fructuosus dolor, non sit: sterilis paenitudo. Tanquam hoc dicit Deus: Ecce indicavi sententiam,. sed nondum protuli; praedixi, non fixi. Quid times, quia dixi, Si mutaris,. mutatur? Nam scriptum est quod paeniteat Deum (Gen 6,6). Numquid: quomodo hominem, sic paenitet Deum? Nam dictum est, Si paenituerit vos de peccatis ves tris, paenitebit et me de omnibus malis quae facturus eram vobis (ler 18,8). Numquid quasi errantem paenitet Deum? Sedi paenitentia dicitur in Deo mutatio sententiae. Non est iniqua, sed iusta.. Quare iusta? Mutatus est reus, mutavit iudex sententiam. Noli terreri. Sententia mutata est, non iustitia. Iustitia integrates manet: quia mutatodebet parcere qui iustus est. Quomodo pertinaci non parcit, sic mutato parcit. Ipse rex est indulgentiae, qui dator est legis. Misit legem, come cum indulgentia. Reum te fecerat lex, absolvit te qui dedit legem. Immo non absolvit: nam absolvere est innocentem iudicare: donat potius peccata converso. Omnes enim sunt rei, qui peccatis suis involuti sunt. Nemo
pptet acquitted: orones veniam deprecemur. Venia vero datur mutato:
Commentary on Psalm 67:3

Let us hear: As wax melts in the presence of fire, so may sinners perish in the presence of God. 7'. Brethren, let sinners perish now before the presence of God. Perish now as sinners, and let sinners not perish. If they begin to live righteously, sinners will certainly perish, but men will not perish. Sinful man; They are two names. Man is just a name, and sinner is also just a name. Of these two names, we know that one was made by God and the other by man. God made man; sin, man 4. Why do you tremble when God tells you: "Let sinners perish before my presence"? What it means is only this: «May what you made perish in you; "I preserve what I created." Now the fire burns in the heat of the word, that is, as we said on another occasion, in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, since it is written in another psalm: There is no one who hides from its heat. That it is the warmth of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle attests: Burning in the Spirit. Therefore, where it says presence of God, put Scripture of God for now. Melt before her. Repent when you hear these things about your sins. If you repent and torment yourself under the heat of the word; If tears even flow, won't you find yourself similar to melting wax, from which in a certain way tears flow? So do now what you fear in the future and you will not have to be afraid later.

8. Therefore, do not dissipate like smoke. You find this and what was previously said written there, perhaps not without reason, since there is a difference between sins. In the same sentence, the psalm put one thing and another. As smoke vanishes, let them vanish, and as wax melts in the presence of fire, so let sinners perish before the presence of God. Who are those who vanish like smoke? Who but the proud, who do not confess their sins, but defend them? Why are they compared to smoke? For the smoke rises and rises high as towards the sky, but the higher it reaches, the more easily it fades and disappears. Consider again what I said: The smoke near the fire and the earth is thicker. It has not yet faded, it has not yet dissipated in the wind. When does it become lighter, fade and disappear? When it has risen a lot. The proud rise against God like smoke against the sky. Therefore, it has nothing left but to perish and die as it rises, as if scattered by the winds of its vanity, in the same way that elevated smoke disappears, spreading with apparent greatness, but not solid. This is the smoke. You see a large mass. You have something to see, but not something to retain. First of all, brothers, detest that punishment; do not defend your sins. If you still commit them, do not defend them. Submit to God. Beat your breasts so that the sins that remain will not be committed again. Make every effort not to commit them and, to the extent possible,

et erimus securi, cum audierimus, Sicut fluit cera a facie ignis, sic pereant peccatores a facie Dei. CAPUT VIL—7. Peccator pereat, ne homo pereat.—Certe, frattes, moda pereant peccatores, et non pereunt peccatores. Si incipiant iuste vivere, peribunt utique peccatores, sed non peribunt homines. Homo peccator, duo nomina sunt: ​​homo unum nomen est, et peccator unum nomen est. In his duobus nominibus intellegimus quia unum horum Deus fecit, alterum horum homo fecit. Hominem enim Deus fecit, peccatorem se ipse homo fecit. Quid ergo contremiscis, quando tibi dicit Deus, Pereant peccatores a facie mea? Hoc tibi dicit Deus: Pereat in te quod tu fecisti, et servo quod ego feci. Et moda ardet ignis in calore verbi, res est in fervore Spiritus sancti, sicut diximus iamdudum, quia scriptum est in alio psalmo, Nec est qui se abscondat a calore eius. Spiritum autem sanctum esse calorem dicit Apostolus, Spiritu ferventes (Rom 12:11). Ergo pro facie Dei, tibi pone interim Scripturam Dei: liquesce ab illa; paeniteat te, cum audis T153] haec de peccatis tuis. Cum autem te paenitet, et cum te ipsum excrucias sub calore verbi, cum etiam lacrimae currunt, nonne cerae tabescenti, et tanquam in lacrimas currenti similis inveniris? Modo ergo fac quod in posterum times, et non habebis quod in posterum timeas: tantum non sicut fumus deficias.

CAPUT VIII.—8. Sicut fumus deficiunt, qui peccata sua defendunt.— Nam utrumque habes ibi positum: forte non sine causa, quia est etiam distantia peccatorum. In ipso uno verb utrumque posit Psalmus: Sicut deficit fumus, deficiant; et sicut fluit cera a facie ignis, sic pereant peccatores a facie Dei. Qui sunt, qui sicut fumus deficiunt? Qui sunt, nisi superbi, non confitentes peccata sua, be your defenders? How do I smoke comparatively? Quia fumus erigit se, extollit se tanquam in caelum: sed quanto fit superior, both facilius evanescit et disperit. Rursus consider yourself quod dixi. Solidior est fumus igni proximus, et terrae proximus; nondum sic evanuit, nondum sic est dispersus in ventos: Tanto autem attenuatur, evanescit, et disperit, quanto se multum extulerit. Quia ergo superbus sic se erected against Deum, quomodo fumus against caelum; restat ut ita deficiat, et tanquam in winds suae vanitatis elatione dissipatus intereat; quemadmodum disperit fumus elatus, túmida, non solida magnitudeine inflatus. Sic est enim fumus: vines magnam molem; Habes quasi quod videas, et non habes quod teneas. Talem ergo poenam, fratres, ante omnia detestamini, nec defendatis peccata vestra: et si adhuc facitis, nolite defendé. Subdite vos Deo, et sic tundite pectora vestra, ut et ipsa quae remanserunt, non fiant. Conamini non faceré, et si fieri potest, nulla facite: si autem fieri non potest ut nulla faciatis, maneat tamen illa pia confessio. S. Ag. 7

do not commit any. If this cannot be, at least let that pious confession remain. You will not miss the look of His mercy, that, if you try to kill everyone and you give it to them in the measure of the help received, He will easily forgive you everything that remains on your path and the effort undertaken. Try only to progress, never give up. If the last day does not find you a winner, may it find you at least fighting, never captive or condemned. 9. Most abundant is the mercy and broad is the love of him who redeemed us with the blood of his Son when we were nothing because of our sins. What he did was already a great thing when he created man in his image and likeness. But, since by sinning we wanted to annihilate ourselves and inherited the inheritance of mortality from our parents and became a mass of sin, a mass of wrath, he was pleased to redeem us by his mercy at such a high price. He gave for us the blood of his only son, who was born, lived and died innocently. He who redeemed us at such a high price does not want those whom he bought to perish. He did not buy them to perish, but to revive them. If our sins overwhelm us, God does not forget what he paid for us, that is, a very high price. But let us not flatter ourselves too much with his mercy if we have not made an effort in the fight against our sins. And if we have committed some, especially capital ones, let us not be under the illusion that his mercy must be such that iniquity is associated with it. Erit enim respectus misericordiae ipsius, ut te conante omnia perimere, et quantum adiuverit petmente, de teliquis quae tibi restant in itinere invento et in conatu comprehenso, facile ignoscat: tantum proficere affecta, non deficere. Si non te invenit dies ultimus victorem, inveniat vel pugnantem, non captum et addictum. CAPUT IX.—-9. Misericordia Dei, quanta erga hominem.—Est autem misericordia Dei abundantissima, et larra eius benevolentia, qui nos sanguine Filii sui redemit, cum propter peccata nostra nihil essemus. Nam ipse aliquid magnum fecit, cum hominem ad imaginem et similarityinem suam creavit. Sed quia nos nihil ficri voluimus peccando, et ttaducem mortalitatis de parentibus duximus, et massa peccati, massa irae facti sumus: placuit tamen illi per misericordiam suam redeeme nos mucho pretio; dedit pro nobis sanguinem Unici sui innocenter nati, innocenter vivostis, innocenter mortui. Qui nos tant pretio re[154]demit, non vult perire quos emit.

Non emit quos perdat: sed emit quos vivificet. Si peccata nostra superant nos, pretium suum non contemnit Deus. Pretium magnum dedit. Nec tamen nobis tantum of ipsius misericordiamur, si non fuerimus conati adversus peccata nostra; nec si aliqua máxime capitalia fecerimus, speremus itafuturam esse misericordiam, ut ei coniungatur iniquitas. "Numquid enim et eos qui nihil egerunt, quemadmodum correcti viverent, sed in pertinacia et duritia animi permanserunt, accusa"

Many did nothing to live corrected, but remained stubborn and hard-hearted and even accused God to defend their sins. Will God place them in the same place as the holy apostles, prophets, patriarchs and faithful, worthy of possessing him, his servants, who walk in chastity, modesty, humility, distributing alms and forgiving what others have suffered? Such is the life of the righteous, such is the life of the saints, who have God as their Father and the Church as their mother 5. Those who do not offend either such Father or such Mother, but live in the love of one and the other, run towards the eternal inheritance without offending either of them, the inheritance is granted. 10. Since it was two fathers who begat us for death, two others begat us for life. The parents who created us for death were Adam and Eve; Those who begot us for life are Christ and the Church 6. My father, who begot me, was Adam to me, and my mother was Eve to me. We were born according to this generation of the flesh, certainly by a gift from God - this gift is not from anyone, but from God - and yet, brothers, how were we born? Certainly to die. Predecessors begat their successors. Did they beget children in whose company they will always live here? No; As destined to die, they gave birth to those who were to succeed them. God the Father and the Mother Church do not engender for this purpose. verunt etiam Deum defending peccata sua, ibi constituturus est, ubi constituit sanctos martyres, ubi constituit sanctos Apostólos, Prophetas, Patriarchas, et fideles suos bene de se merits, sibi servientes, ambulantes in castitate, modestia, humilitate, eleemosynas facientes, ignoscentes quod a quoquam perpessi sunt? Talis est enim via iustorum, talis est via sanctorum tenentium Deum Patrem, tenentium Ecclesiam matrem, nec illum parentem, nec istam offendentes, sed in amore utriusque parentis viventes, et ad hereditatem aeternam properantes, non laeso patre, non laesa matre, datur unicuique hereditas. CAPUT X.—10. Duo parentes ad vitam, et duo ad mortem.—Quia duo parentes nos genuerunt ad mortem, duo parentes nos genuerunt ad vitam. Parentes who genuerunt us ad mortem, Adam est et Eva; parentes qui nos genuerunt ad vitam, Christus est et Ecclesia. Et pater meus qui me genuit ad mortem, Adam mihi Fuit; et mater mea Eva mihi Fuit.

Nati sumus secundum istam progeniem carnis, ex muñere quidem Dei; quia et istud munus non est alterius, sed Dei: et tamen, fratres, quomodo nati sumus? Certe ut moriamur. Praecessores genuerunt sibi successores: numquid genuerunt sibi cum quibus hic semper vivant? Sed tanquam Saint Augustine picks up an idea from Saint Cyprian. In the work The Unity of the Church 6 he had expressed himself in a similar way: "He who does not have the Church as his Mother cannot have God as his Father." They beget eternal life, because they too are eternal. We have eternal life as an inheritance promised by Christ. He, according to that, the Word became flesh and lived among us, growing by being nourished with food. After the passion, death and resurrection he inherited the kingdom of heaven. As a man, he received the resurrection and eternal life. He received it in the man himself. He did not receive it as a Word, because it remains unchanged from always and forever. Since it was that flesh that was resurrected and obtained eternal life, that was resurrected and made alive ascended to heaven, the same has been promised to us. We hope for the same inheritance, eternal life. The whole body has not yet received it, since, although the head is in heaven, the members are still on earth. Only the head will not receive the inheritance and the body will be abandoned. It is the total Christ who will receive it, the total Christ as man, that is, the head and the body. We are members of Christ; Let us wait, then, for the inheritance. When all these things happen, we will receive that good that will not happen and we will avoid the evil that will not happen either. Both are eternal, since he did not promise his own something that was not eternal, nor did he threaten the wicked with something temporary. In the same way that he promised the saints life, happiness, the kingdom, an eternal inheritance without end, so he threatened the wicked with eternal fire. If we still do not love what he promised, let us at least fear what he threatened us with.
Commentary on Psalm 70,4.
Date and place: Unknown.

1. Every soul that attentively sings to God with the words of the psalm must reflect, in doing so, on the dangers in which it finds itself; It is necessary that it be reached by a certain family affection if by chance it suffers at that moment some external tribulation or internal difficulty, and that it refers what it sings to that which it suffers. We have just answered: Deliver me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, from that of the wicked and unjust. Perhaps each of you, when he hears these words from the reader's mouth or when he himself responds, thinks only of some enemy of his own; one who raises slander against him, another who is ready to send him to prison, another who perhaps composes a false writing against him: he calls him a sinner, evil, and wants to get rid of him. You see someone sing; You see him sing with ardour, adapt his face to the words of the psalm, sometimes even watering his mouth with tears, sighing while he sings 2. He who does not know how to discern affections, then praises that man.

SERMO decessuri, qui illis succederent, genuetunt sibi. Deus autem pater et mater Ecclesia, non ad hoc generant: generant autem ad vitam aeternam, quia et ipsi aetetni sunt. Et habemus hereditatem promissam a Christo vitara aeternam. Secundum quod Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (lo 1,14), nutritus crevit, passus, mortuus et resuscitatus accepit hereditatem regnum caelorum. In ipso homine accepit resurrectionem et vitam aeternam, in ipso homine accepit: in Verb autem non accepit; quia incommutabiliter manet ab aeterno in aeternum. Quia ergo accepit resurrectionem et vitam aeternam caro illa, quae resurrexit et vivificata ascendit in caelum, hoc nobis promissum est. Ipsam hereditatem exspectamus, vitam aeternam. Adhuc enim non totum corpus accepit; quia caput in cáelo est, membra adhuc in terra sunt: ​​nec caput solum accepturum est hereditatem, et corpus relinquetur: totus Christus accepturus est hereditatem; totus secundum hominem, id est caput et corpus. Membra ergo Christi sumus, speremus hereditatem: quia cum omnia ista transierint, hoc bonum accepturi sumus quod non trans[155]ibit, et hoc malum evasuri quod non transibit; aeterna sunt enim utraque. Non enim aliquid aeternum promisit suis, et aliquid temporale minatus est impiis. Quomodo vitam, beatitudem, regnum, hereditatem sempiternam sine fine promisit sanctis; sic ignem aeternum minatus est impiis. Si quod promisit nondum amamus, saltem quod minatus est timeamus.
INCIPIT SERMO DE RESPONSORIO PSALMI 70: « DEUS MEUS, ERUE ME DE MANU PECCATORIS»

1. Omnis anima, quae tries to sing voce psalmi Deo, necesse est ut tune de suis propriis periculis cogitet, et familiari quodam tangatur affectu, si quid forte tune vel tribulationis extrinsecus, vel difficultatis intrinsecus patitur, et ad id quod patitur referí quod cantat. Respondimus: Domine, liberate me from manu peccatoris, et from manu facinerosi et iniuriosi (Ps 70,4). Fortasse unusquisque vestrum, cum haec verba a lectore [297] audit, vel ipse responder, non cogitat nisi aliquem inimicum suum, aut qui illi calumniatur, aut qui illum parat mittere in carcerem, qui contra illum forte chirographum falsum conponit: ipsum vocat peccatorem, ipsum facinerosum et iniuriosum, ab ipso se cupit liberari. Vides illum cantore, et cum affectu cantore, vultum etiam verbis psalmi accommodare, aliquando et lacrimis ora rigare, suspirare inter verba cantandi. The text, as it appears here, is strange to Augustine's work. This leads G. Morin to assume that it is an antiphon sung by the people and that it came from a translation prior to the one used by the saint. A further proof is found in the words "we have responded." See the ad hoc note in MA I 296. Beautiful description of a scene that must have been frequent.

He opens and says: «With what affection he listens to the reading. You have to see how he moans, how he sighs! » The other, however, is thinking about that enemy of his, from whom he truly fears some slander, some violence, fraud or deception, and with all his strength, with all his marrow, with his voice, with his face, with his sighs, he says: Deliver me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, from that of the wicked and unjust. He who sings like this, sings like an old man, and understanding it carnally, tries, even if he is old, to sing the new song. If you sing the new song, let the new man sing. What does sing the new man mean? Renew yourself with the desire for a new life, desire something else, sigh to God for something different, be a lover of the kingdom of heaven. More briefly: be a lover of God, love God, love without expecting reward. The devil intended to object to nothing else, and he wanted to convince the holy man Job of this, as if he were an old man, to prevent him from achieving what is promised to the new man, when he says: Does Job worship God for free? If he worships him freely, he conquers the devil; If he does not do so, he is defeated. The slanderer's objection would be valid if Job did not worship God gratuitously. "This is why he worships you," he said, "because you gave him so many good things." God allowed Job to be tempted to show us as an example to imitate the one by whom he knew he was selflessly worshiped. It was known to God, but it was hidden from us. Consider, then, what happened to the perversity of the devil: wanting to show that one was a prevaricator, he made many imitator saints. He did not submit it to himself, but showed it to us.

take us as an example. What then? How did he understand that Job worshiped him freely? For he was not one of those who were grateful while he had and blasphemed when he had not, but he put pleasing God above all his riches, as if to say: “I have the one who gave it to me; Why do I seek what he granted me? 2. I will say, therefore, brothers, that whoever worships God to obtain riches and honors in this world and asks for these things, manifestly does not worship Him gratuitously. He does it for the prize. If God does not grant him these things, he judges that he must be abandoned. On the contrary, he thinks that whoever gives them to him must be more revered. The truth is that no one gives them but him, but if someone else granted them, God forsaken, all lovers of these things would come to him. Lean on God; May he be all your good for you, may he be your true good. After having taken all things from Job, since he could not take away the one whom he selflessly loved, the devil was defeated with Job's own words: The Lord gave him to me, the Lord took him away from me; As it pleased the Lord, so it was done. He did not say, “What am I going to do against the Lord? I will cry for myself, since I cannot defeat him," but: Blessed be the name of the Lord, he said. Only because of his children, whose sin he feared, did he tear his clothes, praying with truly paternal affection for them. She willingly accepted that God would take them away from her, because she was still more willing to hug him. 3. There will be someone who will say: "I do not worship God for riches, he knows that, nor seeking out-of-date and temporary honors."

Qui nescit discernere affectus, iam illum hominem laudat, et dicit: Magno affectu audit lectionem: quomodo gemit, quomodo sigh Ule autem de inimico illo suo cogitat, a quo aliquam calumniam, aliquam vim, aliquam fraudm et circumventionem pertimescit; et totis viribus, et totis medullis, voce vultu suspiriis dicit: Domine, liberate me from manu peccatoris, et from manu facinerosi et iniuriosi (Ps 70,4). Talis qui cantat, vetus homo cantat, et carnaliter intellegens conatur, cum sit vetus, cantore canticum novum. Novus cantet, si novum cantat. Quid est, novus cantet? Desiderio novae vitae innovetur, aliud concupiscat, propter aliud Deo susspiret, sit amator regni caelorum. Brevius dicam: sit amator Dei, Deum amet, gratis amet. Hoc enim et diabolus ille volebat obicere, et in eo volebat convincere sanctum virum Iob, quasi vetus esset, ut ad id, quod promissum est novo, eum pervenire non sineret, quando ait: Numquid Iob gratis colit Deum'? (Iob 1,9). Si ergo gratis colit, vicit diabolum; If not free colit, victus is a diabolo. Valeret enim calumniatoris obiectio, si gratis Iob non coleret Dominum. Ideo te, inquit, colit, quia tanta illi dedisti. Propterea Deus permisit temptari Iob, ut, a quo se sciebat gratis coli, et nobis ostenderet imitandum: Deo enim cognitus erat, sed nos latebat. Videte ergo, quid contigit perversitati diaboli: cum unum vult ostendere praevaricatorem, multos fecit sancti imitatores. Non enim eum

sibi subiecit, sed nobis otendit. Quid ergo? Unde intellectus est Iob quia gratis colebat? Quia non gratias egit cum haberet, et blasphemavit cum non haberet, sed placitum Dei praeposuit ómnibus divitíis suis, tamquam say: Habeo qui dedít, quid quaero quid dedit? 2. Dicam ergo, fratres, quisquís propterea coíit Dominum, ut habeat divitias, habeat honores saeculi, et haec ab illo petit, manifestum est quia non gratis colit: ad praemium colit. Si non ei ista Deus det, deserendus est; qui dederit, amplius colendus existimatur. Et non [298] dat nisi ipse: sed tamen, si alter dedisset, Deo deserto ad illum confugissent istorum amatores. Ad Deum nitere, Deus tibi sit totum bonum, Deus tibi sit verum bonum. Sublatis ergo omnibus rebus, diabolus quia non tulit illum quem gratis amat, etiam ipsius voce diabolus prostratus est: Dominus dedit, et Dominus abstulit; sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est. Non dixit: Et quid sum facturus contra Dominum? Plangam me, quia non eum possum vincere. Sit, inquit, nomen Domini benedictum (Iob 1,21). Solum propter filios suos, quorum timebat peccatum, conscidit ropa sua, orans utique paterno affectu pro eis. rales. Why then? Let us examine this man who worships selflessly and loves selflessly. Why then? «I do not want, he says, riches, I want only what is necessary: ​​nothing is missing in my house, I am healthy, with my wife and my children. "This is enough for me." Still your worship of God is not disinterested. In Job himself God showed it to us. Well, the devil came to fall, who, certainly, with God's permission, had taken away his riches, and not him, because he trampled them in such a way that he hung on God. With God's permission, he also deprived him of his health. Job showed that his worship of God was so gratuitous that he did not even love and worship Him for the health of his body. And the devil did not hurt him in a single limb: from head to toe he left him as if rotten. And this for greater prostration of the devil, so that the triumph would be greater, so that whoever had seduced Adam when he was immortal, would be defeated by a rotten man. He struck him, therefore, with a great wound that extended from his head to his feet; corroded by the work of worms, he still endured his wife who tempted him, becoming an ally of the devil 3. She was the same Eve, but he was not the same Adam. He induced him to blaspheme, so that, losing his patience, he would lose the one whom he selflessly adored. But when could he lose the one he was so close to? What did he respond to his wife who suggested such things to him? You have spoken like a stupid woman. If we have received the goods from the hand of God, are we not going to endure the evils? Here is the disinterested man of worship, who does not give up

scit, ñeque propter expired and temporary honors. Et propter quid? Eliquemus hominem gratis colentem, gratis loverm. Et propter quid? Nolo, inquit, divitias, sufficientiam rerum flew: nihil in domo mea desit, salvus sim cum coniuge, cum filiis meis; hoc mihi sufficit. Adhuc nondum gratis colis Deum. In ipso Iob ostendit hoc nobis: nam diabolus permissu quidem Dei, qui divitias abstulerat, et non ille, ceciderat; quia sic eas calcabat, ut ex Deo penderet. Abstulit et salutem, permisit hoc Deus; et demonstratus est Iob ita gratis colere Deum, ut nec propter ipsam salutem corporis eum coleret et amaret. Et non eum diabolus in uno membro percussit: a capite usque ad pedes putrem fecit; et hoc ad amplificarem subiectionem suam, ut amplius triumpharetur: ut qui seduxerat Adam immortalem, a putri nomine vinceretur. Percussit eum itaque gravi vulnere a capite usque ad pedes; et putrescens vermibus patitur coniugem temptatricem, relictam sibi diaboli adiutricem. Illa ipsa erat Eva, sed ille non ipse Adam. Subiecit blasphemandi suasionem, ut ille amissa patientia amitteret eum, quem gratis colebat. Sed quando amitteret, cui sic inhaerebat? Quid enim mulieri talia diceti respondedit? He reserves himself for those who love him. He wants to show his face to the purified, not in the eye of the flesh, but in the eye of the heart. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Love to see; What you are going to see is not something cheap, it is not something that is blown away by the wind. You will see the one who made everything you love. God does not want you to love the earth, he does not want you to love the sky, that is, the things you see, but himself whom you do not see. Not seeing will not last forever if not loving does not last forever. Love him when he is absent, to enjoy him when he is present. Have desire for the one you are going to possess, for the one you are going to embrace. First adhere by faith; then you will join him in reality. For now, as a pilgrim, you walk by faith and hope.
