1. We will be happy if we perform what we hear and sing. Listening is our sowing; Realizing it is the fruit of the seed. The field in which wheat is planted and produces thorns should not wait for the granary, but for fire. In the same way, those who hear good things and do evil do not wait for the granary of the kingdom of heaven, but for that fire of which it is said: Go into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. By beginning the homily with these words, I wanted to draw attention to your charity, so that your entry into this church will not be fruitless if you hear so many good things and then do not act righteously. I want that, according to the goodness of the sower and the seed, the word of God springs from your customs and from your life, as de videre possimus, fide corda mundemus, caritate sanemus, pace firmamus: quia hoc ipsum unde invicem diligimus, iam ex illo est, quem videre desideramus.
INCIPIT SERMO DE RESPONSORIO PSALMI 74: «CONFITEBIMUR TIBÍ DEUS, CONFITEBIMUR ET INVOCABIMUS NOMEN TUUM»

1. Felices sumus, si, quod audimus et cantamus, etiam faciamus: auditorio enim nostra seminary, operator autem fructus est seminis. Ager, in quo seminatur triticum, et spinas generat, non horreum debent sperare, sed flammam; sic et Mi, qui bona audiunt, et mala operantur, non sibi horreum regni caelorum sperent, sed illum ignem de quo dicitur: Ite in ignem aeternum, qui praeparatus est diabolo et angeüs [301] eius (Mt 25,41). Hoc praelocutus admonuerim caritatem vestram, ne infructuose intretis ecclesiam, audiendo tanta bona, et non bene operan; sed secundum bonitotem seminantis et seminis verbi Dei, ita in vestris moribus et in vestra vita tamcjuam in bona terra ubertimus bonorum

good land, producing abundant fruit from good habits, and thus wait for the farmer who is to come and who is preparing the granary where you are going to be introduced. We just sang: We will confess you, Lord, we will confess you and call on your name. Confessing God, what is it, but humbling yourself before him, not attributing any merit to yourself? For, as the Apostle says, by his grace we have been saved, not by our works, so that no one should be proud: by his grace we have been saved. No just life preceded any that he loved from above and urged him to say: "Let us come to their aid, let us help these men who live justly." He disliked our life, he disliked everything we did, but he did not dislike what he himself did to us. According to this distinction, he will condemn what we did, and save what he himself did. He will condemn the evil deeds of men and save men themselves. Men did not create themselves, but they performed evil actions. What God did in them is a good thing, because he made man in his image and likeness. What God condemns is what man has done wrong, turning away by his free will from the maker and creator and turning to evil. If God condemns him, it is to free man, that is, God condemns what man did and liberates what he himself did 2. 2. We were not good; He took pity on us and sent his only Son to die, not for the good, but for morum fructus exurgat, et speretis agricolam venturum, parantem vobis horreum quo mittamini. Ecce cantavimus, confitebimur tibí Deus, confitebimur et invokebimus nomen tuum (Ps 74,2). Confiten Deo, quid est, nisi humilari Deo, non sibi adrogare merita aliqua? Quoniam gratia ipsius salvi facti sumus, sicut dicit apostolus: Non ex operibus, ne forte quis extollatur; ipsius enim sumus gratia salvi facti (Eph 2,8.9). Non enim praecessit aliqua bona vita, quam ille desuper diligeret et amaret, et diceret: Subveniamus, succurramus istis hominibus, quoniam bene vivunt. Displicuit illi vita nostra, displicuit illi in nobis totum quidquid faciebamus; sed non ei displicuit quod ipse fecit in nobis. Itaque quod fecimus damnabit, quod ipse fecit salvabit: damnabit facta mala hominum, et salvabit ipsos nomines; ipsi enim homines non se fecerunt, sed facta mala fecerunt.

Quod ín eís Deus fecit, quía fecit Deus hominem ad ímaginem et similarityinem suam, bonum est; quod autem per liberum arbitrium aversus a conditore et creatore ipse homo et conversus ad nequitiam male operatus est, hoc damnat Deus, ut hominem liberet: id est, damnat Deus quod fecit homo, et liberat Deus quod fecit ipse Deus. 2. the bad ones; not for the righteous, but for the wicked. Behold, Christ died for the wicked. As follows? There is hardly anyone who dies for a righteous person: but, indeed, perhaps someone dares to die for a good person. Maybe someone will be found who is willing to die for a good person. But for an unjust, impious, iniquitous person, who would want to die, but only Christ, just to the point of sanctifying the unjust? Therefore, brothers, we did not possess any good works; They were all bad. But even though the works of men were such, out of his mercy he did not abandon them and, since they deserved punishment, he, instead of the punishment they deserved, granted the grace they undeserved. He sent his Son to rescue us, not with gold, nor with silver, but with the value of his shed blood, like an immaculate lamb led to sacrifice in favor of the stained sheep, if only stained and not completely blackened. Such is the grace we have received. Let us live, then, in a manner worthy of it, so as not to insult such sublime grace. An extraordinary doctor came to us and forgave all our sins. If we want to get sick again, we will not only be harmful to ourselves, but also ungrateful to the doctor. 3. Let us follow, then, the paths that he showed us, especially that of humility. Such was he made for us. He showed us the path of humility with his precepts and he himself followed it, suffering for us. He would not have suffered if he had not humiliated himself. Who would be able to kill God?

If he hadn't lowered himself? Christ is, in fact, the Son of God, and the Son of God is certainly God. He himself is the Son of God, the Word of God, of whom Saint John says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and the Word was God. He was at the beginning with God. Through him all things were made and without him nothing was made. Who would put to death him by whom everything was made and without whom nothing was made? Who would be able to hand him over to death if he had not humiliated himself? But what was that humiliation like? John himself says it: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Word of God could not be given over to death. So that what could not die could die for us, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The immortal assumed mortality to die for us, to kill ours with his death. This is what God did; This he granted us. The great one humbled himself; After being humiliated, he was put to death; dead, he rose again and was exalted, so as not to abandon us dead in hell, but to exalt us with him in the final resurrection those whom he now exalted through faith and the confession of the just. 4. He left us the path of humility. If we follow it, we will confess the Lord and sing on the occasion: We will confess you, O God, we will confess you and call on your name. You shamelessly invoke the name of the one you do not confess. The first thing you have to do is recognize your sins to prepare the room to whom you invoke 3. Your heart

suum, qui moreretur, non pro bonis, sed pro malis, non pro iustis, sed pro impiis: etenim Christus pro impiis mortuus est (Rom 5,6). Et quid sequitur? Vix enim pro iusto quis moritur; nam pro bono forsitam quis audeat mori (ib., 7). Forte invenitur aliquis qui audeat mori pro bono;, pro iniusto autem, pro impio, pro iniquo quis velit morí, nisi Christus. solus, [302] ita iustus ut etiam iniustos iustificadoret? Nulla ergo, fratres; mei, bona opera habebamus, sed omnia mala. Cum ergo talia essent facta hominum, non deseruit nomines misericordia ipsius; et cum digni essent poena, ille pro poena, quae debenbatur, donavit gratiam, quae non debenbatur; et misit Filium suum, ut redeemeret nos, non auro, non argento, sed pretio fusi sanguinis sui, agnus immaculatus ad victimam ductus pro ovibus maculatis, si vel maculatis, et non totis infectis. Accepimus ergo hanc gratiam: digne vivamus ipsa gratia quam accepimus, ne tantae gratiae iniuriam faciamus. Medicus tantus venit ad nos, dimisit omnia peccata nostra: si volumus iterum aegrotare, non solum in nos perniciosi erimus, sed etiam medico ingrati. 3. Sequamur ergo vias ipsius, quas nobis ostendit, praecipue humilitatis viam, quod factus est nobis ipse: ostendit enim nobis viam humilitatis praeceptis, et fecit illam pariendo pro nobis; non enim pateretur, nisi se humilaret. Quis occideret Deum, nisi se humilaret Deus? Christus

enim Filius Dei, et Filius Dei utique Deus. Ipse est Filius Dei, Verbum Dei, de quo Iohannes said: In principle erat Verbum, et Verbum erat aput Deum, et Deus erat Verbum. Hoc erat in principle aput Deum. Omnia per ipsum jacta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil (lo 1,1.2.3). Quis occideret, per quem omnia facta sunt, et sine quo factum est nihil? Quis illum occidere posset, nisi se ipse humilaret? How do you humiliate yourself? Dicit ipse Iohannes: Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (ib., 14). Verbum enim Dei non posset occidi: ut posset ergo pro nobis mori, quod mori non poterat. Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Immortalis suscepit mortalitatem, ut moreretur pro nobis, et morte sua occideret mortem nostram. Hoc fecit Dominus, hoc nobis praestitit. Magnus humilatus est, humilatus accisus, occisus et resurgens et exaltatus, ut mortuos nos non relinqueret in inferno, sed exaltaret in se in resurrectione mortuorum, quos exaltavit moda in fide et confessione iustorum. 4. Ergo viam nobis humilitatem dedit. Si ipsam tenuerimus, confitebimur Domino, et non sine causa cantamus: Conjitebimur tibi Deus, confitebimur et evocabimus nomen tuum (Ps 74,2). Impudenter enim invokes nomen eius, cui non confiteris: primo confitere, ut pares habi[303]tationem ei, quem invokes. Plenum est enim cor tuum nequitia; The same thought in the Ennarration to Psalm 74:2.

It is overflowing with evil. Confession undoes the impurity that you carry inside you and cleanses the house where the one you invoke must come. Whoever invokes before confessing his sins wants to insult the one he invokes. If you do not dare to invite some saint to your house without first having cleansed it so that his eyes are not offended, do you dare to invoke the name of God to come to your heart, full as it is of evil, without first having eliminated all internal iniquity by confessing your sins? Confession, my brothers, humiliates us; once humiliated, it justifies us; justified, it exalts us. If we are arrogant, God resists us; If we are humble, God exalts us, because he resists the proud and yet gives his grace to the humble, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled; whoever, on the contrary, humbles himself, will be exalted. Returning to God...

1. Let us give thanks to the Lord, our God, and give generous praise to the God to whom it is fitting to sing confessio autem fundit immunditiam, quam geris intus, et mundat domum, quo veniat ille, quem invokes. Nam quisquis antequam confiteatur invoket, iniuriam vult faceré ei quem invoket. Si enim aliquem sanctum non audes invitationre in domum tuam, nisi prius mundaveris domum tuam, ne oculi eius patiantur iniuriam, tu audes in cor tuum plenum nequitia invokere nomen Dei, nisi prius per confessionem fuderis interiorem iniquitatem? Ergo confessio, fratres mei, humilat nos, humilatos iustificat, iustificatos exaltat. Nam si fuerimus superbi, resistit nobis Deus: si fuerimus humiles, exaltat nos Deus; quoniam superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Iac 4:6; 1 Petr 5:5); et qui se exaltat humilabitur, qui autem se humilat exaltabitur (Luke 14:11; 18:14). Conversi ad Deum. Explicit sermo de responsorio psalmi 74.

« DEUS, QUIS SIMILIS TIBÍ? »
1. Gratulatur fidelibus Dei zelo incensis contra idola.—Gratias Domino Deo nostro, et abundantiam laudis illi Deo, quem decet hymnus in
Commentary on Psalm 82:2

a hymn in Zion. Thanks be given to him to whom we have sung with heart and devout voice: O God, who is like you?, because we experience his holy love embedded in our hearts; because you fear him as the Lord and love him as the Father. Thanks to him, who makes himself desired before letting himself be seen and who, at the same time that he is experienced as present, is expected as the one who is to arrive. Thanks to him, whose fear does not distance love, whose love is not an obstacle to fear. We bless him, we honor him, through you and in you. The temple of God is holy, and that temple is you. He already sees how sublime his life is, or his way of living, when the stones of his temple live like this. Think, brothers, what you say and to whom you say it: O God, who is like you? The temples say to your God: O God, who is like you? The living stones say to those who inhabit them: O God, who is like you? Let every creature be presented before your hearts, the earth and all that is in it, the sea and all that it contains, the air and all that it envelops, the sky and all that it encompasses. He spoke and they began to exist; He commanded it and they were created. Let the universe therefore say: O God, who is like you? Let the believing heart say it, let every obedient tongue say it, every devout conscience say it confidently: O God, who is like you? He says it to the one of whom he is not ashamed. A dignified way of speaking appropriate to living stones. 2. May the dead stones experience in themselves the mercy of the living stones! As for dead stones, not Zion. Gratias illi, cui cordis et oris devotione cantavimus, Deus, quis similis tibi? quod eius sanctam caritatem invisceratam sentimus cordibus nostris: quod ipsum tanquam Dominum timetis, tanquam Patrem diligitis. Gratias illi, qui desideratur antequam videatur, et praesens sentitur, et futurus speratur. Gratias illi, cuius timorem non excutit amor, cuius amorem non impedit timor. Ipsum benedicimus, ipsum honoramus, et pro nobis et in nobis. Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos (1 Cor 3:17). Iam videte [163] quantum ille vivat, vel quomodo vivat, quando lapides templi eius sic vívunt. Cogitate, fratres, quid dicatis, et cui dicatis, Deus, quis similis tibi? Lapides lived dicunt habitatori suo, Deus, quis similis tibi?

Occurrat cordibus vestris universe creature; terra et quidquid in terra, mare et quidquid in mari, aer et quidquid in aere, caelum et quidquid in cáelo: Ipse dixit, et facta sunt; ipse mandavit, et creata sunt (Ps 148.5). Ergo, Deus, quis sirhilis tibi? dicat universum cor, dicat universa oboediens lingua, dicat omnis devota conscientia, dicat secura, Deus, quis similis tibi? Illi enim dicit, de quo non erubescit. Dignum est hoc, decet hoc tombstones alive. 2. Christianorum in Paganos pietas.—Nam lapides mortui utinam sentiant in se misericordiam lapidum yivorum. Mortuos dico, nori iljos

I am referring to those with which these churches are built, not even to those in which the artist's chisel works, nor to those that man sculpted to be gods; better, that man sculpted so that they could be called gods without being so; It is not these that I call dead stones, but I call it the men to whom such gods are equal. Living stones are those to whom the apostle Peter speaks and says: You, brothers, contribute to the building of the temple of God as living stones. May, my brothers, the dead stones experience in themselves the mercy of the living stones! Why do we worry? Why do we conceive according to the narrowness or width of our heart? What do we worry about, why do we worry, if not to free one stone from another stone? Living stones have eyes and see; They have ears and hear; They are endowed with hands and with them they act; They have feet and they walk. Behold, they knew their maker, they adore their craftsman and praise their sculptor; The dead stones, however, servants of the stones, look at their gods and are not looked at; they worship and are not recognized as worshipers; They offer sacrifices and become a sacrifice to the devil. If indeed, brothers, you had eyes to see and ears to hear, how difficult it would be for you to see that all the prophecies about Christ have been fulfilled! Would it be too much to examine true codices and non-deceptive oracles? But why don't they see? Why don't they hear? The prophet also said this: Let those who make them and those who put their hope in them be like them. So, are they people without hope or in whom we should no longer expect anything? quibus fabricae istae consurgunt, nec in quibus ferrum artificum operatur, nec quos sculpsit homo, ut dii sint; immo sculpsit homo, ut vocentur et non sint; non ipsos dico mortuos lapides: sed homines dico mortuos lapides, quibus dii similes sunt. Lapides vivi sunt, quos alloquitur apostolus Petrus, et dicit: Et vos, fratres, tanquam lapides vivi coaedificamini templum Dei sanctum (1 Petr 2,5). Utinam ergo, fratres mei, sentiant lapides mortui misericordion in se lapidum vivorum! Quid enim satagimus? quid cordis nostri vel anguish vel latitudine percurrimus? quid curamus, quid studemus, nisi ut lapidem liberemus a lapide?

Lapides enim vivi oculos habent et vident, aures habent et audiunt, manus habent et operantur, pedes habent et ambulant: etenim noverunt factorem suum. At vero lapides mortui, sciunt lapides suos, déos attendunt, adorant, et cognoscuntur; sacrificium inferunt, et sacrificium ipsi diabolo fiunt. Quod ipsi, fratres, si et oculos haberent ad videndum, et aures ad audiendum, quantum erat videre impleri Christi prophetias? Quantum erat attendere verídicos codices, et oracula, sed non fallada? sed quare non vident? Quare non-audiunt? Quia et hic prophetia dicit, Símiles sint illis homines qui faciunt ea, et qui confidunt in eis (Ps 113,8). Ergo desperati et despe-
Commentary on Psalm 82:2

No way. But what can you expect from dead stones? What else do you think, except what we already have written: Is God powerful to make children of Abraham arise from these stones? 3. So then, dearly beloved, since you know to what God we said: O God, who is like you? That is, to him of whom we have no reason to be ashamed, whose inscription we do not read on a stone, but carry it in our hearts; whose name is known to all and lives in those who believe in him; He dwells with those who are submissive to him, he defeats the proud; We already know to whom we said: O God, who is like you? Let not the men whom God made lead us to hate them; On the contrary, they impel us to hate everything that man himself did evil in the man created good by God. Man is a name; a creature name. I seek the maker of this creature. It is God. Is God the creator of man alone? Is it not also true of the beasts, of the fish and the bird, of the angel, of heaven and earth, of the stars, of the sun and the moon and of everything created and governed, whether superior or inferior, whether of the hells or the heavens, united by the bond of unity? Is not God also the architect of all these things? Yes, but he made man in his image and likeness. A being who has a certain resemblance to God is called a man. What degree of similarity? Who is similar to whom? Man is similar to God. What is man, but that you remember him? Also us, men made randi? Absit! Et quid sperandum est de lapidibus mortuis? Quid putatis, nisi quod iam scriptum tenemus, Potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae? (Mt 3,9). 3. Deo vero nec homo comparai debent, multo minus idolum Herculis, cuius titulus refellitur.—Itaque, carissimi, quoniam nostis cui Deo diximus, Deus, quis similis tibi? de quo non erubescimus, cuius titulum non in lapide legimus, sed in corde gestamus: cuius nomen et notum est ómnibus, et vivit in credentibus, habitat in subditis, debellat superbos: quoniam novimus cui diximus, Deus, quis similis tibi? non nos moveant ad odium sui homines, quos fecit Deus, sed moveat ad odíum suí quidquid in homine bene facto a Deo male fecit ipse homo. Homo nomen unum est. Huius creaturae artificem quaero, Deus est. Numquidnam hominis tantummodo creator [164] Deus?

Nonne et pecoris, et piscis, et volatilis, et angelí, et caeli, et terrae, et siderum, et solis, et lunae, et omnium supra infraque conditorum et temperatorum, imorum atque summorum, unitatis vinculo conexorum; nonne istorum omnium artifex Deus? Sed hominem ad imaginem et similaritymem suam fecit (Gen 1, 26.27). Similitudo aliqua dicitur homo, et quanto ad quantum? crux Free of anti-Manichean concerns, the hermeneutics of this Genesis verse is different from that given in Sermon 1:5. The same in sermon 43,3.

in his image and likeness, let us say to our God: O God, who is like you? Although man was made in his image and likeness, he says rightly and truly: O God, who is like you? He added: Remember that we are dust; This is also true, because man, made in the likeness of God, is still far from such likeness; In other words, perhaps that similarity is so distant that it is not even honest to compare it; perhaps the heart of man, the heart of the Christian who cannot say: "to the man God", willingly reads "to the God Hercules"; Not content with reading what was written, he reflects and asks the inscription to whom "the God Hercules" refers - inscription 2 does not speak, but it reads "the God Hercules" -. Who are you referring to? That Hercules says it. Both the inscription and the one to whom it refers are silent; both are meaningless. In what is read is the lie; in what is below, fiction. The inscription accuses whoever wrote it and confuses those who worship it. It is an inscription that instead of recommending a stone-God reveals a foolish man; inscription that falsely attributes the name of God to a fiction and erases the name of the worshiper from the book of the living. He who does not realize that he worships something without senses, to what extent does he possess them?

man. Hit him and heal; put him to death and recover life. Before we said to him: Lord, who is like you? Now we continue telling him, not without logic: Do not be silent or be meek, O God! That? Have we, my brothers, invited God to wrath, to whom we have said: Do not be silent or be meek, O God, whether we are addressing him who sent, or who came and said: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart? The meek and humble of heart is Christ, the Son of God. What to think? He says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and we pray to him: Do not be silent or be meek, O God! It is as if he answered us: "Man, as if that were not enough, since you do not learn from me to be meek, are you trying to induce me not to be meek?" See, brothers, be attentive, help us with your pious attention and chaste prayer; Help us get out of these straits by name. Divine words seem to contradict each other; They seem to affirm the opposite, if we do not have the authentic understanding, which we must receive from him to whom we have said: O God, who is like you? Let us receive what he also assured: I will give you understanding. Let's know these words: I give you my peace, words that Christ pronounces so that Christians may live in peace among themselves. How will they imitate him? How are they going to listen to him, if the divine words themselves are not capable of being at peace with each other? Pay attention, contemplate one as a resonance of contrary words. Come to me and learn from me. What thing? First of all, who is calling? Who are you calling? What does it say? Look

Look at what he did in the man himself, erase what was done by the man against whom he made the quem? Homo ad Deum? Quid est homo, nisi quod memor es eius? (Ps 8,5). Dicamus ergo ad imaginem et similarityinem facti ipsius, Deo nostro dicamus, Deus, quis similis tibi? Addidit enim, Memento quia pulvis sumus (Ps 102,14). Sic longe is a similarityine Dei. Homo factus ad similarityinem Dei: sed ipsa similarity sic distat, ut eam comparati non deceat. Et tamen cor hominis, cor christiani, qui non potest dicere, Homini deo; libenter legit, Herculi deo. Titulus non loquitur, sed vel legitur, Herculi deo. What is the dictum? Ipse dicat de quo dictum. Utrumque mutum, utrumque insensatum: supra mendacium, infra figmentum. Titulus accusans scriptorem, confundens adoratorem. Titulus non commendans lapidem deum, sed indicas hominem stultum. Titulus nomen dei imposings figmento, et nomen cultris delens de libro vivostium. Quam particle sensus in se sentit? 4. Quomodo petitur ut ne taceat, ñeque mitescat Deus.—Quia tamen potens est Deus de lapidibus istis excitare filios Abraham, attendat ibi quoc fecit in nomine. est contra eum, qui hominem fecit. Percutiat et sanet, occidat et vivificet. Cui enim dixit, Domine, quis similis tibi, ei consequenter adiunxit, Ne taceas, ñeque notches, Deus. Who do I see? In isto canticle, fratres mei, ad iracundiam Deum provocavimus, cui diximus, Ne sileas, ñeque mitescas, Deus? Nempe aut ille qui misit, aut ille ipse qui venit, et ait, Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde (Mt 11,29). Mitis et humilis corde Filius Dei Christus. Quid ergo? Ule dixit, Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde: et nos ei diximus, Ne taceas, ñeque mitescas, Deus? Sed responderat nobis: O homo, parum est quia tu non a me discis ut sis mitis, et me vis docere ne sim mitis? Videte, fratres, intendite, adiuvate nos, ut exeamus in eius nomine (adiuvate nos pia intentione, casta oratione) ex his angustiis. Litigare videntur divina eloquia: contrarium putantur sonare, nisi adsit intellectus, et suscipiamus ab illo ipso, cui diximus, Deus, quis similis tibi? quod et ipse dixit, Intellectum tibi dabo (Ps 31,8), suscipiamus. Novimus hoc: Pacem meam do vobis (lo 14,27). Dicit Christus, ut Inter se pacem habeant Christiani. How do I imitatebuntur? quomodo audient, si ipsa divina eloquia pacem inter se habere non possunt? who speaks: I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to the little ones. So it was, Father, because it was so to your liking. All things were given to me by my Father. Here is who speaks: All things were given to me by my Father and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son would reveal him. Sublime greatness and ineffable depth! All things, he said, have been given to me by my Father. Only I know him and I am known only by him. That? Are we excluded? Don't we know him? Where is that: To whom the Son would like to reveal it? 35. Your eagerness and enthusiasm for faith, the aroma of love and the abundance of holy zeal for the house of God is manifested in your voices, which because of their clarity you put as witnesses of your heart. Let the concern for this your will also be manifested in those few faithful of God by whom you are governed. You, brothers, as he said, are the people of God and the sheep of his pasture. You have shepherds who act as God, they also serve as servants and members of the Shepherd. The desire of the crowd and its will to accomplish something finds adequate form to manifest itself in these voices. However, the care that a few have for you must be shown not by words, but by actions. Therefore, brothers, since what belongs to you

I put it to you that you fulfilled it by acclaiming, allow me to demonstrate to you if we are also going to fulfill with deeds what corresponds to us. We have already examined you; Examine us, in case after these voices, witnesses of your heart and your desire, we had been lazy when it came to carrying out what was appropriate to be carried out. May it not happen to us that you are found honest and we are found reprobate! But since, with respect to what you claimed, our desire and yours are identical - although the way of acting cannot be -, we believe, dearly beloved, that it is appropriate to accept your desire and that the decision to act on your desire be expected from us. So that there is no discord among the members of Christ, let them perform all the functions that are proper to them in the body. Make the eye, placed at the top, what belongs to the eye; the ear what corresponds to the ear, and the same the hands and feet, respectively, so that there are no divisions in the body, but that all the members care for it as for themselves. We rejoice and are pleased with your charity, because you obeyed the holy Lord, your bishop and colleague of mine or 4, in what he told you this morning. Continue like this, do not deviate from this path so as not to fall. God's help will be great to achieve what you want if you do what he commands. Well, as I had begun to say 5, what is man, every man, without exception? Or what is the life of men which, as it is written, is

Audi quis vocat. Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine caeli et terrae, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revealsti ea [165] parvulis. lea, Vater, quoniam sic placilum est coram te. Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo. Ecce quis vocat. 'Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Paire meo. Quia nemo cognoscit Filium, nisi Vater; et nemo cognoscit Patrem, nisi Filius, et cui voluerit Filius reveale (Mt 11,25-28). Ingens magnitudeo, et ineffabilis altitudo. Omnia tradita sunt mihi, inquit, a Patre meo. Solus agnosco, just agnoscor. Quid, non remansimus? non agnoscimus? Et ubi est, Cui voluerit Filius reveale? 5. Fidelium quorumdam zelus contra idola.—Animus vester et studium fidei, et flagrantia caritatis, et abundantia zeli domus Dei, apparuit in vocibus vestris, quas satis Claras vestri cordis testes habuistis. Sinite ut appareat et paucotum fidelium Dei, per quos gubernamini, studium citca istam voluntatem vestram. Vos enim, fratres, populus Dei estis, sicut ipse dixit, et oves pascuae eius (Ps 94,7). Habetis in nomine Dei pastores, servos pastoris et membra pastoris. Multitudinis animus et voluntas ad quamquc rem faciendam istis vocibus poterit apparere: paucorum autem cura pro vobis, non vocibus, sed rebus debent ostendi. Itaque, fratres, quoniam iam quod ad vos pertinebat, implestis acclamando; sinite As you can see, two of the previously asked questions remain unanswered: Who are you calling? What does it say?

ut probetur vobis, utrum et quod ad nos pertinet, impleamus agendo. Probavimus you; prove us, if post istas voices testes cordis studü vestri, us in agendis quae agi oportet, according to fuerimus. Absit a nobis ut vos inveniamini probi, et nos reprobi. Sed quoniam voluntas agendi de iis quibus acclamastis, una est et vestra et nostra; modus vero agendi par esse non potest: putamus, caríssimi, ideo oportere, ut voluntas accipiatur a vobis; consilium implendae voluntatis vestrae exspectetur a nobis. Ut membra Christi non discordent, impleant omnia quae in illius corpore sunt, officia sua: faciat oculus in sublimi locatus quod ad oculum pertinet; auris, quod ad aurem pertinet; manus, quod ad manum: pes, quod ad pedem; ut non sint scissurae in corpore, sed Idem ipsum ut pro se invicem sollicita sint membra (1 Cor 12:25). Gratulamur itaque et congratulamur Caritati vestrae, quia sancto domino et collegae nostro episcopo vestro oboedistis in eo quod vobis mane locutus est. Hoc sequimini, ab ista via non recedatis, ne cadatis. Valde enim adiuvat Deus quod vultis, si quod iusserit feceritis. Quid enim, ut dicere coeperam, omnis homo? aut quae est vita hominum, quam, sicut scriptum est, vapor ad modicum apparens? (Jac 4,15). Cogitate ergo, fratres, fragilitatem vestram, humili4
Aurelius of Carthage, the city where he preached this sermon. In the number }.

vapor that appears for an instant? Reflect, then, brothers, on our frailty, our baseness, the condition of the flesh, the rapid passage through this world, and see that only then will it go well with us when all our hope rests in the only person on whom it can be confidently placed. How will our hope rest in it, unless we obey its precepts? 6. Do we perhaps say to you: "Stop wanting such a thing"? On the contrary, we thank the Lord, because you want what God wants. God wills it, he commanded it, he predicted it, he has already begun to put it into effect, and in many places on earth he has already carried it out in part: the extirpation of all superstition of pagans and Gentiles 6. If your desire were for it to begin in this city, that is, you were to ensure that here, before anywhere else, the superstitions of demons were abolished, perhaps it would be a somewhat arduous task, although not one to despair. But if these things were already effectively carried out where they began to be carried out before than here, when there were still no previous examples, with how much more energy do we believe that, in the name of the Lord and with the help of his power, the same thing can be done now also and more effectively, since previous examples can already be presented? 7 You have certainly cried out: "As it happened in Rome, let it also happen in Carthage." If there is already a precedent in the head of the gentility, should not the members also follow it? Reflect, brothers; examine the very books of the gentatem vestram, condicionem carnis, huius saeculi volaticos transitus; et videte quia tune vobis bene erit, si tota spes vestra in illo sit, in quo solo potest firmiter collocari. Quomodo autem ibi erit spes nostta, nisi oboediamus praeceptis eíus? 6. Gratulatur civibus, quod Romanos déos, Romae delectas, nolint stare Carthagine.—Numquid dicimus, Nolite quod vultis? immo etiam gratias agimus id vos velle quod Deus vult. Ut enim omnis Paganorum et [166] Gentilium superstitio deleátur. Deus vult, Deus iussit, Deus praedixit, Deus iam implere coepit, et multis iam terrarum locis etiam ex magna parte complevit.

Si voluntas nostra ab hac civitate inciperet, ut hic primitus aboleri superstitiones daemonum quaereretis; fortasse aliquis arduous labor esset, non tamen desperandus: never vero si facta sunt ista efficaciter ubi fieri coeperunt, et exempla non praecesserant; quanto efficacius in nomine Domini, in adiutorio dexterae ipsius hic quoque effici posse credimus, quando iam praecedentia pronuntiantur exempla? Utique hic clamastis: Quomodo Roma, sic et Carthago. Si in capite Gentium res praecessit, membra non sunt secutura? Cogitate yourself, fratres, warn in libris ipsis Gentium, audite ab eis, in quibus ipsius infelicitatis relicita

useful, hear it from those who remained to show their unhappiness; Get to know their writings, either by listening to them, or by reading them yourselves, and see that they call the gods themselves Romans. Consequently, these gods are also Roman. When, roaring the fury of the pagans, Christians were forced to worship such gods, by refusing to do so they endured their cruelty, which went as far as bloodshed. It was evident that the whole crime of the martyrs whose blood was shed consisted in not worshiping the Roman gods, in refusing to participate in Roman cult ceremonies, in not making supplications to the Roman gods. All the fury, all the envy, had its origin in the name of the Roman gods. They disappeared from Rome, why have they remained here? Pay attention to this, brothers; Do not forget what I have said, retain it. Roman gods! Roman gods! Yes, well, I will say, if the Roman gods disappeared from Rome, why have they remained here? If they had been able to walk they would have said that they fled from there to here. But they did not flee. Did they remain there then, in Rome? The one who is no longer in Rome is the one who was once called the god Hercules. Here, however, he even wanted to present himself with a golden beard. When he no longer exists for you, he wanted to show up here with a golden beard. I was wrong when I said "he wanted to introduce himself." What can an insensitive stone want? Then he wanted nothing, could do nothing, but those who wanted to see him with a golden beard were ashamed of him when they saw him shaved. But I don't know what kind of suggestion was sneaked into the new judge 8. What did he do? He did not intend for such a stone to be worshiped by a Christian; on the contrary, remanserunt; vel audiendo, vel legendo, cognoscite litteras eorum: et videte quia lili et isti dii Romani vocantur. Ergo isti dii vocantur Romani. Et quando Christiani cogebantur, fremente impetu Paganorum, ut eos adorarent, et recusantes, eorum saevitiam usque ad effusionem sanguinis sustinebant; ea videbatur tota culpa martyrum, quorum fundebatur sanguis, quia déos Romanos adorare nolebant, quia caeremonias erga déos Romanos respuebant, quia Romanis diis non supplicabant; et totus Ímpetus, tota invidia non fiebat, nisi de nomine deorum Romanorum. Si ergo dii Romani Romae defecerunt, hic quare remanserunt? Haec ergo, fratres, haec attendite, haec dixi, haec inhíbete. Say Romani, say Romani, say Romani. Si ergo dii Romani Romae defecerunt, hic quare remanserunt?

Si ambulare possent, dicerent quia huc inde fugerunt. Sed non fugerunt: remanserunt ibi, Romae. Qui aliquando dictus est deus Hercules, Romae iam non est. Hic autem etiam barba deaurata esse voluit. Erravi plane, quia dixi, Esse voluit. Quid enim vult insensatus lapis? Ule ergo nihil voluit, nihil potuit. Sed qui deaurari cum voluerunt, of satin erubuerunt. Suggestio itaque nescio quae novo iudici obrepsit. Quid egit? Non egit The proconsul,
Commentary on Psalm 93:12

He tried to irritate that Christian with a superstition that led him to shave him; It did not incline him to reward him, but moved him to take revenge. I judge, brothers, that it was more shameful for Hercules to have his beard cut off than if his head had been cut off. What was put in place by an error of the pagans was suppressed with disgrace to them. Hercules is often called the God of strength. All his strength lies in his beard. Unfortunately for him, it was shiny. What did not shine with the light of the Lord was because its brightness came not from light, but from mourning. 7. Be silent, then; Now look at the god Hercules 9, to whom Christians refer when reading: O God, who is like you? Don't be silent or be meek, O God! This I had set out to demonstrate: how with words, do not show yourself meek, it is asked that not men, but errors, be destroyed. He does not appear meek, then he becomes irritated. But it's about God, so he also has compassion. He becomes irritated and pitied. It is irritated by wounding; He sympathizes as he heals. It is irritated to cause death; He feels sorry to donate his life. In the same man he does both. Therefore, he does not cause death to some and gives life to others, but rather he is angry and meek with the same people. He is angry with errors, he is benign with corrected customs. I will wound and I will heal; I will kill and make alive. Saul himself, later called Paul, he prostrated and raised him up. He prostrated the infidel: he raised the believer. He prostrated the pursuer, raised the

preacher If you don't get irritated, how was Hercules' beard cut? He did this through the faithful, the Christians, through the authorities established by him and subject to the yoke of Christ. Therefore, brothers, accept this willingly and, with the help of the Lord, look forward more happily to other things. Amen.

utique ut a christiano lapis honoraretur; sed ut christianus illi superstitioni ad radendum misceretur: non inclinavit ad obsequendum; sed movit ad vindicandum. Fratres, puto ignominiosius Fuisse Herculi barbam radi, quam caput praecidi. Quod ergo positum est cum errore illorum, ablatum est cum dedecore illorum. Deus fortitudinis solet dici Hercules: tota virtus eius in barba. Malo suo refulsit; quod non fulgebat luz dominica, non a luz, sed a luco fulgebat. 7. Deus irascendo mitis.—Sileant ergo, videant [167] moda, cui Deo legant fideles et dicant, Deus, quis similis tibí? Ne sileas, nec notches, Deus. Hoc susceperam, quomodo non mitescat, non evertendo nomines, sed errors. Non mitescit, ergo irascitur: si mitis est, ergo et miseretur. Irascitur et miseretur: irascitur ad percutiendum, miseretur ad sanandum; irascitur ad mortificandum, miseretur ad vivificandum. In uno nomine facit haec. Non quasi alios mortificans, alios vivificans: sed in eisdem ipsis et irascitur, et mitis est. Irascitur erroribus, mitescit correctis moribus. Ego percuban!, et ego sanabo: ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam (Deut 32,39). Unum Saulum, postea Paulum, et prostravit, et erexit: prostravit infidelem, erexit fidelem: prostravit persecutorem, erexit praedica-

torem. If you don't irascitur, where is Herculi's shaven beard? Fecit enim hoc per fideles suos, per Christianos suos, per potestates a se ordinatas et Christi iugo iam subditas. Itaque, fratres, hoc libenti animo accipite; et in Domini adiutorio cetera prosperius iam sperate.
That is, the God of Christians, who is properly the God of strength,

Date: Between the year 410 and 412. Place: Hippo.

1. When we sang to God we said: Blessed is the man whom you, Lord, teach and instruct with your law. The Gospel of God resounded, and Zacchaeus gave alms. Learn. What better law of God than the holy Gospel? It is the law of the New Testament about which, when you read the prophet, you heard: The days will come, says the Lord, and I will make a new testament with the house of Jacob, different from the one I established with their fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. Testament that was promised then and the promise fulfilled now; promised through
FROM VERSE 12 PSALMI 93: «BLESSED HOMO QUEM TU ERUDIERIS, DOMINE», ETC.

CAPUT I. — 1. Evangelium lex Testamenti Novi. Legis veteris promissa spiritualiter intellegenda.—Cum cantoremus Deo, diximus ei, Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et ex lege tua docueris eum. Ergo Dei Evangelium sonavit, Zacchaeus eleemosynas fecit. Discite. Quae melior enim lex Dei, quam sanctum Evangelium? Lex enim Testamenti Novi, de quo propheta cum legeretur, audistis: Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et consummabo super domum lacob Testamentum novum: non secundum Testamentum quod statui patribus eorum, cum educerem eos de terra Aegypti (Ier 31,31 et 32). Testamentum ibi promissum, hic redditum;
Commentary on Psalm 93:12

prophet, the promise fulfilled by the Lord of the prophets. Read and examine that Testament that is usually called Old. Also then a law of God was promulgated; read it or listen to it, when it is read, and see what was promised there. Land of the earth was promised there; land flowing with milk and honey, but, nevertheless, land. But if we understand it spiritually, seeing that that land did not flow with milk and honey, there is another land that will distill these products, that land of which it is said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. This land here is the land of those who die. Are you looking for milk and honey? Taste and see how sweet the Lord is. Under the name of milk and honey its grace is meant, which is sweet and nutritious. This grace was figured in the Old Testament and made known in the New. 2. Because of those who taste it carnally and expect from God the rewards indicated there, but carnally understood, and want to serve God for the things promised there, that law merited hearing from the apostle Paul that begat children for bondage. Why this? Because the Jews understand it carnally, since understood spiritually it is identified with the Gospel. Therefore he begets children for servitude. To whom? To those who serve God for earthly goods. When they accompany them they are grateful; When they lack them, they burst into blasphemies. Those who serve God for such things cannot serve Him with a sincere heart. They look at those who do not serve our God. Come that

Such have that for which they themselves serve God, and they think in their hearts: "What good is it for me to serve Him? Do I possess as much as he who continually blasphemes? He prays and is thirsty; He blasphemes and belches with satisfaction. Whoever looks at these things is a man, but a man of the Old Testament. Whoever, on the other hand, serves God in the New Testament, must expect the new inheritance, not the old. If you wait for the new inheritance, transcend the earth, step on the tops of the mountains, that is, despise the glory of the proud. But when you have despised and violated him, be humble so that you do not fall from heights. Listen: Lift up your hearts, but towards the Lord, not against the Lord. All the proud have elevated hearts, but against the Lord. You, on the other hand, if you want to have an elevated heart, have it towards the Lord. If you have your heart lifted up to him, he will hold it so that it does not fall to the ground. 3. Then blessed is the man; Blessed is the man whom you teach, Lord. This is what I speak, I proclaim, I expose. Who listens to me? I know who they are: Blessed is the man whom you teach, Lord. The one to whom God speaks in his heart, and when I remain silent, he is the blessed one whom you will teach, Lord, and instruct him with your law. As follows? Up to this point we have sung: and you will instruct him with your law. May you keep him serene in the dark days while the grave is dug for the sinner. Such is the man whom the Lord teaches, such is the one who learns from the Lord through the law, who

promissum per Prophetam, reddítum per Dominum Prophetarum. Testamentum illud quod dicitur Vetus, legite, et videte. Lex Dei data est etiam tune, legite, vel audite quando legitur, et videte quae ibi promissa fuerint. Promissa est tibi terra terrae; terra fluens lacte et melle; thirst tamen terra. Verumtamen si intellegamus spiritualiter (quando non illa terra fluxit lacte et melle), alia est terra quae fluet lacte et melle; terra illa de qua dicitur, Spes mea es tu, portio mea in terra vivostium (Ps 141,6). Haec enim terra morientium est. CAPUT II.—Lac et mel quaeritis? Tústate et videte quam suavis est Dominus (Ps 33,9). Gratia eius significata est nomine lactis et mellis: dulcis et nutritoria est. Haec autem gratia in Vetere Testament figurata, in Novo revelata. 2. Legis veteris servitus, cum Deus colitur propter terrena.—Denique Lex illa, propter eos qui car[168]naliter sapiunt, et talia praemia quaerunt a Deo, et propter illa Deum colere volunt quae ibi promissa sunt, audire meruit ab apostólo Paulo, quia ad servitutem generat (Gal 4:24). Quare? Quia carnaliter intellegitur a Iudaeis. Nam spiritualiter intellecta, Evangelium est. Ergo in servitutem generat. What? Qui propter bona terrena Deo serviunt. Quando illis adsunt, gratias agunt; when desunt, blasphemant. Qui enim propter ea Deo serviunt, vero corde serve non possunt. Attendant enim eos qui Deo nostro non serviunt: vident enim eos habere

propter quod ipsi Deo serviunt; et dicunt in corde suo, Quid mihi prodest quia Deo servio? Numquid habeo tantum, quantum ille qui quotidie blasphemat? Orat, et esurit; blasphemat, et tuctat. Qui ad ista attendit, homo est; homo est from Testament Veteri. Qui vero in Testament Novo Deum colit, novam hereditatem debent sperare, non veterem. If novam hereditatem speras, terram transí, trace vertices montium; hoc est, contemne fastigium superborum. CAPUT III.—Sursum cor.—Sed quando contempseris et calaveris, humilis esto, ne de altitudine cadas. Audi, Sursum cor: sed ad Dominum, non contra Dominum. Omnes superbi sursum cor habent, sed contra Dominum. Si autem vis tu veré sursum cor habere; ad Dominum habe. Si enim ad Dominum habueris cor sursum, ipse tenet cor tuum, ne cadat in terram. 3. Dies maligni ab initio peccati.—Beatus ergo vir, Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine. Ecce loquor, ecce clamo, ecce expono. Who heard me? Scio qui me audiunt: Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine; cui Deus in corde loquitur, et quando ego taceo, ipse est beatus quem tu erudieris, Domine, et ex lege tua docueris eum. Quid sequitur? Huc usque cantavimus: Et ex lege tua docueris eum. Ut mitigates eum a diebus malignis, doñee fodiatur peccatori fovea. Ipse est vir qui eruditur a Domi-
Commentary on Psalm 93:12

He remains serene in the dark days while the grave is dug for the sinner. Listen to what it's about. The days are bitter. Have we not lived unhappy days since we were expelled from paradise? Our ancestors regretted their times and so did their predecessors. No man liked the times in which he lived, but those who come after him like the times of their ancestors and these, in turn, liked those days in which they did not live; This is why they found them flattering. The present produces a more penetrating sensation. I am not saying that it is closer, but that the heart experiences it every day. Every year, ordinarily, when we feel the cold, we usually say: “It has never been so cold; "The heat has never been so great," even though it is the same as always. But blessed is the man whom you teach, Lord, to keep him serene in the dark days while the grave is dug for the sinner. 4. Unfortunate days. Are these days that mark the course of the sun unfortunate? Evil days are caused by evil men; This is how almost everyone is. Among a crowd of evildoers a handful of grain groans. Let us come to the righteous. The unjust are evil and cause unhappy days. What to say about the righteous? Do they not experience evil days? Let us leave aside those who suffer because of the evil men among whom they groan; When you go inside, reflect on yourself, penetrate into the depths of your being, examine yourself well. They will find dark days in themselves.

They don't want war, they want peace — and who doesn't? —. But although no one wants war and everyone desires peace, also those who live justly, when they turn their eyes inward, find war within themselves. Ask me what kind of war. Blessed is the man whom you teach, Lord, and instruct with your law. Behold, a man asks me what kind of war the righteous suffers within himself. Teach him, Lord, with your law. The Apostle speaks: The flesh has desires contrary to those of the spirit, and the spirit desires things contrary to the flesh. Where will I throw the meat if the war cry sounds, if—God forbid—the enemy falls on me? Man flees, but wherever he goes he carries war with him. Notice that I do not say: "If it is bad." Even if he is good, if he lives justly, he finds in himself what the Apostle says: The flesh has desires contrary to those of the spirit and the spirit desires things contrary to the flesh. How come there are good days in this war?

no, ipse est qui ex lege Dei discit a Domino, qui mitigatur a diebus malignis, doñee fodiatur peccatori fovea. Audit quid sit. Maligni dies sunt. Numquid istic, ex quo de Paradiso proiecti sumus, malignancies dies agimus? Et maíores nostri planxemnt dies suos, et avi eorum planxerant dies suos. Nulüs hominibus dies placuerunt, quos vivir egerunt. Sed posterís placent dies maiorum: et illis iterutn illi dies placebant, quos ipsi non sentiebant, et ideo placebant. Quod enim praesens est, aerem habet sensum. Non dico, propius admovetur; sed cor tangit quotidie. Omni anno pterumque dicimus quando frigus sentimus, Nunquam fecit tale ftigus; Nunquam fecited such aestus. Semper facit ipse qui facit. Sed beatus vir quem tu erudíeris, Domine: ut mitiges eum a diebus malignis, doñee ¡odietur peccatori fovea. CAPUT IV.—4. Maligni dies unde.—Maligni dies. Numquid isti dies maligni sunt, quos agitat circulus solis? Faciunt malignancies dies maligni homines: et sic est prope totus munclus. inter turbas malignorum gemit paucitas ftumentornm. Revocemus ad ipsos [169J iustos. Maligni sunt illi, et faciunt malignancies dies: quid ipsi iusti? nonne in diebus malignis sunt et apud se ipsos, praeter quod patiuntur malignas homines, Inter ouns gemunr? Et apud se ipsos, inquam, quando sunt, attendant se, descendant in se, bene se considerant; inveniunt in se dies malignantes.

5. Then there are unhappy days. But let's stay calm. What do we mean by this? Let us not be angry with divine judgment. Let's tell him: It has been good for me to have humiliated myself so that I can learn your justifications. You banished me from paradise, you threw me away from happiness. I live in affliction, between moans. My moan is not unknown to you. But it has been good for me to have humiliated myself so that I can learn your justifications. On bad days I learn to look for the good days. What are the good days? Don't look for them now.

Bellum nolunt, pacem volunt: et quis non? Et cum omnes bellum nolint, et omnes pacem velint, revocat ad se oculos et qui iuste vivit, et bellum in se invenit. Quaere a me quod bellum. Beatus homo quem tu erudíeris, Domine, et ex lege tua docueris eum. Ecce homo quaerit a me, quod bellum in se patiatur iustus; twelve illum ex lege tua, loquatur Apostolus: Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum et spiritus adversus carnem (Gal 5,17). Et ubi proicio carnem, si sonet bellum; yes, quod Deus avertat, hostis irruat? Fugit homo, et secum trahit bellum suum, quocumque it. Non díco, si malus est: prorsus si bonus est, si iuste vivit, invenit in se quod Apostolus dicit, Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem. In isto bello quomodo sunt dies boni? CAPUT V.—5. Dies maligni piis prosunt ad inveniendos dies bonds.— Ergo maligni sunt dies: sed mitigemur. What is it, Mitigemur? Divine judgment non irascamur. Dicamus illi: Bonum est mihi quoniam humiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas (Ps 118,71). De paradiso elisisti, de beatitudine proiecisti: in aerumna sum, in gemitu sum, gemitus meus non est absconditus a te. Sed bonum est mihi quoniam humiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas. In diebus malis disco quaerere dies bonds. Who sunt dies boni? Nolite illos moda quaerere: mihi credite, immo mecum credite, non invenietis. Transibunt dies mali, et venient boni: sed boni venient bonis, malis peiores.
Commentary on Psalm 93:12

The bad days will pass and the good days will come. But good days will come for the good; for the bad ones, worse days. 6. And now I ask you: Who is the man who desires life? I know that everyone's hearts will answer me: "Who is the man who does not want life?" I add: and who loves to see good days? You all answer: "Who is there who doesn't love to see good days?" You have responded well. You love life, you love good days. Certainly when he said: Who is the man who loves life?, any man would answer: "I." Who is the man who loves to see good days? Is not each one of you silently saying, “I”? Listen to what follows: Restrain your tongue from evil. Say now: "I." Seek forgiveness; Now I will find you. The past has already passed. If your tongue had been evil, if you had been a gossip, a informer, a slanderer, a curser: if you had been all these things, let these things pass with the evil days, but do not you pass with them. There is something you can hold on to so you don't pass. Humanity flows like a river, and bad days also flow like a river. Hold on to the wood to avoid being dragged. The river certainly flows. All flesh is hay and all honor of the flesh is like the flower of the hay. He hurries, passes, the hay dries, the flower falls. What do I hold on to? The word of the Lord remains forever.

Seek the peace that we all desire in the mortality of this flesh, in the fragility of this same flesh, in this deceptive vanity. Everyone seek peace. Seek peace and pursue it. Where is? Where do I follow her? Where did it happen? Where does it go, to follow it? He passed by you, but he didn't stop at you. Who do I tell? To the human race; not to each one of you, but to the human race. The same peace passes through the human race. As she passed she cried out to heaven, according to the reading we heard yesterday. And where is he going? Listen to the Apostle. Referring to Christ he said: He is our peace, who made two things one. Peace is, then, Christ. Where is he going? He was crucified, buried, rose from the dead, ascended to heaven. This is where peace is headed. How am I going to follow her? Heart high. Listen how you have to follow it. Every day, in fact, we hear him in a few words when he tells you: Raise your heart. Meditate on it more deeply and follow it. But listen also more fully to follow the true peace, your peace, the peace that endured war for you, the peace that, enduring war for you, prayed for the enemies of peace and said, as He hung on the cross: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do. It was time of war, and peace sprang from the tree. Yes, it sprang up, but then what? He ascended to heaven. Seek peace. How should you follow it? Listen to the Apostle: If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; Taste the things above, not those of the earth. You are dead and your

7. So restrain your tongue from evil and your lips so that they do not speak lies. You, who wanted life, or better, who want life and good days, turn away from evil and do good. 6. Dies boni qua conditione propositi. Etenim et ego interrogates you. Quis es homo qui vult vitam? Scio omnium corda mihi responder, Quis enim homo qui non vult vitam? Addo, Et diligit videre dies bonds? Omnes responderis, Quis est qui non diligat videre dies bonds? Bene responderis; vultis vitam, vultis dies bonds. Certe when he said, Quis est homo qui vult vitam? omnis homo mihi responder, Ego. Quis est homo qui vult videre dies bonds? Nonne in silentio quisque vestrum dicit, Ego? Audi quod sequitur: Contine linguam tuam a malo (Ps 33, 13.14). Dec mode, Ego. Quaeris veniam: te inveniam mode. CAPUT VI.—Transierunt praeterita: fuerit lingua tua maligna, fueris susurro, fueris criminator, fueris calumniator, fueris maledicus; is omnia fueris. Topic: Commentary on Psalm 93,12-13. Date: After the year 396. Place: Basilica of Maiorum, Carthage. 1. We have just sung to the Lord: Blessed is the man whom you teach, Lord, and instruct him with your law, so that you keep him serene in evil days while the grave is dug for the sinner. Therefore, the man instructed by the Lord in the law of God—not the one instructed in the law of God, but the one instructed in it by the Lord—remains serene, while a grave is dug for the sinner. In this world, the happiness of the wicked becomes a pit for sinners. Men, especially the pious, tend to be disturbed by this fact, and those who do not dare to reproach the Lord marvel inwardly that the wicked ordinarily live happily. Those who feel most disturbed are those who, knowing that they live with greater honesty, are

In it he was rich who said: The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it from me. The Lord gave it to me; Let the devil not boast: the Lord took him away from me. Hear it too. Continue like this: Store up for yourself a good foundation for the future, in order to achieve true life. 1. The psalm which we have sung to the Lord, by which we have exhorted each other to worship Him and to fall down and weep before our Maker, invites us to seek more diligently what those words mean: Who made us. No one doubts, unless they are ungrateful, that man was created by God. We know, in fact, because we have read and believed it, that God, among the many things he created, created man in his image. This is the first creation of man; the first human creature. I do not believe, however, voce dicetur: Ego autem sicut olive fruitful in domo Dei (Ps 51,10). This, as I said, no Christian doubts, because God not only created the first man from whom the rest were born, but he himself also creates each of the men today; He, who said to a certain saint of his: Before I formed you in your mother's womb I knew you. Well, he didn't help us and then he abandoned us. He didn't worry about making us and he didn't worry about keeping us. Liberum arbitrium sine Deo quid valeat.—Hoc moda This entire sermon is directed against the Pelagians. For them, being fair or not depends on human will, without the actual intervention of God being necessary. More specifically, of the three moments that he distinguishes in each action, power, willing and realization, Pelagius considers that only the first comes from God, while the other two are due to man. We must thank God for giving us free will and the law to be able to choose good or evil; What happens from there is all the work of man. Intellegite, sapite hoc quod audistis, quantum sit et quale cogitate, et de Deo maiora sentite. Vincit iíle omnem luzem, vincit omnem sonum, vincit omnem intellectum. As it is written, only God is truthful, for every man is a liar. If God is truthful, indeed, the only truthful one, and, on the contrary, every man is a liar, how can man become truthful if not by approaching him who is not a liar? In fact, men are told: Once you were darkness: behold, every man is a liar. To God, however, it is said: In you is the source of light; In your light we will see the light. And since only God is truthful, because God is light and in him there is no darkness, men are darkness, God is light; Man is a liar, God is truthful. When will man become truthful? Come close to him and you will be enlightened. This is what Scripture wanted to demonstrate: that every man, without excluding any, in everything that is his, is a liar; For he is not a liar except in what is his own, and he has nothing of his own except in being a liar. We do not affirm that it cannot be true, but rather that it cannot be true by itself. Therefore, to be truthful: I believed and therefore I spoke. Eliminate the belief; then every man

Topic: Commentary on Psalm 117,1. Date: Pentecost Vigil. As for the year, the opinions of scholars vary greatly: from 397 to 418. Place: Basílica Restituta, in Carthage.

1. We have been warned, and the Spirit of God has commanded us to praise God. We are also given the reason to do it: Because it is good. Although said in a few words, it contains a very deep thought. Praise, he says, the Lord. And as if asking: "Why?" he continued: Because it's good. What more do you want? Or are you looking for something else? Of what goodness? Good has so much power that even the bad guys seek it. For the other things that are called good, from some other good mendacio suo, quoniam qui loquitur mendacium, from suo loquitur (lo 8,44). Dec ergo: Quid retribuam Domino pro omnibus quae retribuit mihi? (Ps 95,12). In Pavore enim meo dixi, et verum dixi: omnis homo mendax (ib., 11). Sed retribuit mihi, non poenam pro mendacio, sed bonum pro malo, et iustificando impium fecit de mendace veracem.
«CONFITEMINI DOMINO, QUONIAM BONUS ES T »

CAPUT I. — 1. Bonus a se solus Deus, a quo cetera bona.—Admoniti sumus, et Spiritu Dei praeceptum est nobis, ut confiteamur Domino: et ea causa dicta est confitendi Domino, quoniam bonus est. Breviter dicitur, quod profundissime cogitatur. Confitemini, inquit, Domino. Et tanquam quaereremus, Quare? responsum est, Quoniam bonus est. Quid plus quaeris, aut si aliud quaeris, quam bonum? Tanta vis est boni, ut bonum quaerant et mali. Sed alia quae dicuntur bona, ab aliquo bono habent ut sint bona: si autem quaerimus omnia bona a quo habent ut sint bona;

They receive being good. And if we inquire from whom all good things receive their being good, let us remember: God made all things and behold, they are good. Therefore there would be no good being if it had not been made by him who is Good. And for what good? For the one that no one has done. There would be no good if it had not been done for Good, which has not been done. Heaven is good, but it is a created good; Angels are good, but created good; Good are the stars, the sun, the moon, the succession of night and day, the seasons, the evolution of the centuries, the course of the years, the shoots of herbs and trees, the nature of animals and, among all these things, man, the creature that can praise. All this is good, but it is a created good. Everything is good because of God, not for itself. He who did this is the Good above all things, for no one created him good, but he is good by myself. And not only for himself, but also for us it is good. Therefore praise the Lord for he is good. 2. Confession is proper to one who praises or one who repents 1. There are some so little educated that, as soon as they hear the word confession in the Scriptures, as if it could only refer to the confession of sins, they immediately begin to beat their chests, as if they were admonished to confess sins. But, so that your charity may know that confession does not refer only to recognizing oneself, recolamus quod dictum est, Et fecit Deus omnia, et ecce bona valde (Gen 1:31). Nullum igitur esset bonum, nisi factum esset a bono. Is there a quali bonus? Quod nullus fecit. Nullum ergo bonum esset, nisi a bono factum esset, quod factum non est. Bonum caelum, sed factum bonum: boni Angelí, sed facti boni: bona sidera, sol et luna, alternatio noctis et diei, temporum vices, volumina saeculorum, cursus annorum, germina herbarum et arborum, naturae animalium, et Inter haec omnia creatura laudattix homo; omnia bona, sed facta bona; et a Deo bona, non a se. Qui fecit haec, super omnia est bonus: quia nullus eum fecit bonus, sed a se ipso bonus est. Nec tamen sibi solí, sed et nobis bonus est. Confitemini ergo Domino, quoniam bonus est. [186] CAPUT II.—2. Confessio duplex, laudantis et paenitentis.— Confessio aut laudantis est, aut paenitentis.

Sunt enim parum eruditi, qui cum audierint confessionem in Scripturis, tanquam nisi peccatorum esse non possit, continuo tundunt pectora; velut iam moneantur confiten pec1 The term confessio has had several meanings in ancient Christian Latin. To the first one, used especially in the context of persecutions, which was equivalent to confessing the faith (confessio fidei), was added that of confessing sin (confessio peccati) and, finally, that of praise (confessio laudis), the latter meaning specifically biblical and which maintains a particularly venerable place in ancient Christian Latin. As an example, suffice the Confessions of the holy preacher. See C. MOHRMANN, The neto Latin Psalter: its diction and slyle, in Studes sur le latin des chrétiens I I p.122-123.

sinner, let us listen to one of whom we can never doubt that he had no sin at all; He exclaimed and said: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. Who said this? He who committed no sin nor was deceit found in his mouth; the only one who could truly say: Behold, the prince of the world is coming, and he will find no sin in me. However, he confesses. But this one who confesses is one who praises, not a sinner. Finally, listen to what he confesses. Listen to the praises, because they are our salvation. What does the sinless Son confess to God the Father? I confess to you, Father, he says, Lord of heaven and earth, because you hid this from the wise and prudent and have revealed it to the little ones. This is the praise that the Father addressed: that he hid such things from the wise and prudent, that is, from the proud and arrogant, and revealed them to the little ones, that is, from the weak and the humble. 3. It is true that there is also a healthy confession of sins. This is why we hear in the psalm that was read before: Put, Lord, a lock on my mouth and a door of temperance around my lips, so that you will not let my heart be inclined to evil words, seeking excuses for my sins. Ask God to put a lock on his mouth. He also exposes and says what he wants to be protected from. There are men, and there are certainly many, who as soon as they begin to be accused are quick to look for excuses. Excusing is looking for causes and motivations why it appears that sin does not taste. Sed ut noverit Caritas vestra, non ad sola peccata pertinere confessionem, audiamus illum, de quo dubitare non possumus quod nullum omnino habebat peccatum, exclamantem et dicentem, Confiteor ubi, Pater, Domine caeli et terrae. Quis hoc dixit? Qui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore eius (1 Petr 2,22): qui solus verissime dicere potuit, Ecce venit princeps mundi, et in me nihil inveniet (lo 14,30). And also confitetur. Be confessor iste, laudator est, non peccator. Denique audi quid confiteatur, audi laudes: et laus ipsa salus est nostra. Quid enim confitetur Deo Patri Filius sine sine? Confiteor tibi, inquit, Pater, Domine caeli et terrae, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revealsti ea parvulis (Mt 11,25). Istam laudem commendavit Patris, quia abscondit haec a sapientibus et prudentibus, id est, superbis et arrogantibus; et revealit ea parvulis, id est, infirmis et humilibus. CAPUT I I I. — 3.

Confessio peccatorum ad salutem necessaria.—Sed quod verum est, est etiam salubris confessio peccatorum. Unde audimus in Psalmo qui primo lectus est, Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium continentiae circum labia mea, ut non declines cor meum in verba maligna, ad excusandum excusationem in peccatis (Ps 140,3 et 4). Rogat Deum, ut custodym det ori suo: et cuius rei custodym exponit et dicit. Sunt enim nomines qui valde abundant; qui cum coeperint accusari,

belongs to you. There is one who says: "The devil did it to me"; another: "Luck was the cause"; a third: "I was forced by fate." Nobody attributes it to themselves. When you want to be your excuser, then your accuser triumphs at your expense. Do you want your accuser, that is, the devil, to suffer and lament? Do what you heard, do what you learned, and say to your God: I said, Lord, have mercy on me; Heal my soul because I have sinned against you. I, the psalm states, I said; Neither the devil, nor luck, nor fate said it. I said; I do not excuse myself, but I accuse myself. I said: take pity on me, heal my soul. Where does your illness come from? Because I sinned against you. 4. Then praise the Lord because he is good. If you are willing to praise, when will you feel safer than when you praise the good? If you want to praise, if you want to utter a confession of praise, what thing can you praise more surely than the Good? And if you want to confess your sins, to whom can you do it more safely than to the Good? You confess to a man and, because he is bad, you are condemned; But if you confess to God, since he is good, you remain purified. If you pay attention to the confession of praise, your intention must be fully devoted to everything that you have to praise profusely, to demonstrate that what you praise is good. Good things are truly praised just as bad things are rightly reviled. You condensed your praise to your Lord in a very short phrase: He is good. If you are also good, praise him for the reason why you are good; but if you are bad, praise him currunt he will excuse himself. Excusare autem est causa quaerere, et causationes innectere, quare ad se non videoatur pertinere peccatum. Alius dicit, Diabolus mihi fecit: alius dicit, Fortuna mihi fecit: alius, Fato compulsus sum: nemo ad se. Cum vis esse excusator tuus, triumphat de te accusator tuus. Vis ergo faceré quod doleat et gemat accusator tuus, id est diabolus? Fac quod audisti, fac quod didicisti; et dic Deo tuo, Ego dixi, Domine, miserere mei; sana animam meam, quoniam peccavi tibi (Ps 40:5). Ego, inquit, ego dixi: non diabolus, non fortune, non fatum. Ego said: I do not excuse myself, sed accuso. Ego dixi, Domine, miserere mei; sana animam meam. Unde enim aegrotat? Quoniam peccavi tibi. 4. Utraque confessio, laudis et peccati, debita Deo. Confitemini ergo Domino, quoniam bonus est.—Si laudare vis, quid securius laudas, quam bonum? Si laudare vis, si confessionem laudis habere vis, quid securius laudas, quam bonum?

Si peccata tua confiteri vis, cui tutius quam bono? Homini, quoniam malus est, confiteris, et damnaris: Deo, quoniam bonus est, confiteris, et purgaris. Si confessionem laudis atiendas, quidquid copióse laudaturus es, circa hoc occupata est intentio tua, ut ostendas bonum esse quod laudas. Bona enim recte laudantur, sicut mala recte f 187J vituperantur, Breviter tibi dicta est laus Domini Deí tui, Bonus est,

also so that you are good. Well, if you are good, you are good because of him who is good; and if you are bad, you are only bad because of yourself. Flee from yourself and draw near to him who made you, because by fleeing from yourself, you follow yourself; and by following you, you join him who created you. 5. How many things do you desire, oh bad man! You are certainly bad. Tell me, what do you want but good? You don't want a horse if it's not good; You don't want a farm if it's not good; Likewise you want a good house, a good wife, a good tunic, good coats. And you only want to have a bad soul! But don't you realize that by being bad and seeking good things, you are contradicting yourself? If you are looking for good things, first be what you are looking for. And if, being bad, you found many good things, of what use will they be to you, since you lost yourself? Love your good souls and hate your bad souls. If you love him from whom all good comes, you too will be good. Hate your bad things, choose the good ones. 6. What does it mean to hate your bad things? Confess, repenting, your sins. Everyone who repents and confesses his sins becomes angry with himself, and, in some way, with repentance, he takes revenge on himself for what displeases him. God hates sin. If you also hate in yourself what God hates, you are already united to God by some desire, by hating in yourself the same thing that he hates. Let it be against you, CAPUT IV.—Si et tu bonus es, lauda unde es bonus: si malus es, lauda unde sis bonus. Si enim bonus es, ab illo bonus es: si malus es, a te malus es. Fuge te, et veni ad illum qui fecit te: quia fugiendo te, sequeris te; et sequendo te, haeres in eo qui fecit te. 5. Homo malus vult bona omnia praeter se ipsum.—Quanta bona quaeris, homo male? Certe malus is: dic mihi quid velis, nisi bonum? Equum quaeris, nonnisi bonum; fundum quaeris, nonnisi bonum; domum quaeris, nonnisi bonam; uxorem quaeris, nonnisi bonam; tunicam nonnisi bonam, caligam nonnisi bonam: animam solam malam. Nonne tibi ipse es contrarius, qui bona quaeris, cum sis malus? Si bona quaeris, prius esto ipse quod quaeris. Si autem malus fines bona invenisti, quid tibi prodest, quia tu peristi? Amate good spirits vestras: hate habete bad souls vestras. Be loving illum a quo est omne bonum, boni eritis. I hate habentes bad vestra, bona eligite. CAPUT V.—6. Peccatum puniendum aut a Deo aut ab homine paenitente.—Quid est, odio habere mala tua?

Paenitendo confiteri peccata tua. Omnis enim paenitens, et peccata sua paenitendo confitens, irascitur sibi; et quodammo paenitendo vindicat in se quod displicet sibi. Deus enim odit peccatum. Si et tu oderis in te quod et Deus odit, interim aliqua volúntate coniungeris Deo, dum hoc in te odisti quod odit et Deus. Saevi in ​​te, ut Deus intercedat tibi, et non damnet te. Peccatum enim

so that God looks out for you and does not condemn you. Without a doubt, sin must be punished. This deserves sin: punishment and condemnation. Sin necessarily has to be punished, either by you or by him. If he is punished by you, then he will be punished without you; If, on the other hand, he is not punished by you, then he is punished with you. Praise the Lord therefore, for he is good. Praise him as much as you can and love him as much as you can. Pour out your hearts in his presence; Well, God is our help, because he is good.

May you sing praising his gifts, may you shed tears for your sins, praise the Lord because he is good, because his mercy is eternal. Not only the remembrance of our sins, but also the praise of our Lord, is called confession 2, since, even when we do one of the two things, we do not do it without the other. For we accuse ourselves of our wickedness with the hope placed in his mercy, and at the same time we praise his mercy with the memory of our iniquity. Let us therefore praise the Lord because he is good, because his mercy is eternal. There are those who think that bad creatures exist because they offend the sense of the ignorant 3. But nothing could be more false. God made all things excellently good, because he is good. To others it seems that God is unjust 4 because many times his faithful have to endure hard and harsh misfortunes in this temporal life. But those who see this this way are mistaken, because he punishes every child, not the one who rejects, but the one who receives, because his mercy is eternal.

Topic: Commentary on Psalm 117,1. Date: Probably the eve of Pentecost in the year 397. Place: Probably Carthage. 1. Praise the Lord for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.' To what the Holy Spirit exhorted us through the words of the psalm, to which we responded hallelujah (which in Latin translates as praise the Lord), to this the Holy Spirit himself now exhorts you through our voice: Praise the Lord because he is good, because his mercy endures forever. Let it be sine dubitatione puniendum est: hoc debentur peccato, punitio, damnatio. Puniendum est peccatum, aut a te, aut ab ipso. Si punitur a te, tune punietur sine te: si vero a te non punitur, tecum punitur. Confitemini ergo Domino, quoniam bonus est. Laúdate quantum potestis, amate quantum potestis: effundí te coram íllo corda vestra, Deus adiutor noster (Ps 62,9); quoniam bonus est.
