Let us say all this in our confession, because, if there is something contrary to punish our mortality, he, because he is good, always works well. And if he corrects us with bodily pain and labor, he will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant forever, because his mercy endures forever. Is there anything more good than our God? Men blaspheme; and not only do they not humiliate themselves, but they even boast about their crimes. However, he makes the sun rise on the good and the evil, and makes it rain on the just and the unjust. Is there anyone more compassionate than our God? Men continue in their clumsiness and iniquities, and he never tires of calling them to conversion. Is there anything more good than our God, from whom we receive so much comfort even in tribulation? Who is more compassionate than he towards us, for if we convert, we can change the future sentence? Let us praise the Lord because he is good, because his mercy is eternal. Praise of anything is not authentic praise, but praise of the Lord our God. If it has been said with truth: How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!, he himself appears evil to those with a perverse heart. Who among men praises the Lord, because to him, now converted, he is good, who when he was perverse seemed bad to him; Who praises him, I repeat, except the one who became good from perverse, so that he begins to praise what he previously reproached and admire what he previously despised? And because by his own malice he was evil, and with the grace of God he has corrected himself, deliqui (Ps 118,67). Dicamus haec in confessione: quia, si quaedam supplicio nosttae mortalitatis adversa sunt, ille tamen bonum facit, quoniam bonus est. Et si temporalibus dolotibus et laboribus emendamur, non in finem irasceiur, ñeque in aeternum indignabitur (Ps 102,9): quoniam in saeculum misericordia eius. Quid tam bonum quam Deus noster? Blasphemant nomines, nec solum non humilantur, sed etiam superbiunt in sceleribus suis; et facit ille solem suum oriri super bonds et malo, et pluit super iustos et iniustos (Mt 5:45). Quid tam misericors quam Deus noster? Perseverant homines in flagitiis et facinoribus suis, et eos ille ad conversionem vocare non cessat. Quid tam bonum quam Deus noster, a quo et in pressura solacia tanta percipimus? Quid tam misericors quam Deus noster, cuius etfuturem sententiam mutati mutamus? Confiteamur Domino quoniam bonus est, quoniam in saeculum misericordia eius.

Non omnium rerum laudes confessiones sunt, sed laudes Domini Dei nostri. Si enim verissime dictum est, quam bonus Deus Israel rectis corde (Ps 72,1), malus utique videtur perversis corde. Quis autem hominum nisi ex perverso fit rectus, ut tamquam convictus laudare incipiat quod antea reprehendebat, et mirai quod antea contemnebat, confitens Domino, quoniam sibi iam recto bonus est, qui perverso videbatur malus? Et quoniam sua malitia perversus erat, ipsius autem gratia [41] correct
Commentary on Psalm 117:1

It is convenient for him to confess that his mercy is eternal. We are the bad ones; he, the good one; we are good because of him and bad because of ourselves. He is good to us when we are good, and He is also good to us when we are bad. We are cruel to ourselves, and he is compassionate to us. He calls us to conversion; waits for us to convert; He forgives us if we convert and crowns us if we do not depart from him 5. 3. Let us praise the Lord because he is good, because his mercy is eternal. The confession of sins always seemed worthy of fear to men, but before a male judge. Because many times whips, whips with straps, iron hooks and fire are used to extract a confession. And sometimes the limbs succumb sooner to the torments caused to break the bond of the body, than the spirit to the pains caused to divulge the secret of the crime. The executioners urge and increase all kinds of torments 6, but in vain the insides are opened and torn when the conscience is closed in the negative. Why is a man afraid to confess in the midst of such atrocious torments, if not because, after having confessed, he is usually punished? Anyone who confesses in front of a man is punished; But whoever confesses before God, he is free. And it is not surprising. Man seeks to know through man what he who seeks does not know. God, on the other hand, who commands us to confess, knows what we did not want to confess est, simul oportet confiteatur quoniam in saeculum misericordia eius. Nos mali, bonus ille: nos ab ipso boni, a nobis mali: bonus ille nobis bonis, bonus ille nobis malis. Nos saevientes in nos, ille misericors erga nos. Vocat, ut convertamur: expectat, doñee convertamur: ignoscit, si convertamur: coronat, si non avertamur. 3. Confiteamur Domino quoniam bonus est, quoniam in saeculum mercy eius. Confessio etiam peccatorum timenda semper hominibus visa est, sed apud hominem iudicem. Nam saepissime flagellis et quibusque verberibus, ungulis quoque et ignibus agitur, ut eruatur ore confessio; et aliquando prius cedunt membra tormentis, ut corporis compago solvatur, quam doloribus animus, ut secretum facinoris propaletur. Instant carnifices, crebrescunt omnia genera tormentorum; thirst frustrates laniando aperiuntur viscera, cum clauditur denying conscientia. Cur autem in tantis cruciatibus homo metuit confiten, nisi quia confessi solent puniri?

Qui confessus fuerit homini, punitur: Deo qui confessus fuerit, liberatur. Nec mirum. Quaerit homo ab homine quod ille qui quaerit ignorat; Deus autem, qui monet ut confiteamur, novit quod confiten nolebamus, nec Note the parallelism of the phrases, a skill of the former professor of rhetoric. See supplementary note 43: Torture, p.758,

and learns nothing from our confession. He who forgives us temporal death, how much more will he not free those who confess from eternal death, a death due to our sins, which he already knew before we confessed them? 4. You may say, "Why does God ask me to confess what he already knows?" When man demands this of man it is because he ignores it. Why do you think God does this, if not because he wants you to recognize the sin, to be punished by you and to be erased with his forgiveness? Because how do you want to be forgiven for what you don't want to acknowledge? Listen to what the psalm says, and if you are awake, recognize your voice in it: I acknowledged my sin and did not hide my iniquity. I said: I will declare my crime against me to the Lord, and you have forgiven the impiety of my heart. Hear the same thing in another psalm: For I acknowledge my iniquity and my crime is always before me. Therefore, it was not impudent to say to God, Turn your face from my sins. God deigns to look away from man's sin when man himself seeks to become aware of his sin, saying in God's ear: And my sin is always before me. For the same reason, it should not be understood that God turns his face away because he does not know sin, but because he forgives it. Therefore, if you, man, are afraid to confess to a judge-man because he is evil or because he is forced to comply with the severity of the law, confess safely to the Lord, because he is good and because his mercy is eternal. tune discit quando confessi fuerimus. Quanto ergo magis confitentes a sempiterna morte liberat, qui nostris iniquitatibus, quas et ante quam confiteremur noverat, a temporali morte parcebat. 4. Dicis fortasse: Quid a me quaerit Deus, ut confitear quod ipse iam novit? Nam homo, ab homine cum hoc quaerit, ignorat. Quid whores, nisi quia Deus vult, a te ut peccatum tuum cognoscendo puniatur, et ab illo ignoscendo solvatur? Nam quomodo illum cupis ignoscete, quod tu non vis agnoscere? Audi psalmum, et, si evigilas, advette ibi vocem tuam: 'Peccatum, inquit, meum cognovi, el faetnus meum non operui. Dixi, proloquar adversum me delictum meum Domino, et tu dimisisti impietatem coráis mei (Ps 31,5). Audi in alio psalmo: [42] Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego agnosco, et delictum meum ante me est semper (Ps 50,5). Non itaque impudenter dicebat Deo, averte faciem tuam a peccatis meis (ib., 11).

Tune enim ab hominis peccato faciem Deus digntur avertere, cum homo ipse ad peccatum suum faciem suam curat advertere, ut in Dei auribus dicat, et peccatum meum ante me est semper. Nec ideo dicitur Deus avertere faciem, quia non cognoscit, sed quia ignoscit. Si ergo propterea times, homo, confiten homini iudici, quia malus est, aut quia severitatem legis implere compellitur, securus confitete Domino, quoniam bonus est, quoniam in saeculum misericordia eius,
Topic: Parallelism between Ps 118,133 and Rom 7,14. Date: Between the year 412 and 416. Place: Basilica Tricilarum,

1. Without a doubt, brothers, the one who said Direct my steps according to your word and let no evil dominate me, wanted to remove a great burden and a heavy bondage of iniquity. Let us see, then, when man is dominated by evil, to understand what we hear from the mouth of the person praying and what we ourselves have prayed when responding. As I think, we have all responded to the holy psalm with pious and truthful affection, praying and saying to our God: Direct my steps according to your word and let no evil dominate me. From the terrible slavery of this tyrant we have been redeemed with precious blood. And what did it profit him to have received a law that commands and commands, but does not help, so that we are prisoners under its dominion before the grace of God arrives? In vain does he threaten the law when it is iniquity that dominates. The law is not corporal; It is not carnal. As God who gave the law is spirit, so the law is, without a doubt, spiritual. What is it
DE VERBIS PSALMI 118: «GRESSUS MEOS DIRECTS», ETC. ET APOSTOLI (Rom 7): « LE X SPIRITUALIS EST, EGO AUTEM CARNALIS», ETC. AGAINST PELAGIANS

CAPUT I. — 1. Iniquitatis in hominem dominatus ante gratiam.—Sine dubio, fratres, gravem quamdam sarcinam et grave iugum iniquitatis vitare cupiebat, qui Deo dicebat: Gressus meos direct secundum verbum tuum, et non dominetur mihi omnis iniquitas (Ps 118,133). Videamus ergo quando homini dominetur iniquitas; ut intellegamus quid orantem audierimus, et quid responding etiam nos ipsi oraverimus. Omnes enim ad sanctum Psalmum, quan[188]tum arbitror, ​​devotee et veraci corde responderimus, orantes et dicentes Domino Deo nostro: Gressus meos direct secundum verbum tuum, et non dominetur mihi omnis iniquitas. Ab huius pessimae dominae dominatu, pretioso sanguine redempti sumus. Et quid proderat Legem accepisse iubentem ac minantem, et non adiuvantem, ut sub illa essemus rei ante gratiam Dei? Frustra Lex minatur, quando iniquitas dominatur. Lex enim non est corporalis, non est carnalis: sed quoniam Deus spiritus est qui Legem dedit, procul dubio Lex S. Ag. 7

What does the Apostle say? We know therefore that the law is spiritual, but I am of flesh, sold to the power of sin. Do not be surprised, oh sold to sin!, if the one to whom you are sold dominates you. Listen to the apostle John: Sin is evil. Against this tyrant we invoke the Lord when we say: Let no evil dominate me. 2. The sold man screams; listen to the redeemer. Man gave himself over to the dominion of evil through free will and received as a price the small pleasure of the forbidden tree. It is he himself who cries: Direct my paths, which I have crooked; direct my steps, those that I lost with my free will. Lead them according to your word. What does it mean: direct them according to your word? May my steps be straight, because your word is also straight. «I, he says, am bowed under the weight of evil; but your word is the standard of truth. Correct me, crooked, according to your rule, that is, according to your word. Therefore direct my steps according to your word, and let no evil dominate me. I sold myself, rescue me; I sold myself with my free will; rescue me with your blood. Let pride be ashamed in the seller and grace glorified in the redeemer. For God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. 3. The law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold to the power of sin. I don't know what I do, because I don't do what I want. I don't do what I want, says the carnal; does not accuse spiritualis est. Sed quid ait Apostolus? Scimus enim quia Lex spiritualis est; ego autem carnalis sum venumdatus sub peccato. Noli ergo mirari, o venumdate sub peccato, si tibi dominetur cui es venumdatus. Audi apostolum loannem: Peccatum iniquitas est (1 lo 5,17). Contra talem ergo dominam invokemus Dominum, cui dicimus: Gressus meos direct secundum verbum tuum, et non dominetur mihi omnis iniquitas. CAPUT II.—2. Captivitas hominis ex peccato.—Venumdatus clamat, redemptor exaudiat. Ipse homo se vendidit per liberum atbitrium sub dominant iniquitate, et accepit pretium exiguam de arbore vetita voluptatem. Ipse ergo clamat: Itinera mea directs, quae ego distortioni: Gressus meos directs, quos ipse meo arbitrio depravavi: directs secundum verbum tuum. Quid est, direct secundum verbum tum? Ut recti sint gressus mei, quia rectum est verbum tuum. Ego, inquit, distortus sum sub pondere iniquitatis, sed verbum tuum est regulate veritatis: me ergo a me distortum, correct tanquam ad regulam, hoc est, ad verbum rectum.

Ergo, Gressus meos direct secundum verbum tuum, et ne dominetur mihi omnis iniquitas. Sold me, redeem me: sold me arbitrio meo, redeem me sanguine tuo. In venditore erubescat superbia, in redemptore glorietur gratia. Deus enim superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Iac 4,6). 3. Adversarius gratiae refutatur experiment propriae infirmitatis.— Lex enim spiritualis est; ego autem carnalis sum, venumdatus sub peccato. Quod enim operor I ignore: non enim quoí flew ago. Non quod flew ago,
Parallelism between Ps 118,133 and Rom 7,14

to the law, but to himself; because the law, which is spiritual, is guiltless; It is the sold carnal man who incurs guilt. He doesn't do what he wants. When he wants he can't, because when he could he didn't want to. By wanting evil, good lost its power. Already in captivity, he speaks and says: I don't do what I want. I do not do the good that I want to do, but the evil that I hate, that is what I do. Not what I want. A man contradicts you: "You certainly want it." I don't do what I want. “You completely do what you want.” I don't do what I want. Believe me, brother, I don't do what I want. «Oh, if you wanted it, I believe you would do it; but you do not do good because you do not want to! » I don't do what I want. Believe me, my brother, I know what happens inside me. I don't do what I want. You are a contradictor of grace 1, not a judge of conscience. I know that I don't do what I want, and you say: "you do what you want"? No one knows the innermost part of man, but the spirit of man that is in him. 4. You are also a man. If you don't want to believe me, pay attention to yourself. Do you live in a corruptible body that burdens the soul, so that the flesh has no desire against the spirit nor the spirit against the flesh? Is this strife not taking place within you? Is there not within you a lust of the flesh that resists the law of reason? If nothing in you resists the other part, think about where the one and the other are. If your spirit does not disagree with your flesh, which desires the opposite, be careful, lest your reason go in accordance with your flesh; think that carnalis dicit: non Legem, sed se accusat. Nam Lex spiritualis non habet culpam: carnalis venumdatus incurrit in culpam. Non agit quod vult: cum vult non potest, quia quando poterat noluit. Per malum velle, perdidit bonum posse; et captivus iam loquitur, et dicit captivus; Non quod flew ago. Non enim quod voló, jacio bonum: sed quod odi malum, hoc ago (Rom 7,14,15). Non quod flew. Et contra homo: Vis prorsus. Non quod flew ago. Omnino quod vis, agis. Non quod flew ago: crede mihi, frater, non quod flew ago. O si velles, ageres: quia non vis, non agis bonum. Non quod flew ago: crede mihi, novi quid in me agatur; non quod flew ago. Contradictor gratiae, non es arbiter conscientiae: ego me novi non quod voló agere, et tu dicis: Quod vis agis? Nemo scit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est (1 Cor 2:11). [189] CAPOT III.—4. Lucía carnis et spiritus.—Et tu homo es; si non vis credere mihi, intende tibi.

Itane tu ita vivis in hoc corruptibili corpore, quod aggravat animam (Wis 9:15), ut caro non concupiscat adversus spiritum tuum, et spiritus adversus carnem tuam? Is this rixa non est in te? Nulla est concupiscentia carnis, quae resistat legí mentis? Si nihil in te alteri resistit, vide totum ubi sit. Si spiritus tuus a carne contra concupiscente non dissentit, vide ne forte carni mens tota consentiat:

Maybe there is no war because there is a perverse peace. Perhaps you agree on everything with the flesh and that is why there is no strife. What hope do you have of ever winning if you haven't started fighting yet? If, on the other hand, you delight in the law of God according to the inner man, you see another law in your members that is repugnant to the law of your reason; If you delight in the latter, if you feel yourself bound by it, free in mind and a servant in the flesh, if this is already the case, pity the man who says: I don't get what I want. Do you want that concupiscence to reside in you that is diametrically opposed to your reason? If you do not want to deprive yourself of such an enemy, you are a man of evil desire. I, I confess, want to totally eliminate everything that is revealed against my reason and litigates with contrary delight, everything that exists of such in me. If, with God's help, I do not consent to it, I do not want to have anyone to litigate with. For me it is much more desirable not to have an enemy than, having one, to defeat him. Is not that movement by which the flesh desires against the spirit mine? Or am I actually made of a different nature? The movement is mine, and the resistance to which I do not consent is also mine. I have a free part that resists the relics of slavery. I want to be whole and healthy, since everything is me. I do not want my flesh to be separated from me forever, like a stranger, but to be healed all with me. If you don't want this, I don't know what you think of meat. I think that you judge that I do not know where it comes from, as if it came from enemy people. This is false, it is heretical, vide ne forte ideo non sit bellum, quia pax perversa est. Forte in totum carni consentís, et mile rixa est. Quam spem habes quod possis aliquando vincere, qui nondum coepisti pugnare? Si autem condelectaris legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem, vides autem aliam legem in membris tuis repugnantem legi mentis tuae (Rom 7,22,23); si hac condelectaris, hac ligaris, liber es in mente, servus in carne: si iam ita est, compatere potius homini they say ti: Non quod flew ago. Tu enim non vis ut concupiscentia illa quae resistit mentí tuae, omnino non sit in te? Mali voti homo es, si tali adversary non vis carere. Ego, fateor tibi, quidquid in me rebellat adversus mentem meam, et litigat mecum delectatione Contra, quidquid tale in me est, omnino interficere flew. Et si ei forte adiuvante Domino, non consentio; nolo habere cum quo litigem. Multo est mihi optabilitus, inimicum non habere, quam vincere.

Neque enim illud ipsum quod caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, non est meum: aut vero ex contra natura compactus sum? Et illud meum est, et quod ei non consentio, meum est. Pars aliquantum liberates, resistit reliquiis servitutis. Totum sanum sit flew, quia totus sum ego. Nolo ut a me caro mea, tanquam extranea, in aetemum separetur, sed ut mecum tota sanetur. Si hoc tu non vis, nescio quid de carne you felt: arbitror te putare nescio quid unde sit, quasi of contrary people. Falsum est, haereticum est, blasphemum
Parallelism between Ps 118,133 and Rom 7,14.

It is blasphemous, because only one is the author of the mind and the body. When he created man, he did one thing and another, and he united both in unity: he subjected the flesh to the soul and the soul to him. If the former is always obedient to its master, the latter will also always be submissive to its owner. Do not marvel if the one who abandoned the superior suffers punishment from the inferior. The flesh has desires contrary to those of the spirit and the spirit contrary to those of the flesh. They wage war on each other so that you don't do what you want. Therefore Paul says: I do not do what I want, because the flesh desires against the spirit and I do not want it to have these desires. It is a great thing for me not to consent; However, I wish to lack desire itself. Then I don't do what I want. I want the flesh not to desire against the spirit, and I cannot. This is what I have said: I don't do what I want. 5. Why do you slander me? I say: I don't do what I want; and you say: "You do what you want." Why do you slander me? Ungrateful to the doctor; why do you slander the sick person? Let me pray to the doctor: Rescue me from the slanders of men and I will keep your precepts. I will keep them for your redemption, not for my power. Therefore, I do not attribute salvation to myself, which I do not yet possess, but I ask it of the doctor. You, on the contrary, defender of nature 2, I wish you were!, not presenting a false defense of the healthy one, but begging the doctor for the not yet healthy one; you, defender of nature, better yet, enemy of it, while pareest: mentís et carnis unus est artifex. Ipse quando hominem creavit, utrumque fecit, utrumque coniunxit: carnem animae subdidit, animam sibi. Si semper illa staret sub Domino suo, semper et ista oboediret dominae suae. Noli ergo mirai si ea quae deseruit superiorem, poenas patitur per inferiorem. Caro enim concupiscit adversus spiritum, spiritus autem adversus carnem. Haec enim, inquit, invicem adversantur, ut non ea quae vultis faciatis (Gal 5:17). Inde et iste: Non quod flew ago. Concupiscit enim caro adversus spiritum, et nolo concupiscat: pro magno habeo si non consentiam, opto tamen ut caream. Ergo, Non quod flew ago. Flew enim ut non concupiscat caro adversus spiritum, et non possum: hoc est quod dixi: Non quod flew ago. CAPUT TV.—5. Naturae falsus ingratus medical defender.—Quid mihi hic calumniaris? Ego dico: Non quod flew ago; et tu dicis: Quod vis agis. Quid mihi calumniaris?

You ungrateful doctor, why did you slander me? [190] Sine ut medicum rogem: Redime me a calumniis hominum, et cus. todiam legem tuam (Ps 118,134). Custodiam per redemptionem tuam, non per potestatem meam. Ideo mihi sanitatem, quam nondum habeo, non arrogo; quia medicum rogo. Your autem naturae defender; quod utinam esses, non quasi sanae defensionem falam adhiberes, sed pro nondum
The Pelagian. See supplementary note 42: Christian grace, p.758.

While you praise the creator for healthy nature, you actually exclude the savior of the sick. He who created healthy nature that fell by himself, raises it by himself. This is the faith, this is the truth and this is the foundation of the Christian faith. One and one. A man through whom ruin came and another through whom our settlement came. For the first, the collapse; for this second, the rebuilding. He who did not remain standing fell; he who never fell lifts him up. He who abandoned him who stands firm has fallen; and he who stands firm descended to him who was lying on the ground. 6. If, then, the flesh has desires against the spirit, so that in this very case you do not do what you want, since you want it not to do this and you cannot do it, at least keep your will attached to the grace of God and persevere firmly with his help. Tell God what you sing: Direct my steps according to your word and let no evil dominate me. What do you mean: let no evil dominate me? Listen to the Apostle: Let sin reign in your mortal body. And what is queen? To obey your desires. He did not say, "Have no ill wishes." How can I not have evil desires in this mortal flesh, where the flesh desires against the spirit and the latter against the former? Accomplish this: Do not reign sin in your mortal body to obey its desires. If such desires exist, do not obey them so that iniquity does not dominate. Do not make your bodies sana medicum rogares: I never see your naturae defender, vel potius oppugnator, dum quasi de natura sana laudas Creatorem, excludis a languida Salvatorem. Qui creavit, sanat; ruentem per se ipsam, levat per se ipsutn. Ipsa fides est, ipsa veritas, hoc est christianae fidei fundamentum. Unus et unus: unus homo per quem ruina, alius homo per quem structura; per illum ruina, per hunc structura. Cecidit qui non mansit, erigit qui non cecidit. Ruit ille quia resignit manentem, manens ille descendit ad iacentem. 6. In lucía carnis et spiritus quid faciendum.—Si ergo concupiscit caro adversus spiritum, ut in hoc ipso non quod vis agas, quia vis ut non concupiscat, et non potes; teñe saltem in gratia Domini voluntatem, et in eius adiutorio persevera: dic ei quod cantasti: Gressus meos direct secundum verbum tuum, et ne dotninetur mihi omnis iniquitas. Quid est, ne dominetur mihi omnis iniquitas? CAPUT V.—Audi Apostolum: Non regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore. Quid est: Non regnet? Ad oboediendum desideriis eius.

Non dixit: Noli habere desideria mala. Quomodo enim in hac carne mortali, ubi caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem non habeo desideria mala? Illud ergo fac. Ñon regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore ad oboediendum desideriis eius. Etsi sunt desideria, non eis oboediatur, ne iniquitas dominetur. Nec exhibitatis membra vestra weapon
Parallelism between Ps 118,133 and Rom 7,14

weapons of injustice at the service of sin. Do not let your members become weapons of evil and you will not be dominated by any iniquity. But even that, that your members do not become weapons of iniquity, do you earn it with your strength? I repeat: do you give it to yourself? Even if they do not become weapons of evil, there is still evil within those members, in those illicit desires, even if they do not reign. How are they going to reign if they don't have weapons? A part of you, your body, the lust of your flesh, rebels against you because of illness. That languor is a tyrant. If you want to be victorious over your tyrant, invoke Christ the emperor. 7. I already know what you were going to say to me or what you are saying to yourself. Whoever you are, you who listen to me, I also know what evil is dictating to you internally. When you do not recognize the rescue of the redeemer, you have not yet freed yourself from the yoke of evil. I know what you are saying to yourself: “Look, my flesh desires against the spirit; desires adultery, but does not consent to it, I do not approve of it nor decide to do it. Not only do I not commit it, but I also do not consent to committing it; Not only do I not commit it externally in the flesh, but I do not even follow the rebel with my thoughts. Do I consent to that enemy, do I go after him when he fights? I don't do any of that. You see that no evil dominates me. Is that so? It's true? If so, thank the one who granted you that it is so. Do not want to arrogate this to yourself, lest you lose what you have received and begin to pray in vain. Have you not iniquitatis peccato (Rom 6:12). Non fiant membra tua arma iniquitatis, et non dominetur tibi omnis iniquitas. Sed etíam hoc, ut non fiant membra tua arma iniquitatis, numquid tu tibi viribus tuis praestas? Hoc ipsum, inquam, hoc ipsum quod non fiant membra tua arma iniquitatis, tu tibi praestas viribus tuis? Cum enim non fiunt membra tua arma iniquitatis, est quidem iniquitas in membris tuis, in desideriis illicitis, sed non regnat. Quomodo regnat, qui arma non habet? Pars tua, caro tua, concupiscentia carnis tuae languore rebellat adversus te. Languor iste tyrannus est: si vis te tyranni esse victorem, Christum invokes imperatorem. 7. Gratiae adversarius sub iugo est iniquitatis.—Nam scio quid mihi eras dicturus, vel quid apud te ipsum moda dicas. Quisquís talis hic es, et audis me, scio quid tibi intus loquatur iniquitas. Adhuc enim sub iugo es iniquitatis, quando non agnoscis pretium Redemptoris. Scio quid tibidicas.

As we really should be, we must understand that we are all included: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. As they went, they cried, throwing the seed; When they return they will come singing, bringing their sheaves. Where are they going and where are they coming from? What do they sow with tears? What seeds are they? What bundles? They go to death, they come from death. They come when they are born, they come when they are resurrected, sowing good works, collecting an eternal prize. Because our seed is all the good things we do; our bundles, what we will receive in the end. If the seed is good, if the works are good, what is the reason for tears, since God loves a joyful giver? 2. Consider, first of all, dearly beloved, that these words refer mainly to the martyrs. No one has spent as much as those who spent themselves, as the apostle Paul points out: I also will spend myself for your souls. Confessing Christ, they spent themselves; also fulfilling with his help what is said: You sat at a sumptuous table, know that it is appropriate for you to prepare similar things. What is the sumptuous table, but that on which we receive the body and blood of Christ? What does it mean, know that it is appropriate for you to prepare similar things, if not what Saint John says: In the same way that Christ gave his life for us, we must also give our lives for our brothers? Look how much they spent. But did he certainly perish?

ron, if they received from the Lord the security of even a hair? Will the hand perish when not even the hair perishes? Will the head perish when not even a hair disappears? Let us therefore always sow with good works, while we have time, because the Apostle says: He who sows sparingly will reap very little. Who isn't forced to get going since they entered life? A child is born and, as he grows up, he is on the move; His death is the end of the road. You have to reach the end, but with joy. Who is there who does not cry on this evil path of ours, when the same newborn begins life with tears? The psalm wants to recommend the prayers of the saints, those of pilgrims, those of those who are weary in this world, those of lovers, those of those who cry, those of those who are constantly sighing for the eternal homeland until, once seen, those who are now despondent are satisfied. Truly, my brothers, while we live in the body, we are pilgrims far from the Lord. A pilgrim who does not cry does not desire the homeland. Shed tears if you want what you don't yet have. They have become bread to me: they comforted the groaning, they satisfied the hungry. My tears were my bread day and night. As? When I am constantly told: Where is your God? What righteous person has not shed those kinds of tears? He who has not cried has not regretted being a pilgrim. With what face does someone who did not sigh arrive to the homeland?

Daos tells how he sings against Goliath, who boasted of himself, and recommends you to David, who, appearing weak before men, was very brave with the help of God. What is man? Here it says what man is: Since you have manifested yourself to him. Then the whole man exists: if God manifests himself to him; but, if it is not revealed to him, man is nothing. What is a man to whom God has not manifested himself? Man is similar to vanity; His days pass like a shadow. Then what is man, since you have manifested yourself to him, and the son of man, since you value him? What do you mean you appreciate him? That it pleased you to choose him and place him in a very high and sublime position by virtue of your goodness, not his merits. chordarum psallam tibi, iam cantore in praeceptis, hoc est hilariter praecepta rompiere. CAPUT IX.—9. De suis viribus ne homo praesumat.—Et ut noveritis. fratres, quia gratia hoc implet, nemo debent de viribus suis praesumere: hoc est enim praesumere de gratia Dei. Vocat enim te Deus, et iubet ut facias: sed ipse dat vires, ut quod iubet, impleri possit. Tibi autem capax fides adhibenda est, ut inundatione gratiae humilies te, supplices Deo, nihil de te praesumas; spolies you Golia, induas David. Ad hoc pertinet quod in eodem psalmo dicitur, quod iam commemorare coeperamus, Quid est homo? Hoc enim monet, ne de se praesumat homo. Nam videte quomodo incantat adversus Goliam, qui de se praesumebat; et commendat ibi David, qui infirmus in hominibus, in Deo firmissimus erat. Who is homo? Et dicit quid sit homo: Quoniam innotuisti ei. Hoc est totus homo, si innotescat illi Deus: si autem non illi innotescat Deus, nihil est homo. Quid est homo, cui non innotuit Deus? Homo vanitati assimilatus est, dies eius velut umbra praetereunt.

Ergo, Quid est homo, quoniam innotuisti ei; et filius hominis, quoniam aestimas eum? Quid est, do you estimate eum? Placuit tibi elect illum, et constituere in aliquo superiore et eminentiore loco: misericordiae tuae est, non meritorum ipsius. 10. Seek what is unique about man; you will find sin. Look for what is unique about man; you will find the lie. Erase sin, and everything you find in man is a gift from God. Therefore, let no man love what is his 5. What the Apostle says can also refer to this: let no one seek what is his. Sometimes they hear this from readers and believe that they have the right to steal other people's property. Distinguish who tells you: "Do not seek what is yours." Sometimes a bad advisor says it; other times, a good doctor. God is the good doctor. When you hear him say, "Do not seek what is yours," don't take it that way. Something good is what God advises you. What we said: "seek what is yours", refers to your sin. Do not seek sin and do not seek what is yours. Do not look for lies and do not look for what is yours. The truth comes from God; the lie, of yourself. 11. When the devil occasionally suggests something to you, he imprisons those who consent, but he does not force those who do not want to. He does not seduce or drag anyone, except those whom he finds in some way already similar to him. Find someone who desires something, and the desire opens the door to the devil's schemes. He admonishes you to achieve what you see you want. Enter man through these two doors: that of desire and that of fear. Close them and in this way you fulfill what the Apostle said in

Today's reading: Don't give the devil a chance. With these words the Apostle meant that, if the devil enters and takes possession, it is because the man opened the door for him to enter. 12. Since the man to whom God has not manifested himself and whom he does not esteem is nothing, he gives him his grace, finding in him something punishable and forgiving him everything when he recognizes himself as a sinner, to crown him when he believes. What did God find in men when he came, but something to condemn? That's how it is; Think and see, brothers, how both among the Israelite people and among the Gentiles he found nothing that was not worthy of punishment. Therefore, he wanted to descend to sinners in a humble way, not as a judge, to forgive them, first offering mercy by forgiving sins and then being able to show his severity by punishing sin. Let us not abuse, that is, let us not misuse, his mercy, and we will not experience the rigor of his justice. Thus, everything that man is comes from God manifesting himself to him. That he grants him his grace, the one that David boasted about. Goliath, arrogant, puffed up, conceited of himself, of his strength, was the first to put on his own person the weight of the total victory of the entire army of which he was a part. And since all pride is characterized by audacity of face, he was knocked down by the stone that hit his forehead. Thus the forehead that contained the impudence of his pride was destroyed and the one that carried the humility of the cross of Christ conquered.

CAPUT X.—10. Proprium hominis nihil nisi peccatum et mendacium.—Quaere quid sit hominis proprium, peccatum invenies. Quaere quid sit hominis proprium, mendacium invenies. Tolle peccatum, et quidquid consideraveris in homine, Dei est. Non ergo amet homo quod proprium est. Etiam ad hoc potest pertinere illud quod dicit Apostolus: Nemo quod suum est, quaerat (1 Cor 10:24). Aliquando enim audiunt illud homines a Lectoribus, et aedificantur ad auferendas res alienas. Interest quis tibi dicat, Noli quaerere quod tuum est. Aliquando enim dicitur a malo suasore, aliquando autem dicitur a bono doctore. Deus bomas est doctor. Quando ergo audis a Deo, Noli quaerere quod tuum est; noli sic accipere, quomodo dici solet. Aliquid boni est, quod te monet Deus. Quod dicebamus, quaere quid sit tuum, invenies peccatum. Noli ergo quaerere peccatum, et non quaeris tuum: noli quaerere mendacium, et non quaeris tuum. Veritas enim a Deo est, mendacium abs te. CAPUT XI.—11. Duae ianuae diabolo tentatori, cupiditas et timor.— Et si diabolus aliquando aliquid suggerit, consentientem tenet, non cogit invitum. Non enim seducit ille aut trahit aliquem, nisi quem invenerit ex aliqua parte iam similem sibi. Invenit enim eum aliquid cupientem: et cupiditas aperit ianuam intranti suggestioni diaboli. Invenit illum aliquid timentem, monet ut fugiat, quod illum invenit timere; monet ut adipiscatur, quod illum invenit cupere: et per has duas ianuas cupiditatis

Ibi enim voluit ostendere Apostolus, quia quamvis intret et possideat diabolus; homo illi tamen locum dedit, ut posset intrare. 12. Reos omnes Christus invenit.—Ergo quia nihil est homo cui non innotuit Deus et quem non aestimat Deus; dat illi gratiam suam, inveniens in illo quod damnet, et donans omnia confitenti, ut coronet credentem. CAPUT XII.—Quid enim invenit Dominus in hominibus quando venit, nisi quod damnaret? Omnino, fratres, cogitate et videte; sive in the populo Israelitarum, sive in Gentibus, non invenit nisi quod damnaret. Et ideo ad peccantes humilis voluit vinore, non iudex, cum parcit illis, ut primo praerogaret misericordiam donando peccata, et sic postea redderet severitatem puniendo peccata. Non abutamur, id est, non male utamur misericordia eius, et non sentiemus severitatem eius. Ergo hoc est homo totum, quod ei innotescit Deus, quod dat illi gratiam suam, unde praesumebat David: Golias autem de se, de viribus suis, superbus, elatus, inflatus, primo totam victoriam universae partis suae in se uno constituit. Et quia omnis superbia habet impudentiam frontis, in ipsam frontem lapide veniente deiectus est. Evacuata est frons quae habebat impudentiam superbiae suae; et vicit frons quae habebat humilitatem crucis Christi.

13. For the same reason, we also wear the sign of the cross on our foreheads. Who can understand this? I tell you this, brothers, because there are many who sign themselves with it and do not want to understand. God seeks creators of his signs, not merely painters. If you carry on your forehead the sign of Christ's humility, you also carry in your heart the imitation of his humility. We also said, brothers, that he who opens the doors of desire and fear gives entry to the devil. But what desire and what fear is it about? We desire the kingdom of heaven and are afraid of hell. But in the same way that those doors, the desire for temporal things and the fear of temporal punishments frequently draw in evil and give way to the devil, so the desire for eternal things and the fear of equally eternal punishments make room in the heart for the word of God. 14. Briefly, brothers, if we want to live well, let us love what God promises us more than what this world promises us. Let us also fear more what God threatens us with than what this world threatens us with. Is what I have told you too much or too long? You are presented with the temptation of some fraud; You want to cheat to get money. God promises those who do not steal the eternal kingdom of heaven. The desire for money overcomes you. But who doesn't want the kingdom of heaven? However, to desire earthly things more is to sin; To sin is to love what is present more, not to believe what is in the future; wanting more what man sees and not

to desire what God promises, since what man sees can be taken away from our eyes, can be lost; But what God promises us cannot at the moment be contemplated with the carnal eye, and when someone manages to obtain those promises they no longer fear losing them, because there is no one more powerful than the one who grants them. Therefore, brothers, adhere with love to the promises of God, and thus the desires of this world will not overcome you. 15. Now the temptation of fear comes to us. Anyone can tell you: "Witness falsely for me." First he promises you something; and if you do not let yourself be carried away, if you put the promises of God before the insinuations of men, greed will not overcome. He tempts you with threats and begins to put horrible things before your eyes. Maybe he is one of the powerful people in the city, one of the potentates of this world. It seems that he is capable of carrying out his threats. You are overcome by the fear of imminent evil, from which God could certainly deliver you, if it seemed to him that it would be for your good; and if I didn't want to push it away from you, you should understand that I wouldn't allow it to happen to you if I didn't know that it was useful to you. God himself removed the fire from three boys. Has God changed because he did not spare the martyrs the sword? The same was the God of the three boys as that of the Maccabees. The first escaped from the fire; the latter were tormented with him. Both, however, through the eternal God. They did not appreciate their temporal life, nor did the others allow themselves to be defeated by temporal threats.

CAPUT XIII.—13. Crucis signum in fronte quid significet-—Propterea et nos signum ipsum crucis in fronte portamus, qui illud intellegit. Hoc dico, fratres, quia multi illud faciunt, et intellegere nolunt. Factorem quaetit Deus Signorum suorum, non pictorem. If you bear in fronte signum humilitatis Christi, bear in corde imitationem humilitatis Christi. Diximus autem, fratres, eum daré locum diabolo, qui illi aperit ¡anuas cupiditatis aut timoris: sed cupiditatis cuius, aut timoris cuius? Nam et regnum caelorum cupimus, et gehennam timemus. Sed quomodo illae ianuae, cupiditas rerum temporalium, et timor poenarum temporalium trabit plerumque ad nequitiam, et dat locum diabolo: sic cupiditas rerum aeternarum, et timor poenarum aeternarum facit locum in corde verbo Dei. CAPUT XIV.—14. Cupiditatis tentatio.—Breviter ergo, fratres, si volumus bene vivere, plus amemus quod promittit Deus, quam quod promittit hic mundus; et plus timeamus quod minatur Deus, quam quod minatur hic mundus. Numquid magnum aliquid aut longum est quod diximus? Venit tentatio tibi alicuius fraudis, vis faceré fraudm, ut acquiras pecuniam: promittit Deus fraudm non facientibus sempiterna regna caelorum, vincit te cupiditas ad pecuniam. Nam quis est qui nolit regna caelorum? Sed plus velle terrena, hoc est peccare: plus velle quod praesens est, non credere quod futurum est; plus [202] velle quod videt homo, et non desiderare quod promittit Deus: cum id quod videt homo,

etiam ab oculis potest auferri, etiam possessum potest amitti; id autem quod promittit Deus, nec oculo carnis videri interim potest; et cum quisque ad Dei promissa pervenerit, non timet ne amittat; quia nemo est potentior illo qui dedit. Itaque, fratres, haerete caritate promissis Dei; et non vos superabunt cupiditates saeculi. CAPUT XV.—15. Timoris tentatio.—Rursum timoris tentatio advenit: dicit tibi quisque, Dic pro me falsum testimonium. Primo promittit: sed cum non deceperit, si forte praeponas promissa Dei pollicitationi hominum, non vincit cupiditas; per comminationem tentat, et incipit minari horribilia. Potens est forte in civitate, potens in saeculo, videtur posse faceré quod minatur. Vincit te timor praesentis mali: quod et posset a te utique Deus avertere, si hoc illi videretur prodesse tibi; et si nollet avertere, intellegere duties quia non tibi permitteret evenire, nisi et hoc sciret prodesse tibi. Avertit ignem a tribus pueris idem Deus. Numquid mutatus est Deus, quia non avertit gladium a martyribus? idem ipse Fuit Deus trium puerorum, qui Fuit Machabaeorum. Illi de igne evaserunt (Dan 3), illi ignibus cruciati sunt (2 Mach 7): utrique tamen in Deo sempiterno vicerunt. 16. Therefore, do not be afraid of the man who threatens you. Well, what is man? Akin to vanity, his days pass like a shadow. Consequently, either it will not harm you and that shadow will pass before it can send its sting to you; God can do everything. Or, if it were allowed to harm you, it will only temporarily harm your shadow, that is, what is transitory to you, your temporary life, your old life. Because until the very moment of death we carry something of the old man. He can harm you in your temporal life, but no one can take away your eternal life; He will be able to remove the impediment that keeps you here; but you will be united to God, with whom you were already in relationship, first by faith and then by charity. 17. Therefore it is elegantly said in the psalms about the wicked man: Like a sharp razor you deceived. In this way the spirit of God mocks him. What do you see special about the knife? Not that men can perish through it, but the end for which it was made. It was manufactured to cut hair. What is more superfluous in the story than these? With how much diligence, with how much care, with what thoroughness, with how much effort he sharpens to shave the hair! The evil man behaves in the same way: He moves away, thinks, rethinks, thinks again, puts deception upon deception, looks for tricks, prepares assistants, buys false witnesses: he sharpens the knife. What are you going to do with the righteous, but shave off what is superfluous?

18. In this way, brothers, if you want to be prepared to fulfill the will of God - something that I recommend to you and that I recommend first of all to myself; Furthermore, he who speaks with confidence recommends it to all of us, if we want to be willing to fulfill the will of God, let us not love the fleeting things of this life, let us not think that what is called happiness in this world is happiness. Those foreigners believed the same thing. They put all their happiness in the temporal and all their sweetness in a shadow, not in the light itself, not in reality itself. Pay attention to the last words of this psalm, written against Goliath. They are very clear words, in very simple language, such that they do not need an interpreter or commentator. By the mercy of God they are so clear that no one can say: «Look, he said this as he wanted; he interpreted it according to his wit; "He understood it however he wanted." They are written like this so that no one finds excuses. They were given by David who spoke, that is, for a new life, the life of Christ, a life that was given to us through him, despising the old life, the old happiness of men, and despising those who place their hope in it and those who obtain it and rejoice in it.

CAPUT XVI.—16. Bono malus nihil veré nocet, sed prodest.—Itaque noli timere hominem minantem tibi. Quid est enim homo? Vanitati assimilatus est; dies eius sicut umbra praetereunt. Aut non tibi nocebit, et ante transitibit illa umbra, quam ad te aculeus eius transiré potuerit; potens est enim Deus: aut si permissus fuerit nocere, ad tempus nocebit umbrae tuae, id est, rei transitoriae tuae, vitae temporali tuae, vitae veteri tuae. Usque enim ad ultimum mortis portamus aliquid veterís hominis. Temporalem vitam ille nocere potest, aeternam tibi vitam nenio potest auferre. Tollet tibi impedimenta, quibus hic teneris; et haerebis Deo, cui te iam praemissa spe, caritate colligaveras. CAPUT XVII.—17. Homo malus novacula acuta.—Propterea in Psalmis elegantissime dicitur de homine malo, Sicut novacula acuta fecisti dolum (Ps 51,4). Sic illi insultat-Spiritus Dei. Quid attendit in novacula? Non quia occidi homines de novacula possunt: ​​sed ad quam rem facta est novacula. Facta est autem ad radendos capillos. Quid tam superfluum in corpore, quam capilli? How much instantia, how much study, how much caution, how much intentione acuitur, ut raddat capillum? Sic et homo malus tollit se in partem, cogitat, recogitat, excogitat, ponit fraudra super fraudm, quaerit machinationem, ministers parat, false testes comparat, acuit novaculam. Quid facturus iusto, nisi superflua rasurus?

CAPUT XVIII.—18. congratulations non in temporalibus [203]ponerda.— Itaque, fratres, si vultis parati esse ad sequendam voluntatem Dei, quod vobis dicimus, et nobis primum dicimus; immo omnibus dicit ille, qui securus dicit: si volumus parati esse ad sequendam voluntatem Dei, non amemus ista quae transeunt, non putemus ipsam esse felicitatem, quae dicitur in hoc saeculo. Hoc enim putabant illi alienigenae; totam felicitatem in rebus temporalibus, totam suavitatem in umbra dondebant, non in ipsa luz, non in ipsa veritate. Ideo in isto psalmo, qui ad Goliam est, attendite posteriora Psalmi: oronino lucidissimis verbis et enodatissimo sermone, qui non quaerat interpretem aut expositorem; thirst mercy Dei ita sunt posita, ut nemo dicat, Ecce hoc quomodo voluit dixit, et pro ingenuity suo interprétate est, sensit ut voluit: sic sunt posita, ut nemo se excuset. Posita sunt autem a David dicente, id est, a nova vita, Christi vita, vita quae per Christum nobis data est; insultans vitae veteri, felicitad veteri hominum, et illis qui in eam spem ponunt, et illis qui adípiscuntur eam, et in illa gaudent. CAPUT XIX.—19. Felicitas impiorum nonnullis scandalum. Superflua petens propiiio Deo non exauditur.—Videntur enim iusti laborare in hoc saeculo, et iniusti feliciter in hoc saeculo vivere: et quasi dormiat Deus, neglegens res humanoe, illi plerumque extolluntur impunitate, isti plerum-

What can he use in this way from the abundance of present goods, whether God took it from him or did not give it to him? Wouldn't this be an act of mercy? 21. However, someone will say, “I did well, I did not steal anything from anyone, and you did not listen to me. From what I own I give to the poor; I took nothing from anyone. I beg you, grant it to me. You ask for a farm as if it doesn't mean that someone else is left without it. If you were told: "Sell that property," you would be frightened as if faced with a curse and you would take it as an insult. You hold a grudge inside you because you heard from a man the invitation to sell it, as if you could buy it unless someone else sells it. And so, if it is a bad thing to sell, therefore to desire and long to buy, you look for a bad thing for another. You think it is a good thing to find a wallet full of money 8 lost on the street and, when you pick it up, you exclaim: "God put it at my hand," as if you could find something without someone else having lost it. Why do you not rather desire the other good riches, which everyone can possess together with you without any fear? You desire gold; You want justice better. You can't get gold if someone else doesn't lose it. Both of you embrace justice and live with it. 22. But let us return to the psalm so that you may understand, dearly beloved, what foreigners they are who judge that there is no other happiness than the present. Do you think you are worthy of God granting you all these things? Think about how you use them. If he has not granted them to you, know that it is beneficial rerum praesentium, ut auferat illi eam Deus, non illi eam det? Nonne tune est mercy? CAPUT XXI.—21. Cupiditas temporalium quomodo [204] in proxitnum iniqua.—Et dicet: Bene feci, et nihil alienum abstuli, et non me exaudisti: ex eo quod habeo do genti, non tollo alicui; Anyway, your day. Quasi vero det tibi villam, nisi alius perdat villam. Si dicatur tibi, Vendas villam tuam; tanquam maledictum exhorrescis, iniuriam tibi factam whores; odium servas in pectore, quia hoc audisti ab homine, ut vendees villam: quasi emere possis, nisi alius vendet. Itaque quod valde cupis emere, et optas emere, si malum est I will sell, alii malum quaeris. Bonum est invenire saccellum solidorum in via: quod cum inveneris, dicis, Deus mihi dedit; quasi possis invenire, nisi alius perdat. Quare ergo non optas illorum thesaurorum bona, quae tecum omnes sine anguish valeant possidere? Desideras aurum, desidera iustitiam. Habere aurum non potes, nisi alius amittat: iustitiam both complectimini, et both dilatamini. CAPUT XXII.—22.

It's your fault that the good Father does not give it to you. Because also when your son cries for you to give him a beautiful knife with a gold handle, no matter how much he kicks, you don't give it to him, because he can cut himself with it. Save me, Lord, from the hand of the children of foreigners, whose mouth utters vanities and whose right hand is a right hand of wickedness. And explains what is meant by vanity and what is meant by right. By the right of evil he understands the happiness of only this world. Not because it is not found in the good, but because these, when they possess it, possess it in the left hand, not in the right. In their right hand they have eternal happiness; the temporal one, on the left. The desire for eternal things and happiness should not be mixed with the desire for temporal things, that is, for present and temporary happiness. This is what it means: your left hand does not notice what your right hand is doing. Therefore, his right is the right of evil. 23. See how they speak vainly and how they have a wicked right. Let's all hear it; it suits you. Let us hear it so that you do not turn the ears of a merchant, since it was said to the servant: "You must give and I must demand." We also said yesterday 9 that we are the ones who give, but it is someone else who demands. Our sisters, not wanting to listen, act as if they did not want to tolerate the presence of the tax collector 10. Therefore, let no one take from here reasons for flattery

without reason. It is one thing not to have received and quite another to not have wanted to receive. Whoever rejects the gift of God, makes himself guilty of the refusal. As it was said to the servant administrator: "Why did you not give?", so it will be said to the servant for whose benefit the other was appointed administrator: "Why did you not give?" If there had been no one to give, you would have an excuse. There will be nothing to answer in God's judgment if the readers make themselves heard even if the commentators remain silent. The word of God is announced everywhere and it was rightly said: His voice spread throughout the earth; The heat of the word of God expands everywhere and there is no one who hides from its heat. Let us hear and act, brothers; and if we want to walk in hope, let's not make excuses. Often the beggar who asks for a coin sings the commandments of God to you at the door of your house.

scias quia prodest tibi quia non dat patet bonus. Quia et filius tuus quando plorat, ut des illi formosum cultellum manubrio deaurato; quantum vult ploret, non illi das unde laedatur. 25. See how he wants the man of new life to be, how he wants the man who belongs to the shepherd horns, to the grace of God and to the milk with which we nourish ourselves. Pay attention: His sons are like shoots rooted, his daughters are adorned in the likeness of the temple. Maybe this is why the sisters didn't want to listen to us. Well, whether they like it or not, they have to listen to us; Decide to come to the temple with the humility of David and not with the arrogance of Goliath. But will we have to explain these things? Are they dark? Men speak vanities and are considered foreigners. They do not belong to the kingdom of Christ, to the kingdom of him to whom we call Yadre ours. They are considered foreigners. What do you call happiness? His children, like well-rooted shoots, like descendants of descendants: «He has many children, a multitude of grandchildren; In case of death, he is calm. As if a disaster couldn't wipe out millions of men! His children, like well-rooted shoots. Let us grant that he has children like well-rooted shoots. Does it not often happen that the fire also burns the shoots in the forest? His daughters are adorned in the likeness of the temple. Their granaries are full, overflowing with fruits of all kinds, as we say to those who swim in abundance: “There is no room for more; "He doesn't know how much he has." A pantry is filled and still

there are plenty of fruits; Possessions abound, larders burst with one thing and another. 26. His sheep are fruitful, they multiply with their births. Few enter; They give birth and many come out: they multiply with their births. The year before there were so many; This year there are many more. He enjoys and is happy. Goliath becomes arrogant and, emboldened by this happiness, challenges him to a fight: «Who can defeat me? Who dares to fight with me? Don't men who swim in abundance say this? Doesn't everyone think about it daily within themselves? He owns a little more than his neighbor. Doesn't he also say: "Who can help me?" or "If my neighbor insults me, won't I stand up to him?" See if he is not representing Goliath, who challenges him to a fight. But David advances without any weapon of war, provided only with a few stones. Let the good man cast down all pride, as did the martyrs, who cast down the unjust. When these seemed to be victors, they were defeated, because in the former the devil, their leader, was defeated. 27. Consider that other happiness. His sheep multiply with lambing, his oxen are well fatted. There is no gap in the fence. This is usually done with stones. There is no gap or exit point in the fence. Everything is whole, everything perfect, everything in plenitude. There is no shouting in its squares either: there are no fights, everything is peaceful. Notice that he describes a happiness like that of the innocent, so that no one says to himself: "He said this about those who steal things."

CAPUT XXV.—25. Felicitatem saeculi quisquís magni pendil, alien est.—Videte qualem velit esse hominem de vita nova, qualem velit esse hominem ad vasa pastoralia pertinentm, et ad gratiam Dei, et ad lac quo nutrimur. Filii eorum sicut novellae constabilitae: quasi propago propaginís. He has many filias, many nepots; securus est adversus casus mortis. Quasi non millia hominum plerumque unus casus absumat. Filii eorum sicut novellae constabilitae. Ecce puta sint filii sicut novellae constabilitae: nonne aliquando etiam novellas silvis vicinas silvarum ignis absumit? Filiae eorum ornatae sicut similarity templi. I quote hinc transeamus: consulendum est modesty feminarum. Ipsae potius habendo cognoscant quid habeant, quod nos commemorando erubescimus. Filiae eorum ornatae sunt sicut similarity templi. Cellaria eorum plena, eructantia ex hoc in hoc. "others." It does not refer to this; Mention of such things is made elsewhere. It is very clear that criminals have to be punished. That rich man who was overtaken by a region of barrenness did not seek foreign fruits, and who, finding himself burdened by not having where to store worldly fruits and not seeing the poor in whom a treasure for heaven could be stored, said: I will destroy my barns; I will make bigger ones and fill them. Brothers, in the same way that in the Gospel the one who enjoys temporal happiness is insulted, even though it comes from private property and not from the theft of other people's things, in the same way in this psalm temporal happiness is despised so that the soul, renewed and regenerated by the grace of milk, learns to desire perpetual and everlasting happiness. See how the ideas are linked. His children, like well-rooted shoots. His daughters are adorned in the likeness of the temple. Their granaries, overflowing with fruits of all kinds. your. Videte qualem congratulatem quasi innocentium describat: ne dicat sibi quisque, Sed hoc dixit de illis qui rapiunt res alienas. Non est hinc dictum aliquid: alibi fit talium mentio. exit, nor shouting in their squares. They called the town that has all that happy. But who said it? Those whose mouth spoke vanity. They were described above. 28. And what do you say? Those called the town that has all that happy. What do I say? Blessed are the people whose God is the Lord. Therefore, the people are happy who, instead of adorned sons and daughters, instead of the fatness of oxen, instead of the fertility of sheep, instead of full barns, instead of firmness of houses, instead of peace, disputes and chieftainships; Instead of all this happiness, he wants to possess his God, to have the One who created all things, instead of possessing them, and to be able to say: It is good for me to be united with God. Beatum dixerunt populum cui haec sunt. Sed qui dixerunt? Quorum os locutum est vanitatem. Superius enim descripti sunt. CAPUT XXVIII.—28. Beatus populus quis.—Tu autem quid dicis? Nam illi beatum dixerunt populum cui haec sunt. Ego quidd? Beatus populus cuius est [207] Dominus Deus ipsius. Ergo ille est beatus populus, qui pro filiis suis et pro filiabus ornatis, pro crassitudine boum, pro fecunditate ovium, pro plenitude cellariorum, pro integrate aedificiorum, pro pace ac litibus et iurgiis civilibus, pro ista omni felicítate, Deum suum vult possidere, ut ipsum habeat pro omnibus, qui condidit omnia, et dicat, Mihi autem adhaerere Deo, bonum est (Ps 72,28): colat eum gratis; colat quando ista dat, et quando aufert, et quando non dat: et nihil sic timeat, quam ne ipse se auferat. Itaque christianus populus, fratres, qui dicit in corde suo, Quidquid vult auferat, se ipsum mihi non auferat, Beatus est populus, cuius est Dominus Deus ipsius.
Commentary on Psalm 143:9
XXXIII Topic: Commentary on Salt 143,9. Date: Between the year 405 and 411. Place: Unknown.

1. The reason why it is written: O God, I want to sing to you a new song, to sing for you on the ten-stringed harp, is because the ten strings of the harp are the ten commandments of the law.' Singing and chanting is usually the business of lovers 2. The old man is imbued with fear; The new one is in love. That is why we also distinguish two Testaments, one old and the other new, which, according to the Apostle, are prefigured in the two sons of Abraham, one of the slave woman and the other of the free woman: They are, he says, the two Testaments. Slavery belongs to fear; freedom, love. The Apostle says: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear; rather, you received a spirit of adopted sons that makes us exclaim: Abba, Father! John also says: In charity there is no fear; On the contrary, perfect charity drives away fear. Therefore it is charity that sings the new song. That servile fear rooted in the old man can

CAPUT I.—1. Caritate cantatur canticum novum.—Quoniam scriptum est, Deus, canticum novum cantabo ubi; in psalterio decem chordarum psallam tibi; decem chordarum psalterium, decem praecepta Legis intelleguntur. Cantare autem et psallere, negotium esse solet amantium. Vetus enim homo in timore est, novus in amore. Ita etiam duo Testamenta discernimus, vetus et novum, quae in allegoria dicit Apostolus etiam in Abrahae filiis figurari, one of ancilla, alter of libera: Quae sunt, inquit, duo Testamenta (Gal 4,22.24). Servitus enim pertinet ad timorem, libertas ad amorem. Dicit enim Apostolus: Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore; sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba, Pater (Rom 8:15). Dicit et Ioannes: Timor non est in caritate; sed perfect caritas foras mittit timorem (1 lo 4,18). Caritas
The same topic is discussed in sermon 9. In sermon 34,1 he will say: "Singing is an expression of joy and, if we think about it better, it is something proper to love."

have a ten-stringed psaltery, because the law of the ten commandments was also given to the carnal Jews, but they cannot sing the new song in it. He is subject to the law and is incapable of complying with it. He carries the musical instrument, but does not play it; The psaltery weighs him down, it does not serve as an ornament. Whoever, however, is under grace, and not under the law, he fulfills the law, because it is not a burden for him, but an honor; nor is it a torment for him who fears, but an adornment for him who loves. Ignited in the spirit of love, he now sings the new song with the ten-stringed psaltery. 2. Thus says the Apostle: He who loves another has fulfilled the law. For you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in these words: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor never causes evil. The fullness of the law is charity. The Lord, who had said: I did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it, gave the disciples this precept so that they could fulfill the law: I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. We should not be surprised if the new commandment sings the new song, because, as has been said, the ten-stringed psaltery symbolizes the commandments of the law, and the fullness of the law is love. The Apostle only wanted to remember a few chords, to understand the rest from them, when he says: You shall not commit adultery, no maergo cantat canticum novum. Nam timor ille servilís in veteri homine constitutus, potest quidem habere psalterium decem chordarum, quia et Iudaeis carnalibus data est ipsa Lex decem praeceptorum: sed cantore in illa non potest canticum novum; sub Lege est enim, et implere non potest Legem. Organum ipsum portat, non tractat; et oneratur psalterio, non ornatur. Qui autem sub gratia est, non sub Lege, ipse implet Legem: quia non est eí pondus, sed decus; nec tímenti tormentum est, sed amanti ornamentum. Spiritu enim dilectionis accensus, iam in psalterio decem chordarum cantat canticum novum. CAPUT II.—2. Lex impletur caritate.—Nam sic dicit Apostolus: Qui enim diligit alterum, Legem implevit. Nam, Non adulterabis, Non homicidium facies, Non furaberis, Non concupisces; et si quod est aliud mandatum, in hoc sermone recapitulatur, Diliges proximum tuum tanquam te ipsum. Dilectio proximi, malum non operatur. Plenitudo autem Legis, caritas (Rom 13:8-10).

Dominus etiam quia dixerat, Non vení ÍO/[208]vere Legem, sed adimplere (Mt 5,17); propterea tale mandatum discipulis dedit, unde Lex ab eis posset impleri: Mandatum, inquit, novum do vobis, ut vos invicem diligatis (lo 13,34). Non ergo mirum, si mandatum novum cantat canticum novum: quia, sicut dictum est, psalterium decem chordarum decem praecepta sunt Legis, et plenitudo Legis dilectio est. Commentary on Psalm 143:9

defects, etc. Because just as there are two commandments of love in which, says the Lord, all the Law and the Prophets are contained, making it very clear that love is the perfect fulfillment of the law, in the same way these ten commandments were given on two tables. Of them, it is said, three are written on one table and the remaining seven on another. As the first three refer to the love of God, so the remaining seven look to the love of neighbor. 3. This is the first of the three: Listen, Israel: the Lord your God is the only God, you shall not make idols or any other statues of what is in heaven above, nor of what is on earth below, and the rest of the things by which he determines the worship of the only God, abandoning fornication with idols. The second commandment is: You shall not take the name of the Lord, your God, in vain. The third refers to the observance of the Sabbath. I believe that all three, because they are a trinity, refer to the love of God. Because the unity of divinity takes its beginning from the Father; That is why the first commandment speaks above all about the only God. In the second we are warned not to consider the Son of God a creature, thinking that he is unequal to the Father. All creatures, says the Apostle, are subject to vanity. There we are commanded not to take the name of God in vain 4. The gift of God, which is the Holy Spirit, promises eternal rest,

figured in the Sabbath. Therefore we keep the Sabbath spiritually if we do not perform menial work. Also in their carnal sense they were prohibited to the Jews on the Sabbath day. And whoever wants to understand menial jobs spiritually, listen to what the Lord says: Everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin. Because sin is not only what appears to men as clumsy or unjust 5, but also everything that, having the appearance of goodness, is done only with temporal aims and not for the sake of eternal rest. Whatever anyone does, if it is done to gain a temporal reward, is a servile work, and therefore does not keep the Sabbath. We have to love God with selflessness; Nor can the soul rest except in that which it loves. Eternal rest will not be given except in the love of God, who alone is eternal. This is perfect sanctification and the spiritual Sabbath of Sabbaths. Therefore, since we are sanctified in the Holy Spirit, who is there who is not moved to understand this great mystery: that in the three commandments that refer to God, the third deals with the Sabbath? Of all the things that, according to Scripture, in the book of Genesis God did, only the seventh day, which means Saturday, was sanctified.

intellegantur, ubi ait, Nam, Non adulterabis, Non homicidium facies, etc. Nam sicut duo sunt praecepta dilectionis, ex quibus Dominus dicit totam Legem Prophetasque penderé (Mt 22,37-40), satis ostendens dilectionem esse plenitudinem Legis: ita ipsa decem praecepta in duabus tabulis data sunt. Tria quippe dicuntur in a tabula esse conscripta, et septem in altera. Sicut autem illa tria pertinent ad dilectionem Dei, ita septem cetera dilectioni proximi deputantur. CAPUT III.—3. Praecepta tria ad Deum pertinentia. Sabbatum spirituale. Sabbatum sabbatorum.—Primum est illorum trium: Audi, Israel; Dominus Deus tuus, Dominus unus est (Deut 6,4). Non facies tibí idolum aut cuiusquam similarityinem, ñeque quae in cáelo sursum, ñeque quae in terra deorsum; et cetera quibus ad unius Dei cultum relicta idolorum fornicatione constringit. Secundum autem praeceptum est: Non accipies nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum. Tertium, de observatione sabbati (Ex 20,2-11). Credo propter Trinitatem tria praecepta pertinent ad dilectionem Dei. Unitas enim divinitatis a Patre habet exordium: inde primum praeceptum of one Deo máxime loquitur. Admonemur autem secundo praecepto, ne Filium Dei creaturam putemus, si eum acceperimus inaequalem Patri. Omnis enim creatura, sicut dicit Apostolus, vanitati subdita est (Rom 8:20): ibi autem praecipitur, ne nomen Domini Dei riostri in vanum accipiamus. Iam vero donum Dei, quod est Spiritus sanctus, promittit

requiem sempiternam, quae sabbato figuratur: unde nos sabbatum spiritualiter observamus, si non faciamus opera servilia. Ab his enim etiam carnal intellectu Iudaeis sabbato prohibentur. Quia autem spiritualia vult intellegere opera servilia, audit Dominum dicentem, Omnis qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati (lo 8,34). CAPUT IV.—Peccatum autem non solum illud est, quod in turpi aut iniquo facto apparet hominibus; sed etiam si habeat speciem boni operis, et tamen propter mercedem temporalem fiat, non propter requiem sempiternam. Quodlibet enim quisque facit, si hoc animo facit, ut terrenum emolumentum consequatur, serviliter facit, et ideo sabbatum non observat. Free enim amandus est Deus: nec anima potest nisi in eo quod diligit, requiescete. Aeterna autem requies ei non datur, nisi in dilectione Dei, qui solus aeternus est; et ipsa est perfection sanctificatio, et spirituale sabbatum sabbatorum. mother. The second, this: Thou shalt not kill. The third: You will not fornicate. The fourth: Thou shalt not steal. The fifth: You will not bear false testimony. The sixth: You shall not desire your neighbor's wife. The seventh: You will not desire anything from your neighbor. The Apostle adapts perfectly to this order when he says: Honoring father and mother is the first commandment. It is investigated and it is not found that it is the first of the decalogue. This is the new song, the grace of the New Testament, which separates us from the old man who was made at the beginning of the earth, earthly. But what does he say through the prophet who thanks the grace of God for having reconciled us with God through the forgiveness of sins and for having renewed us by eliminating past old age? He extracted me, he says, from the depths of misery and the miry mire; He planted my feet on the rock, directed my steps and put a new song in my mouth, a praise to our God. This is the new song that sings with the ten-stringed psaltery. No one praises

You shout at God, or sing a hymn to Him, unless your words and actions are in harmony, loving God and your neighbor. Nor should the rebaptizing Donatists 6 think that they belong to the choir of the new song. This song is not sung by those who, due to their impious pride, have separated themselves from the Church that God wanted to spread throughout the earth. Also in another place the prophet says: Sing to the Lord a new song, sing to the Lord all the earth. He who does not feel solidarity with the whole earth in praise and does not depart from the old man, he does not sing the new song, he does not play the ten-stringed psaltery, because he is an enemy of charity, the only fullness of the law, which contains the ten commandments that refer to the love of God and neighbor.

If we praise Him on this pilgrimage, while we are passing through, how will we praise Him in the house from which we will never leave? Living a happy life, where God is contemplated without the slightest doubt, where he is loved without discomfort and praised without end, this will be our life: seeing God, loving him, praising him. If we already praise him when we believe, how will we praise him when we see him? How will vision praise him, if faith praises him in this way? The Apostle says: While we live in the body, we are pilgrims, far from the Lord; we walk in faith, not in vision. Now it is by faith, then it will be by vision. Now we believe what we do not see; then we will see what we believed. He who believes does not feel confused, because it is true that he will see. Our Lord first built faith in us. A poor Christian, of humble condition, who sighs with tears in the midst of daily fatigue, sees this and, perhaps, says in his heart: "What good is it for me to have become a Christian? Am I better than he who is not, than he who does not believe in Christ, than he who blasphemes against God? The psalm warns him: Do not put your trust in princes. What delights you, hay flower? All flesh is hay, says the prophet; He not only says it, but proclaims it. The Lord spoke aloud to him: Proclaim, he said. And he answered him: What shall I proclaim? All flesh is hay and all honor of the flesh is like the flower of the hay. The hay dries up, the flower falls. So does everything perish? No way. The Word of the Lord remains forever. Why does hay delight you? See he perishes. Do you want not to perish? Subject yourself to the Word. This psalm also tells us this. Perhaps the poor and humble Christian set his eyes on a rich and powerful pagan; He contemplated the flower of the hay and perhaps preferred to choose it as his protector rather than God. The psalm addresses this: Do not put your trust in princes or in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. say. We have already spoken of the thoughts of the impious, illustrious rich man, who dressed in purple and linen and feasted splendidly every day; With his death all his thoughts perished. The beggar Lazarus was at their doors, full of ulcers and wanted to be satisfied with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table, and no one gave them to him; The dogs came and licked his sores. I want to see you here, Christian. Both their lives have been exposed. God is powerful to give health in this life, eliminate poverty and grant what is necessary to the Christian. But if this did not exist, what would you choose: to be like the beggar or to be like the rich? Don't be fooled. Listen to the ending and notice which is the wrong choice. Without a doubt, that beggar, pious as he was and overwhelmed by temporal fatigue, thought that one day that life would end and he would reach eternal rest. They both died, but the thoughts of that beggar did not perish on that day. At his death it came to pass that he was taken to Abraham's bosom. That day all his illnesses were cured. And since Lazarus, a Hebrew word, translated into Latin means "helped," the psalm rightly warns: Blessed is he whom the God of Jacob helps. When your spirit goes out and your flesh returns to the land from which it came, your thoughts will not perish, because your hope is in the Lord your God. This is learned in the school of the teacher, who is Christ; This is what awaits the soul of the faithful believer; this is the true reward of the Savior. quia ibi scriptum invenit, itnmo ibi scribi iussit. Mortui sunt ambo, sed illius pauperis non illa die perierunt cogitationes. Contigit enim mori inopem illum, et auferri ab angelis in sinum Abrahae: in illa die sanatae sunt omnes cogitationes eius. Topic: Commentary on Prov 9:12 (according to the version of the Seventy). Date: Before the year 410. Place: Possibly Hippo. 1. If we listen carefully to the divine words, perhaps, and not without reason, what is written will draw our attention: Son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbor. If, on the other hand, you become evil, you will only hasten the evils. How can this be understood correctly? In the same way that we are happy about the honest life of our neighbor, it also saddens us when it is perverse. If one thinks that this was said as an exhortation, since the wise man is wise for the benefit of himself and those whom he invites to seek wisdom, why, if he becomes evil, only he will hasten the evils, since it has been said about the advice of such people: bad conversations corrupt customs? What else does the voice of charity affirm: If one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with him; And if one member suffers, do all suffer with him? It will find, with the help of the Lord, its solution if first of all we have as defined, fixed and immutable, and this with complete certainty, that no good will be good in the place of another and no evil will be bad in the place of another. This is why the Apostle says: Each one of us will carry his own burden. And in another place: Each of us will be responsible for ourselves. Again: Each one examines his work, and then he will find glory only in himself and not in another. The prophet Ezekiel says nothing else: The soul of the father is mine, the soul of the son is mine; The soul that sins will die. With this text he tries to explain that neither bad children will be able to rely on the goodness of their parents, nor will good children be oppressed by the evil of bad parents. Taking into account this statement, true and untouchable, made mainly for us, it only remains to find out what we are obliged to do by office; We will distinguish the effect of our salvation, which we desire, and the effect that our neighbor demands of us.
