Because you are good, you rejoice in the goodness of another, not with borrowed kindness, but with reciprocal love. In the same way, if you are bad, you are not bad because of the evil of others, but because of your own evil. And because of this your very evil you do not love your neighbor as yourself. You don't even love yourself. You love evil, your staunch enemy, which does not come to you from outside, but you yourself engender it within yourself. You encourage it against you so that it can more easily defeat you. Thus you clearly convince yourself that you hate yourself by loving the one by whom you are clumsily defeated. The divine word that says: He who loves evil hates his soul could not be wrong. 3. From this it follows that the good, by virtue of the goodness by which he is good, rejoices in the goodness and is saddened by the evil of others. Thinking about this neighbor - that is what is properly called whoever cares for you from close quarters, that is, whoever looks at you with mercy - if you were wise, you would be wise for yourself and for him. Not because he is going to be good for your good, but because to be good he has to be a lover of your good. If, on the other hand, you become evil, you will only hasten the evils, not with others. Nor will he be evil for your evil, but in the face of your evil he will be merciful. Your wickedness saddens him, but he does not incur his punishment. It makes him sad, but he does not participate in his injustice. Bad, you will only hasten evils, not in the company of your neighbor, because the sadness that the good person feels for you is for his good and for your evil. His sadness is an indicator of his love and your downfall. That is why it is written: Obey your leaders; They watch over your souls as those who have to give an account of them, so that they do so with joy and not with sadness, something that does not suit you. It is not convenient for you to also carry their sadness. It is not convenient for them to be sad because of your injustice. XXXVI Topic: Commentary on Prov 13,7-8. Date: Perhaps the year 410. Place: Unknown.

1. We have just read the Holy Scripture. She, or rather, God, who impels us through her to speak to you, etiam scriptum est, Ohoedientes estofe praepositis vestris: ipsi enim vigilant pro animahus vestris tanquam rationem reddituri: ut cum gaudio hoc faciant, et non cum tristitia; ñeque enim expedit vobis (Hebr 13,17). Vobis ergo non expedit illarum tristitia praegravari. Nam illis expedit de nostra malitia contristan. Bonds ergo upcoming deputa; et esto bonus, tuo quidem bonus, non illorum; et ipso non abs te tibi dato, sed divinitus impertito. Quid enim habes quod non accepisti? (1 Cor 4:7). Atque ita, Si sapiens fueris, tibi sapiens eris, et proximis tuis, quibus bonum est de tua bonitote laetari. Si autem malus evaseris, solus hauries mala, non etiam illi, quibus et hoc bonum est de tua malitia contristan. SERMO

DE EO QUOD SCRIPTUM EST IN PROVERBIIS SALOMONIS, «SUNT QUI SE DIVITES AFFECTANT, NIHIL HABENTES; ET SUNT QUI SE HUMILIANT, CUM SINT DIVITES. REDEMPTIO ANIMAE VIRI DIVITIAE EIUS: PAUPER AUTEM NON SUFFERT MINAS» (CHAP. 13, V. 7. 8)

CAPUT I. — 1. Expositio verborum Scripturae.—Sancta Scriptura, quae moda in auribus vestris lecta est, admonuit nos, immo per illam Deus This text will be variously commented on in the sermons of the anti-Pelagian era. See, among those that make up this volume, sermon 13:3 and 30:10. Other texts can be seen in KUNZELMANN, Die Cbronologie der Sermones des hl. Augustinus: MA II 352 note 3, 1-7
Commentary on Prov 13:7-8

invites us to search and examine together with you what what was read is and what it means: There are those who pretend to be rich without having anything, and there are those who humiliate themselves by being rich. We must not think or believe that divine Scripture is concerned with those riches of which the proud boast; I mean of these visible and earthly riches, either so that we appreciate them, or so that we suffer for not having them. "What does it profit a man, says someone, to be rich if he has nothing?" The Scripture refers to this one and rebukes him. But one should not even desire to be, or imitate, or overestimate the one whom one seems to have praised, if one thinks of temporal and earthly riches. There are, he says, those who humiliate themselves by being rich. We dislike the person who, having nothing, presumes to be rich. Will we be pleased with someone who, being rich, humbles himself? Maybe we like him not because he is rich, but because he humbles himself. 2. Let's consider this too. It is not indecent, nor dishonest, nor useless that the Holy Scriptures have wanted to recommend us to the humble rich. Nothing is to be feared as much in riches as pride. For this reason, the apostle Paul warns Timothy: Command the princes of this world not to act arrogantly. He was not afraid of riches, but of the disease of riches. This is nothing other than great arrogance. Great is the spirit that, living among riches, is not tempted by this disease; es mayor qui iubet nobis loqui ad vos, quaerere vobiscum et pertractare quid sit, et quid sibi velit quod lectum est: Sunt qui se divites affectant, nihil babentes; et sunt qui se humiliant, cum sint divites. Non enim arbitrandum est, ñeque omnino credendum, quod de istis divitiis, quibus inflantur supetbi, de visibilibus istis dico atque tetrenis, curaverit Scriptura sancta nos admonere, ut vel eas pro magno habeamus, vel non habere timeamus. Quid enim prodest homini, ait aliquis, qui se divitem videri affectat, cum nihil habeat? Istum Notavit Scriptura atque reprehendit. Sed nec Ule valde admirandus aut imitandus est et pro magno habendus, quem videtur in laude posuisse, si temporals atque terrenas divitias intellexeris. Et sunt, inquit, qui se humiliant, cum sint divites. Ule recte displicet nobis, qui cum nihil habeat, se divitem affectat. Crux? Iste placet nobis, qui cum sit dives, humiliat se? Forte placet quia humiliat se: non tamen placet quia dives est. CAPUT II.—2.

Divitiarum morbus, superbia.—Accipiamus ergo et hoc: non indecorum est, nec inhonestum, nec inutile, quod Scripturae sanctae nobis commendare voluerint humiles divites. Nihil enim in divitiis tam timendum est, quam superbia. Denique apostolus Paulus hoc admonet Timotheum: Praecipe, inquit, divitibus huius mundi, non superbe apere (1 Tim 6:17). Non enim divitias expavit, sed morbum divitiarum. Morbus autem divitiarum is superbia magna. Nam grandis animus
See supplementary note 34; Pride and riches, pJ56,

than his riches; His victory lies not in desiring them, but in despising them. Great is the rich man who does not consider himself great because he is rich. Whoever for this reason considers himself great is arrogant and indigent. It overflows in his flesh; in the heart beggar. It's swollen, not full. Consider two wineskins; one is full; the other, inflated; both are equally large, but not equally full. If you only look at them, you are deceived. If you feel them you will notice it. He who is full manages with difficulty; the one that is inflated rises quickly. 3. Ordain, he said, the rich of this world. If he adds: of this world, it is because there are those who are not of this world. Who are these? Those who have as leader and head him of whom it was said: Although he was rich, he became poor for us. If only him, what was his use? Look what follows: so that with their poverty we could become rich. The poverty of Christ, I believe, did not bring us money, but justice. Where does your poverty come from? Of having become mortal. Therefore, true riches consist in immortality. There will be true abundance where there is no poverty. Since we could not have become immortal if Christ had not become mortal for us, for this very reason, being rich, he became poor. It does not say: he became poor having once been rich, but: being rich, he became poor... He took poverty and did not lose his wealth. Internally rich, externally poor. God, hidden in his wealth,

est, qui Inter divitias isto morbo non tentatur: maior animus divitiis suis, qui eas vincit, non concupiscendo, sed contemnendo. Magnus est ergo dives, qui non se ideo magnum putat quia dives est: qui autem ideo se magnum putat, superbus et egenus est; in carne crepat, in corde mendicat; inflatus est, non plenus. Utres autem duos si videas, unum plenum, alterum inflatum; in utroque eadem est magnitudeo, sed non in utroque eadem plenitudo. If you attend, you will fail; si appendis, inventes: qui plenus est, difficile movetur; qui inflatus est, I quote aufertur. 3. Divites non huius mundi. Pauperlas et divitiae Christi.—Praecipe, ergo, inquit, divitibus huius mundi. Non adderet, huius mundi, nisi quia sunt et divites non huius mundi. Who sunt divites non huius mundi? Quorum princeps et caput est ille, de quo dictum est, [216] Pauper pro vobis factus est, cum esset dives. Sed si ille solus, quid profuit? Vide quid sequitur: Ut illius paupertate vos ditaremini (2 Cor 8,9). Puto quia paupertas Christi non nobis attulit pecuniam, sed iustitiam. Paupertas autem illius unde? Quia mortalis effectus est. Ergo divitiae verae immortalitas: ibi enim veracopia, ubi nulla indigentia. CAPUT III.—Quia ergo nos immortales fieri non possemus, nisi pro nobis Christus mortalis esset effectus: ideo pauper factus est, cum dives esset. Et non ait, Pauper factus est, cum dives Fuisset; sed, Pauper factus est, cum dives esset: paupertatem assumpsit, et divitias non amisit. Intus
Commentary on Prov 13:7-8

He manifests himself as a man in poverty. Look at its riches: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was in God and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. Everything was done by him. Is there anyone richer than the one by whom all things were made? The rich can own money, but they cannot create it. Since his riches were to be commended, consider his poverty: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. With his poverty we have been enriched, since the bag of our sins was torn thanks to the blood that flowed from his flesh, flesh that the Word took to dwell among us. By that blood we put off the clothes of iniquity to put on the stole of immortality. 4. The good faithful are all rich. Let no one despise himself; Although he is poor in the pantry, he is rich in conscience. He who is rich in conscience sleeps more peacefully on earth than he who is rich in gold wrapped in purple. The heart purified from all crime, no evil concern awakens in it. Keep in your heart the riches that the poverty of your Lord brought you. Furthermore, he placed himself as your guardian. So that the riches he gave you do not perish in your heart, let him who gave them keep them. All the good faithful are rich, but not rich of this world. Not even they themselves experience its riches; They will experience them later. The root is green, but during the winter, even the green tree is like the dry one.

During the winter, both the dry and the green tree are devoid of the honor of leaves; both are devoid of the honor of fruits. Summer will come and will distinguish one from the other. Leaves will sprout from the living root and it will be filled with fruit. The dry land will remain sterile in summer as well as in winter. For that the granary is prepared; The ax is applied to this, to be sent to the fire once cut. Our summer is the arrival of Christ. Our winter is the time when Christ remains hidden. Our summer, the revelation of Christ. For this reason, the Apostle addresses this recommendation to good and faithful trees: You are dead and your life is hidden with Christ in God. Dead, yes; but dead in appearance, because you are alive at the root. Wait for the summer to come, when he will continue and say: When Christ, your life, will appear, then you yourselves also will appear with him in glory. These are rich, but not of this world. 5. Nor, however, are the rich of this world despised. He also won them with his poverty who, being rich, became poor for us. If he had despised them and had not wanted to have them among his own, the Apostle would not have ordered these words to Timothy: Ordain the rich of this world. Among those who are rich in faith, there are those who are rich in this world. Give them orders, since they too have become members of that poor man. Tell them what you fear in them about riches: not to act arrogantly or put hope in the uncertainty of

dives, foris pauper. Latens Deus in divitiis, apparens homo in paupertate. Vide divitias eius: In principle erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principle apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum jacta sunt. Quid ditius eo, per quem facta sunt omnia? Aurum habere dives potest, creare non potest. Cum itaque istae eius divitiae commendatae essent, vide paupertatem eius: Et Verbum caro factum est, et habU tavit in nobis (lo 1,1.2.3.14). Hac eius sumus paupertate ditati: quia sanguine eius, qui manavit de carne eius, quod Verbum caro factum est, ut habitaret in nobis, conscissus est saccus peccatorum nostrorum. Per sanguinem illum abiecimus pannos iniquitatis, ut indueremur stola immortalitatis. 4. Omnes boni fideles divites sunt intus. Hiems et aestas nostra quae.—Omnes ergo divites boni fideles. Nemo se contemnat, pauper in celia, dives in conscientia. Dives quippe in conscientia securior dormit in terra, quam dives in purple. Ibi non excitat sollicitudo maligna, compuncto corde de scelere. Serva divitias in corde tuo, quas tibi contulit paupertas Domini Dei tui. Immo ipsum adhibe tibi custodem: ne pereat de corde quod dedit, servet ipse qui dedit. CAPUT IV.—Omnes ergo divites boni fideles, sed non divites huius mundi. Denique divitias suas nec ipsi sentiunt; sentient posts. Vivit radix, sed hiemis tempore etiam viridis arbor aridae similis est. Time

quippe hiemis et arbor quae aret, et arbor quae viget, utraque nuda est honore foliorum, utraque vacua honore fructuum: veniet aestas, et discernet arbores: viva radix folia producit, impletur fructibus; arid inanis aestate, sicut híeme, remanebit. Itaque illi horreum praeparatur, huic securis adhibetur, ut amputata in ignem mittatur. Sic aestas nostra, Christi est adventos: hiems nostra, Christi occultatio: aestas nostra, Christi revelationtio. Denique arboribus bonis et fidelibus hanc allocutionem praebet Apostolus: Mor tui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cutn Christo in Deo. Certe mortui: sed mortui specie, I lived in radice. Attende autem venturum tempus aestatis, quomodo sequatur, et dicat: Cum autem Christus apparuerit vita vestra, tune et vos cum ipso apparebitis in gloria (Col 3,3.4). Hi sunt divites, sed non huius mundi. 5. Divites huius mundi non contempti a Christo. Di\2Yl~\vitiarum inanitas et periculum.—Nec tamen et divites mundi contempti sunt. Et ipsos lucratus est sua paupertate, qui cum dives esset, propter nos pauper effectus est. Nam si eos comtempsisset, et in numero sanctorum habere noluisset, non Timotheo, sicut dicebam, Apostofus praecepisset, ut et ipse praeciperet: Praecipe, inquit, divitibus huius mundi non superbe sapere. inter hos qui fide sunt divites, sunt quidam divites huius mundi. Praecipe illis, quia et ipsi membra illius pauperis facti sunt. Praecipe illis quid in
Commentary on Prov 13:7-8

the riches. That's where the rich man's pride comes from: placing hope in the uncertainty of riches. If he looked reasonably at their uncertainty, he would never become arrogant; rather he would always be full of fear. The richer he was, the more attentive he would be not only thinking about this life, but also about that. There were many poor people who found themselves safer in the midst of the disorders of this world. Many were sought and captured for being rich. Many regretted having been, since they could not possibly have been forever. Many regretted not having followed the advice of their Lord, which says: Do not store up treasures on earth, where moth and rust eat away at them and where thieves break in and steal. Rather, store up treasures for yourselves in heaven. I'm not telling you to lose them, but to change their place. Many did not want to do so and regretted not having obeyed when they lost not only their things, but also themselves because of them. Command the rich of this world not to act arrogantly. Let what we have heard in the Proverbs of Solomon be fulfilled in them: There are those who, being rich, humble themselves. It is possible, thinking about temporal riches. Be humble. Find greater joy in being a Christian than in being rich. Don't inflate yourself, don't exalt yourself. Look at the poor brother; Do not be afraid to call yourself the brother of the poor. No matter how rich he is, Christ is greater, who wanted his brothers to be those for whom he shed his blood.

6. But, lest the rich say that they did not know what to do with their wealth, the Apostle warns Timothy to give them advice on what they should do, and not just a precept on what they should avoid. After saying: Nor put your hope in the uncertainty of riches, lest you think that you had lost hope, he added: but in the living God, who abundantly grants us everything to enjoy. Temporal goods must be used, eternal goods must be enjoyed 2. But what are they to do with their riches? Be rich, he said, in good works. Give with ease. This is what wealth must be used for, so that you do not have difficulty in donating. The poor man wants to, but he can't. The rich want and can. Give easily, make others participate, lay for yourself a good foundation for the future, to achieve true life. This life is false. Deceived by this falsehood, he who wore purple and linen despised the ulcerous beggar who was at his door. But the other, licked by the dogs, acquired for himself an eternal treasure in the bosom of Abraham, and if he did not abound in wealth, he did abound in pious and excellent will. That rich man who thought he was great for living wrapped in purple and linen, died and was buried. What did you find? An eternal thirst; flames that would not go out. Fire succeeded the purple and the linen. That tunic was burning that he couldn't get rid of. Banquets are followed by thirst and the desire for a drop of water from the beggar's finger, as he desired crumbs from the rich man's table. But the need

illis timeas a divitiis. Non superbe sapere, ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum. CAPUT V.—Inde enim superbit dives, quia sperat in incerto divitiarum. Nam si incerta divitiarum prudenter attenderet, nunquam superbiret, sed semper timeret: quanto esset ditior, tanta fietet sollicitior, et secundum hanc vitam, non solum secundum illam. Multi enim in istis saeculi perturbationibus securiores pauperes fuerunt. Multi autem propter suas divitias quaesiti et cortepti sunt. Multi se habuisse planxerunt, quod semper habere minime potuerunt. Multos paenituit consilium sui Domini non recepisse, qui dixit: Nolite vobis thesauros condere in tena, ubi tinea el cometura exterminat, et ubi jures effodiunt et jurantur: sed thesaurizate vobis thesaurum in caelis. Non dico vobis ut perdatis, sed ut migretis. Multi enim hoc faceré noluerunt, et non se oboedisse doluetunt; quando non solum sua perdiderunt, sed propter illa et ipsi perierunt. Praecipe ergo divitibus huius mundi non superbe sapere: et fiet in eis quod audivimus in proverbial Salomonis, Sunt qui se humiliant, cum sint divites. Et secundum ist divitias temporal fieri potest. Sit humilis: plus gaudeat quia christianus est, quam quia dives est. Non infletur, non extollatur: attendat pauperem fratrem, non dedignetur frater pauperis appellari. Quantumcumque enim dives sit, ditior est Christus, qui fratres suos esse voluit pro quibus sanguinem suum fudit.

CAPUT VI.—6. Divitiae ad quid prodesse possunt.—Tamen ne dicerent divites, non se habere quid faciant de divitiis suis, admonuit Timotheum, ut eos etiam consilio regeret, non solum praecepto cohiberet: cum dixisset, Ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum; ne se spem perdidisse arbitrarentur, subiecit, Sed in Deo vivo, qui praestat nobis omnia abundantr ad fruendum: temporaria ad utendum, aeterna ad fruendum. Sed de divitiis suis quid faciant? Divites sint, inquit, in operibus bonis, facile tribuant. Hoc prosint divitiae, ne sit tibi difficultas tribuendi. Vult enim pauper, et non potest: vult dives, et potest. Vacile tribuant, communicent, thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in juturum, ut apprehendant veram vitam (1 Tim 6:17-19). Nam ista vita false est. Huius vitae falsitate deceptus tile in purpura et bysso, iacentem ulcerosum pauperem ante suam ianuam contemnebat. Sed Ule linctus a canibus, thesaurum sibi aeternum in Abrahae gremio comparabat, et si non abundanti facúltate, pia tamen et opima volúntate. lile autem dives, qui sibi magnus videbatur in purpura et bysso, [218] mortuus sepultus est in inferno. Et quid invenit? Aeternam sitim, inefficient flames. Successit ignis purpurae et bysso: ea tunic ardebat, qua se exspoliare non poterat. Pro epulis ariditas, et desiderium guttae de digit pauperis, sicut illi
See supplementary note 48; Vsar and enjoy ("uti et frui"), p.760,

That man's condition was temporary; this one remains. Consider this, the rich of this world, and do not act arrogantly. Give easily; involve others. Lay for yourself a good foundation for the future, where the truly rich are, but not of this world, to achieve true life. 7. Perhaps this is what divine Scripture intimates when it says: There are those who pretend to be rich without having anything, thinking about the rags that are arrogant. If it is difficult to tolerate a proud person who is rich, who will tolerate one who is also poor? Better are those who, being rich, humble themselves. However, Scripture attests that it refers to other riches. He continued with these words: His riches are the ransom of the man's soul; The poor man does not tolerate threats. We must think that the poor person is poor with I don't know what other type of poverty and that the rich person is poor with I don't know what other type of wealth. Those who are rich in heart are more profoundly rich, full of strength, exuberant with piety, full of charity, rich with themselves, rich within themselves. There are those who pretend to be rich by being poor, that is to say: They believe they are just by being unjust. We must think about those riches. The Scripture stated why it said: His riches are the ransom of the man's soul. «Understand, he said, what riches I recommend. When I said: There are those who pretend to be rich without having anything and there are those who, being rich, humiliate themselves, you thought about those temporal, earthly and visible riches. I'm not referring to them; in which ones am I penmicarum de mensa divitis. Be illius egestas praeteriens, huius poena permanens (Luke 16:19-26). Hoc attendant divites huius mundi, et non superbe sapiant. Vacile tribuant, communicent: thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum; ubi sunt veri divites, sed non huius mundi: ut apprehendant veram vitam. CAPUT VIL—7. Divitiis interioribus divites.—Forte ergo hoc admonuit Scriptura divina, ubi ait, Sunt qui se divites affectant, nihil habentes, propter superbos pannosos. Si enim vix toleratur dives superbus, pauperem superbum quis ferat? Meliores sunt ergo illi qui se humiliant, cum sint divites. Verumtamen de alus divitiis se dicere Scriptura testatur: secuta enim adiunxit, Redemptio animae viri divitiae eius; pauper autem non suffert mines. Intellegere debenmus ex alia nescio qua paupertate pauperem, et ex alus nescio quibus divitiis divitem.

Altius enim divites, in corde divites, pleni fortitudine, opimi pietate, abundant caritate, secum sunt divites, interiors sunt divites. Sunt autem qui se divites affectant, cum sint pauperes: iusti sibi videntur, cum sint iniqui. Divitias quippe illas intellegere debenmus: quoniam aperuit Scriptura quid dixerit, Redemptio animae viri divitiae ipsius, intellege, quas tibi divitias commendem. Quoniam dixi, Sunt qui se divites affectant, nihil habentes; et sunt qui se humiliant, cum sint divites; temporal and earthly and visible islands

"And I say it below: His riches are the ransom of the man's soul." Of those who do not have the ransom of the soul because they are evil and try to appear fair, because they are hypocrites, of those he says: There are those who pretend to be rich without having anything. They want to appear just without having the gold of justice in the deposit of conscience. Those, however, of whom it was said: Blessed are the poor in spirit because theirs is the kingdom of heaven, are full, being all the more humble as they are richer. 8. Why do you seek riches that flatter human and carnal eyes? Gold shines, but faith shines more. Choose what you have in your heart. Try to be full within, where God sees your wealth, although man does not. Do not despise what you have inside because man does not see it. Do you want to prove that even in the eyes of the wicked, faith shines brighter than gold? Does not the greedy master praise the faithful slave? He says that there is nothing more valuable than him; Furthermore, it testifies that it is priceless. "I have a slave, he says, who is priceless." Do you expect me to tell you why? Maybe he dances well, or maybe he's an excellent cook. It's not about that. Listen to the praise of something internal: "No one is more faithful." Do you, man, like the faithful slave and do you not want to be a faithful servant for God? Think you have a slave; Also think that you have a master. You could have bought your slave, not created. Your Lord created you with his word and redeemed you with his blood. If you debased yourself in divitias cogitabas: ego autem non ipsas dico, sed quas dicam consequenter admoneo; Redemptio animae viri, divitiae ipsius sunt. Ergo qui non habent animae redemptionem, quia iniqui sunt, et iustos se videri affectant, quia hypocritae sunt, ipsi sunt de quibus ait, Sunt qui se divites affectant, nihil habentes: iustos se volunt videri, cum in celia conscientiae non habeant aurum iustitiae. Et sunt pleni, mucho humiliores, quanto ditiores: de quibus díctum est, Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum (Mt 5,3). CAPUT VIII.—8. Interiores divitiae, fides, auro praeferenda.—Quid ergo quaeris divitias, quae oculis humanis et carneis blandiuntur? Lucet aurum: sed plus luzet fides. Choose quid in corde habere debenas. Intus plenus esto, ubi divitias tuas Deus videt, homo non videt. Nec tamen quia homo non videt, ideo you must contemnere quod intus habes. Vis videre, quia et oculis iniquorum plus luzet fides, quam aurum? Quomodo laudat etiam avarus dominus servum fidelem?

Nihil íllo dicit esse pretiosius: immo eum omnino pretium non habere testatur. Habeo servum, inquit, non [219] habet pretium. Do you expect your unde? Forte bene saítat, aut optimus coquus est. Non: attende interiorem laudem. Nihil, inquit, fidelius. Placet tibi, homo, servus tuus fidelis, et tu non vis esse Deo servus fidelis? Attend quia habes servum tuum, attende quia habes et Dominum. Servum tuum potuisti comparae, non creare: Dominus tuus et verbo suo creavit te, et sanguine suo redemit te, Si viluisti tibi, recolé

To your detriment, look at the price. And if you have forgotten him, read the Gospel, your instrument 3. You love faithfulness in your slave; Can not your Lord seek it in his servant? Give what you demand from others. Return to your superior what you enjoy when your inferior gives it to you. You love the slave who faithfully guards your gold. Do not despise the Lord who mercifully guards your heart. Everyone has eyes to praise fidelity, but only when they demand that it be kept to themselves. When it is demanded of them, they close their eyes; They don't want to see how beautiful she is. Or perhaps out of stupid folly they do not want to give it so as not to lose it, in the same way that anyone is afraid to give money: after having given it, they do not possess it? This is not how fidelity happens. It is given and it is had. Wonderful saying! Furthermore, if you don't give it, you don't have it. 9. His riches are the ransom of the man's soul. No wonder God despised that rich man full of vanity. In this way he admonishes us not to imitate the behavior of him who, when a time of many fruits occurred, was more troubled by abundance than by scarcity. He thought to himself and said: What shall I do? Where will I store my harvest? After much thought and reflection, he believed he had found the right decision. He works good and not evil. And not for herself, but for her husband, so that he who lives may no longer live for himself, but for him who died for all and rose again. For her husband, then, she works good; in the presence of God he works it. She serves him, she is dedicated to him, she always strives to please him. 7 to sermon 19. Refers to Photinus, bishop of Srrmio, from the 4th century. XXXVIII Topic: Continence and resistance. Date and place: Unknown.

1. The Lord commands us two things in this laborious life: contain ourselves and endure. We are charged with continence in those things that in this world are called good and resistance to evils, which also abound in this world. The first is called continence; to the second, resistance. They are two virtues that purify the soul and make it capable of divinity. To curb concupiscence and dominate voluptuousness, so that we are not seduced by what flatters us for our harm or weakened by what is called prosperity, we need continence, that is, not trusting in earthly happiness and seeking to the end the happiness that has no end. In the same way that it is characteristic of continence not to trust vitae meae. Et quid ibi facies? Ut contempler delectationem Domini (Ps 26,4). Et laudetur in portis vir eius. Beati qui inhabitant in domo tua; in saecula saeculorum laudabunt te (Ps 83,5).

CAPUT I.—1. Duae virtutes huius vitae.—Dúo sunt quae in hac vita veluti laboriosa nobis praecipiuntur, continere et sustinere. Iubemur enim continere ab his quae in hoc mundo dicuntur bona, et sustinere ea quae in hoc mundo abundant mala. Illa continentia, is sustinentia vocatur: duae virtutes quae mundant animam, et capacem faciunt divinitatis. In frenandis libidinibus et coercendis voluptatibus, ne seducat quod male blanditur, et enervet quod prosperum dicitur, continentia nobis opus est: non credere felicitati terrenae, et usque ad finem quaerere felicitatem, quae non habet finem. Ut autem est continentiae, felici1
See note 1 to sermon 20, p.314.
Continence and resistance

in the happiness of this world, so it is characteristic of endurance not to give consideration to the unhappiness of this world. In both abundance and poverty we must wait on the Lord to give us what is truly good and pleasant and to remove from us what is truly evil. 2. The goods that God promised to the righteous are reserved for the end; likewise the evils that threaten the wicked. The good and evil of this world are mixed. Not only the good ones have them, nor only the bad ones. Whatever you call good in this world, both the good and the bad have it. For example, bodily health is possessed by the good and the bad. You can find riches in both good and bad times. We see that descent into children is a common gift to the good and the bad. There are good people and there are bad people who enjoy longevity. Any other kind of good that you want to list in this world you will find mixed in the good and the bad. In the same way, anything hard or sad is suffered by both the good and the bad: hunger, illness, pain, damage, oppression, deprivation. This occasion of tears is common to all. It is easy to see that the goods of this world are found in the good and the bad, and that the evils are also suffered by both. This is why the feet of many stagger when they walk along the path of the Lord and try to get out of the way. Many turn aside and turn away from him, since they had thought and purposed in

His mind will serve God to abound in earthly goods and avoid and lack evils. Having proposed this and having established it as a reward for their piety and religiosity, when they see that they grow weary, that the wicked flourish, they deny God as if they had lost their reward, as if they had been deceived by the one who called them, as if he had ordered them to work in vain by the one who deceived them in the reward. Where do these wretches turn, separating themselves from him by whom they were made and clinging to those things that were made? When what has been created begins to fade, where will be the lover of time who lost eternity? 3. Therefore, God wants us to believe in him for those goods that he will only give to the good and for those evils that he will only give to the bad. At the end of time both will appear. What is the reward of faith or, even more, how can it be called faith if you want to see now what you must have? You should not see what you have to believe, but believe what you have to see; Believe while you do not see, so that when you see, you will not be ashamed. We believe while it is the time of faith, before the time of reality arrives. Thus says the Apostle: While we are in this body we are pilgrims far from the Lord. We walk by faith. We walk by faith when we believe what we do not see. We will have reality when we see him face to face as he is. The apostle John also distinguishes in his letter the time of faith and the time of reality.

It is tiring, but this is the work that receives the other as a reward. Do not be lazy in doing that from which you expect a reward. If you yourself had hired a day laborer, you would not give him his salary before he had practiced it at work. You would tell him: "Work and then you will receive." I wouldn't tell you: "Give it to me and then I'll work." This is how God works too. You, fearing God, do not deceive your hired servant; Is God, who commands you not to deceive the hired worker, going to deceive you? However, you may not give what you promised. Even if the delusion of falsehood does not exist in your heart, there is certainly scarcity in human fragility that can cause difficulty. Hoc est primum praeceptum, iioc est initium religíonis et vitae nostrae, fixum habere cor in fide, et figendo cor in fide vivere bene, abstinere ab ómnibus seductoriis, sustinere mala temporalia; et quamdiu illa blandiuntur et illa minantur,

so that you do not get carried away by the former or give in to the latter. Having, therefore, continence and endurance, once the temporal goods have passed, when no evils can befall us either, you will have God as your good and you will not suffer any evil. What were we told in the reading? Son, as you approach serving God, remain in righteousness and fear and prepare your soul for temptation. Humble your heart and endure: that it may grow in the last days of your life—not now, but in the last days—so that it may grow in the last days of your life. How far, we think, will it grow? Until it becomes eternal. At present, human life, although it is long and seems to be long, in reality decreases rather than increases 2. Pay attention and see it; reflect and see that it is so. A man was born. For example, God has established that he should live seventy years. As he grows, we say that life is added to him. Is it added or removed? Of the seventy years he has already lived sixty; He has ten left. He has diminished what he had predetermined, and the longer he lives, the less he has left. In this way, here, by the fact of living, life decreases, it does not grow. Keep what God promised you, so that it grows in the last days of your life. 6. Modo enim vita humano, quamdiu producitur et videtur produci, decrescit potius quam crescit. Attendite and video, ratiocinamini and video quia decrescit. Natus est homo: verbi gratia, constituit illi Deus vitae suae septuaginta annos: Accedit illi vita, dicimus, crescendo. Accedit, did you decide? Ecce de septuaginta annis vixit sexaginta, remanserunt decem: diminutum est quod erat propositum; et quanto plus vivit, mucho minus illi restat.

If the judge decrees exile, it is a punishment; Greed orders it, and it is a joy. What thing, no matter how great, can wisdom impose on you that greed cannot also impose on you? Still, when greed tells you to, you do it. And once what this vice orders is done, what will you have? A house full of gold and silver. Have you not read: Although man walks as in shadow, he wanders in vain. He accumulates treasures, and he does not know for whom? Why did you sing and say to God: Hear my tears, that is, Give ear to my tears? Why don't you listen to the words of the one you want to hear your tears? If you will give up your greed, he will invite you to his wisdom. When you have received the yoke of wisdom, will it be a tiring task? It certainly will be. What do you accumulate through wisdom? You accumulate for yourself. Wake up, stay awake, have the heart of an ant. We are in summer; collect what is useful to you for the winter. This expression appears frequently in Augustinian sermons. In addition to the present, sermon 42,2; 345.3 (=Frangipane 3); 86.11 and 114 A 4 (=Frangipane 9). Traiectitium was called the transfer of goods from one region to another across the sea. In connection with this, there was the foenus traiectitium (sermon 42,2). XXXIX Topic: Commentary on Eclo 5,8-9. Date and place: Unknown.

1. We have heard, brothers, God saying through the mouth of his prophet: Do not delay in converting to God, nor defer et amatur mundus. Quid, if tranquillus esset mundus? Formoso quomodo haereres, qui sic amplecteris foedum? Flores eius quomodo colligeres, qui ab spinis non revocas manum? Non vis relinquere mundum, relinquit te mundus, et sequeris mundum. Cor ergo mundemus, carissimi: et non perdamus sustinentiam; sed percipiamus sapientiam, et teneamus continentiam. Transit labor, venit requies: transeunt false delicious, et venit bonum quod concupivit anima fidelis, cui inardescit et suspirat omnis peregrinus in saeculo: patria bona, patria caelestis, patria contemplationis Angelorum; patria ubi nullus civis moritur, quo nullus hostis admittitur; patria ubi habeas sempiternum Deum amicum, ubi nullum timeas inimicum.

Christ put the kingdom of heaven up for sale and priced it in a glass of cold water. When it is a poor person who gives alms, it is enough for him to give a glass of cold water. Alms always benefit those who have changed their way of life. You give to poor Christ to redeem your past sins. XLI Topic: Commentary on Eclo 22,28. Date and place: Unknown.

1. When the divine Scriptures were read, not all of whose phrases can be explained here, I focused my attention on a little phrase, small in terms of the number of words, but large in terms of its richness of meaning. With the help of the Lord, and as far as the mediocrity of my strength allows, I have chosen to serve with it the great expectation of your charity and to serve you from the pantry of the Lord, from which I feed together with you. The phrase I am talking about is this: Be faithful to your neighbor in his poverty to also enjoy his goods. Let us first consider it as it sounds, as you can understand it.
(Apparebit una simul cum sermone 339 [PL 38,1480], buius editionis)
DE EO QUOD SCRIPTUM EST ECCLESIASTICI 22,28: «FIDEM POSSIDE CUM PÓXIMO IN PAUPERTATE IPSIUS, UT ET BONIS EIUS PERFRUARIS»

1. Vides amico in eius paupertate servanda.—Cum divinae Scripturae legerentur, de quarum sententiis ómnibus nunc loqui non valemus, animadverti unam sententiam, verborum numero brevissimam, pondere autem sensus amplissimam, unde elect, adiuvante Domino, huic tantae expectationi Caritatis vestrae, pro virium nostrarum mediocritate I will serve, and I will minister to the voices of cellario Dominico, unde et ego vobiscum vivo. Haec ergo sententia est, de qua loquor: Fidem posside cum proxima in paupertate ipsius, ut et bonis eius perfruarís. Accipiarmjs hanc pri-
Commentary on Eclo 22:28

everyone, even those who do not search any mystery in the divine Scriptures. Be faithful, he said, to the poor in their poverty, to also enjoy their goods. «So it must be, says one who understands it in its most obvious sense; When a friend is poor, trust should not be withdrawn; you have to stay by his side; Friendship should not be changed because wealth has changed; Confidence must be maintained consciously affirmed. If my friend was only when he was rich, and now that he is poor he is not, he was not my friend, but money. If, on the other hand, the man was my friend, whether the gold remains or goes, he is the same friend who was. Why should he not be a friend who, although he has lost the treasure, has not lost his heart? If I had bought a horse, once the tack and saddle were removed, perhaps I would not despise it without them. And the friend whom I like dressed, do I already dislike him stripped? Very well, therefore, the divine Scripture orders, correctly and healthily accommodating itself to the customs of men: Be faithful to your neighbor in his poverty.

to him for fidelity, even when he is poor, to enjoy his goods when riches come to him and you enjoy them with him. He has fidelity along with him. He is poor, but he has a great possession: fidelity. You, who wanted and were preparing to possess an inheritance with him, if there were one that you possessed jointly, how much more closely do you possess fidelity with him? Perhaps your friend is such that some evil man can take possession of him. Could he possibly take away his fidelity? What does it mean: to also enjoy your goods? Since the poor can become rich, so that you, who did not despise him in his poverty, may enjoy his riches. 3. I like the first part of this phrase, according to such popular sense. The second, on the other hand, I confess, I dislike. If you stay by the friend's side in his poverty so that, when he is rich, you can enjoy his riches, you still do not love the friend, but something different in him. Faith and hope are two good friends, but greater than them is charity. In divine things, says the Apostle, three things remain: faith, hope and charity; but the most excellent of them is charity. Seek charity. I ask a person about his friend. «Tell me, please, do you remain faithful to him in poverty?» «Indeed, he says; I heard this in the Scripture, I kept it in my heart and I retain it in my memory; I remember it with pleasure and with greater pleasure I fulfill it. I heard the holy word: Be faithful to your neighbor in his poverty. And I ask you:

2. So that you also enjoy its goods. What are you saying? We move on to the second part of this sentence. We have such esteem for our friend that we say: "We must remain at his side and maintain confidence in him in times of poverty, to also enjoy his goods." One who is now poor will become rich, and he will not allow you to share in his riches, since, being arrogant, you are upset by his poverty. Join mum ut videtur sonare simpliciter, ut eam possunt intellegere omnes, etiam qui nulla Scripturarum divinarum secretiora rimantur. Fidem, inquit, posside cum proximate in paupertate ipsius, ut et bonis eius perfruaris. Verum est, inquit, qui simpliciter audivit: quando amicus pauper est, non ei frangenda est fides; permanendum cum illo est, nec mutanda amicítia facúltate mutata; sed servanda fides, volúntate firmata. Amicus enim meus, si cum dives esset, amicus Fuit; cum pauper est, amicus non est; non ipse mihi amicus, sed aurum eius Fuit. Si autem amicus meus ipse homo Fuit; et manente auro, et recedente auro, ipse est qui Fuit: quare ergo moda non sit amicus, qui et si perdidit thesaurum, non perdidit animum? Equum si emerem, detractis ornamentis et strato, nudum forte non despicerem; et amicus mihi vestitus placuit, exspoliatus displicet? Bene ergo praecipit Scriptura divina, salubriter omnino et accommodatissime moribus hominum, Fidem posside cum proxima tuo in paupertate ipsius. 2. Qua spe servanda fides amico pauperi.—Ut et bonis eius perfruaris. Quid ergo? accesontes ad posteriorem partem huius sententiae, talem cogitationem habebimus de amico, ut dicamus nobis: Manendum est cum illo et servanda illi fides est in paupertate eius, ut et bonis eius perfruamur? Erit enim dives qui modo pauper est, et non te admittet
See complementary note 54: Saint Augustine and friendship, p.762.

ad divitias suas, cuius paupertatem superbus antea fastidisti. Posside ergo cum illo fidem, etiam cum pauper est, ut et bonis eius perfruaris, quando illi accesserint divi[248]tiae, et cum illo gaudeas in eis. Posside cum illo fidem: pauper est, sed magnam possesionem habet fidem. Qui parabas cum illo et volebas possidere terram, si baberet terram, quam possideretis simul, quanto firmius cum illo possides fidem? Talis est enim forte amicus tuus, ut ei possit aliquis improbus auferre possessionem: numquid poterit auferre fidem? Quid est ergo, Ut et bonis eius perfruaris? Utique quia ex paupere poterit fieri dives, et perfrueris divitiis eius, quia eius paupertatem non aspernatus es. 3. Non spe venturae ipsi felicitatis temporalis.—Prior quidem pars sententiae huius, secundum istum intellectum popularen!, placet mihi; later tamen, fateor, offendit me. Si enim propterea manes cum amico in paupertate eius, ut quando dives fuerit, perfruaris divitiis eius; adhuc non amicum, sed aliud aliquid amas in amico. Fides et spes duae amicae bonae sunt, et maior his caritas. Manent, inquit Apostolus, tria haec, fides, spes et caritas; maior autem horum est caritas: sectamini caritatem (1 Cor 13:13; 14:1). Interrogation ergo amicum of amico. Dec mihi, obsecro te, fidem possides cum isto in paupertate eius? Plan, inquit: audiví enim hoc in sacra Scriptura, et commendavi cordi meo, et in memoria mea reposui; libens recoló, libentius fació. Audivi enim sanctum verbum,, Fidem posside cum proximate in paupertate ipsius. Et ego: Quare hoc
Commentary on Eclo 22:28

«Why are you doing this? For what follows: to also enjoy his goods? What are you waiting for? "So that, when he is rich, I say, and riches come to him, he may allow me to enjoy them because I did not disdain his evils." «Allow me to continue asking you: How would you behave with this poor man, to whom you have not denied fidelity, if he never became rich, if he were poor until death? Would your faithfulness end because he disappointed your hope? Would you regret having been faithful to the poor because you could not possess gold with the rich? If you think humanly; Furthermore, if you think the truth, this question of mine will disturb you and you will tell me: "What you say is true. It is a good thing to be faithful to your neighbor. But if one is faithful to one's neighbor with the hope of reaching his riches to share in his company, with all certainty, when this poor man has died without ever possessing the riches that we expected, we will repent of all that good; "What we knead well, we spread poorly." You see how the meaning of this phrase has to be investigated more deeply; It is not possible to limit oneself to an ordinary understanding. As founded on the authority of God, it must be understood in such a way that it suggests to us, orders us, imposes on us 2 something superior where our hope does not feel disappointed nor regret having possessed fidelity. Otherwise you will not understand the sentence.

rich This poor man was sick in a way so worthy of compassion that he did not even enjoy bodily health, the ordinary heritage of the poor. I was sore; the dogs licked his ulcers. No wonder the Lord Jesus, lover and giver of fidelity, paid more attention to the fidelity of the poor than to the gold and pleasures of the rich. He paid more attention to the assets of the poor than to the elevation of the rich. For this reason he gave the name of the poor man and judged that the name of the rich man should be kept silent. There was, he says, a certain rich man who dressed in linen and purple, who feasted lavishly every day; There was also a certain poor man named Lazarus. Doesn't it seem as if you were reading in a book in which you found the name of the poor man written and not the name of the rich? It is the book of the living and the just, not that of the proud and evil. The rich man's name was known to men; that of the poor, ignored. The Lord works the other way around: he points out that of the poor and remains silent about that of the rich 3. That rich man did not want to share fidelity with the poor. They both died. with him, since he did not have fidelity in common either. Father Abraham, says the rich man, sends Lazarus to dip his finger in water and let it fall on my tongue, because I am burned in these flames. It was answered: Remember, son, that you received many good things in life, and Lazarus, on the other hand, many bad things: so now he rests and you are tormented. Furthermore, there is an abyss between you and us that is impossible to cross in one direction or the other. He found himself denied the mercy he had denied. He realized how true it is that there will be a judgment without mercy for those who did not have it. He who in due time did not take pity on the poor, later took pity on his brothers. Send, he says, Lazarus. I have five more brothers. Tell them what is happening here, so that they do not also end up in this place of torment. Instead of carrying out his will, he was told: If you do not want to come to this place of torture, you have Moses and the prophets there; listen to them. He used to laugh at the prophets in the company of his brothers. In fact, I believe without a doubt that, speaking with his brothers about the prophets, who exhorted good and forbade evil, who terrified with future torments and promised eternal goods, he laughed at everything, commenting with them: "What is there after death? What will be the memory of corruption? What will the ashes feel? They will all get there and be buried. Has anyone been heard of coming back from there? Remembering these

With his words he wanted Lazarus to return to his brothers so that they would no longer say: "Has anyone returned from there?" To this also he found an adequate and dignified response. It seems that he was a Jew, and that is why he had said: Father Abraham. Before him, God shows himself benevolent towards sins. If God is not benevolent towards sins, will there be anyone who is not guilty? Through almsgiving, men purify themselves from those faults and sins without which it is impossible to go through this life. There are two kinds of alms: giving and forgiving; give the good you possess and forgive the evil you suffer. How briefly the Lord and good teacher, who shortened the word on the earth, so that it would be fruitful and not burdensome, summarized these two kinds of alms, listen to him: Forgive and you will be forgiven, he said; give and it will be given to you. Forgive and you will be forgiven refers to the second; Give and it will be given to you, the first time. With that alms with which you forgive a man you lose nothing. Immediately ask for forgiveness from whoever offended you, you forgave them and you lost nothing. The other type of alms by which we are ordered to give to the needy seems burdensome, because what each person wants, that same thing he will no longer possess. 2. CAPUT I.—1. Vines necessaria.—Initium bonae vitae, cui vita etiam aeterna debentur, recta fides est. Est autem fides, credere quod nondum vides: cuius fidei merces est, videre quod credis. Tempore igitur fidei tanquam tempore sementis, non deficiamus, et usque in finem non deficiamus: sed perseveremus, doñee quod seminavimus metamus. Cum enim aversum esset genus humanum a Deo, et iaceret in delictis suis, sicut Creatore opus habebamus ut essemus, sic Salvatore ut revivisceremus. Iustus Deus damnavit hominem, misericors Deus liberat hominem. Deus Israel ipse dabit virtutem et fortitudinem plebi suae: benedictus Deus (Ps 67,36). Be accipiunt credentes, non accipiunt contemnentes.

2. Vides magnum Dei donum.—Nec de ipsa fide tamen ita gloriandum est, quasi aliquid nos possimus. Non enim fides nihil est, sed magnum aliquid: quam si habes, profecto accepisti. Quid enim habes, quod non accepisti? (1 Cor 4:7). Videte, carissimi, unde Domino Deo gratias agatis: ne in aliquo dono eius ingrati maneatis, et propter hoc quod ingrati estis, quod accepistis perdatis. Laus fidei explain to me millo moda potest, sed a fidelibus cogitari potest. CAPUT II.—Porro si ex aliqua parte, ut dignum est, cogitetur, quis digne cogitet, quam multis donis Dei ipsius praeferatur? Et si minora Dei dona in nobis debenmus agnoscere, quanto magis illud quod ea superat, debenmus agnoscere? 3. Dei in hominem benefits. Aliud intellectus et aliud ratio.—A Deo debenmus esse quod sumus. Quia quod non nihil sumus, nisi a Deo a quo habemus? Sed sunt et ligna, sunt et lapides, a quo nisi a Deo? We ergo quid plus? Non vivunt ligna et lapides: nos autem vivimus. Sed adhuc nobis idipsum vivere [255] cum arboribus frutetisque commune est. Dicuntur enim et vites vivere. Nam si non viverent, non scriptum esset: Occidit in grandine vincas eorum (Ps 77,47). Vivit, cum viret; arescit, cum moritur. Sed vita ista non habet sensum. Why do we expand? Sentimus. Quinquepartitus corporis notus est sensus. Videmus, audímus, olfácimus, gustamus, tactu etiam per totum Corpus nostrum mollia diiudicamus et dura, áspera et lenia, calida et frígida. est

hard from soft, rough from soft, hot from cold. There are, therefore, five senses in us. But animals also have them. We have, then, something more. But, my brothers, just by considering these things that we have enumerated, how much thanksgiving, how much praise do we not owe to the Creator? And what do we have more? The mind, reason, discernment; Beasts, birds, and fish do not have this. With this we are the image of God. Indeed, Scripture narrates that we were created. And to show that we were not only put before them, but also placed before them, that is, that they are subject to us, he adds the following: Let us, he said, make man in our image and likeness and have power over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky and the beasts and serpents that crawl on the earth. Where does such power come from? To be the image of God. Hence it is said to some as a reproach: Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding. It is one thing to know and another to know the reason. We have the reason even before we understand; On the contrary, we cannot understand if we are not right. For this reason, man is an animal capable of reason; To put it more clearly and quickly, a rational animal of whose nature reason is part; Before understanding, he possesses reason: insofar as he wants to understand what reason precedes him. 4. This in which we are superior to the beasts we must cultivate with the utmost care, renew it in a certain way and reform it. But who can do it, but the architect who ergo it in nobis sensus quinquepartitus: sed hunc habent et bestiae. Habemus ergo aliquid amplius nos. Et is tamen quae enumeravimus, fratres mei, siconsiderus in nobis, quantam de his gratiarum actionem, quantam Creatori laudem deben? Sed tamen amplius quid habemus? Mentem, rationem, consilium, quod non habent bestiae, non habent volucres, non habent pisces: in eo facti sumus ad imaginem Dei. Denique ubi Scriptura nartat quod facti sumus, ibi subiungit, ut nos pecoribus non solum anteponat, sed et praeponat, id est, ut ea nobis subiecta sint: Faciamus, inquit, hominem ad imaginem et similarityinem nostram, et habeat potestatem piscium maris, et volatilium caeli, et omnium pecorum, et serpentium quae repunt super terram (Gen 1:26). Unde habeat potestatem? Propter imaginem Dei. Unde quibusdam dicitur increpando: Nolite esse sicut equus et mulus, quibus non est intellectus (Ps 31,9).

Be aliud est intellectus, aliud ratio. Nam ratioem habemus et antequam intellegamus; sed intellegere non valemus, nisi rationem habeamus. Est ergo animal rationis capax: verum ut melius et citius dicam, animal rationale, cui natura inest ratio, et antequam intellegat iam rationem habet. Nam ideo vult intellegere, quia ratio praecedit. manna does not rain, we will die. The Lord prepares his table for us by arranging the readings in such a way that in the prophet Isaiah we are promised something and in the Apostle we are told: Having these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every stain in the flesh and in the spirit, bringing sanctification to perfection in the love of God, as if the prophet and the Apostle were the same reading. What does the Apostle say? Having these promises, dearly beloved; There it does not say what promises, not because they do not exist there, but because the reader did not start somewhere else. In this way the reader's mind tried to find out what promises the Apostle is referring to: Having these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every stain in the flesh and in the spirit. A great task and no small fatigue falls upon us: to cleanse ourselves of every stain in the flesh or in the spirit. No one undertakes this task without having heard the promised reward. If, then, no one undertakes the task of cleansing the flesh and the spirit without being incited by the reward, I do not know how it happened that the reader began not with the promise of the reward, but with the presentation of the task to be performed. But God did not want to disappoint the attentive reader. If perhaps you were hesitant to undertake the task of cleansing the flesh and spirit because you had not heard the reward, go to the beginning of the Apostle's reading. But if you are looking for the promises, pay your attention to the end of the prophet's reading. Where the prophetic reading ends is the promise; where that of the Apostle begins, there is the entrusted task.

Will someone say: Am I going to cleanse myself from every stain in the flesh and in the spirit in order to possess the land and live on the mountain? Without a doubt, it is necessary to investigate what it means to possess the land and to live in the mountains, lest perhaps men expect to receive extensive possessions and, instead of eliminating the desire to possess, they prolong it even more, increase it and despise it as something of little importance, thinking that they can acquire even greater things from that type of thing. Who does not despise a portion if he is promised to possess a hundred? Or who does not despise the pleasures of a meal, perhaps poor and frugal, if he is told: "If you do not abstain, you will not be able to attend that most sumptuous and sumptuous dinner?" Those who abstain from certain present things in this way in no way repress their desire to possess. And the greater these desires are, they despise lesser things, fearing to lose what they so strongly desire. This is the desire. Is he not a miser who despises a hundred folios to acquire a thousand? Topic: The shepherds (Ez 34,1-16). Date: Around the year 410, or 414. Place: Hippo or Carthage. 1. That all our hope resides in Christ and that he is all our glory, true and salutary, know it, serve you, be friends. Et quid est daturas amicis? Quod in se ipso otendit resurgente. Coronabuntur, et convertentur in gloriam caelestem, et erunt aequales Angelis Dei (Luke 20:36). Nulla erit corruptio, nulla titillatio. Non ibi nobis dicetur, Mundate vos ab omni coinquinatione carnis et spiritus. Non laborabimus, nec nobis promittetur praemium; quia iam accepimus. Nec nobis dicetur ut gemamus; quia iam laudamus. Sicut enim caro mortalis convertitur in corpus angelí; sic et gemitus convertetur in laudes. Hic paenitentia, et pressura, et gemitus: ibi laudes, laetitia, et gaudium. Post ergo, moda non est laetitia. Are you located? In spe. Nondum tenes, sed sperando gaudes: quia qui promisit non potest decipere; quia qui promisit, habet et dat.

In being Christians, the focus must be on our own usefulness; In the fact of being superior, one should only think about yours. There are many who, being Christians, without being superior, reach God, perhaps walking an easier and faster path, since they carry a smaller burden. We, on the contrary, leaving aside the fact of being Christians, and according to that, we must give an account of our lives to God; We are also superior, and according to this we must give an account to God of our service. If I tell you this it is so that, having compassion for us, you will pray for us. The day will come when everything is put to trial. That day, although it is still far away for the world, for each man it is the last of his life. God wanted to keep one and the other hidden: when the end of the world will come and when the end of this life will be for each of the men. Do you want not to fear that hidden day? Make sure you are prepared until it arrives. Since superiors are appointed to take care of those over whom they are in charge, they should not seek in the act of presiding their own usefulness, but that of those they serve; Whoever is superior in such a way that he takes pleasure in being so, seeks his own honor and looks only to his comforts, feeds himself and not the sheep. Listen, as sheep of God, and consider how God constituted you in security, in a manner christiani sumus, propter nos est: quod autem praepositi sumus, propter vos est. Let us see what the divine word, which flatters no one, says to shepherds who feed themselves and not the sheep. Behold, you drink its milk, you cover yourselves with its wool, you sacrifice the fattest sheep and you do not feed my sheep. You did not comfort the weak: you did not care for the sick, you did not bind the wound, you did not reduce the stray, you did not seek the lost sheep: you destroyed the strong one. Thus my sheep were scattered for want of a shepherd. Shepherds are reproached for feeding themselves and not the sheep, what they love and what they neglect. What do they love? You drink its milk, you cover yourself with its wool. Therefore the Apostle says: Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not feed on milk? We think that the milk of the flock is everything that the people of God donate to their superiors to sustain this temporal life. The Apostle spoke of this in the words that I have just remembered. 4. Although the Apostle preferred to work with his hands and not seek milk from the sheep, he clearly said that he had the right to receive it and that the Lord had ordained that those who announce the Gospel should live by it. People like him made use of this right, not usurped, but given. He went even further by not even accepting what was owed to him. He certainly forgave what was owed to him, but the other demanded what was undue. He went beyond the law. Perhaps the one who, upon taking the sick man to the inn, said: If you spend anything more, I will return it to you upon your return, meant that one. What more can we say about those who do not need the milk of the flock? That they are more merciful, or better yet, that they exercise the duty of mercy more generously. They can, and what they can they do. Let these be praised, but let the others not be condemned. Nor did the Apostle demand what was given. However, he wanted all the sheep to bear fruit and not be barren without the abundance of milk. In fact, on one occasion finding himself in great need, chained for confessing the truth, the brothers sent him something to help his need and destitution. He responded by thanking them with these words: You did well in helping my needs. I learned to be enough with what I have. I know how to live in abundance and I know what it is to suffer hardship. I can do everything in him who comforts me. All in all, you did well to send something for my needs. To show what he was looking for in the good they had done, lest there be among them shepherds who feed themselves and not the sheep, he does not so much rejoice that they have relieved his need, but rather he rejoices in their fruitfulness. What were you looking for there? I do not seek what is given, he said, but

Lactis percipiendi potestas data pastoribus.—Et quidem Apostolus quanquam elegerit manibus suis transigí, et nec ipsum lac quaerere ab ovibus (2 Thess 3,8); tamen lactis percipiendi potestatem habere se dixit, et sic Dominum disposuisse, ut qui Evangelium annuntiant, de

Respondit autem illis gratias agens, et dixit: Bene fecistis communicare necessitatibus meis. Sed ut ostenderet, in eo quod illi bene fecerunt, quid ipse quaereret, ne inter illos esset qui se ipsos pascunt, non oves, non tam suae gaudet subventum esse necessitati, quam illorum gratulatur fecunditati. 13. She who was weak, he said, you did not strengthen her. He says this to bad pastors, to false pastors, to those who seek their interests, not those of Jesus Christ; to those who enjoy the comfort that milk and wool give them, completely neglecting

the sheep and not strengthening the one that was sick. There is a difference between the weak and the sick, although we say that the sick are weak. I think that we should make a difference between the weak and the sick, that is, the one who is not well. We, brothers, establish a difference. Perhaps we could find others with greater attention; or perhaps another more expert or enlightened by the light of the heart could better distinguish what we try to distinguish at all costs. But so that you do not feel disappointed, I am going to say what I feel, regarding the words of Scripture. In the weak it is to be feared that temptation will come and break him. The sick person, on the other hand, already suffers because of some desire, and this same desire prevents him from entering the path of God and submitting to the yoke of Christ. Look at those men who want to live righteously, who have determined to live this way, and yet are not so willing to endure evil as prepared to do good. It belongs to Christian firmness not only to do good, but also to tolerate evil. Those who seem eager to do good, but are unwilling or unable to tolerate imminent suffering, are the weak. Those who, through an evil desire, being lovers of the world, withdraw from good works, lie sick and languid; These, due to their own illness, as if they were without any strength, cannot do any good. Such was the soul of that paralytic: those who were carrying him, not being able to present him to the Lord, opened the roof and left him through.

that was lost you did not redirect it and that which was lost you did not look for it; 16 Therefore, listen to what he says next about these negligent, nay, evil shepherds: My sheep were scattered for want of a shepherd and became prey for all the beasts of the field. Lurking wolves steal them, roaring lions snatch them when the sheep are not united to their shepherd. Although the shepherd is present, for those who do wrong he is not a shepherd. not in the hardness of the mountain. They also have Scriptures, also sacraments. These do not belong to the mountain, and even if they are there, it is bad to remain there. Lost in the mountains and hills, they abandon the flock, abandon the unit and the cadres defended against wolves and lions. May God call them to get out of there, may he himself call them. Right now you will hear him calling: “My sheep have gone astray,” he says, “through every mountain and high hill, that is, through all the swelling of earthly pride.” There are also good mountains: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me. But notice that your hope is not in the mountains: My help comes to me from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Do not think that you offend the holy mountains when you say: My help comes to me, not from the mountains, but from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. The mountains themselves also shout this to you. It was Monte who cried: I have heard that there are schisms among you, and that each one of you says: I am of Paul, I of Apollo, I of Cephas, I of Christ. Raise your eyes towards this mountain, listen to what it says, but do not stay on it. Listen to what he says below: Was Paul crucified for you? Therefore, after having lifted your eyes to the mountains, from which help comes to you, that is, to the authors of the divine Scriptures 4, fix your attention on him who, with all his strength, with all his bones, cries out: Lord, who is like you? And so you can say calmly, without causing confusion, habent Sacramenta. Non sunt ista montium: sed cum inveniuntur in montibus, male remanetur in montibus. Errando enim in montibus et in collibus, deserunt gregem; deserunt unitatem, deserunt munitas cohorts adversus leones et lupos. Inde ergo revocet Deus, ipse revocet.
