the lost, comfort the weak, heal the sick, bind up the broken; He frees some from these, the others from those, who are unknown to each other. She, however, knows them all, because she is mixed with all of them. For example, in Africa there is the party of Donatus, not the Eunomians 5, and mixed with the party of Donatus is the Catholic party. In the East, where Donato's party does not exist, there are the Eunomians, and with them there is the Catholic Church. She is like the vine that grows and spreads everywhere; those, like useless branches, cut with the farmer's pruning shears because of their sterility, so that the vine can be pruned, not to be cut down. The branches remained where they were cut. The vine, on the other hand, grows in all places and knows its branches, those that remained in it, and has close to it those that were cut off from it. It leads the lost, since, referring to the cut branches, the Apostle also says: God is able to graft them back. Whether you think about the lost sheep from the flock or the trunks cut from the vine, God is able to bring the sheep back to the flock and graft the trunks back in, because he is the supreme shepherd, the true farmer. They scattered over the entire face of the earth; and there was no one to look for them or anyone to lead them back, that is, none of the bad shepherds; There was no one looking for them, that is, no man.

As I live, says the Lord God. See how it begins. These words are like an oath from God, a testimony of his life. As I live, says the Lord. The shepherds died, but the sheep are safe; the Lord lives. As I live, says the Lord God. Which shepherds have died? Those who seek their interests, not those of Jesus Christ. Will there be and will pastors be found who do not seek their interests, but those of Jesus Christ? There will be them, and they will be found; They are neither missing nor will they be missing. Let's see what the Lord says when he swears that he lives; Perhaps he says that he is to take the sheep from the bad shepherds, who feed themselves and not the sheep, and give them to the good shepherds, who feed the sheep and not themselves. As I live, says the Lord God, my sheep have become a prey to all the beasts of the field, because there was no shepherd. Again he speaks to the shepherd; before and now. It does not say: because there are no shepherds. For such sheep, who are led astray to their evil and lost to their evil, there is no shepherd; and if it is present, since in being present there is light, it is not light for the blind. And the shepherds did not seek my sheep; They fed themselves and not my sheep.
Therefore, shepherds, listen to the word of the Lord:

in ea ubique quaerit errantes, comfortat infirmos, curat languids, alligat confractos, alios ab istis, alios ab illis non se invicem scientibus. Sed tamen illa omnes novit, quia cum ómnibus fusa est. Verbi gtatia, est in África pars Donati, Eunomiani non sunt in África; sed cum parte Donati est hic Catholica. Sunt in Oriente Eunomiani, ibi autem non est pars Donati; sed cum Eunomianis ibi est Catholica. Illa sic est, tanquam vitis, crescendo ubique diffusa: illi sic sunt, tanquam sarmenta inutilia, agricolae falce praecisa merit sterilitatis suae; ut vitis putaretur, non ut amputaretur. Sarmenta ergo illa ubi praecisa sunt, ibi remanserunt. Vitis autem crescens [281] per omnia, et sarmenta sua novit quae in illa manserunt, et iuxta se quae de illa praecisa sunt. Inde tamen revocat errantes: quia et de ramis fractis dicit Apostolus, Potens est enim Deus iterum inserere illos (Rom 11,23). Sive dicas oves errantes a grege, sive dicas ligna praecisa de vite; nec ad revocandas oves, nec rursus ad inserenda ligna minus idoneus est Deus; quia ille summus pastor, ille verus agricultural. Et in omnem faciem terrae disperse sunt; et non fuet qui requireret, non fuet qui revocaret. Non Fuit, sed in illis pastoribus malis: Non Fuit, sed homo, qui requireret. CAPUT IX.—19. Malis pastoribus oves unde securae.—Propterea,
V? See additional note 59: The Eunomians, p.764,

20. Therefore, shepherds, listen to the word of the Lord. What shepherds? This is what the Lord God says: Behold, I am above the shepherds and I will require my sheep at their hands. Listen and learn, sheep of God. God claims his sheep from the shepherds, and claims their death from their hands. In shepherds, audite verbum Domini: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus Deus. Videte unde coepit. Tanquam iuratio est Dei, testificatio vitae suae. Live ego, Dominus said. Mortui sunt pastors: sed securae sunt oves, vivit Dominus. Vivo ego, said Dominus Deus. Qui autem pastors mortui sunt? Sua quaerentes, non quae Iesu Christi (Phil 2:21). Erunt ergo, et invenientur pastores non quae sua sunt quaerentes, sed quae Iesu Christi? Erunt plane, et invenientur; plan nec desunt, nec deerunt. Videamus ergo quid dicat Dominus, qui se dicit vivere: utrum dicat ablaturum se oves a pastoribus malis, pascentibus seipsos, non oves; et daturum se eas pastoribus bonis, pascentibus oves, non se. Vivo ego, dicit Dominus Deus, nisi pro eo quod factae sunt oves meae in comesturam ómnibus bestiis campi, eo quod non esset pastor. Rursus pastorem dicit, et paulo ante, et nunc. Non ait, Ex eo quod non sint pastors. Ovibus enim talibus male errantibus, male pereuntibus non est pastor, et si praesens est pastor: quia et cum praesens est lux, non est caecis lux. Et non quaesierunt pastors oves meas, et paverunt pastors se ipsos, oves autem meas non paverunt. 20. Ovium interitus quomodo pastori imputatur.—Propter istud, pastors, audite verbum Domini. Sed qui pastors audite? Haec dicit Dominus Deus: Ecce ego super pastors, et inquiram oves meas de manibus eorum. Audite et discite, oves Dei: a malis pastoribus inquirit Deus oves suas, et de manibus eorum inquiret mortem earum. Dicit enim alio
The shepherds (Ez 34,1-16)

Another place says by the same prophet: Son of man, I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel, you will hear a word from my mouth and make it known to them from me. If I say to the sinner: You are going to die, and you do not warn him, so that the wicked may turn from his evil way, he, as an evil one, will die for his crime; but I will ask you to account for his blood. If, on the other hand, you warned the wicked from his evil way, so that he would depart from it, and he did not do so, he will die for his crime, and you will have freed your soul. What is this, brothers? You see how dangerous it is to remain silent. The sinner dies and dies justly; He dies for his impiety and his sin; The shepherd's negligence caused him to die. He could have found a living shepherd who would say to him: As I live, says the Lord; but he found one negligent; Although he was president and sentinel to give the warning, he did not warn; the one dies justly; and the other, precisely too, is condemned. If, on the contrary, thus says the Lord, if you say to the wicked whom I have threatened with the sword, "You are going to die," but he neglects to avoid the imminent sword, and it comes and kills him, he will die because of his sin, but you spared your life. For this reason, it is up to us not to remain silent; You, however, have to listen, even when we remain silent, to the words of the pastor in the Holy Scriptures. 21. Let us see, then, what he had proposed to deal with: if he takes the sheep from the bad shepherds and gives them to the good ones. I see that, indeed, he takes the sheep from the bad shepherds. By

This says: Behold, I am coming upon the shepherds and will take my sheep out of their hands; I will remove them from feeding my sheep; and they will feed themselves no more. When I tell them to feed my sheep, they feed themselves, not my sheep. I will remove them, so that they do not feed my sheep. How do you remove them so that they do not graze your sheep? Do what they say, but don't do what they do. As if to say: "They say my thing, they do their thing." He could have said: 'Do calmly what they do; "I will condemn them for living badly, but I will forgive you, because you have followed those who are your superiors." If I had said this, I repeat, I would have terrified the bad shepherds, who feed themselves, not the sheep. But it instils fear not only in the blind man who leads, but also in the blind man who follows him - for he does not say: He who leads falls into the pit, but he who follows him does not fall, but rather: If a blind man guides another blind man, they both fall into the pit; That is why he warns the sheep, telling them: Do what they say; Don't do what they do. When you do not do what bad shepherds do, then they do not feed you; When you do what they say, I feed you. They proclaim my precepts and do not fulfill them. "With tranquility, some say, we follow our bishops." Heretics often say this when they are convinced by the manifest truth: “We are sheep; "They will give an account of us." They certainly give a bad account of your death. The bad shepherd will give a bad account of the death of the evil sheep. Perhaps

in loco per eumdem prophetam: Fili hominis, speculatorem dedi te domui Israel: audies ex ore meo sermonem, et praemonstrabis eis ex me. In eo cum dixero peccatori, Morte morieris, et non fueris locutus, ut caveat impius a via sua; Ule facinorosus in suo facinore morietur, sanguinem autem eius de manu tua exquiram. Tu autem si praenuntiaveris facinoroso viam eius, ut avertatur ab ea, et non fuerit aversus a via sua; Iste in facinore suo morietur, et tu animam tuam liberabis. What is it, frattes? Videtis quam tú tacere peticulosum? Moritur ille, et recte moritur: in impietate sua et peccato suo moritur; neglegentia enim eius occidit eum. Nam pastorem inveniret vivostem, qui ait, Vivo ego, dicit Dominus: sed cum fuerit neglegens, non admonente illo qui ad hoc est praepositus et speculator, ut [282] admoneat, et ille iuste moritur, et iste iuste damnatur. Si autem dixeris, inquit, impio, Morte morieris, cui ego gladium fuero comminatus, et Ule neglexerit vitare imminentem gladium, et venerit gladius, et interfecerit eum; Ule in sin suo morietur, tu autem animam tuam liberasti (Ez 33,2-9). Propter hoc, ad nos quidem pertinet non tacere; ad vos autem, etiamsi taceamus, de Scripturis sanctis verba pastoris audire. CAPUT X.—21. Oves a malis pastoribus quomodo reducit Deus. Ovis errantem pastorem sequendo non secura.—Videamus ergo, quia sic pro-

posueram, utrum auferat oves a pastoribus malis, et det eas pastoribus bonis. Video eum auferentem oves a pastoribus malis. Hoc enim dicit: Ecce ego ipse super pastors, et inquiram oves meas de manibus eorum, et avertam ab eis, ut non pascant oves meas; et non pascent adhuc shepherds semetipsos. Cum enim dico, Pascant oves meas; illi se pascunt, non oves meas. Avertam, ut non pascant oves meas. Quomodo avertit, ut non pascant oves ipsius? Quae dicunt, facite; quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite (Mt 23,3). Tanquam diceret, Mea dicunt, sua faciunt. Si diceret, Facite securi quod faciunt, ipsos damnabo male vivos; vobis autem parcam, quia secuti estis praepositos vestros: si hoc diceret, deterreret bad shepherds, pascentes non oves, sed se. Sed quoniam terret non solum caecum ducentem, sed et caecum sequentem (ñeque enim ait, Cadit in foveam, ducens, et non cadit sequens: sed, Caecus caecum ducens, ambo in foveam cadunt [ib., 15,14]); admonuit oves, et ait, Quae dicunt, facite; quae faciunt, faceré nolite. Cum enim non facitis quae faciunt mali pastores, non vos ipsi pascunt: cum autem facitis quae dicunt, ego vos pasco: mea enim dicunt, et non faciunt. Securi, inquiunt, sequimus episcopos nostros. Dicunt hoc saepe haeretici, quando veritate manifestissima convincuntur: Nos oves sumus, illi de nobis reddent rationem. Reddent plane malam de morte vestra. De morte ovis malignae

Does the sheep live because its skin is presented? The shepherd is reproached for having neglected the lost sheep, which is why it fell into the jaws of the wolf and was devoured. What is the benefit of having marked skin? The father of the family claims the life of the sheep. Behold, the bad shepherd presents the skin. Account for the skin. Can the shepherd lie? Whoever will judge him later saw it from above; He tells her the words, the facts and sees her thoughts. The bad shepherd accounts for the skin of the dead sheep. «I announced your words to him, and he did not want to follow them; "I made every effort to keep him from straying from the flock, and he did not obey me." If he says this and thereby tells the truth—God knows if he says the truth—he gives a good account of the bad sheep. If, on the other hand, God sees that he neglected the lost sheep, that he did not look for the one that was lost, what good does it do him to have found the skin to present? I would have brought her back to the flock, so as not to have to show the dead woman's skin. If, then, the person who did not look for it when it was lost did not give a good account, what account will the one who lost it give? This is what I hear: If the bishop of the Catholic Church does not account for the sheep, if he does not look for it when it is lost from the flock of God, what account must the heretical bishop give who not only did not lead it back from its loss, but also led it to it? 22. But let us see, as I said, how God separates the sheep from bad shepherds. I already said it before: Do what reddet malus pastor malam rationem. Numquid ideo vivit ovis, quia assignatur pellis ipsius? Increpatur pastor, quia neglexit ovem errantem, et propterea in fauces lupi irruit, ut devoratetur. Quid illi prodest, quia affert pellem signatam? Paterfamilias vitara ovis inquirit. Sed ecce malus pastor attulit pellem: reddat de pelle rationem. Forte menturus est? Videbat desuper, who posts iudicat. Cui verba ille ficta numerat, cogitationes inspicit. Reddat pastor malus rationem de pelle ovis mortuae. Clamavi ei verba tua, et sequi noluit: dedi operam ut a grege non aberraret, et non obtemperavit. Plan si hoc dicat, et verum dicat (novit autem ille utrum verum dicat), reddit bonam rationem de ove mala. Si autem inspicit Deus quia neglexit errantem, quia non quaesivit pereuntem; quid [283] prodest quod invenit pellem quam referret? Ipsam revocaret, ne pellem mortuae demonstraret. Si ergo non bonam rationem reddit, quia non quaesivit errantem; qualem reddet, qui fecit errantem?

Hoc est quod dico: Si in Catholica episcopus constitutus non bonam rationem reddit de ove, si non quaesierit errantem a grege Dei; qualem rationem redditurus est haereticus, qui non solum non revocavit ab errore, sed etiam impulit in errorem? 22. Pastor malus non in eo quod de suo, sed in eo quod de Dei profert, audiendus.—Sed videamus, ut dixi, quomodo revocet Deus oves * The shepherd was obliged to present the skin as proof that the sheep had been devoured by the wolf, not sold or stolen.

They say, but don't do what they do. It is not they who feed you, but God; Whether shepherds want it or not, to get to the milk and wool, they must announce the word of God. You who preach that one should not steal, you steal, says the Apostle to those who say good things and practice evil. You listen to him who preaches, do not steal; do not imitate the one who steals. If you would like to imitate the thief, he will appease you with his action; It supplies you with poison, not food. But if you hear that he says something, not about his harvest, but about God's...—grapes cannot be gathered from brambles, for it is also the word of the Lord: No one gathers grapes from brambles or figs from thistles—; You should not slander God in a certain way by saying: “Lord, you have not loved me, because you cannot gather grapes from brambles; and in another place you told me about some: Do what they say, but do not do what they do; That is to say, those who do evil are brambles. How do you want me to gather the grape of the word from the brambles? He will answer: «That grape is not a product of the brambles; What sometimes happens is that the branch gets tangled in the hedge and the grape hangs in the middle of thick brambles, but it does not come from the roots of these. If you are hungry and have nowhere to get them, put your hand in carefully so as not to lacerate yourself with the brambles, that is, so as not to imitate the actions of the bad guys; and take the grape that hangs in the midst of the brambles, but which is the fruit of the vine. The food of the cluster will come to you; The torment of fire is reserved for the brambles.

to pastoribus malis. Iam commemoravi: Quae dicunt, facite; quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite. Et non vos ipsi pascunt, sed Deus: quia velint nolint pastors, ut perveniant ad lac et lanam, verba Dei dicturi sunt. Qui praedicas non furandum, furaris (Rom 2:21), dicit Apostolus ad eos qui bona dicunt et mala faciunt. Tu audi praedicantem, ne fureris: noli imitari furantem. If furantem imitari volueris, ipse te pascit facto suo: tibí venenum subministrat, non cibum. Si vero hoc ab illo audis, quod non dicit de suo, thirst for Dei; non potest quidem uva de spinis legi (nam et ipsa Domini sententia est, Nemo colligit de spinis uvam, et de tribulis ficus [Mt 7,16]): nec ideo tamen quasi calumnieris Domino tuo, et dicas, Domine, noluisti me, quia fieri non potest, de spinis legere uvam: et rursus dixisti mihi de quibusdam: Quae dicunt, facite; quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite. Nempe mala facientes utique spinae sunt. Quomodo vis de spinis me colligere uvam verbi tuí? Respondebitur: Non est illa uva spinarum; sed aliquando increscens sarmentum implicat se in sepem, et pendet uva interdense spinarum, sed non surgit de radice spinarum. Tu si esurieris, et aliud non habes unde sums, caute manum mitte, ne lacereris ab spinis, id est, ne facta imiteris malorum; et lege uvam inter spinas pendentem, sed de vite nascentem. Ad te peryeniat botri alimentum: spinis servatur ignis tormentum,
The shepherds (Ez 34,1-16)

23. I will tear my sheep from their mouths and hands, he said, and they will no longer be their pasture. This same thing is said in the psalm: Do not all those who work iniquity know that they devour my people like bread? And they will no longer be their pasture, for this is what the Lord God says: Behold, I myself. I separated the sheep from the bad shepherds, telling them, as I said, not to do what they do; That is, let the unsuspecting and carefree sheep not do what the bad shepherds do. And what does it say? To whom does he give what he took from them? To the good shepherds perhaps? It doesn't indicate it. What shall we say then, brothers? Are there no good shepherds? Is it not said elsewhere in the Scriptures: And I will give them shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed them with discipline? Just as he does not give to good shepherds the sheep he takes from bad ones, as if there were no good shepherds left anywhere, he says: Will I accept them? He had said to Peter: Feed my sheep. What to think, then? When the sheep are entrusted to Peter, the Lord does not say: I will feed my sheep, do not do it, but: Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep. Or perhaps because Peter is no longer here—he was already received into the rest of the apostles and martyrs—there is no one to whom the Lord of the sheep can say with confidence: Feed my sheep? Perhaps, forced by necessity, he goes down to carry out the job of tending his sheep, because he has no one to entrust it to and not wanting to abandon them? So it seems, so it continues: This

says the Lord God: Behold, I, that is, he to whom we said, You who feed Israel, look; You who guide Joseph, the people established in Egypt, like sheep. Israel, already spread among the peoples, is Joseph himself. You know, in fact, that Joseph emigrated to Egypt; This happened when the brothers sold it. The Jews sold Christ; Not without reason, also among the apostles Judas was the one who sold him. Christ began to be among the Gentiles, there he was honored, there his people grew, his shepherd did not abandon him. Awaken, he said, your power and come save us. He is already doing it and he will do it. It goes like this: Behold, I myself will seek my sheep, I will visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock. The bad shepherds did not worry; They did not rescue them with their blood. As he visits, he said, the shepherd his flock on the day. On what day? When there are storms and clouds, that is, rain and fog. Rain and fog are the misplacement in the world, a great darkness that arises from the appetites of men and a dense fog that covers the earth. It is difficult for the sheep not to get lost in the middle of this fog. But the shepherd does not abandon them. He looks for them, he pierces the fog with sharp eyes, unhindered by the darkness of the clouds. He sees them, he calls the lost one anywhere, so that what is said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: The sheep that are mine hear my voice and follow me. In the midst of the scattered sheep I will look for my own, I will take them out of every place where they are lost in the day of clouds and storm. When it's hard to find them, then I will find them.

CAPUT XI.—23. Ovium curam Deus ipse suscipit.—Et extraham oves meas, inquit, de ore eorum, et de manibus eorum: et non erunt eis adhuc in cibum. Hoc et in Psalmo dicitur: Nonne cognoscent omnes qui operantur iniquitatem, qui devorant populum meum in cibum pañis? Et non erunt eis adhuc in cibum: quoniam haec dicit Dominus Deus, Ecce ego ipse. Abstuli a malis pastibus oves meas, monendo, ut dixi, ne quod faciunt, faciant; Id est, ne quod faciunt malí pastors, faciant impustrae et neglegentes oves. Et quid ait? Cui dat quod illis abstulit? Forte bonis pastoribus? Non hoc sequitur. Et quid dicemus, fratres? Nonne sunt pastores boni? Nonne alio loco Scripturarum dicitur: Et constituam eis pastors secundum cor meum, et pascent eas cum disciplina (Jer 3,15). Quomodo ergo oves, quas malis pastoribus tollit, non dat bonis; sed tanquam omnino nusquam remanserint boni, dicit, Ego pascam? Petro dixerat, Pasee oves meas. Quid ergo facimus? Cum Petro [284] commendantur oves, non ibi dixit Dominus, Ego pascam oves meas, non tu: sed, Petre, do you love me? Walk oves meas (lo 21.17). An forte quia moda non invenitur Petrus (iam enim assumptus est in requiem Anostolorum et martyrum), non est cui dicat securus Dominus ovium, Pasee oves meas; et quodammodo quasi necessitate descendit ad officium pascendi oves suas, non habens quibus commendet, nec tamen deserens? Hoc enim videtur sequi, Haec dicit Dominus Deus, Ecce ego ipse. Cui dicebamus, qui pascis Israel, intende; what do you deduce tanquam oves

loseph, populum in Aegypto constitutum. Iam diffusus in Gentibus Israel, ipse est Joseph. Nostis enim quia migravit loseph in Aegyptum: vendetibus fratribus factum est (Gen 37,28). Vendiderunt Christum Iudaei: non sine causa et inter Apostólos ipse ludas venditor Fuit. Coepit esse Christus in Gentibus, ibi honoratus est, ibi crevit populus eius, non eum deserit pastor eius. Excita, inquit, potentiam tuam, et veni, ut safe facías nos (Ps 79,2.3). Plan facit, et faciet. Ait enim: Ecce ego ipse, et inquiram oves meas; et visitabo eas, sicut visitat pastor gregem suum. Non curaverunt mali pastores: non enim suo sanguine redemerunt. Sicut visitat, inquit, pastor gregem suum in die. In quali die? Cum fuerit nimbus, et clouds: id est, et in pluvia, et in nebula. Pluvia et nebula, error saeculi huius: caligo magna arises from cupiditatibus hominum, et nebula valida contegens terram. Et difficile est ut non errent oves in ista nebula: sed pastor non deserit eas. Inquirit eas, penetrat nebulam oculis acutissimis, non impeditur calígine nubium: videt, undique errantem revocat: in tantum ut fiat quod dicit in Gospel, Quae sunt oves meae, audiunt vocem meam, et sequuntur me (lo 10,27). In medio ovium dispersarum, sic inquiram oves meas, et educam eas ab omni loco quo disperse sunt illie, in die nubis et nimbi. Quando difficile est eas inveniri, tune ego inveniam. Crassa nebula est, pinguis nimbus est: oculos eius nihil latet.

24. I will bring them out from among the people, I will gather them from the regions, I will bring them into their own land and feed them on the mountains of Israel. He established the authors of the divine Scriptures as mountains of Israel. Feed there to do it safely. Whatever you hear that it comes from there, delight your taste; reject what is strange. Do not get lost in the fog, listen to the voice of the shepherd. Gather on the mountains of the Holy Scripture. There are the delights of your heart; There is nothing poisonous, nothing strange; There are lush pastures. You come in health, feed in health on the mountains of Israel. And in the streams and in every place on earth. In these mountains that we are showing have their headwaters the streams of evangelical preaching, when his voice spread throughout the land and every place on earth became joyful and fruitful for the sheep that are to be fed, I will feed in good pastures on the high mountains of Israel and they will have their sheepfold there, that is, the place where they rest, where they say: "It is good"; where they say: "It's true, it's clear, they didn't deceive us." They will rest in the glory of God, as in his sheepfolds. And they will sleep, that is, they will rest, and they will rest in complete delight. 25. They will feed in rich pastures on the mountains of Israel. I already said who the mountains of Israel were, the good mountains to which we lift our eyes so that help may come to us. But our help comes to us from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. For this reason, so that not even in the 24. Montes Israel, ubi pascua bona.—Et educam eas de gentibus, et colügam eas de regionibus; et inducam eas in terram earum, et pascam eas super mountains Israel. Constituit montes Israel, auctores Scripturarum divinarum. Ibi pascite, ut securae pascatis. Quidquid inde audieritis, hoc vobis bene sapiat: quidquid extra est, respuite. Ne erretis in nebula, audite vocem pastoris: colligite vos ad montes Scripturae sanctae; ibi sunt deliciae cordis vestri, ibi nihil poisonum, nihil alienum; Ubérrima pascua est: vos tantum sanae come, sanae pascimini in montibus Israel. Et in vivís, et in omni habitatione terrae. A montibus enim, quos ostendimus, manaverunt rivi praedicationis evangelicae, cum in omnem terram exiit sonus eorum (Ps 18,5): et facta est omnis habitatio terrae ad pascen[285]das oves laeta atque fecunda. In pascua bona pascam eas, et in montibus dtis Israel.

Erunt stabula earum illic: hoc est, ubi requiescant, ubi dicant, Bene est; ubi dicant, Verum est, manifestum est, non fallimur. In gloria Dei requiescent, tanquam in stabulis illis. Et dormient, hoc est, requiescent; et requiescent in deliciis bonis. 25. Spes ovium in solo Deo.—Et in pascua pingui pascentur super mountains Israel. Iam dixi mountains Israel, mountains bonds, quo levamus oculos, ut nobis inde auxiliúm veniat. Sed auxilium nostrum a Domino, qui fecit caelum et terram (Ps 120,1.2). Ideo ne vel in montibus bonis
The shepherds (Ez 34,1-16)

good mountains to put our hope, he said: I will feed my sheep on the mountains of Israel; Furthermore, so that you would not remain in the mountains, he immediately added: I will feed my sheep. Lift your eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to you; but listen to him who says: I will feed. Your help is in the Lord, who made heaven and earth. 26. And I will give them rest, says the Lord God. But, to make them rest, what did he worry about beforehand? What his previous concerns were he says later: This is what the Lord God says: I will seek the one that is lost; I will call the one that was lost; I will bind up the ravine, I will strengthen the weak, and I will guard the rich and strong: all things that the bad shepherds did not do, who fed themselves, not the sheep. The Lord does not say, “I will appoint other shepherds to do this,” but rather, “I myself will do it; "I will not entrust my sheep to anyone else." Be calm, brothers; Be confident, you sheep. It is we who have to fear, as if the good shepherd were missing. 27. Conclude in this way: And I will accept them with justice. Keep in mind that only he feeds them like this; he who feeds them with justice. What man can judge another man? Everything is full of reckless judgments. anyone, he hardly knows it himself. Still, to a certain extent, he knows what it is today. On the other hand, what will be tomorrow, not even he himself knows. According to the prophet Jeremiah, the partridge cried, gathered eggs that it did not lay, accumulating riches, but without judgment. Unlike this partridge who accumulated his wealth without judgment, this shepherd feeds with judgment. Why without judgment? Because he gathered what he did not beget. Why this one with judgment? Because he breeds what he begot. We are talking about the good shepherd. Good shepherds either do not exist or are hidden. If there aren't any, why are we wasting time? If they are hidden, why aren't they talked about? In that partridge some of our elders and the commentators on Scripture before us saw significance to the devil, who gathers what he did not give birth to 7. He is not a creator, but a deceiver, accumulating his riches without judgment. He does not care if one goes astray in this way and another in another. Christ feeds you with judgment, distinguishes the sheep that are his from those that are not. The sheep that are mine, he says, listen to my voice and follow me. 30. Here I find all the good shepherds in one. There is no shortage of good shepherds, but they are found in only one. Those who are divided are many. Only one is advertised here, because unity is recommended. Perhaps you will say that now we do not speak of shepherds, but of a single shepherd, because the Lord cannot find someone to entrust his sheep to. So he entrusted them because he found Pedro. On the contrary, in Peter himself he recommended unity to us. There were many apostles and only to one it is said: Feed my sheep. Far be it from us to say that good shepherds are now lacking; far from us who are missing, far from his mercy who does not produce and establish them for us! In fact, if there are good sheep, there are also good shepherds, since good shepherds come from good sheep. But all the good shepherds are in one, they are one thing. They feed, it is Christ who feeds. The husband's friends do not say that it is their own voice, but rather that they enjoy the husband's voice. Therefore, it is he himself who feeds when they feed. He says: It is I who feed; for in them his voice is found, in them his charity. To the same Peter to whom he entrusted his sheep, as if he were his "alter ego", he wanted to do one thing only with himself, in order to entrust him with the sheep. And responded: Master. Et iterum: Do you love me? And responded: Master. Et tertio: Do ​​you love me? And responded: Master. Confirmat caritatem, ut consolidet unitatem. Tamen ut pauca commemoremus, Legem attende, primum Dei Testamen13 Here Augustine mentions the facts that the Donatists denounced: having handed over the sacred books to the persecutors and having offered incense to the idols during the persecution of Diocletian. The reason for this accusation against the Catholics came from the fact of being in ecclesiastical communion with Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, who had been consecrated, along with two others, by Bishop Felix of Abtungi, upon whom such suspicions fell. That was the occasional reason for the schism. See supplementary note 62: Origin of the Donatist schism, p.765. Augustine responds by inviting them to distinguish between concrete people and the Church itself.

Ipsa adhuc dicit, ubi pascis, ubi cubas Throughout this paragraph, Augustine speaks as a grammarian. The distinctio verborum was one of the school practices. To understand it, we must remember that ancient writing did not separate words, and an adequate distinction between them was absolutely necessary to capture the meaning of the text. In his work Christian Doctrine III 2,2-5, the saint gives the rules on how to proceed in this regard in the case of the Bible: "when the reader does not know with certainty how it should be punctuated or how it should be pronounced, he should consult the rule of faith that he has received from the clearest texts of Scripture or from the authority of the Church."

7. What is said about the Lord? Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, and between rams and goats. I am the one who judges. Great security, brothers; It is he who judges; the good ones be safe. No adversary corrupts the judge, no lawyer will entangle him, no witness will deceive him. But the greater the security of the good, the greater the fear of the wicked. He who judges is not one from whom something can be hidden. Will God, at the time of judgment, go to look for witnesses through whom he will know who you are? How can the one who knew what you were going to be be wrong about who you are? He will question you; not another about you. The Lord, d:ce, questions the righteous and the wicked. He questions you, but not to learn from you, but to confuse you. Having, then, such a judge, whom no one will deceive against us, no one for us, let us conduct ourselves in such a way that we do not fear the coming judgment, but hope and desire it. Is wheat afraid of being introduced into the granary? On the contrary, he desires it vehemently and craves it. Do sheep fear being placed on the right? On the contrary, nothing seems longer to them than the waiting time until this happens. These, when they pray, say with all their heart and with all sincerity: Your kingdom come. At these words the heart of the wicked man trembles and his tongue hesitates. How do you say your kingdom come? It will certainly come. How will he find you? Behave in such a way that you are safe being a sheep. And if there is something of error or sin in your conscience, you have the medicine.

There are many who learn quietly and teach riotously, and, having a patient teacher, they are cruel to the learner. Who does not notice how calmly Scripture itself teaches us? Someone comes, reads the commandments of God, reads them and understands them; He calmly understands them, drinking from the quiet fountain, grazing on what is tender and clean. Another comes to hear something from his mouth. He becomes indignant, he becomes upset, blaming the slowness of someone who takes a little longer to understand, and disturbing him makes him understand even less what he had been able to hear calmly. 10. The fact that I say this, brothers, does not mean that harshness does not sometimes have to be corrected, since the utmost tranquility of the truth also does so when saying: Oh foolish ones and slow of heart to understand! But it must be done with that love through which we want to introduce restlessness into men; It is to instill in them the effort to maintain attention and perhaps to calm the cloud in their mind, which they contracted from the business of the world; thinking perhaps of useless things, they cannot hear what is useful. And even if someone sees this slowness in himself, we rebuke him to pray to God to free him from it and grant him the truth. Our negligence must also be corrected if, because of it, we do not understand what we hear. If this slowness persists once we are accused of it, we have to pray to God. Such doctors should not be censored. But they must be those who with bitterness, out of envy, trample the pastures and muddy the

sources. Perhaps what they know they want to know in such a way that others do not know it. Men of evil minds, full of infernal zeal, livid not in body, but in heart, read it and understood. When asked, they respond: "Are you so interested in me entrusting these things to you?" Are you worthy of reading and listening to these things? Why do you cloud the water? The fountain flows for both. Why do you step on grasses that are common? It was not you who gave the rain for them to be born. 11. There is another aspect to these words. It does not seem that the understanding that I propose is absurd. There are men who believe that a good conscience is enough for them in their righteous life, and they do not worry about what others think of them. Perhaps a man sees another with a good conscience, but sees that he lives with a certain negligence, that he frequently associates with anyone and anywhere, that he knows that an idol is nothing and yet sits down to eat meats consecrated to it; The conscience of the former is weak and he is encouraged to do not what is the result of deep knowledge, but what is simply suspicion. A man like you, your brother, cannot enter your conscience, although God knows it. Let your conscience be before God, but let your life be before your brother. If he, suspecting something bad about you, is disturbed and feels impelled to do something that he believes you do, since you live this way, what does it matter that the belly of your conscience has drunk the pure water, if he has a troubled life due to your negligence? 4

12. When such are corrected not to act in that way, you hear them respond to us and say: "The Apostle said: If I wanted to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." I accept it; I gladly acknowledge that it is a phrase of the Apostle. But didn't you read anything else in it? Please everyone in all things, just as I please everyone in everything, not seeking what is beneficial to me, but what is beneficial to all, that they may be saved. Did you not also hear the same Apostle when he said: Do not be a stumbling block to the Jews and Greeks, nor to the Church of God? On the one hand, the Apostle says: If I wanted to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ; On the other hand, he himself affirms: Please everyone in everything, just as I please everyone in everything. He explains what he says on the one hand: Our glory is the testimony of our conscience, and on the other: We take care to do good not only before God, but also before men. If you listen to it calmly, if the water in your mind doesn't get muddied

mind, perhaps I will be able to explain it to you to the best of my ability. There are men, rash judges, detractors, gossipers, gossipers, inclined to suspect what they do not see, also inclined to boast about what they do not even suspect: Against such such, what do we have left, but the testimony of our conscience? Nor, brothers, do we seek our glory in those whom we wish to please, nor should we seek it, but rather their salvation, so that, living well, they may not go astray by following us. Be imitators of us if we are imitators of Christ; If we are not imitators of Christ, let them be so directly. Of course also because of those who said: Please everyone in everything, just as I please everyone in everything. One thing and another is clear, calm, clean, not clouded. The sheep (Ez 34,17-31)

We are the people of his pastures and the sheep of his hands. If you are good, let him be praised who made you good, not you, who by yourself could do nothing but be bad. Why do you want to change the order of truth so that when you do something good you want to be praised and when you do something bad you want to reproach the Lord? He who said: Let your works shine before men, he himself said in the same place: Do not do your righteousness before men. But as these things seemed contrary to you in the Apostle's mouth, they also seem to you in the Gospel. If you do not muddy the water of your heart and recognize the peace of the Scriptures here, you too will be at peace with them. If, on the other hand, you do not want to be at peace with them, you enter into litigation with yourself, but they do not lose their peace. Thinking of those who, boasting, praise themselves before men and broadcast their good works, so that they put the end of them in the praise of men and, in a certain way, even consider the praise of men as the reward due to them, the Lord said: Truly I say to you, they have already received their reward. Against them it is said: Beware of doing your justice before men. This is the reason you continue: to be seen by them. They did not set their intention further; Its purpose ends here. Do not do in front of men what you do that is good, to be seen by them, as if the end of your good work were to be seen by them. Do not act like this to be

seen by them. The purpose of the phrase was not to be seen by men, before whom he wants our good works to be, but rather it says: Let your works shine before men, so that they may see your good works. He did not stay here, he did not find the end here, but he led you higher and took you out - you would fall, in fact, if you were in yourself - and placed you where you were safe. See, he said, your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. Do not be irritated because he is glorified. Stay by his side and you will be glorified in him. So that no flesh may boast, says the Apostle, in his presence. So will we remain inglorious? No. He himself says: Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord. The testimony of our conscience is glory to us, because it is in it. For if our glory is to please ourselves, and in fact we take pleasure in ourselves, let us know that he who pleases himself pleases a fool. 14. Let us be concerned, brothers, not only to live well, but also that our life is upright in the presence of men; Let us not only try to have a good conscience, but also, as far as our weakness allows, as far as the vigilance of human frailty allows, let us try not to do anything that could lead to bad suspicion in the weak brother, lest, by eating herbs and drinking clean water, we trample the pastures of God, and the weak sheep eat what has been trampled and drink what is turbid. Ah! The Lord says: I judge between sheep and sheep.

The evil son calls himself righteous, but he did not clean his way out. Listen, my brothers, to this sentence, brief for the number of its words, but great for the weight of the truth. Why does your heart tremble when you hear in the divine books: They came from among us, but they were not ours, if that evil fortress, through which you push, impel and fan the sheep, allows your heart to tremble? But I am not the one who announces the Church spread throughout the world. The prophets, the apostles announced it, the Lord himself announced it spread throughout the earth. To us, as already living by day, the apostle John says: Dearly beloved, we are children of God. And yet, since we are still night, how does it continue? And what we will be has not yet been manifested. We know that when he appears we will be like him, because we will see him as he is. But this is the reward, not the work. If you approach being ugly, and you see yourself as such, do not accuse the mirror. Go back inside; the mirror does not deceive you; Don't fool yourself. Judge yourself, be saddened by your ugliness, so that when you leave and walk away sad, with the ugliness corrected, you can return beautiful. But even if you judge yourself without flattery, judge your neighbor with love. To judge you have there what you see. It may happen that you see something bad that causes you to stain yourself; It may happen that your neighbor himself confesses his evil to you and declares to his friend what he had concealed from his enemy. Judge what you see. What you don't see, leave it to God. When you judge, love the man, hate the vice 4. Do not love vice for man nor hate man for vice. The man is your neighbor; vice is the enemy of your neighbor. You love your friend when you hate what hurts him. If you believe, you work, because the righteous live by faith. 6. I am talking about what abounds in human things. Sometimes someone who was a friend of both of you is an enemy of your dearest friend. If, of three friends, two begin to be enemies, what will the third do? He wants, he asks you, he demands that you hate with him the one whom he began to hate, and he tells you these words: "You are not my friend if you are a friend of my enemy." What one tells you, the other tells you. There were three of you. There were three of you; two began to enter into discord; you remained If you go with this one, you will have the other as your enemy; If with the other, you will have the first; if with both, both will murmur. Behold cum foedus accesseris, et foedum te ibi videris, noli aecusare speculum: ad te redi, non te fallit speculum, tu te noli fallete. Iudica de te, contristare de tua foeditate; ut cum abieris et discesseris tristis, foedus, correctus possis rediré formosus. Cum ergo iudicaveris te ipsum sine adulatíone, judica et proximum cum dilectione. Est enim quod [323] iudices, quod vides. Fieri enim potest ut aliquid mali videas, unde sordescas. Fieri potest ut malum suum ipse proximus tuus tibi confiteatur, et prodat amico quod texerat inimico. Quod videris, iudica: quod non vides, Deo dimitte. Quando autem judicas, dilige hominem, oderis vitium. Noli propter hominem diligere vitium, nec propter vitium odisse hominem. Homo proximus tuus est: vitium inimicum proxima tuo. Tune amas amicum, si oderis quod nocet amico. If you believe, believe; quia iustus ex fide vivit. CAPUT VI.—6. This, to which you do not pay attention: Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. Whoever hates is a murderer. Can you now say "what do I have to do with a murderer?" Whoever hates is a murderer. You did not prepare a poison, you did not go out to wound your enemy with your sword. You did not look for a hitman, nor did you arrange the place or the time. Anyway, you didn't commit the crime. You only hated and killed yourself before the other. Learn, therefore, justice so that you hate only vices, loving men. If you do this and do justice, in such a way that you prefer that vicious men be healed rather than condemned, you will have done a good job in the vineyard. Exercise in this, my brothers. 8. With them the miser torments himself and in them the merciful finds help. As divine justice distributes its goods, rightly executed actions are manifested in them and sins are punished through them. For gold and silver and all earthly possession is an exercise of humanity and a torture for the desire to possess. When God distributes such things to us men, He shows in them how much He is capable of despising the spirit of him whose riches are none other than the same one who gives them. No one can appear to despise a thing if he has not become its possessor. Also those who do not possess it can despise it. But whether such contempt is only feigned or real, it is seen only by God, who is the scrutinizer of hearts. But before men, so that they can serve as models of imitation, we cannot see the intention of the one who despises except in the hands of the one who distributes. When God grants these things to perverse men, he shows through them how even good things torment the spirit of him to whom the one who gives so much seemed vile. It provides the good with opportunities to do good; He torments the wicked with the fear of harm. Gold and silver are, therefore, the property of him who knows how to use both well. For even among men themselves it must be said that someone possesses something when he uses it well. In effect, what he does not manage fairly, he does not own in law. What he does not possess with right, even if he says it is his, this will not be the voice of the just possessor, but the shamelessness of a shameless usurper. Therefore, if man, not without reason, calls something his own, not because he has taken possession of it out of an iniquitous and foolish desire to possess, but because he has administered it with power full of prudence and just moderation, with how much more reason does God say that gold and silver are his, since he created it with immense goodness and administers it with a most just dominion, so that, without his will and dominion, neither the evil ones, to punish their greed, nor the good ones, for the exercise of mercy, could they have the gold and silver? Because neither good nor bad can make wealth exist, nor distribute and order that some have it and others lack it. 5. If gold and silver were given only to the evil ones, it could rightly be thought that they were evil things. If they were given only to the good, one might rightly think that they were a great good. Gold can be possessed holy, the good also have it. If you want to know that they are not good because of the gold, the bad ones also have it. Furthermore: if you want to know that poverty is not misfortune, there are some happy poor people. If you want to know that poverty is not happiness, there are certain poor unfortunates. Therefore, gold and silver are distributed to men by God, the creator and administrator of everything, so that, in themselves, by their nature and kind, they are a good, although not the supreme and supreme good; To the extent of the position they occupy in the gradation of beings, they manifest the one who is worthy of being praised for being the creator of everything; so also that its abundance does not make the good proud nor its scarcity depress them, and that the bad, on the other hand, blind them by being offered to them and torment them by being taken from them. 6. In no way can a thing created for the praise of its maker and for the proof of the good and the punishment of the bad be justly condemned. In all truth, God says that what is his is what he not only created with most generous kindness, but also distributes with most provident moderation. When the Lord in the Gospel calls this type of thing mammona of iniquity, he means that there is another type of mammona, that is, other riches that no one can possess except the just and the good, and which are called mammona of iniquity, because it is iniquity that calls them riches. Justice, however, knows that there are other riches with which the inner man adorns himself, as the blessed one says.

Peter: who is rich before God. Such riches are said to be just because they are given as a reward for good and just actions. They are called true riches because whoever possesses them will not feel need. The others are called unjust riches not because gold and silver are unjust, but because it is unfair to call riches that which does not eliminate need. What's more, the more each one will feel need the greater the need he has if he loves them. How to call riches those that, al. increase, they increase scarcity; to those that, the older they are, not only do they not provide satiety, but rather inflame the desire to possess in their lovers? Do you judge someone rich who would be content with less if he had less? We see some who, having little money, find joy in small gains. But once they began to abound in gold and silver, although they are false riches, if you offer them little, they reject it. You think they are already satisfied, but it is false. For a greater amount of money does not close the jaws of greed, but rather expands it much more; It does not turn them off, but rather turns them on. They reject the glass because they long for the river. Whoever wanted to increase his wealth so as not to need and now has more so that he needs more, should he be called richer or more needy? 7. [1] Manichean influence on Augustinian exegesis.—The procedure of contrasting texts from the Old and New Testaments, attempting to demonstrate their mutual contradiction, is not original to the Manichaeans, of whom Saint Augustine speaks in this sermon. It was already a topic of pagan-Christian controversy. The pagan Celsus opposes the legislation of Moses to that of Jesus (ORÍGENES, Contra Celsus VII 18). Already in a generically Christian environment it was carried out by some Gnostic sects, but above all by Marcion, who even composed a book titled Antithesis, in which he collected how much his way of understanding was in contradiction between both Testaments. All this based on the doctrine itself. On the other hand, Manichaeism has had no small influence on Augustinian exegesis. Above all, he has nurtured his interest in allegorical exegesis, which allowed him to overcome the problem of the morality of the Old Testament. We also owe it to Manichaeism that Augustine dealt preferentially, especially in the first part of his life, with the OT. If the saint has put so much effort into defending the truth of the Bible, for example, the harmony between the four evangelists or the unity between one alliance and another; if it has accentuated the dividing line between the canonical books and the apocrypha; if he was concerned with determining the canon of inspired books; If he insisted on their authenticity against the theory of interpolations and, finally, if he attached so much importance to the comparison between the manuscripts containing the sacred books, all of this is largely due to Manichaeism. See A. ALLGEIER, Der Einfluss des Manicháismus auj die exegetische Vragesteüung bei Augustin, in Aurelius Augustinus. Die Festschrift der Górres-Gesellschaft zum 1500 Todestage des heiligen Augustinus (Cologne 1930) p.13; P. MONCEAUX, Le manichéen Faustus de Milev (Paris 1924). [2] The rules of Scripture.—Scripture, as a special book that has God as its author, requires certain rules of interpretation that distinguish it from other books. The rules referred to in this text consist of understanding the Trinity of persons under the word God. According to her, it is not necessary to always explicitly mention each of the three to understand their presence. Frequently, through his sermons, Augustine will appeal to the rules of Scripture.

Limiting ourselves to those included in this volume, we can cite S.2,5 (when the prophet speaks, it is God who speaks); 12,2 ("world" must be understood as a group of sinners); 22,1-2 (what is still future is narrated as having already happened); 32,6 (the allegorical meaning of things or words varies from text to text—pro locis Scripturarum—, and that depends on the circumstances—quo pertinent caetera circumstantiae ipsius lectionis). [3] Manichean Christology.—Manichean Christology, related to Gnosticism, is also full of similarities with Catholicism, but each of them corresponds to another dissimilarity that makes them irreconcilable. Catholics and Manichaeans recognize that Christ is the Word, the Son of God and the Savior of men. But the Manichean faith is vitiated by other postulates. The first brings its origin from the Trinitarian aspect. Both recognize the existence of a Father, of a Hün v Ae- a

Holy Spirit; but for the Manichaeans, these last two are in no way hypostases, and even less persons, in the Catholic sense; They are forces, not distinct from the Father. Some accept the incarnation for soteriological reasons; but the Manichaeans defend points unacceptable for a Catholic. The first is the plurality of incarnations, one of them in the serpent of paradise who opened Eve's eyes and taught her the science of good and evil (Against Faust XV 9; The Heresies 46); another in the historical person of Jesus. The second point of disagreement is the conception of this incarnation. For the Manichaeans it did not really exist: everything was a fiction, an appearance. Christ was neither born of a woman, nor was he baptized, nor tempted, etc. Walking bodily with his disciples, eating, drinking, suffering the passion, being crucified, dying, etc., was all a simulation. In accordance with his dogmatic postulates, Christ could in no way have taken human flesh. However, they normally speak of the passion and crucifixion of the Lord, but they understand something else, namely, the martyrdom that the divine part that is imprisoned in matter and that needs to be freed is suffering. It is what they call the Iesus patibilis. [4] Liturgical singing.—In his sermons Saint Augustine continually alludes to the fact of singing the psalms. The custom must have been introduced in Africa at the beginning of his pastoral activity, not without resistance from some whom the saint had to refute (see Retractions I I 11). Augustine had reasons to defend it despite his theoretical reservations, because he knew how much it is capable of moving and elevating God's spirits. His Milanese experience in this regard, before being baptized, was written in beautiful words in Confessions X 33,49. There are doubts about the way it was carried out. Some texts indicate that a singer sang the verses, and the people responded with a chorus. Other texts, however, suggest that the entire town sang the entire psalm alternating in two choirs. See in this regard F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.421.424. [5] Historicity of the biblical facts.—These words are repeated almost verbatim in S.8,2 (= Frangipane 1).

In both texts he responds to a certain category of people who sought, on the one hand, to save the value of everything contained in the Bible, and, on the other, denied the historical reality of the facts, especially those that contained something wonderful, stating that they were impossible. According to this tendency, God had wanted the facts to be recorded in writing to mean something through them. «Let no one say: surely it is written that the water turned into blood as a plague of the Egyptians; but only to mean something, not because it was true, since in reality it could not be done" (S.8,2; see the same regarding the flood in The City of God XV 27,2). For Augustine, such a way of arguing is an insult to the omnipotence of God: "Whoever speaks in this way seeks the will of God in such a way that he offends his power" (S.8,2). What difference does it make, says Augustine, to affirm that God could mean something through words than through actions, since in Him words are actions? As he will say below, everything is easy for God, because he does everything with his word. On the other hand, Agustín reminds them that wanting to look for meaning in a fact that did not exist is totally absurd. With his words: wanting to build in the air. The spiritual meaning, which Augustine does not deny, is based on the historical truth of the event, in its literal sense. Hence the insistence on affirming that it took place exactly as it had

been read. In the next issue he will emphasize both things. Isaac was certainly born, but it also meant something. [6] The spiritual meaning of the Old Testament.—In a few words it sets forth the relationship between the Old and the New Testaments. The problem of the function of the Old Covenant, once Christ arrived, is as old as Christianity. Already in the gospels the voice of those who wanted to abolish it can be heard. It will be Jesus who says that He did not come to abolish it, but to perfect it (Mt 5:17). The problem is raised by Saint Paul with no less intensity (Rom, 1 Cor, Gal) and, behind him, by many generations of Christians. The problem was related to many fields of struggle. First of all, the anti-Jewish controversy; In fact, being forced to reject the Jews, at the same time the Christians accepted their Scriptures; then the anti-Gnostic and anti-Marcionite controversy, heretics who denied value or, in the best of cases, interpreted the pages of the Old Testament from their heterodox doctrinal assumptions. It also had its impact on the anti-pagan struggle, in that there were no shortage of those who used the immoralities of the God of the Old Testament to combat Christianity (see Contra Celsus, by Origen). The problem was posed to Saint Augustine above all by the presence of the Manichaeans; Furthermore, he had experienced it in his own flesh (Conf. V 14,24). This explains the frequency with which he speaks on the subject, following the centuries-old tradition. The solutions given can be reduced to three: full and literal acceptance of the Old Covenant (Ebionites); denial of all historical value and purely spiritual interpretation (Epistle of Barnabas); Finally, the Pauline, which, maintaining the historical value, also accepts the spiritual significance: Old and New Covenant meet as sign and reality, symbol and content, figure and figurative thing. In this conception, the one adopted by Augustine, the Old Testament had its value and maintains it, although always ordered to the New Testament; specifically, to Christ and the Church. "Almost all the pages of Scripture speak of nothing other than Christ and the Church" (S.46,33). The former not only temporally precedes the latter, but also prepares and determines it. As M. Pontet says (La exégése de saint Augustin prédicateur p.311): "The New Testament comes not only after the Old, but also because of it."

In the OT the New is hidden, and in the New the OT is manifested (The Catechesis of Beginners 4,8) or, as it says in this same sermon (n.9): «The OT is a figurative promise; the NT is the promise understood spiritually. Then the Lord expressed himself in ways suited to the capacity of intellection of those carnal men; Now, with the arrival of Christ, man can now grasp the true meaning and spiritual value hidden under so many material promises. The need for each biblical text to express a literal meaning led him to the famous controversy with Saint Jerome. [7] Exodus and Christian life.—In Augustinian work we frequently find this conception of the march of the Hebrew people through the desert as an image of the Christian life. The crossing of the Red Sea means baptism, through which, whoever has received it, is freed from the Egypt of sin and becomes a pilgrim on earth in search of his homeland, the promised land, in the midst of trials and temptations. See S.352,4-6 and S.363,4; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 26,11-12; 28.9; The catechesis of beginners 20; Against Faust X I I 29-30. This interpretation is not original to Saint Augustine. It belongs to the entire Christian tradition before him, and found its normal development in

liturgical catechesis. It can be seen at length in J. DANIELOU, Sacramentum futuri (Paris 1950) p.l31ff. [8] Extension of the Church.—For Saint Augustine, the Church does not begin to exist at the moment of Christ's coming into the world. All the saints of the Old Testament already belonged to it. In this text he tells us about Abraham. In others he will trace it back to Abel himself (Enarrac. to Psalms 90 I I 1; 128,2). All those righteous had Christ as their head, like us. What we believe as already happened, they believed as future (Enarrac. al psalm 36,3,4. See Y. CONGAR, Ecclesia ab Abel. Festschrift für K. Adam [Dusseldorf 1952] p.79-108, specifically p.81-86). Also the martyrs of the OT are Christian martyrs. Christ gave them strength, helped them and crowned them, like the later martyrs. The entire S.300 can be read for this purpose. This conception must be taken into account when discussing the extra formula Ecclesiam nulla salus, which was emphasized by Africans, both Donatists and Catholics. Augustine had his own explanation, because for him Christianity is "the true religion", to which all those who are saved belong, even if they are dissidents. [9] The sinner and the sin.—This distinction, which so irritates Marcuse, between the sin and the sinner is a fundamental idea of ​​the spirituality of Saint Augustine. Hatred due to sin should not be an obstacle to fulfilling the Christian precept of love for the person, even if he or she is a sinner. We must love man and hate vice (S.49,5). In short, it is about distinguishing between what is the work of God and what is the work of man (S.223 D 4 = Wilmart 4). In each of us two names come together: man and sinner; God made man, man made himself a sinner (S.13,8; 22,7). Or in other words, God made nature; the man, the vice. Vice must be cured to save nature (S.19,1), the latter formulation that reveals the Pelagian controversy. Man, therefore, must not love what is his own, but what is the work of God (S.32,10). See also Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 12,13. Outside of preaching, Letter 153,3. [10] Pro]ethical vision of the saints of the OT.—Augustine is convinced of the spiritual meaning of what is narrated in the OT, a meaning that has become evident in the revelation brought by Jesus.

But it goes further, to the point of attributing to the same characters in the OT the awareness of the symbolic value of their actions; even more so, to carry them out to signify that value, although certainly such knowledge was nothing more than obscure, in shadows. Here he is right; If such knowledge did not exist, it would be logical that Isaac would have been angry at feeling deceived by his youngest son. For Augustine, everything in the Bible, both in one Testament and in another, goes beyond common human behavior, is a sure sign of some mystery, that God wants to indicate something to us. This tendency of Augustine is explained by his desire to defend the patriarchs and the Bible, which speaks about them, from the denunciations of the Manichaeans. [11] The Donatist schisms.—The Donatist church, which so deeply wounded the unity of the African Church, had to experience within itself the bitterness of division. The reasons were various, including those of a doctrinal nature. In this regard, the most relevant case was the excommunication of the secular theologian Tyconius by the primate of Carthage Parmenian in the year 373. As of greater importance, however, the internal schisms that followed must be classified. The first—rogatist—was its initiator Rogato, bishop of Certenna, who reproached his co-religionists for excessive violence. The separation took place

in the year 370. Also worthy of mention is that of the Claudianists, which emerged in Carthage in 392, when Claudianus, bishop expelled from Rome, did not want to submit to the primacy of Carthage; Their separation was brief, as he and his supporters were later admitted to the unit. The greatest of all was, without a doubt, that of Maximian, Primian's opponent to the see of Carthage, whom he managed to excommunicate in a council of 43 bishops on his side, and, in turn, was excommunicated and deposed by another council of 310 bishops on the opposing side, in 394. Augustine will not miss the opportunity to remind the Donatists of this stormy history of the community. Where there is division, there is no charity; and where there is no charity, there is no unity. And where this is missing, the Church of Christ is not there. [12] Etymologies.—Augustine refers to the etymology of the word. Vicente (Vincentius) comes from vincens, vincere (to conquer). The recourse to etymology is not typical of Augustine or Christian authors. As a literary resource, its use was widespread among the Greeks and Romans. Christian authors picked up the technique, but gave it another purpose: exegetics and apologetics. The etymologies, true or false, it matters little, they were used in the fight against the pagan gods, against the institutions of their cult and also against the heretics themselves. However, its most common use was exegetical. They were mainly applied to the Hebrew names present in the Bible, both prosopographical and topographical. Casts of these interpretations abound in Christian antiquity. Thinking about Saint Augustine, it is worth mentioning that of Saint Jerome (The Translation of Hebrew Names), which he knew. But it also extended to the remaining proper or common names that expressed the contents of the Christian faith, and there was no shortage of etymologies conceived only as word games. [13] God's correction and fraternal correction.—The comparison of God with a father who is good and severe at the same time is a thought that frequently appears in Augustinian sermons. A father's love does not prevent him from punishing his son; Furthermore, love is shown in punishment. In this sense all the setbacks that God sends us must be seen. They are the discipline that God uses to educate us. Even if it is difficult, we must follow it and never deviate from it (S.21,8; 22,3). At the same time, God's behavior is to be a model for human behavior.

As God corrects, so we must also correct our brother; This thought is fundamental in Augustinian spirituality. Fraternal correction is a sign of spiritual progress (Commentary on the letter to the Galatians 56; Rule 4; City of God I 9; Faith and works 3; Letter 78,8). The saint cannot escape how difficult it is (Letter 95,3). It must be done in the right way and at the right time (City of God I 9; Letter 110,2; S.16 A, 7-8 = Denis 20) and always with love (S.163 B 3 = Frangipane 5). [14] The "competent."—The competent were the catechumens who were preparing to receive the sacrament of baptism. They had to register at the beginning of Lent or even earlier. They were only accepted when the testimony of their Christian neighbors was favorable in the sense that they lived according to Christian morality. They were presented by godfathers and godmothers. During Lent they prepared for the solemn encounter with Christ, and the bishop gave them special attention in his preaching. During the forty days they fasted daily, except on Sundays and Holy Thursday; They didn't go to the bathrooms; They were forced to maintain marital continence. The preparation also carried with it some rites or "sacraments" such as scrutiny, renunciation of Satan, etc. A moment of special importance was the traditio symboli, the delivery of the

creed or symbol of faith, which took place fifteen days before the Easter Vigil. The bishop explained it to them, and they, with the help of the godparents, had to learn it by heart for the following Sunday, when the redditio symboli took place, that is, proclaiming it before the Christian community. Once the person being baptized knew what he should believe, the prayer of the Lord's Prayer was given to him, this rite also called the traditio of the Pater. This took place eight days before the Easter Vigil, after the redditio symboli. The catechumen had to learn the Lord's Prayer by heart in order to recite it with the community on the solemn night of baptism. The order of the two traditions was not accidental, but was based on theological foundations. Saint Augustine says in a sermon to the competent on the day of the redditio symboli and, contemporaneously, of the traditio of the Pater noster: «How are they going to invoke him in whom they have not believed? (Rom 10:14); For this reason, you did not receive first the prayer and then the symbol, but first the symbol, so that you would know in whom you were to believe, and then the prayer, so that you would know whom to call on” (S.56,1). See in this regard F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.459-464, or the introduction by Saint PÓQUE to the volume Sermons pour la Páque, by Saint Augustine: Sources Chrétiennes 116 (Paris 1966); C. EICHENSEER, Das symbolum Apostolicum beim Hl. Augustinus (St. Ottilien 1960). [15] Eve and the Church.—The comparison between Adam's dream and the death of Christ on the cross, from whose sides Eve and the Church were born, respectively, is a very frequent theme in Augustinian pages. In addition to the present, it appears in sermons 218,14; in Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 120,2; and, much more frequently, in the Enarrations to Psalms 40:10; 56.11; 103 I I 4.6;^ 126.7; 127.11. Outside of preaching, in Against Faust X I I 8; The genesis against the Manichaeans I I 24,57; The city of God XV 26; XXII 17. The idea is not original. He probably took it from Saint Ambrose (Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Luke Nor is Saint Ambrose the first to propose it. It already appears in Tertullian (The Soul 43,10). Other authors, with identical interpretation or with minimal variants, can be seen in J.

DANIELOU, Sacramentum futuri p.37-44. [16] The Jews and Jerusalem.—The Jews received the prohibition of setting foot in Jerusalem from several emperors: Hadrian (EUSEBIUS OF CAESÁREA, Ecclesiastical History IV 6); Septimius Severus (TERTULIAN, Apologetic 21 and Against the Jews 13) and Constantine (S. JOHN CHRYSOSTOMO, Homily III against the Jews). According to Saint John Chrysostom, Constantine dispersed the Jews who had dared to enter Jerusalem against the imperial order throughout the various regions of the Empire, after having cut off their ears, so that they could serve as a lesson to the others. Note that Augustine mentions the emperor as a Christian. [17] The dispersion of the Jews.—Here Augustine gives a reason for the Jewish diasnora: they have been dispersed throughout the world to contribute to the spread of Christianity. In what way? As guarantors of the truth of the Scriptures; more specifically, of the prophecies. To pagans who object that such prophecies were falsified to show as such what was written post eventum, Christians present the Jewish Scriptures. Their value is all the greater because they come from a part hostile to Christianity, as the Jews always were. This idea is repeated very frequently in the Augustinian pages. It is a constant theme in the Epiphany sermons (S.200,3; 201,3; 202,3; 204,3; 274,2). inside
Additional notes

preaching, see also Ennarrations to Psalms 40:14; 56.9; 58 I 22; Treatise on the gospel of Saint John 37,7. Outside of preaching, The concord of the evangelists I 14,22; I 26,40; Letter 137, 4.16; The city of God XVIII 47, etc. In this sense they can be called capsarii (the slave who carried the books to the children who went to school or the one who carried the lawyer's books to the court). See Ennarration to Psalm 40:14, In this same sermon he calls them custodians, guardians of our books (Scriptures). The idea of ​​presenting the Jews as guarantors of the truth is not original to Augustine either. It already appears, for example, in LACTANTIUS, Divine Institutions IV 16. Everything previously said does not mean that, in other places, Augustine sees such a diaspora as a punishment for the crime of the crucifixion of the Lord. See S.47.5; Ennarration to Psalm 40:12; 52.9; 56.14; 62.18, etc. Such was the most common opinion among previous parents. See TERTULLIAN, Against the Jews 10,13; Apologetic 21; SAINT CIPRIANO, The vanity of idols 10; SAINT HILARIO, Commentary on Psalm 51:14. And among the Greeks, ORIGINS, Against Celsus I 47; IV 32. About Saint Augustine and the Jews you can read B. BLUMENKRANZ, Die Judenpredigt Augustin. Ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der jüdisch-christlkhen Beziehungen in der ersten ]ahrhunderten (reprinted from the 1st edition of Basel 1946; Paris 1973). Also J. ALVAREZ, Saint Augustine and the Jews of his time: Augustinus 12 (1967) 39-50. [18] Theophanies.—The theophanies of the Old Testament were very frequently the object of attention on the part of the early Christian theologians. The normal thing was that they referred them to the Son, almost always guided by apologetic interests. Starting from the undisputed principle of the philosophy of time, that God was absolutely transcendent and, therefore, invisible, the apologists could conclude from such manifestations of God to the existence of two divine persons, against the pagans and Jews (SAINT JUSTIN, Dialogue with Trypho 127,2-5). Against the Marcionites, Tertullian could show that there was unity between the two Testaments, since Jesus, Son of God, had already made himself present in the Old Testament (TERTULLIAN, Against Marcian II 27). In the same way the Sabellians were attacked, demonstrating that the Father and the Son are different persons (NOVATIAN, Treatise on the Trinity 8). The problem took on greater heights with the Arian controversy.

It was these heretics who used such an interpretation to defend their aberrant ideas. In fact, by attributing them to the Son, they found an argument to distinguish him essentially from the Father and show his inferiority, as one is visible and the other invisible; one mutable and the other immutable. In this historical context, Augustine's reflection on the theophanies is introduced. He discussed them in detail in Cnrtns 147 and 148 and, above all, in his work The Trinity, books TI v TTT. HIS principle, taken from Saint Ambrose, is the following: not only the Father, but the three divine persons are invisible in their nature, since all three are equally God. One cannot, therefore, deny the Father the manifestation of himself and attribute it only to other people, based on the fact of invisibility. The subjects of the theophanies will be both the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The context will tell in each case which of the three people has manifested. A key principle on which Saint Augustine insists is this: Whatever the person who manifests himself, he never does so in his own essence or substance, but through a visible creature. The fact that the Old Testament fathers saw God does not in any way mean that they contemplated the divine essence. See J. LEBRETON, Saint Augustin théo-

logien de la Trinité. Son exégése des théophanies: MA I I 821-836, and B. STUDER, Zür Theophanie-Exegese Augustins. Untersuchung zu einem Ambrosíus-Zitat in der Schrift Be videndo Deo (Epist. 147) (Rome 1971). [19] The immutability of God.—One of the attributes that Saint Augustine most frequently places in God is immutability. For him, sticking to the Greek tradition of the verb einai, it is only what remains immutable (Confes. VII 11,17); To be truly is equivalent to being immutable, which only God is (Ennarration to Psalm 134:4); Furthermore, the name of immutability is being (S.7,7). Hence God is called, without further ado, IS. This text is not unique; in Confessions In comparison with Him, the other things that are are not (Ennarration to Psalm 134,4). Here is the comparison between man and Him: in Him there is only IS; while in man there is also what was and what will be, what in God is, only IS. «Behold the great ES, the great ES. Compared to Him, what is man? what is anything that is? Who will understand that BEING?..." (Enarration to Psalm 101 I I 10). You can read A. TRAPE, La nozione del mutabile e dell'immutabile secondo Sant'Agostino (Tolentino 1959). [20] The rule of truth.—In this text, Saint Augustine incidentally exposes the exegetical norms that he explained more calmly in The Christian Doctrine I I I 27,38. The function of the exegete is to always search for the authentic meaning of the texts, that is, what the sacred author wanted to express, something that is not always easy, especially in especially obscure texts. In these cases, it is common for two or more options to be presented with the same degree of probability. For this circumstance, the only norm that the saint presents is that they agree with the rule of faith, which is at the same time the norm of truth; that are in accordance with the regula veritatis (true) and do not contradict the regula fidei (orthodox). In other words, we could talk about authentic interpretation and valid interpretation. The latter is the one that agrees with the rule of faith; that one, which reflects what the sacred author actually meant. If the latter is not true, there should be no fear in staying with the former.

Furthermore, God himself may have wanted the darkness in the hagiographer's words to expand the richness of his word: while searching for the authentic one it is possible to find many valid ones, all of them willed by God, which does not mean accepting the plurality of literal meanings, which here is indirectly rejected: when speaking of two according to faith, he speaks of only one intended by the writer: "whatever the author has thought." Among the two that conform to the faith, only one was intended by the author. On the problem of the multiple literal meaning of Scripture according to Saint Augustine, once highly discussed, see M.
