AVILES, Augustinian Book of Exegetical Ideas: Augustinus 20 (1975) 326-334: "The literal sense, plurality of senses?", where he exposes the various opinions. [21] Augustinian Trinitarian Doctrine.—In his Trinitarian doctrine, Saint Augustine obviously remains within the Western tradition. In opposition to the Easterners, who took as their starting point the Trinity of persons, to conclude in the unity of nature, the Westerners started from the unity of God to, from it, derive the Trinity of persons. Such is the setting of his masterful work The Trinity. The Greek-speaking theologians expressed the mystery through the terms one ousía, three hypostasis; Latinos, on the other hand, through a substantial

tia, three personae, as Augustine writes in this text. However, the saint tries to speak of an essentia (The Trinity VIII 4,7), instead of a substantia, because this term suggests the existence of different attributes, while in God they are identified with his essence (The Trinity V 3; V I I 10). On the other hand, he also does not agree with the term person, because it invites us to think of separate individuals. However, he accepts it for its anti-modalist or anti-Sabelian force, and at the same time as a tribute that must be paid to the imperfection of human language when it tries to express the mystery of God (The Trinity V 10; V I I 7-9). [22] The ages of the world.—Augustine, following the baptismal catechesis, divides the history of humanity into seven epochs (Genesis against the Manichaeans I 23,35-41; Against Faust We currently live in the sixth, which began with the coming of Jesus Christ and will conclude with his return, to give way to the last and definitive, the seventh, which will have no end. Starting from these assumptions, it is easy to understand Augustine's assertion that what remains is less than what is past. But he has no illusions about an immediate return of the Lord nor does he venture to speculate about the number of years. The Gospel has clearly said that it is not convenient for us to know (Mark 13:32) and any effort in this direction is doomed to failure (The City of God XVIII 53). To learn more about Augustine's thoughts on the duration of this world, read Letter 199. In general, on the ages of the world, A. LUNEAU, L'histoire de salut ¿hez les Peres de l'Église. La doctrine des ages du monde (Paris 1964). About Augustine, starting on page 285. [23] Temporality according to Saint Augustine.—"From whatever point it is placed, profane history, sacred history, personal or collective, the time lived by man always appears affected by a regrettable ambivalence: it is a vector and factor at the same time of hope and despair, the means through which better-being is realized and, at the same time, this incurable wound opened in the flank of man through which his being spills and is destroyed." Perhaps the first of these two aspects, time as a vector of hope, as oriented towards a happy consummation, as faith teaches, is less known than the other negativist and defeatist aspect.

Possibly the expressive beauty of the saint when he talks about time that leaves and does not return has contributed to this; of human life, which, when it lengthens and it seems that way, in reality it decreases rather than increases (S.38,5); of man, who, as soon as he is born, begins to leave (S.31,4); of the beginning of life, which is nothing other than the introduction of the possibility of death, as he says in this sermon, or when he expresses in a dramatic tone the succession of generations. It is worth quoting a text from the Enarration to Psalm 127:15: «Your children are small; You caress them, they caress you, but do they want to remain such? You want them to grow, you want them to increase in age. But consider that, when one (age) arrives, the other dies; When childhood arrives, childhood dies; Adolescence arrives, childhood leaves; With the arrival of youth, adolescence ends; When old age arrives, youth disappears; making an appearance of death, every age perishes. How many stages of life you wish to arrive, as many stages of life you wish to perish. In reality they don't exist. On the other hand, should the children born to you on this earth live with you or rather should they cast you out and succeed you? Do you rejoice when they are born, so that they cast you out? Children, at birth, seem to say this to their parents:

Hey, think about leaving here now; Now it is our turn to perform the comedy, and human life is nothing else. There may be nothing in this matter of literature or rhetoric, but that does not nullify the truth that was expressed in the text. The modern man, who insists so much on the subject, considers Saint Augustine as a classic. Therefore, this negativist vision of time and life in Augustine cannot be denied; But to do full justice to the saint, it is important not to forget the other aspect of his conception of time, to which we referred previously. Above all, it is worth reading H. I. MARROU's little book L'ambivalence du temps de l'histoire chez Saint Augustin (Montreal-Paris 1950), from which we have taken (p.57) the lines with which we begin this note. [24] Social condition of women.—In this text, Saint Augustine reflects the customs of his time: on the one hand, how widespread adultery was (see n.9,12 of this same sermon); then the legal interior situation of the woman and, finally, scenes of family life. Roman law considered adultery a crime only when committed by the woman. This already appears in the law of the time of Augustus (Lex lulia de adulterüs co'ércendis, prior to the year 18 BC). Ancient custom allowed the husband's revenge on the adulteress or punishment only after a family council, in everything similar to a trial. Under the legislation of Julian the Apostate, the father of the adulterous woman (paterfamilias) was permitted to kill her and the adulterer if they were caught in her or her husband's home. His rights were limited: he was obliged to divorce her; Otherwise, he was considered a pimp and fell under the law. The punishment for the adulteress who was denounced consisted of banishment and confiscation of a third of her property, along with the loss of a part of the dowry she had given upon marriage. Constantine's legislation introduced the maximum penalty, or death penalty. See A. BERGER, Encyclopedic Diclionary of Roman Law (Philadelphia 1963). Although women had already resigned themselves to this state of affairs, to the point of having convinced themselves that it was lawful for men to do what was forbidden to them, Christian preachers, going beyond the legal point of view and based on religious reasons, insist on proclaiming the absolute equality of both sexes in this regard.

It has been human perversity, not divine truth, that has led to this situation. In these lines, the saint refers to the coémptio, that is, a contractual form of acquisition of power over the wife by the husband (manus) through a fictitious sale and purchase (mancipatio), through which the woman and, consequently, the power over her, ceased to belong to the domain of the paterfamilias and passed to that of the husband. Christ has purchased both husband and wife with his blood; Therefore, both owe him fidelity, which is specifically expressed in the mutual fidelity of the spouses. What the husband believes he can demand from the wife by virtue of the coémptio, the same he is obliged to give by virtue of the emptio (purchase) effected by Christ. Therefore, not only the woman must be faithful; As a Christian, and regardless of whether the laws favor him, the husband must be faithful with the same fidelity that he demands of his wife. Finally, in this text by Augustine it becomes clear how little by little the women became aware of the fact of the equality preached by the bishop and even dared to confront their husbands. At the same time, the character of those men is reflected, with

contemporary and countrymen of the saint, who were as enthusiastic in applauding and acclaiming him in church as they were in insulting and cursing him for having interfered in his private affairs, such as his married life, or also cursing the day and hour in which his wife went to church. A common argument of Augustine is to derive the term virtus from vir (male). How does a man boast of virility when it is proven that he does not have it, but rather is a victim and slave of a passion, while his wife is "virile" or virtuous? See on this purpose F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.244-256. [25] Public shows.—Agustín refers to two of the shows most appreciated by his fellow citizens: the games in the amphitheater and those in the theater. The first, called muñera (gifts), because they were given free of charge by the rich, consisted fundamentally of hunting wild beasts and fighting gladiators. Romanianus, for example, Augustine's former protector, gained popularity by paying for such festivities. The theater consisted of the pantomimic representation of all kinds of dishonesties, taken mainly from those attributed by mythology to the gods, which were sung to the sound of a zither. Agustín very frequently directed his attacks against one type or another of shows that competed with him. In other times he too, and especially his friend Alypius, was passionate about them. The beautiful pages of F. van der Meer (Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.84-94) corresponding to the chapter entitled Pompa diaboli deserve to be read, to get an idea of ​​how deeply rooted attendance at such spectacles and their character were in those people. [26] The use of marriage.—For Saint Augustine, the immoderate use of marriage is a sin, and there are many who see in it a Manichean aftertaste. He repeats the idea frequently. See S.278.9; 351.5. Against the two letters of the Pelagians I I I 5,14; The perfection of justice in man 8,18; Enchyridion 78.21. When is marriage used immoderately? In general, when instincts prevail over the control of reason. Such sin becomes a moral imperfection for the saint, which is easily forgiven through prayers, fasting, alms, etc. You can read the purpose D. Covi (The end of sexual activity according to Saint Augustine.

Order of nature and purpose of the sexual act: Augustinus 17 [1972] 47-65, especially: "The veniality of an immoderate use in the marital act", p.64-65; P. LANGA, Saint Augustine and the progress of the theology of marriage [Rome 1977] [dacty.] p.173). On the other hand, it is necessary, according to the Bishop of Hippo, that the marriage act be directed towards procreation: "The union of both sexes is exempt from sin only when it takes place with the aim of procreating" (S.351,5). [27] The marriage "tables."—The tabulae (the tablets on which writing was done) were the written attestation of the marriage contract. They are also called nuptiale instrumentum. Documents in this regard appear already at the beginning of the imperial era. The writing of the contract was not a requirement for its validity, but simply proof that it had taken place. Among other things, they contained provisions regarding the dowry to be delivered by the woman: amount, method of payment and restitution, due to dissolution, death or divorce. There it also stated, as Augustine recalls in this text, that the woman was taken with the purpose of procreating children (liberorum procreandorum causa). They were read before witnesses (S.51,22). In S.37,7, the saint calls them instruments of your purchase (instrumenta emptionis tuae), that is, of the purchase of the wife by the husband. Ade-

In addition to the texts mentioned, Augustine also speaks of them in the Ennarration to Psalm 80:21 and The City of God XIV 18. [28] Sacramentum.—The term sacramentum has several meanings in the Christian Latin language of antiquity. In addition to meaning sacrament, in the traditional sense of the word, it is applied with the value of mystery and sacred rite. See C. COUTURIER, Sacramentum et "mysterium" dans Voeuvre de saint Augustin, in H. RONDET-LE LANDAIS, Études Augustiniennes (Paris 1953). In this text it has the meaning of a rite with symbolic value. In this sense, Christ is the life of all of them, insofar as they point towards him and have him as their end. In him, the symbol becomes reality, "since in Christ what is visibly celebrated among the Jews is understood with vitality." On the Christian origin of this term, see C. MOHRMANN, «.Sacramentum» dans les plus anciens textes chrétiens, in Études sur le latin des chrétiens I p.233-244. [29] The fact and the intention.—It is normal that Augustine, when he speaks of the surrender of Jesus by Judas, associates the same surrender on the part of the Father or the self-surrender on the part of Jesus himself. In addition to the present sermon, consult Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 62:4; Treatises on the first letter of Saint John 1,1; Ennarrations to Psalms 61,62; 65.7; 93.28. Although both the delivery on the part of the Father and that of Jesus himself are missing in this sermon, it is proven through biblical texts (Rom 8:32, for the first, and Eph 5,2,23,25 and Gal 2,20 for the second). In this association of traditiones there is always an implicit or explicitly formulated question: why, if everyone did the same thing, is Judas reproached for the act, and the Father and Jesus are praised for the same thing? Augustine's response always goes in the same direction: we must not look at the fact, but at the intention with which it was carried out: Judas, for money; the Father and Jesus, for our benefit. In this way, it begins to discuss the benefits that such an action brought us. On other occasions he will use the aforementioned fact to show how God can take advantage even of bad actions; benefit that cannot be attributed to those who were its material authors, but to God who willed it and foresaw it and, in view of it, permitted such actions. [30] Abortion in ancient times.—The plague of abortion was also widespread in ancient times, although the means were more rudimentary.

Here Augustine speaks of prostitutes who take potions in order to provoke him. In this regard, it is interesting to remember what Oribasius, personal physician of the Emperor Julian the Apostate, writes in his Book of Cure Methods, in a chapter titled Remedies to Cause Menstruation, although in fact he talks about abortion: "Make a juniper concoction that will corrupt the living fetus and send it out once dead. Also the juice of centaura maior roots produces the same result, and likewise the juice of calamita drunk and applied. The same applies to myrrh and oil; and if you anoint your virile member with a mixture of them, the woman will not conceive. Those who use these medicines do not need to use a second one, namely a lupine concoction applied with myrtle and honey and poultices of lupine flour. Add the juice of the centaura minor: by applying it, the woman is freed. The same effect is produced by cyclamen juice spread on the lower abdomen; Corruption is, in fact, very strong when applied in a pessary with honey. Elaterium (drank) or applied corrupts fetuses. Castoreum, with polio or calamite, has been used to cause the expulsion of the fetus, as has cabbage juice applied with lolium flour (lolium) to make

"The rest comes out (placenta that remains inside)." Text taken from A. NARDI, Procurato abortion nel mondo greco-romano (Milan 1971) p.507-508. As you can see, everything was trusted to the effect of certain plants. But it was not only prostitutes who used such methods. Husbands also resorted to them, as indicated by Saint Augustine (Marriage and Lust I 15,17). And Saint Jerome tells us about virgins consecrated to the Lord who even lost their lives in their abortion attempts. In Letter 22,13 to Eustace he writes: "Some (virgins), upon realizing that they have conceived in crime, think of poisons to abort and, frequently, when they too die, they are sent to hell, guilty of three crimes: as suicides, as adulteresses towards Christ and as parricides of an unborn child." [31] Augustine's argument.—The Manichaeans, to show their theory of the opposition between the Old and the New Testament, confront the text of the book of Job, according to which the devil was in the presence of God, and another of the Gospel, according to which God is only seen by those with pure and upright hearts. Augustine's response presents several aspects. First, he defends the text of Job, arguing that there are different ways in which one can be in the presence of God and different ways in which the word "God spoke" can be interpreted: he could do it directly or through another. Then move on to direct attack; In the text, he says, it is not written that the devil saw God, as they claim. Spontaneously his thought goes to the temptations of Jesus as a similar case, and from them he argues ad hominem. If the devil, when speaking with Jesus, saw the body, it is because he had it, something they deny. If he saw Jesus and did not see his body, he had to see the substance of God, something impossible, according to the words of the Gospel that they accept. He then presents them with another dilemma: does the devil see the sun? If you see it, the sun is not God (the Manichaeans considered it a part of divinity); If he does not see it, at least the evil ones see it, thus contradicting the New Testament.

In either of the two hypotheses they cannot find a way out. [32] The sentence of the judge.—The explanation of this phrase can probably be obtained from the following words from the life of the saint written by his deacon Pontius: «So, then, the judge read the sentence from his tablet; sentence that can be said without recklessness inspired by the Holy Spirit; sentence worthy of such a bishop and such a witness of Christ; In short, a glorious sentence, in which he was called the standard bearer of our religion and enemy of the gods, adding that his death was to be a lesson for his people and his blood, the first sanction of the law. Nothing more complete, nothing more true than this sentence. In fact, everything that is said in it, even said by a Gentile, turns out to be divine things... Cyprian had been our standard bearer, since he taught us to raise the flag of Christ. He was an enemy of the gods, because he ordered their simulacra to be destroyed. His death was, indeed, a lesson for his people, since he was the first to consecrate the first fruits of martyrdom in the province of Africa for many who were to follow him with the same type of death..." Life of San Cipriano 17, in D. RuizBÜENO, Actas de los mártires (BAC, Madrid 2 1958) p.724-750; specifically, p.747. The sentence can also be found in the Martyrdom of Saint Cyprian, o.c, p.756-761. [33] Homoioteleuton.—The Spanish translation does not allow us to capture all of Augustine's expressive particularities such as homoioteleuton or similiter desinens, that is, the conclusion with the same sound of two or more sentences (the rhyme). Note in the Latin text the subsequence of

the same verbal form: «... aadisti,... audú/z,... hiisti,... asczndisti,... suspendwíz,... adhibuisti,... sadisti,... punir//',... discussz'ííz',... audz'íti,... punisti,... pepercisti». This rhetorical figure is omnipresent in Augustinian sermons. Someone who has had the humor to count such assonances lists the figure of 4,254 examples in the Sermons to the People alone (M. I. BARRY, Saint Augustin, the Orator: a Study of the rhetorical qualities of saint Augustine's "Sermones ad populum" [Washington 1924] p.256). On this aspect of Augustinian sermons, see also J. OROZ, La rhetoric en los sermons de San Agustín (Madrid 1963) p.285-304. [34] Pride and riches.—The association of riches and pride is frequent in Augustine. From the latter evil comes to the former, which in themselves cannot be evil, but good, since they are a gift from God (S.15 A,5 = Denis 21; 56,4,6). In this text, as later in S.36,2, he calls it illness (morbus). Elsewhere (S.39,4; 61,10; 85,3), worm (vermis). If pride is what corrupts riches, in turn nothing exists as capable of engendering the former as these (S.36,2; 61,10; 85,3). On the other hand, the deleterious effect of pride is something repeatedly affirmed by the saint. His entire thought on the matter is expressed in the following phrase of the Rule: "For all other types of vices provoke bad works, but pride lies in wait for good works themselves to cause them to perish" (1:8). With a similar phrase he stated in his work Nature and Grace: «The other vices have their strength in bad actions; Only pride must guard against good works” (27:31). [35] Excommunication.—Excommunication, or temporary expulsion from the Church, was relatively common in the early Church. "When it was a real scandal, an adultery known in the city, a pact with heretics, blasphemy or apostasy from the faith, or crimes that fell under the sanction of the law, such as murder or serious mistreatment, the bishop excommunicated the guilty person from the Church" (F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.490). Since the sin that motivated the excommunication had been public, readmission to the Christian community took place only after the corresponding public penance. In Augustine's time, excommunication was considered a great dishonor with no small consequences on social life itself.

In this text, the holy bishop remembers that he was not fond of resorting to these extreme measures, always to avoid greater evils. [36] Ethnicus.—Ethnicus is the simple Latin transcription of the Greek term, with the meaning of pagan, gentile. Thus, the first Christian writings in Latin and the Vulgate. In the fourth century, however, it seems that this meaning was no longer understood by everyone; hence the need for Augustine's explanation of the present text, which does not happen only on this occasion. See S.82,4,7: "The Ethnicians, that is, the Gentiles and pagans." These two terms have a pejorative meaning in Saint Augustine, in opposition to gentes. While this expresses those people who have not believed in Christ because it has not been announced to them, those denote those who have positively rejected him. For greater precision on the meaning of these terms, read P. BORGOMEO, L'fígjise de ce temps dans la prédication de saint Augustin (Píirís 1972> p.49-73. T371 The codex.—The oldest form of the book, in papyrus, was the label (volume): it was formed by sheets of this material joined together and rolled around to a small stick (umbellicus) The way of writing varied depending on whether it was a literary text or

a document. In the first case it was written horizontally, based on successive columns; in the second, it transverses the letter, that is, perpendicular to the horizontal fibers. Although the label continued to be used for documents even during the Middle Ages, in new materials, already from the 1st century AD. It began to be replaced by the codex (codex), as, above all, parchment was imposed on papyrus. The codex now has the form of the current book. It is made up of several notebooks linked together, each of which can vary in the number of pages. The pagination of them began in a second moment. First only the notebooks; then the folios, with single pagination, that is, not on both sides. [38] Augustinian interiority.—«The doctrine and experience of Saint Augustine is dominated by the continuous call to interiority. Man is worth what he is in his interior, in the presence of God, who reads in hearts; The truth that illuminates him dwells in the inner man, and the Holy Spirit builds there the temple of God. It is necessary for man to enter into himself to rise above his being and encounter God" (M. PELLEGRINO, Itinerario spirituale [Cuneo 1964] p.l). Part of this interiority is the interrogatio coráis, a scrutiny of consciousness equivalent to a kind of psychoanalysis. It is a fundamental principle of Augustinian spirituality; In the heart, in fact, God speaks individually: "This is what the Lord says to you from within, where only you can hear" (S.21,6). Hence the frequency with which in the sermons of this volume the holy preacher invites his listeners to examine his heart, which is why he was defined on more than one occasion as a "modern man" (S.34,7; 47,17; 47,23; 49,5; 49,8, etc.). We find the precise formulation of his thoughts on the matter in his work The True Religion 72: «You do not want to go outside; enter into yourself; The truth dwells in the inner man; and if you see that your nature is mutable, transcend yourself. The return to interiority is the first step to conversion. From the exterior to the interior; from the interior to the superior. Such is the Augustinian synthesis. [39] Sin.—As a pastor, in this text Augustine explains to his faithful when sin occurs, which implicitly entails a definition of it.

Explicit definitions are not rare in the saint's works; Quite a few of them have become justly famous for their conciseness and precision of concept. We remember: "Sin is a deed, saying or desire against the eternal law" (Against Faust XXII 27) or, even more briefly, "sin is aversion to God and conversion to creatures" (Free Will II 19,53). In the present text, Augustine emphasizes disordered love; What he means by disordered love can be gathered from a text in S.33,3, in which he considerably extends the scope of sin. This exists not only when something is done that is clumsy or unfair, but also when good works are carried out in themselves, but guided by temporary intentions or purposes. Any work that is not done for the conquest of eternal rest has nothing good other than the appearance (species). Consequently, everything that is not aimed at obtaining eternal life, that is, God, is disordered. [40] The mother Church.—One of the bases on which the parallelism that Augustine, following other authors of Christian antiquity (Tustino, Irenaeus, etc.), establishes between Eve and the Church is based, is motherhood. Both are mothers. From Eve, united to Adam, the men of ancient humanity were born; From the Church, united to Christ, new men are born. Thus in the present text. In others, Augustine establishes a variant. Maintaining the principle of the motherhood of the Church,

The begetting of new children does not come from his union with Christ, but from the union with divinity itself (S.22,9; 57,2). On the other hand, Eve is not the only type of motherhood of the Church. Augustine also finds it in Mary, the Mother of the Lord: both are virgins and mothers. He develops the theme at length in the Christmas sermons. «She (the Church) is also a virgin and is a mother: a mother for her bowels of charity, a virgin for the integrity of her faith and piety. She gives birth to the peoples, who are members of that one person of whom she is the body and wife; so also in this she is similar to that Virgin, because she is the mother of unity among many" (S.192,2. See also S.188,4; 191,3; 195,2, etc.). You can read on the subject R. PALMERO RAMOS, “Ecclesia Mater” in San Agustín. Theology of the image in anti-donatist writings (Madrid 1970). [41] The "exemplum."—With these phrases Augustine shows himself fully Roman in education. As a student first and then as a professor of rhetoric, he has frequently had to deal with the exemplum, as one of many arguments in favor of a cause or, simply, to cause a delectatio in his listeners (see QUNTILIANO, Institutio oratoria V 11). But rhetoric does nothing more than assume what the fundamental conceptions of a people are. Everyone knows the prestige that the examples of their ancestors enjoyed among the Romans, as an expression of the mos maiorum that was considered ideal. Furthermore, the moral education of young people was nourished by examples taken from national history offered for their admiration or imitation (read H. I. MARROU, Storia della educazione dell'antichita [Rome 2 1966] p.314). In law, the exempla or antecedent cases had legal force. [42] Christian grace.—The reader unfamiliar with the language of Pelagius may easily be deceived. He and his followers also spoke of grace, but by that term they understood other things; specifically, nature created by God with free will to choose good or evil, the natural law discovered by reason, the law of Moses, the example of the holy patriarchs and, above all, that of Christ, etc. These "graces" touched the man only from the outside. Augustine will try to clarify the terms, taking only nature as his focus in this text.

He does not deny that she is a grace; It is effectively so, insofar as God has given it freely; but he affirms that this is not the grace of which he normally speaks; grace that will be clarified throughout the sermon: the grace by which we are God's people (n.5); by which we have been made believers (n.7); for which we are Christians (n.9); It is the grace of Christians that comes to us through Christ-the-man mediator (n.12). [43] Torture.—Torture in order to obtain the confession of the alleged prisoner was not always accepted in the life of the Roman people. It was introduced, and with extreme harshness, only in the imperial era, when power took more authoritarian forms. The higher spheres of society were excluded by law from it. The torments to which the victims were subjected were truly atrocious, as this text indicates. It was practiced not only in civil courts, but also in ecclesiastical courts. When the Emperor Constantine granted the bishops judicial power, they did not hesitate to use the systems then in use to carry out their function. Augustine's letter 133.2 states this explicitly. After exhorting the imperial official Marcellinus with these words: «Do not lose the paternal diligence that you showed in the interrogations, when you extracted from them the confession of

so many crimes with only lashes with rods, without stretching their limbs on the rack, without tearing their skin with iron nails, without using fire," he continues: "This mode of coercion is used by liberal arts teachers, parents and, frequently, the bishops themselves use them in their lawsuits." [44] Tractatus.—St. Augustine frequently uses the terms tractare, tractator, tractatus. In Christian language they acquired a meaning that they lacked in classical Latin and are equivalent to sermo. At least in Augustine's language. He indifferently uses one term or another, even within the same work. For example, in the Retractions, prologue 1, he divides his writings into books, letters and treatises (as also in The Christian Doctrine IV 18,37 and Letter 224,2), and a little later, in II 67,94, he divides them into books, letters and sermons to the people. In the present text the sermon is called a treatise. However, considering the works of Saint Augustine that moderns call Sermons and those others that are called Treatises, scholars perceive some non-substantial differences between them. Thus, M. PONTET (L'exégése de saint Augustin prédicateur p.218) can write: "What characterizes the sermon and opposes it to the treatise is perhaps not so much the science, more precise in the latter, more diffuse and more human in the former, but rather the collective atmosphere of fairly intense piety and prayer." C. Mohrmann, in turn, is of the opinion that "the treatise differs from the sermon in its didactic rather than edifying tone" ("Tractatus, tractare, sermo", in Études sur le latin des chrétiens, I I p.70). [45] Augustine's reasoning.—Note the thread of Augustine's reasoning. Firstly, according to tradition, he divides the ten commandments into two groups, which correspond to the two tables. One of which includes the first three, which have God as their object, associating each of the precepts with each of the divine persons. Of special interest is to see how the second applies to the Son. The word "vain" in the precept reminds him of Saint Paul's phrase, according to which every creature is subject to vanity (Rom 8:20). From this creature-vanity association it is easy for him to affirm that those who consider Jesus as a creature, that is, the Arians, take the name of God in vain. It is an example of Augustine's exegetical procedure, which frequently proceeds through the purely external association of identical sounds.

The same example already appeared in S.8,18 and 9,4. [46] The reiteration of baptism.—The Donatists defended that baptism administered by a heretic was not valid. Consequently, they baptized again those who, coming from the Catholic Church or another Christian sect, became part of Donato's church. The problem is not specifically Donatist, since it had previously disturbed the peace of the Church and led to bitter disputes between the episcopal sees of Carthage and Rome. In this regard, there were two traditions: the African one, and with it the entire Church of the East, which they rebaptized, and the Roman one, along with the Alexandrian one, which were limited to a laying on of hands. The fight broke out sharply between Saint Cyprian and the bishop of Rome Stephen. Both were strongly attached to the traditions of their respective churches. The arguments adduced by Saint Cyprian in favor of the reiteration of the sacrament, arguments that were later appropriated by the Donatists, were the following: heretics do not possess the Holy Spirit nor the grace of God. What they do not have, they cannot give {Letter 70,2). Outside the Church there is no salvation; Christ has entrusted his sacraments to the apostles and their successors alone; It is invalid, therefore, that administered by those who are not in
Supplementary Notes

communion with them (Letter 69,1; 74,7). Since heretics do not have true faith in the Trinity, they do not fulfill the precept of Christ, although they materially use the evangelical formula (Letter 73,5). With the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian, the controversy died down until the Donatists revived it with force. Against the Donatists, referring specifically to this issue, Augustine wrote Baptism and The Only Baptism. [47] Order in love.—That man cannot live without loving has just been well established. The problem consists in choosing precisely the object of love, in ordering love. It is worth quoting the following text from the work Christian Doctrine: “He who values ​​all things lives justly and holyly. This will be the one who has love ordered, so that he neither loves what should not be loved, nor fails to love what should be loved, nor loves more what should be loved less, nor loves equally what requires more or less love, nor, finally, loves less or more what should be equally loved. No sinner should be loved as a sinner. Every man, as man, must be loved for God, and God for himself. And since God must be loved more than all men, each one must love God more than himself. We must also love another man more than our own body; because all things must be loved for God, and the man who is foreign to us can enjoy God with us, of which our body is not capable, which lives from the soul with which we will enjoy God" (I 27,28). [48] ​​Use and enjoy (“uti et frui”).—We find here the typically Augustinian theory of use and enjoy (uti et frui). The saint frequently deals with it, both in his preaching and outside of it. See S.177,8 and the Ennarration to Psalm 121,3 for the first case. For the second, see The Customs of the Catholic Church I 3,4; The 83 issues 30; The Trinity X 10,13 and The City of God However, where he explains the theory in more detail is, perhaps, in Christian Doctrine I 3,3ff, talking about the interpretation of Scripture. This is conceived as a set of signs that refer to other realities—res—. These, says Agustín, are divided into three classes: some, which should be enjoyed; others, those that should be used; others, finally, that it should be used and enjoyed.

Those that should be enjoyed make us happy; those that we must use help us achieve blessedness (3,3). What is enjoyment? Adhere to a thing for the love of itself. Using, on the other hand, consists of directing to the achievement of what we love, if it truly deserves to be loved, that which we use (4,4). Finally, what things should be enjoyed? The realities to be enjoyed are only the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, that is, the Trinity (5,5). The rest must help us achieve it. The concrete formulations of such theory are slightly different depending on texts and contexts. Augustine uses it with philosophical, theological and mystical value. See R. LORENZ, Fruitio Dei bei Augustin: Zeitschr. F. Kirchengesch. 63 (1950-51) 75-132. [49] The health of Saint Augustine.—On the health of the saint we present the conclusion of Dr. B. Legewie in Die korperliche Konstitufion und die Krankheiten Augustins: MA I I 21: «Augustine had a healthy, although delicate physical constitution. He was not very resistant to unusual efforts, whether mental or, above all, physical. Despite

of all, it always provided maximum services. Their complaints about their lack of work capacity were due, among other things, to an intense desire to perform even better. "He was extraordinarily resistant to the most serious illnesses, which visited him only rarely in his life." These diseases are referred to in Confessions I 11,17 (stomach pain, in Tagaste); V 9,16 (a serious infection, in Rome); I X 4,12 (intense toothache, in Casiciaco); Letter 38.1 (could only be lying down, due to cracks in the body); Letter 118.34 (fevers); S. PoSIDIO, Life 29 (an infection), in addition to the chest pain that he used as an excuse for abandoning the chair of rhetoric at the time of his conversion (Confessions IX 2,4). To this we must add the weak voice that complains in this place and several others. In addition to the aforementioned article, you can see F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, Shepherd of Souls p.313ss (health) and 529ss (weakness of voice). [50] The freedom of the Lord.—This phrase, or others similar to it, is found repeated with great frequency in the preaching of the saint regarding the acts of Jesus. Through it he intends to free Jesus-God from the ignominy of having endured so many things that belittle his divinity. Emphasizing that he did it because he wanted to, and not because he was forced by external elements, he can go further and present a precise will in so many humble acts of Jesus. As proof, the present text of S.218,1 suffices: "Since what he suffered in his mortal flesh was not out of necessity, but of free will, there are reasons to believe that in each of the events of his passion he wanted to mean something." It is a whole scheme of Augustine's thinking that can be schematized like this: Jesus could have avoided those things; If he didn't, it was because he wanted to teach us something. It is so common that it is not worth giving examples. [51] Saint Augustine and the grammarians.—This is not the only place in Augustinian preaching where we find this indifference to the rules of a pure language, as expounded by the grammarians. In the Enarration to Psalm 36 I I I 6 it is expressed as follows: «What do I care about grammarians? "I prefer that you understand barbarism before, because I appear very rambling, you are left deserted." And in the Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 2,14: "Let us say it calmly without fearing the ferula of the grammarians, if by doing so we arrive at a solid and certain truth."

See also the Enarrations to Psalms 50:19; 123.38, etc. All of this is nothing other than what he had precisely formulated in Book IV of The Christian Doctrine, in which he gives norms for exposing the Holy Scripture. It goes like this: "When the use of a Latin word involves obscurity or ambiguity, and the vulgar expression avoids both the one and the other, do not follow the advice of the learned, but speak as the unlearned do..." (10,24). This indifference is more theoretical than practical. As H. I. Marrou says, “if you want to see to what extent Augustine followed this rule in practice, you are surprised to find that he really did not take it into account. Their language is of perfect correctness and even of relative purity, taking into account the time. Augustine never risks using directly, or using a term on his own, an expression that is not Latin. It is advisable to note the precautions one takes before using a vulgarism or a neologism" (Saint Augustin et la fin de la culture antique [Paris 1947] p.536-540). Generally, the texts in which he expresses a certain disdain try to justify, not Augustinian words, but translations of less fortunate biblical passages.

from the Latin point of view. In such cases a conflict arises between love for the Latinites and respect and veneration for the divine word. [52] The dream of Jesus in the boat.—The interpretation that Augustine gives here of the dream of Jesus in the boat is very frequent in his preaching. The variants from text to text are minimal and all agree on the fundamental idea, based on the following comparisons: the sea is the world; the storm, temptations of different kinds; the boat, the heart of the believer; Christ who sleeps, symbol of an extinguished faith. About the symbolism of the sea in Saint Augustine you can read H. RONDET, Le symbolisme de la mer chez Saint Augustin, in Augustinus Magister I I p.691-701. The interpretation of the gospel story is also found in Sermons 63; 81.8; 75, 163 B (=Frangipane 5); Ennarrations to Psalms 25 I I 4; 45.5; 90.11; 93.25; 54.10; 147.3; 108.5; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 49,19. Such an interpretation is not original with Augustine. It is already found in Saint Ambrose (Exposition of the Gospel of Saint Luke VI 39ff), who, in turn, must have taken it from Origen. [53] Saint Augustine and riches.—Saint Augustine was never rich. This deprived him of the freedom that having abandoned immense riches for Christ granted to certain of his contemporaries, such as Saint Basil, Saint John Chrysostom, Saint Ambrose or Saint Paulinus of Ñola. This phrase that he repeats almost verbatim in S.61,12 ("what is superfluous for you, is necessary for the poor") undoubtedly entails great moral demands. But Augustine, dealing with wealth and the duty to give alms, does not reach the radicalism of the previously mentioned authors. It is enough to remember a text from Saint Ambrose: «When you give alms to a poor person, you do not give it to them from your own. You usurp for yourself only what is common and has been given for the use of all" (Naboth 12:53), or in this other: "Nature generated the common law; usurpation created private law” (The Duties of Ministers I 132). Saint John Chrysostom is no less radical. See the Homily on Lazarus 2,4, where he maintains the same idea that the rich man, when he gives alms, does nothing other than restore to the poor what is his. An approach to these ideas by Augustine can be seen in Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 6,25; Ennarration to Psalm 131,4-6. [54] Saint Augustine and friendship.—Saint Augustine intensely cultivated friendship throughout his life.

He did not leave any treatise written about her, contrary to other authors of antiquity. However, everything he wrote and spoke about this human and Christian virtue was considerable. The pages of his works and his sermons are dotted with allusions, brief comments, definitions, etc., which generally reveal his personal experience, both positive (the joy she caused him) and negative (the pain of the loss). About her you can read M. A. MCNAMARA, Friendship in Saint Augustin (Friburg-Suisse 1958). The work deals extensively with Augustine's friendships, and only briefly with the concept, characteristics, qualities, etc., of friendship as such. [55] The obscurity of the Scriptures.—The reason for the obscurity of so many texts of Scripture frequently worried Augustine in his sermons. It is, however, in the work Christian Doctrine I I 6,7 where he speaks in more detail about the subject. In this text he exposes two reasons why God's wise pedagogy allows and desires such obscurities: to invite us to search and to increase our satisfaction in finding. The dark passages are those that found the allegorical interpretation,

of highly pedagogical value. In effect, allegory values ​​the truth, excludes the unworthy; It involves a universalist exegesis, avoids boredom and disgust, excites desire, exercises in search and, finally, rewards with the satisfaction of discovery. See in this regard J. PEPIN, Saint Augustin et la fonction protreptique de l'allégorie: Recherches Augustiniennes I (1958) 244ff, whose conclusions we have just collected. The same author shows how, fundamentally, Augustine's views are identical to those of earlier Christian and even pagan traditions. [56] "Orator... senator... imperator."—Here Augustine lists three very high spheres of social life at that time. Perhaps today's man is shocked by the fact that the speaker is placed next to the senator or the emperor himself. But that's how it was in reality; The entire culture was aimed at the mastery of the word. It is not in vain that Marrou calls rhetoric the queen subject; as an instrument at the service of the orator, it constituted the culmination of normal training, which consisted of three degrees: litterator school, which taught reading and writing; of the grammaticus, who taught syntax and the classics, and, finally, of the rhetor, who introduced the ars bene dicedi or rhetoric. The aforementioned Marrou says about this: «But the teaching of rhetoric, to the extent that it was a conquest of the verb, assumed an absolute value and became, in a certain way, an end in itself. Nothing could be conceived greater. It refers specifically to the Hellenistic era, but the situation was not essentially different in Augustine's time. In this regard, you can see the excellent book by the aforementioned author Storia dell'educazione nell'antichita (Rome 2 1966). [57] Faith and understanding of faith.—For Saint Augustine, the first step of knowing the content of Christian revelation is climbed through faith; Only in a second moment does its understanding take place. Relying on the LXX version of Is 7,9 ("if you do not believe you will not understand"), for the saint faith is the condition for understanding; the understanding or intelligence of faith is its reward (merces: S.33 A, l = Denis 23; 43,1; meritum: S.126,1). The order is, therefore, fides, intellectus: S.118,1; Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 29,6.

Trying to do otherwise is trying to go too fast, like wanting to advance by burning through stages and altering the order of time (praepropere, praepostere; S.126,1; 33 A 1), with the consequence of not being able to reach the intended goal. So aren't we acting irrationally? Not at all, Saint Augustine will say. In another order of things, faith is preceded by reason; that is, faith is rational. Letter 120,1,3 is clear on this matter: "If it is reasonable that in order to have access to certain things whose greatness means that they cannot yet be understood, faith precedes reason, without a doubt reason itself precedes faith, due to the fact that there is a certain reason that persuades us of that." There is no other way of reasoning in this sermon: understand (the reasons there are) for you to believe; believe so that you may understand what you have believed. Specifically, Augustine invites his listeners to understand his words (which invite them to believe), so that they effectively believe in the word of God; Then he invites them to believe in the word of God so that they can understand it. In brief, the process is as follows: reason prepares the act of faith; then the act of faith and, finally, the understanding of the content of faith. You can read E. G IL SON, Introduction al'étude de saint Augustin (Paris 1949) p.31ff; M. LOEHRER, Der Glaubensbegriff des Hl. Augustinus (Einsiedeln-ZürichKóln 1955); discussion in E. PRZYWARA, Augustinus (Leipzig 1934)

p.40ff. Keep in mind that Augustine gradually developed the concept, extension and depth of faith. [58] Parmenian.—Of Spanish or Gaulish origin, according to Optatus of Milevi (The Schism of the Donatists I I 7), this priest was chosen upon the death of Donatius the Great to succeed him as bishop of Carthage and, consequently, as the highest de facto authority of the Donatist Church. In its dissemination he played a leading role during the long years of his government (363-391 or 392). During this period, important events took place in the life of his Church, such as the excommunication of the layman Tyconius (who through his writings exerted so much influence on Saint Augustine) and the Rogatist schism (on this, see note 16 to S.4: The Donatist schisms p.81). Writer and theologian, one of his works was titled Against the Church of Traitors; Only fragments are known of it. From Augustine we preserve a work entitled Against the Letter of Parmeniano. [59] The Eunomians.—Heretical sect that receives its name from Eunomius, Arian bishop of Cyzicus from 360 onwards. He had to resign, because his followers did not want to give obedience to a heretical pastor. His doctrine represents the most extreme Arianism. The Son is not only a creature, but is unequal to the Father, anomoios; hence the name Anomeos, which is also used to refer to the followers of the sect. For him, the essence of God is totally comprehensible to human intelligence. Together with his teacher Aetius, he distinguished himself for having introduced Aristotelian logic into theological reasoning. His theology thus becomes pure rationalism. His position forced the Padí Saints to react against him by insisting on the transcendence of God and, at times, on a negative theology. [60] The Physiologus.—The source common to all must be the Physiologus. Of this bird he says the following: «There is a bird, called partridge, fraudulent in the extreme; The prophet Jeremiah says of her: 'the partridge cried, and gathered what it had not procreated, acquiring riches without judgment; but in the middle of her days they will abandon her, and in the end she will appear foolish' (Jer 17:11).” The Physiologus says that the partridge is quite cunning, in that it steals the eggs of others, that is, of other partridges, and hatches them itself; but he cannot possess the fruit of his fraud, because he will lose the foreign chicks he carries.

When they hear the voice of their mother, that is, the one who laid the eggs, they immediately fly to her and associate with their natural parents. Thus, having fulfilled a function, disappointed in his love, he who uses his efforts in vain for the benefit of others, in addition to paying what he deserves for his fraud, is left as a fool, alone and with nothing. Similar to that is the devil, who strives to kidnap what has been gathered together by the eternal Creator; If in truth it manages to gather together some foolish people lacking the vigor of their own sense, and nourishes them with bodily pleasures, when the little ones hear the voice of Christ, using the spiritual wings that faith grants, they entrust themselves to Christ, who immediately receives them with paternal care and love in the shadow of his wings, and gives them to the Church to nourish them" (see F. J. CARAMODY, Phisiologus latinus. Editions préliminaires. Versio B [Paris 1939] p.45-46). [61] The Donatists before the Emperor.—Excepting the short government of Emperor Julian the Apostate (361-363), who was neutral, all the remaining emperors vigorously defended the cause of the Catholic Church with their legal force and coercion, seeking the peace of the Empire and religious unity. In fact, the laws against

Donatism were increasingly severe, reaching their climax in the year 411, after the conference that saw bishops from both sides brought together before Marcellinus, the imperial representative as arbitrator, and which assigned victory to the Catholic Church. Such protection motivated the continued accusation of the Donatists: relying more on the strength of the emperor than on that of truth, and the negative stance of the sect towards imperial power. In this text, Augustine reminds them that they did the same, that is, turning to the emperor. Indeed, they forced Constantine to intervene in the dispute, recognizing Caecilian against Majorinus as bishop of Carthage (see note 20 to this sermon: Origin of the Donatist schism p.661); and when, immediately afterwards, in the year 313, he granted important economic privileges to the orthodox clergy, that is, to Caecilian and all those who were in communion with him, the Donatists appealed to the emperor to send them judges from Gaul (see Letter 88,2, by Augustine, and OPTATO DE MILEVI, The Schism of the Donatists I 22). Constantine orders that delegations from both sides appear in Rome to be judged by the city's bishop Miltiades and others from the area, instead of the Gauls requested by the Donatists. The sentence was favorable to Ceciliano, and Donato was convicted. Not accepting the decision of these bishops—Augustine's words in this text: “you did not abide by the judgment of the bishops; "As many times as you were defeated, you appealed again" - they went again to the emperor asking to be judged by Gallic bishops, not Roman or Italian. The emperor calls a second council, this time in Arles, southern France, with bishops from the area. Once again the cause was lost by Donatism. See W. H. C. FREND, The Donatist Church (Oxford 1952) p.l41ff. [62] Origin of the Donatist schism.—In these few lines he refers to the events that gave rise to the Donatist schism, very different from other schisms. Briefly stated, its development was as follows: Upon the death of the bishop of Carthage Mensurius, which occurred in the year 311, against the claims of two clerics named Botro and Celestio, the deacon Cecilianus was chosen as his successor. This was not well regarded by some as an enemy of the "mystique of martyrdom" and an abusive cult of martyrs.

Furthermore, instead of being consecrated by twelve bishops, as was the African custom, it was only consecrated by three, of not very glorious fame, one of whom, Felix of Abtungi, was suspected of having handed over the sacred books during the persecution of Diocletian, that is, of being a "traitor." Ceciliano came into conflict with a group of seniors whom he reproached for having squandered precious vessels for their own benefit. On the other hand, the chosen bishop had reproached Lucilla—the lady mentioned in the sermon—for the custom of kissing the bones of supposed martyrs before receiving communion. This earned him, in addition to the enmity of the rich and fanatical lady, of Spanish origin, the reputation of being an enemy of the martyrs. All of this invited us to question the validity of his consecration. Immediately, Second of Tigisis, primate of Numidia—the sermon also talks about him—set out and appeared in Carthage with seventy bishops from the area. Considering Caecilian's consecration invalid and supported by Botro, Celestius, the seniors and Lucilla, he appointed an interim administrator—the aforementioned oor Augustine—and called a council, which was held in the year 312. Lucilla, with her money and skill, managed to have Caecilian deposed and Mavorinus elected in his place. Since Caecilian did not accept the decision of the council, there were two bishops in Carthage, two clergy, two Churches, a schism. Mayorinus died soon, and in 313 he was succeeded by Donatus, after whom the sect received its name and was the first

great organizer of it. The problem was, however, very complex and not only doctrinal or religious. That's why it lasted until the Muslim invasion. [63] The Circumcelians.—Augustine's anti-Donatist works make frequent mention of this group, and he always speaks of them with horror. An example taken from the work Against Gaudentius, Donatist bishop I 28,32 is enough: «Who does not know this class of men, as active when it comes to committing acts of horrendous cruelty as they are idle when it comes to carrying out any profitable work; as cruel in killing others as they are vile in causing it to themselves; who sow terror especially in the fields, disregarding them, and prowl around the farmers' pantries to look for food...? These are terrorist gangs from the Roman province of Numidia that targeted, above all, Catholic institutions and clergy. The Augustinian pages are full of his violence. It can be seen especially Contra Cresconio, Donatist grammarian I I I 42,46-48,53, in which he makes a long enumeration. On many occasions, at least, they showed themselves to be the armed wing of Donatism in its fight against the rival Catholic Church. They certainly belonged to the Church of Donatus and were distinguished by their religious fanaticism. They called themselves saints, warriors of faith and soldiers of Christ; They especially venerated the martyrs and, to achieve such a title, they despised death; Furthermore, they sought it, now by provoking the pagans, now by violating imperial laws, or by committing suicide by iron, fire or cliffs. His battle cry was “Praise to God” (Deo laudes). There is agreement on this. The divergences begin when it comes to defining more precisely the social class of these people: free or slaves? If free, did they form a special class? There is also debate about their religious status: were they monks or not?, and about the reasons for the revolt: were they purely religious, or should they rather be considered social revolutionaries? The latter theory has been highly favored in recent years mainly, although not exclusively, by scholars of the socialist area. According to them, it would be an anti-Roman mass movement of a religious-social type, which fought with terrorist means, on the one hand, for the elimination of classes, the liberation of slaves, and the economic and legal improvement of the situation of the poor; on the other, due to the extension of Donatism.

The various theories about this North African phenomenon can be seen in E. TENGSTRÓM, Donatisten und Katholiken. Soziale, wirtschaftliche und politische Aspekte einer nordafrikaniscben Kirchenspaltung (Gothenburg 1964) p.24-78. [64] The catechumenate.—The reception of the sacrament of baptism was preceded in Christian antiquity by a period of different duration, depending on the case, but always long, unless the imminence of death shortened it. This period was called the catechumenate. A catechumen was, therefore, someone who had decided to become part of the Christian community and had registered, but was not yet baptized. Entry into the community was carried out with the reception of certain "sacraments"; the first of which was the sign of the cross on the forehead; then an exorcism by which the evil one was ordered to leave that person; the last was the "sacrament" of salt, as a symbol of incorruption. Once these signs were received, the catechumen was already considered a Christian and regularly attended church, although only to the first part of the liturgical celebration, that is, the liturgy of the word. Once the sermon was over, as Augustine says in this text, the catechumens were dismissed and remained to continue the sermon.

eucharistic sacrifice only the baptized faithful (fideles). The act of dismissal was called missa. For quite a few, the catechumenate lasted a lifetime, since they did not dare to receive baptism due to the moral demands it entailed. They preferred to receive it at the end of their days, perhaps on their deathbed, trusting in the absolute forgiveness of sins it conferred. Saint Augustine himself was not baptized as a child because there was a fear that in his youth he would lose the grace of the sacrament. About this way of proceeding and the motivations, both things that the saint disapproves, you can read Confessions I 11,17-18. When the preparation for baptism was immediate, they were called competent (see note 3 to S.5: The competent p.93). You can consult I. RODRÍGUEZ, The catechumenate in the discipline of Africa, according to Saint Augustine, in Missiological Weeks (Burgos 1955) p.160-174; F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, shepherd of souls p.453-459.
